questions.title: Playbook YAML Structure
questions.situation: You're creating your first Ansible playbook to configure web servers. Understanding the basic structure is essential.
questions.code:
Option A:
- hosts: webservers
  tasks:
    - name: Install nginx
      apt: name=nginx state=present

Option B:
---
- name: Configure webservers
  hosts: webservers
  tasks:
    - name: Install nginx
      apt:
        name: nginx
        state: present
questions.question: Which of the following is the correct minimal structure for an Ansible playbook?
options: Option A - hosts and tasks are the only required keys
Option B - must start with --- and include name for the play
Both are valid - name is optional but --- is best practice
Neither - ansible_connection and become are required
questions.explanation: Both structures are technically valid. The YAML document marker (---) is optional but recommended for clarity. The play name is also optional but helpful for readability. The minimal structure only requires 'hosts' and 'tasks'. However, Option B follows best practices with the document marker and descriptive play name.

questions.title: Idempotency in Ansible
questions.situation: Your team runs the same playbook multiple times per day. Understanding idempotency ensures safe, predictable automation.
questions.code:
# Running this playbook twice:
- name: Ensure nginx is installed
  apt:
    name: nginx
    state: present

First run: Changes made
Second run: ?
questions.question: What does idempotency mean in the context of Ansible?
options: The playbook will fail on the second run because nginx is already installed
The playbook will skip all tasks on subsequent runs for performance
The playbook produces the same result regardless of how many times it's run
The playbook requires a --force flag to run multiple times
questions.explanation: Idempotency means that running a playbook multiple times produces the same result as running it once. Ansible modules are designed to be idempotent - they check current state and only make changes if needed. In this example, the second run would show 'ok' (no change) rather than 'changed' because nginx is already installed.

questions.title: Handlers and Notify
questions.situation: You're configuring nginx and need to restart the service only when the configuration file changes.
questions.code:
- name: Update nginx config
  template:
    src: nginx.conf.j2
    dest: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
  notify: restart nginx

handlers:
  - name: restart nginx
    service:
      name: nginx
      state: restarted
questions.question: When do handlers execute in an Ansible playbook?
options: Handlers run at the end of the play, only if notified and only once
Handlers run immediately when notify is called
Handlers run before each task that notifies them
Handlers run at the beginning of the playbook execution
questions.explanation: Handlers are special tasks that run at the end of a play (after all tasks complete), but only if they were notified by a task that reported 'changed'. Even if multiple tasks notify the same handler, it only runs once. This is perfect for restarting services - you want to restart nginx once after all configuration changes, not after each individual change.

questions.title: Inventory Host Patterns
questions.situation: You have inventory groups for different server types and environments. You need to target only production web servers.
questions.code:
[webservers]
web1.example.com
web2.example.com
web3.example.com

[production]
web1.example.com
db1.example.com

[staging]
web2.example.com
db2.example.com
questions.question: Which hosts will the pattern 'webservers:&production' target?
options: All hosts in webservers group OR production group (union)
All hosts in webservers group EXCEPT production group (difference)
Invalid syntax - will cause an error
All hosts in webservers group AND production group (intersection)
questions.explanation: The '&' operator performs an intersection - it targets hosts that are in BOTH groups. In this case, only web1.example.com is in both webservers AND production, so only that host will be targeted. The ':' operator is union (OR), '&' is intersection (AND), and '!' is exclusion (NOT).

questions.title: Ansible Vault for Secrets
questions.situation: Your playbook contains encrypted passwords using Ansible Vault. You need to run it in GitLab CI without exposing the vault password.
questions.code:
# Encrypted vars file
$ANSIBLE_VAULT;1.1;AES256
303233...encrypted content...

# How to decrypt in CI?
questions.question: What is the recommended way to use Ansible Vault in a CI/CD pipeline?
options: Store vault password in git repository with playbook
Use --ask-vault-pass flag and enter password interactively
Store vault password in CI environment variable and use --vault-password-file
Commit decrypted files to repository for CI use
questions.explanation: The secure approach is: 1) Store vault password in CI/CD secret environment variable (e.g., VAULT_PASSWORD), 2) Create a temporary password file from the env var, 3) Use ansible-playbook --vault-password-file=/tmp/vault_pass. Never commit vault passwords or decrypted secrets to git. Interactive prompts don't work in CI. Modern alternative: use cloud provider secret managers (AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault) instead of Ansible Vault.

questions.title: Ansible Role Directory Structure
questions.situation: You're creating a reusable role for nginx deployment and need to understand the standard directory structure.
questions.code:
roles/nginx/
├── tasks/main.yml
├── handlers/main.yml
├── templates/
├── files/
├── vars/main.yml
├── defaults/main.yml
├── meta/main.yml
└── README.md
questions.question: Which directories are automatically loaded when using an Ansible role?
options: All main.yml files in standard directories are automatically included
Only tasks/main.yml is required; all other directories are optional
You must explicitly import each directory in tasks/main.yml
The role will fail if any standard directory is missing
questions.explanation: Ansible automatically loads main.yml from standard directories (tasks, handlers, vars, defaults, meta) if they exist. You don't need to explicitly import them. Only tasks/main.yml is technically required for a role to function. The vars/ and defaults/ difference: vars have higher precedence and can't be overridden easily, while defaults have lowest precedence and are meant to be overridden.

questions.title: Dynamic Inventory Sources
questions.situation: Your infrastructure uses AWS auto-scaling groups. Instances are constantly created and destroyed based on demand.
questions.code:
# Static inventory
[webservers]
10.0.1.10
10.0.1.11

# Dynamic inventory script
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import boto3
# Query AWS for current instances...
questions.question: What is the primary benefit of using dynamic inventory over static inventory?
options: Dynamic inventory is faster because it caches results
Dynamic inventory allows grouping hosts by arbitrary attributes
Dynamic inventory is required for Ansible to work with cloud instances
Dynamic inventory automatically discovers current infrastructure state from cloud providers
questions.explanation: Dynamic inventory scripts query infrastructure in real-time (AWS, Azure, GCP, VMware, etc.) to get the current list of hosts, eliminating manual inventory maintenance. This is critical for auto-scaling environments where instances come and go. Modern approach: use inventory plugins (aws_ec2, azure_rm, gcp_compute) which are more efficient than custom scripts. You can also group by tags, regions, etc.

questions.title: Privilege Escalation (become)
questions.situation: Some tasks in your playbook need root privileges (installing packages), while others should run as the normal user (cloning git repos).
questions.code:
---
- hosts: webservers
  become: yes
  tasks:
    - name: Install nginx
      apt: name=nginx
    
    - name: Clone app repo
      git:
        repo: https://github.com/app.git
        dest: /home/deploy/app
      become: no
questions.question: What is the difference between 'become: yes' at play level vs task level?
options: Task-level become always takes precedence, overriding play-level setting
Play-level become cannot be overridden at task level
Both settings must match or Ansible will error
become is only valid at play level, not task level
questions.explanation: Task-level become overrides play-level become. This allows you to set become: yes for the entire play (convenient for system administration tasks), then selectively use become: no for specific tasks that should run as the regular user. Best practice: set become at the most appropriate level (play, block, or task) to minimize privilege scope.

questions.title: Loops and Iteration
questions.situation: You need to install multiple packages in a single task instead of writing separate tasks for each package.
questions.code:
# Old way (deprecated):
- name: Install packages
  apt:
    name: "{{ item }}"
  with_items:
    - nginx
    - git
    - curl

# New way:
- name: Install packages
  apt:
    name: "{{ item }}"
  loop:
    - nginx
    - git
    - curl
questions.question: Which is the modern, recommended way to loop over items in Ansible?
options: with_items - it's the original and most stable syntax
loop - it's the modern, unified syntax replacing with_* lookups
for_each - consistent with Terraform syntax
Both with_items and loop are equally recommended
questions.explanation: 'loop' is the modern, recommended way to iterate in Ansible (introduced in 2.5). It replaces the many with_* lookup plugins (with_items, with_dict, with_fileglob, etc.) with a single, consistent syntax. with_items still works but is considered legacy. For the package use case, many modules now accept lists directly: apt: name=['nginx', 'git', 'curl'], which is even better.

questions.title: Conditional Execution (when)
questions.situation: You have a task that should only run on Ubuntu systems, not CentOS. The condition checks ansible_facts['distribution'].
questions.code:
- name: Install nginx on Ubuntu
  apt:
    name: nginx
    state: present
  when: ansible_facts['distribution'] == 'Ubuntu'
questions.question: When is the when clause evaluated in a task?
options: Before connecting to the host - if false, the host is skipped entirely
After connecting but before gathering facts
After facts are gathered but before the task module executes
After the task runs - determines if changes are applied
questions.explanation: The 'when' clause is evaluated after facts are gathered (assuming gather_facts: yes) but before the task module executes. If the condition is false, the task is skipped and marked as 'skipped' in output. This is why you can use ansible_facts in when clauses. The task module is never invoked if when evaluates to false, saving time and avoiding potential errors.

questions.title: Error Handling and Recovery
questions.situation: You're running a playbook that attempts to stop a service that might not exist on all hosts. You don't want the playbook to abort if the service doesn't exist.
questions.code:
- name: Stop legacy service if it exists
  service:
    name: old-app
    state: stopped
  # This might fail on some hosts
questions.question: How can you continue playbook execution even if a task fails?
options: Use failed_when: false to never consider the task failed
Use ignore_errors: yes to continue despite failures
Use rescue blocks to handle errors gracefully
All of the above are valid approaches depending on the scenario
questions.explanation: All three approaches are valid for different scenarios: 1) ignore_errors: yes continues execution but still logs the failure, 2) failed_when: false redefines what constitutes failure (e.g., failed_when: result.rc != 0 and result.rc != 2), 3) block/rescue/always provides try-catch-finally logic for complex error handling. For this specific scenario, checking if the service exists first with a stat task is even better.

questions.title: Ansible Galaxy and Role Dependencies
questions.situation: Your playbook depends on several community roles from Ansible Galaxy. You want to ensure all team members use the same role versions.
questions.code:
# requirements.yml
---
roles:
  - name: geerlingguy.nginx
    version: 3.1.4
  - name: geerlingguy.docker
    version: 6.1.0

# Install with:
ansible-galaxy install -r requirements.yml
questions.question: What is the purpose of the requirements.yml file in an Ansible project?
options: Lists system package requirements that must be installed before running playbooks
Specifies Ansible roles to download from Galaxy or git repos with version pinning
Defines Python library dependencies for custom Ansible modules
Contains inventory requirements for the playbook to run
questions.explanation: requirements.yml specifies external roles (from Ansible Galaxy, GitHub, or other sources) that your playbook depends on. It supports version pinning to ensure reproducible deployments. You can also specify collections: in the same file (Ansible 2.9+). This is similar to package.json for Node.js or requirements.txt for Python. Always commit requirements.yml to version control and run ansible-galaxy install before running playbooks.

questions.title: Jinja2 Templates and Filters
questions.situation: You're creating a dynamic configuration file that needs to adjust based on the number of items in a list.
questions.question: What will be the output of {{ my_list | length }} if my_list contains ['a', 'b', 'c']?
options: Error - length filter doesn't exist
'abc'
questions.explanation: The length filter returns the number of items in a list, string, or dictionary. In this case, it returns 3. Jinja2 provides many useful filters: default (set default values), regex_replace (pattern matching), to_json/to_yaml (format conversion), join (concatenate), and more. Filters are chained with the | operator. Understanding filters is crucial for effective Ansible templating.

questions.title: Performance Optimization Strategies
questions.situation: Your playbook runs against 500 servers and takes 45 minutes. You need to reduce execution time significantly.
questions.code:
# Current ansible.cfg:
[defaults]
forks = 5
gathering = implicit
host_key_checking = True

# Optimization options?
questions.question: Which strategy provides the biggest performance improvement for large inventories?
options: Increase forks to 50-100 for parallel execution across more hosts
Use gathering = smart to cache facts between playbook runs
Enable pipelining to reduce SSH overhead
All of the above combined provide significant speedup
questions.explanation: Performance optimization requires multiple strategies: 1) Increase forks (default 5) to parallelize across more hosts - try 50-100 for large inventories, 2) Use gathering = smart to cache facts between runs, 3) Enable pipelining = True to reduce SSH connections, 4) Disable host_key_checking in controlled environments, 5) Use async for long-running tasks, 6) Use strategy = free to not wait for all hosts per task. Combined, these can reduce runtime by 70-90%.

questions.title: Testing Roles with Molecule
questions.situation: Your team is developing custom Ansible roles and needs a standardized way to test them before deploying to production.
questions.code:
# Molecule test sequence:
molecule create   # Create test instance
molecule converge # Run the role
molecule verify   # Run verification tests
molecule destroy  # Cleanup

# Or simply:
molecule test
questions.question: What is the primary purpose of Molecule in Ansible development?
options: Molecule generates Ansible roles from templates
Molecule provides automated testing framework for Ansible roles with multiple drivers (Docker, Vagrant, EC2)
Molecule is a GUI tool for visualizing playbook execution
Molecule converts Ansible playbooks to other IaC tools like Terraform
questions.explanation: Molecule is a testing framework for Ansible roles. It automates the testing lifecycle: create test environment (Docker, Vagrant, cloud), apply the role, run verification tests (using TestInfra, Ansible itself, or other tools), and cleanup. This enables test-driven development (TDD) for infrastructure code. Molecule supports multiple scenarios, different platforms, and integrates with CI/CD. Essential for maintaining reliable, reusable Ansible roles.

questions.quizTitle: GitOps with Argo CD: Multi-Environment Repository Structure Quiz
questions.title: Choosing a Repo Strategy
questions.situation: You have 8 microservices, each with its own CI pipeline. Developers push code changes daily. The platform team manages the Kubernetes manifests. A junior developer just pushed a Helm values change directly to the app repo and accidentally broke staging. The team lead asks you to propose a repo layout that prevents this from happening again.
questions.code:
# Current structure (single repo per service):
my-service/
├── src/
├── Dockerfile
├── ci/
│   └── pipeline.yaml
└── k8s/
    ├── base/
    ├── dev/
    └── prod/

# What the team lead wants:
# - App devs can't directly change prod manifests
# - Platform team reviews all deployment config changes
# - CI pipeline still auto-deploys to dev
questions.question: Your team is adopting Argo CD and needs to decide how to organize the Git repositories for application code and Kubernetes manifests.
options: Keep manifests in each app repo but add a CODEOWNERS file to protect the k8s/ directory
Move all Kubernetes manifests to a separate config repo with branch protection and require platform team review for staging/prod changes
Use a mono-repo for all services and manifests with path-based access controls
Store manifests in a separate branch of each app repo so platform team can manage them independently
questions.explanation: Separating application code from deployment config into different repos is the most common pattern with Argo CD. It gives you clear ownership boundaries: developers own the app repo, the platform team owns the config repo. Branch protection rules on the config repo mean no one can push directly to main without review. CI pipelines can still auto-update dev values in the config repo via a bot commit, while staging and prod changes require a pull request. CODEOWNERS helps but still lets developers push to the same repo. A mono-repo works for small teams but gets unwieldy at scale. Separate branches in the same repo create confusion about which branch Argo CD should watch.

questions.quizTitle: GitOps with Argo CD: Multi-Environment Repository Structure Quiz
questions.title: Kustomize Overlay Structure
questions.situation: Your team just created a new config repo. You have three environments: dev, staging, and prod. Each environment runs in a different Kubernetes cluster. Dev needs 1 replica with debug logging, staging needs 2 replicas, and prod needs 3 replicas with resource limits enforced. A colleague suggests putting everything in flat directories per environment, but you want to avoid duplicating the entire manifest set three times.
questions.code:
# Your colleague's proposal (lots of duplication):
config-repo/
├── dev/
│   ├── deployment.yaml    # 1 replica, debug logging
│   ├── service.yaml       # identical across envs
│   └── configmap.yaml
├── staging/
│   ├── deployment.yaml    # 2 replicas
│   ├── service.yaml       # identical across envs
│   └── configmap.yaml
└── prod/
    ├── deployment.yaml    # 3 replicas, resource limits
    ├── service.yaml       # identical across envs
    └── configmap.yaml
questions.question: You need to set up the directory structure in your config repo so Argo CD can deploy the same app to three environments using Kustomize.
options: Use Kustomize with a base/ directory for shared manifests and overlays/ for per-environment patches that only change what differs
Use Helm with a single values.yaml per environment since Kustomize doesn't support per-environment config
Keep the flat structure but use Git branches (dev, staging, prod) instead of directories to separate environments
Use a single directory with environment variables injected at deploy time by Argo CD's built-in templating
questions.explanation: Kustomize's base + overlays pattern is exactly designed for this. You put shared manifests in base/ and only the differences in each overlay. For example, the overlay for prod might just be a patch that sets replicas: 3 and adds resource limits, while the service.yaml stays in base/ since it's identical. This avoids the duplication problem where you have to update service.yaml in three places. Helm is also a valid tool, but the question is about Kustomize, and Kustomize absolutely supports per-environment config. Git branches for environments is an anti-pattern because it makes it hard to see what's different between environments and leads to painful merge conflicts. Argo CD doesn't have built-in templating that replaces Kustomize or Helm.

questions.quizTitle: GitOps with Argo CD: Multi-Environment Repository Structure Quiz
questions.title: Bootstrapping Multiple Applications
questions.situation: You just finished setting up Argo CD in your cluster. Now you need to create Application resources for each service in each environment. Doing this manually through the UI or kubectl is going to be painful and error-prone. Your team lead says, 'There has to be a better way than clicking through the UI 45 times.' You need an approach that's itself GitOps-managed.
questions.code:
# You currently create apps one at a time:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: payment-service-prod
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/org/config-repo
    path: apps/payment-service/overlays/prod
    targetRevision: main
  destination:
    server: https://prod-cluster-api:6443
    namespace: payments
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true

# You need 44 more of these...
questions.question: You need to register 15 microservices across 3 environments in Argo CD without manually creating 45 Application resources.
options: Write a shell script that generates all 45 Application YAML files and apply them with kubectl
Use the Argo CD CLI to batch-create applications from a CSV file
Use the App of Apps pattern: create one parent Application that points to a directory containing all child Application manifests
Use Argo CD Projects to automatically generate Applications for each service
questions.explanation: The App of Apps pattern is a core Argo CD concept. You create one 'root' Application that watches a directory in your config repo. That directory contains Application manifests for all your services and environments. When you add a new service, you just add a new Application YAML to that directory, and the root app picks it up automatically. This keeps everything in Git (true GitOps) and avoids manual steps. A shell script works but isn't GitOps since those resources aren't managed declaratively. The Argo CD CLI doesn't have CSV import. Projects define RBAC and allowed sources, they don't auto-generate Applications.

questions.quizTitle: GitOps with Argo CD: Multi-Environment Repository Structure Quiz
questions.title: ApplicationSet for Environment Matrix
questions.situation: Your App of Apps setup works, but maintaining 45 Application YAML files is getting tedious. Every time someone adds a new service, they have to create three nearly identical Application files (one per environment). Last week someone forgot to create the staging Application for a new service, and it wasn't caught until a week later. You want a single template that automatically creates Applications for all service/environment combinations.
questions.code:
# What you want: ONE template that generates all 45 apps
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: ApplicationSet
metadata:
  name: all-services
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  generators:
    - ???
  template:
    metadata:
      name: '{{service}}-{{env}}'
    spec:
      source:
        repoURL: https://github.com/org/config-repo
        path: 'apps/{{service}}/overlays/{{env}}'
      destination:
        server: '{{clusterUrl}}'
questions.question: You want to generate Argo CD Applications automatically for every combination of service and environment without maintaining individual Application manifests.
options: Use a List generator with every service-environment pair manually listed
Use a Matrix generator that combines a List of services with a List of environments to produce all combinations
Use a Git directory generator pointed at the apps/ directory since it auto-discovers subdirectories
Use a Cluster generator that creates one Application per registered cluster
questions.explanation: The Matrix generator is the right tool here. It takes two or more generators and produces the Cartesian product. You define a list of services and a list of environments (with cluster URLs), and Matrix gives you every combination. A List generator would work but defeats the purpose since you'd manually list all 45 pairs. The Git directory generator is useful but only gives you one dimension (it finds directories, not the cross-product of services x environments). The Cluster generator creates one app per cluster, not per service. The Matrix generator is the most scalable approach because adding a new service means adding one entry to the services list, and it automatically gets deployed to all environments.

questions.quizTitle: GitOps with Argo CD: Multi-Environment Repository Structure Quiz
questions.title: Helm Values File Organization
questions.situation: Your team decided to use Helm for a new service because it needs complex templating. You have a Helm chart in your config repo and need separate values for dev, staging, and prod. The dev environment should use an in-cluster database, staging should use a shared RDS instance, and prod should use a dedicated RDS with read replicas. You need Argo CD to apply the correct values file for each environment.
questions.code:
# Your Helm chart structure:
charts/order-service/
├── Chart.yaml
├── templates/
│   ├── deployment.yaml
│   ├── service.yaml
│   └── configmap.yaml
├── values.yaml            # defaults
├── values-dev.yaml        # in-cluster postgres
├── values-staging.yaml    # shared RDS
└── values-prod.yaml       # dedicated RDS + read replicas

# How do you tell Argo CD which values file to use?
questions.question: You are switching from Kustomize to Helm for a service and need to structure values files so Argo CD picks the right config per environment.
options: Use Argo CD environment variables to dynamically select the values file at sync time
Create separate Helm charts per environment, each with its own values.yaml
Use Argo CD's parameter overrides in the UI to set values per environment
Set the valueFiles field in the Application spec's Helm source to point to the environment-specific values file
questions.explanation: The Argo CD Application spec has a helm.valueFiles field that lets you specify which values files to layer on top of the default values.yaml. For your prod Application, you'd set valueFiles: [values-prod.yaml]. Argo CD applies them in order, so environment-specific values override the defaults. This keeps everything in Git and is easy to review in PRs. Argo CD doesn't have environment variables that select files dynamically at sync time. Creating separate charts per environment means massive duplication of templates. UI parameter overrides work but aren't stored in Git, which breaks the GitOps model.

questions.quizTitle: GitOps with Argo CD: Multi-Environment Repository Structure Quiz
questions.title: Sync Policy for Production
questions.situation: Your dev and staging environments have automated sync enabled, and it works great. Changes merged to main are deployed within minutes. Now the VP of Engineering asks, 'Why isn't prod doing the same thing?' The platform lead pushes back, saying automated sync in prod is risky. Last month, a bad config change in staging took 20 minutes to detect because the automated sync applied it instantly. You need to propose a sync policy for production.
questions.code:
# Current staging config (auto-sync ON):
syncPolicy:
  automated:
    prune: true
    selfHeal: true
  syncOptions:
    - CreateNamespace=true

# Proposed prod config - which is safest?
# Option A:
syncPolicy:
  automated:
    prune: true
    selfHeal: true

# Option B:
syncPolicy: {}
# (manual sync only)

# Option C:
syncPolicy:
  automated:
    selfHeal: true
  syncOptions:
    - ApplyOutOfSyncOnly=true
questions.question: Your team is debating whether to enable automated sync for production Applications in Argo CD.
options: Enable full automated sync with prune and selfHeal in prod, same as staging, to maintain consistency across environments
Use manual sync for prod so every deployment requires a human to click Sync in the Argo CD UI or run argocd app sync
Enable automated sync with selfHeal but disable prune, and add a sync window that only allows syncs during business hours
Disable sync entirely and use kubectl apply directly for prod deployments
questions.explanation: For production, the sweet spot is usually automated sync with selfHeal enabled but prune disabled, combined with sync windows. SelfHeal means if someone manually edits a resource in the cluster (kubectl edit), Argo CD reverts it back to what's in Git. That's important for production to prevent config drift. Disabling prune means Argo CD won't automatically delete resources that are removed from Git, which prevents accidental data loss from a bad commit. Sync windows restrict when syncs can happen, so a merge at 2 AM doesn't auto-deploy when no one is watching. Full auto-sync with prune in prod is risky because a bad merge can delete resources. Fully manual sync loses the drift-correction benefit. Kubectl apply bypasses GitOps entirely.

questions.quizTitle: GitOps with Argo CD: Multi-Environment Repository Structure Quiz
questions.title: Managing Secrets in the Config Repo
questions.situation: You're setting up the config repo for a service that connects to PostgreSQL. Each environment has different credentials. A new team member asks, 'Can't we just put the Secret manifests in the repo? It's a private repo.' You need to explain why that's a bad idea and propose the right approach for Argo CD.
questions.code:
# What the new team member proposed (DON'T DO THIS):
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: db-credentials
  namespace: orders
type: Opaque
data:
  # base64 is NOT encryption
  DB_PASSWORD: cHJvZC1wYXNzd29yZC0xMjM=
  DB_HOST: cHJvZC1kYi5leGFtcGxlLmNvbQ==

# $ echo 'cHJvZC1wYXNzd29yZC0xMjM=' | base64 -d
# prod-password-123
# Anyone with repo access can read this!
questions.question: You need to store database credentials for each environment in your config repo without exposing them in plain text.
options: Use Sealed Secrets or SOPS to encrypt secrets before committing them, so only the cluster can decrypt them
Store secrets in a .gitignore'd file and copy them manually to each cluster
Use Kubernetes ConfigMaps instead of Secrets since ConfigMaps are not base64-encoded
Keep secrets in the private repo since base64 encoding provides sufficient protection for internal teams
questions.explanation: Sealed Secrets (from Bitnami) or SOPS (from Mozilla) let you encrypt secrets so they can safely live in Git. Sealed Secrets uses asymmetric encryption: you encrypt with the cluster's public key, and only the Sealed Secrets controller in the cluster can decrypt them. SOPS encrypts individual values in YAML files using KMS, PGP, or age keys. Both work well with Argo CD. Base64 is encoding, not encryption. Anyone with read access to the repo can decode the values. A .gitignore'd file breaks the GitOps model since it's not tracked in Git. ConfigMaps store data in plain text too, and they're not designed for sensitive data. For the most secure option, consider External Secrets Operator, which pulls secrets from Vault or AWS Secrets Manager at runtime, keeping them out of Git entirely.

questions.quizTitle: GitOps with Argo CD: Multi-Environment Repository Structure Quiz
questions.title: Environment Promotion Workflow
questions.situation: Your CI pipeline builds a new image, pushes it to the registry, and updates the dev values in the config repo. You need a promotion flow where the same image tag is tested in staging before going to prod. Right now, developers manually edit the staging and prod values files to update the image tag, which is error-prone and slow. Last week someone promoted to prod with a typo in the image tag, causing a rollout failure.
questions.code:
# CI pipeline updates dev automatically:
# values-dev.yaml
image:
  repository: registry.example.com/order-service
  tag: "v1.4.2"  # CI just updated this

# values-staging.yaml
image:
  repository: registry.example.com/order-service
  tag: "v1.4.1"  # still on old version

# values-prod.yaml
image:
  repository: registry.example.com/order-service
  tag: "v1.3.8"  # even older
questions.question: You need to design a process for promoting a new container image version from dev through staging to prod using GitOps.
options: Use a single values file for all environments with Argo CD parameter overrides to set the image tag per environment
Use Argo CD Image Updater to automatically detect new images and update all environments at once
Tag the config repo with environment-specific Git tags (e.g., staging-v1.4.2) and point each Application at its tag
Create a promotion script or CI job that opens a PR to update the image tag in the next environment's values file, triggered after successful tests
questions.explanation: A promotion pipeline that opens PRs is the standard GitOps promotion pattern. After CI deploys to dev and tests pass, a job opens a PR to update staging's values file with the same image tag. A human (or automated test gate) approves the PR, Argo CD syncs staging, and after staging tests pass, another PR promotes to prod. This gives you an audit trail (PRs), review gates, and eliminates manual typos. Parameter overrides in Argo CD bypass Git and break the GitOps model. Argo CD Image Updater auto-updates based on tag patterns, but you don't want all environments updated simultaneously since that skips testing. Git tags for environments create a complex workflow that's hard to track and roll back.

questions.quizTitle: GitOps with Argo CD: Multi-Environment Repository Structure Quiz
questions.title: Debugging OutOfSync Status
questions.situation: It's Monday morning. You check Argo CD and see that the payment-service-prod Application has been OutOfSync since Saturday. No one on your team merged anything to the config repo over the weekend. The app is running fine, but the OutOfSync status is making the on-call engineer nervous. You need to figure out what happened.
questions.code:
$ argocd app diff payment-service-prod
===== apps/Deployment payment-service/payment-service ======
--- /tmp/live-manifest.yaml
+++ /tmp/desired-manifest.yaml
@@ -18,7 +18,7 @@
     spec:
       containers:
       - name: payment-service
-        resources:
-          requests:
-            memory: "512Mi"
+        resources:
+          requests:
+            memory: "256Mi"

# The live cluster has 512Mi but Git says 256Mi
questions.question: Your production Application in Argo CD shows OutOfSync, but you didn't make any changes to the config repo.
options: The Argo CD repo cache is stale and needs to be cleared with argocd cache clear
Someone used kubectl edit or a mutating admission webhook to change the resource requests directly in the cluster
Argo CD lost connection to the cluster over the weekend and is showing a stale diff
The Helm chart was updated upstream and Argo CD is comparing against the new chart version
questions.explanation: The diff clearly shows that the live cluster has different values (512Mi) than what Git specifies (256Mi). Since no one changed Git, someone (or something) changed the live cluster directly. The most common culprits are: someone ran kubectl edit to quickly fix a memory issue, or a mutating admission webhook (like a VPA - Vertical Pod Autoscaler) automatically adjusted the resource requests. This is exactly why selfHeal is valuable in production: if enabled, Argo CD would have reverted this change back to what Git says. Without selfHeal, the drift persists until someone syncs manually. The diff output is real and accurate, so it's not a cache issue. Argo CD connection issues would show as Unknown status, not OutOfSync.

questions.quizTitle: GitOps with Argo CD: Multi-Environment Repository Structure Quiz
questions.title: Controlling Sync Order with Sync Waves
questions.situation: You added a Kubernetes Job that runs database migrations to your config repo. The Job and the Deployment are in the same Argo CD Application. When you sync, Argo CD applies them at the same time. The new Deployment starts before migrations finish, hits missing columns, and crashes. You need to control the order.
questions.code:
# migration-job.yaml - needs to run FIRST
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: db-migrate-v42
  annotations:
    ???: ???
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: migrate
        image: registry.example.com/order-service:v1.5.0
        command: ["python", "manage.py", "migrate"]
      restartPolicy: Never

# deployment.yaml - needs to run AFTER migration
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: order-service
  annotations:
    ???: ???
questions.question: Your application needs its database migration Job to complete before the Deployment rolls out, but Argo CD applies them in the wrong order.
options: Add argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave annotations with a lower number on the Job and higher on the Deployment
Split them into two separate Applications and configure an Argo CD sync dependency between them
Add an initContainer to the Deployment that waits for the migration Job to complete
Use Argo CD's sync-order field in the Application spec to define the resource apply sequence
questions.explanation: Sync waves are Argo CD's built-in mechanism for ordering resource application. You add argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "0" to the migration Job and argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "1" to the Deployment. Argo CD applies wave 0 first, waits for those resources to become healthy (the Job must complete), then applies wave 1. This is clean and declarative. An initContainer would work but it couples the migration logic to the Deployment and runs the migration on every pod restart, not just during deployments. Splitting into separate Applications adds unnecessary complexity. There's no sync-order field in the Application spec; sync waves use annotations on the individual resources.

questions.quizTitle: GitOps with Argo CD: Multi-Environment Repository Structure Quiz
questions.title: Multi-Cluster Argo CD Architecture
questions.situation: You currently have Argo CD installed in each cluster independently. This means three Argo CD instances to maintain, three sets of credentials, and three UIs to check. The CTO wants a single pane of glass for all deployments. But the security team is concerned about a single Argo CD having credentials to all clusters, especially production.
questions.code:
# Current setup: one Argo CD per cluster
dev-cluster:    argocd namespace → manages dev apps only
staging-cluster: argocd namespace → manages staging apps only
prod-cluster:    argocd namespace → manages prod apps only

# Option A: Hub-and-spoke (single management cluster)
mgmt-cluster: argocd namespace → manages dev + staging + prod

# Option B: Hub-and-spoke with separate prod
mgmt-cluster: argocd namespace → manages dev + staging
prod-cluster: argocd namespace → manages prod only

# Option C: Argo CD per cluster + Argo CD UI aggregation
Each cluster has its own Argo CD, with a dashboard that aggregates all three
questions.question: Your company runs separate Kubernetes clusters for dev, staging, and prod. You need to decide how to set up Argo CD to manage all three.
options: Install Argo CD in a management cluster and register all three clusters as destinations using argocd cluster add
Keep one Argo CD per cluster and use Argo CD Notifications to send deployment events to a shared dashboard
Install Argo CD only in the management cluster for dev and staging, but keep a separate Argo CD in the prod cluster for isolation
Use a single Argo CD instance running in dev that deploys to all clusters since dev is the least restricted environment
questions.explanation: Option C is the pragmatic middle ground. You get a single UI for dev and staging (the environments where you want fast feedback and unified visibility), while production keeps its own Argo CD with tighter access controls and a separate credential boundary. This satisfies the security team because the management Argo CD never has credentials to the prod cluster. It satisfies the CTO because developers get a single pane of glass for their day-to-day work. A fully centralized setup (Option A) is simpler to operate but creates a security blast radius concern. Running Argo CD from the dev cluster is a bad idea because dev is typically the least secured environment. Notifications to a dashboard give you visibility but not unified management.

questions.quizTitle: GitOps with Argo CD: Multi-Environment Repository Structure Quiz
questions.title: ApplicationSet Git Generator Auto-Discovery
questions.situation: You configured an ApplicationSet with a Git directory generator to auto-discover services. When a team adds a new service directory to the config repo, Argo CD should create an Application automatically. But the team added the auth-service directory 30 minutes ago, and nothing happened. The existing services are working fine.
questions.code:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: ApplicationSet
metadata:
  name: all-services
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  generators:
    - git:
        repoURL: https://github.com/org/config-repo
        revision: main
        directories:
          - path: apps/*
  template:
    metadata:
      name: '{{path.basename}}'
    spec:
      source:
        repoURL: https://github.com/org/config-repo
        path: '{{path}}'
        targetRevision: main
      destination:
        server: https://kubernetes.default.svc

# Config repo structure:
apps/
├── order-service/     ✓ Application exists
├── payment-service/   ✓ Application exists
└── auth-service/      ✗ No Application created
    └── kustomization.yaml
questions.question: You set up an ApplicationSet with a Git directory generator, but new services aren't being picked up automatically.
options: The ApplicationSet controller has a default polling interval of 3 minutes, so you just need to wait a bit longer or configure a webhook
The Git directory generator only detects directories that contain a Chart.yaml file, not kustomization.yaml
The auth-service directory was added but the commit wasn't pushed to the main branch yet
ApplicationSets only scan directories at initial creation and need to be deleted and recreated to pick up new directories
questions.explanation: The ApplicationSet controller polls the Git repository at a configurable interval (default is around 3 minutes). If the directory was just added, the controller may not have polled yet. You can speed this up by configuring a Git webhook that notifies Argo CD of changes, reducing detection time to seconds. The Git directory generator detects any directory matching the glob pattern, regardless of what files it contains. It doesn't require Chart.yaml specifically. The commit being on a different branch is a reasonable guess but the scenario says it was added 30 minutes ago (and existing services work, confirming the repo connection). ApplicationSets absolutely do re-scan on each poll cycle, they don't need recreation. In practice, if it's been 30 minutes, you should also check the ApplicationSet controller logs for errors.

questions.quizTitle: GitOps with Argo CD: Multi-Environment Repository Structure Quiz
questions.title: GitOps Rollback in Production
questions.situation: At 3 PM, a new version of the payment service was deployed to prod via a merged PR. At 3:15 PM, error rates spike to 40%. The on-call engineer runs kubectl rollout undo deployment/payment-service, which brings back the old version. But 2 minutes later, Argo CD syncs and redeploys the bad version because it's what Git says. The on-call engineer is panicking.
questions.code:
# Timeline:
# 15:00 - PR merged: image tag v2.1.0 → v2.2.0
# 15:05 - Argo CD syncs, deploys v2.2.0
# 15:15 - Error rate spikes to 40%
# 15:17 - kubectl rollout undo → reverts to v2.1.0
# 15:19 - Argo CD selfHeal kicks in → redeploys v2.2.0 💀

$ argocd app history payment-service-prod
ID  DATE                 REVISION
4   2026-04-14 15:05:00  abc123f (main)
3   2026-04-14 09:30:00  def456a (main)

# What's the right way to roll back in GitOps?
questions.question: A bad deployment just went to production and you need to roll back. But you're using GitOps with Argo CD, so kubectl rollout undo won't stick.
options: Disable Argo CD auto-sync, then use kubectl rollout undo to revert the Deployment
Revert the PR in Git (git revert the merge commit), which creates a new commit that Argo CD will sync to roll back the change
Use argocd app rollback payment-service-prod to go back to the previous Argo CD revision
Delete the Application in Argo CD, fix the issue, then recreate it
questions.explanation: In GitOps, Git is the source of truth. The correct way to roll back is to revert the bad commit in Git. Run git revert <merge-commit-hash> and push it to main (or open and immediately merge a revert PR). Argo CD detects the new commit and syncs back to the previous good state. This gives you a clean audit trail: the Git history shows exactly when the bad change went in and when it was reverted. Disabling auto-sync and using kubectl rollout undo is a temporary band-aid that will break again when sync is re-enabled. argocd app rollback exists but is only for emergencies and is not recommended as the standard approach because it puts the cluster in a state that doesn't match Git. Deleting the Application is destructive and may remove the running resources (depending on finalizer settings). For the immediate 3 AM emergency, disabling sync temporarily while you prepare the Git revert is a valid tactic, but the actual fix must go through Git.

questions.title: Right-Sizing Your Compute
questions.situation: You're running a web application that experiences predictable traffic spikes during business hours (9 AM - 6 PM) and needs to handle CPU-intensive image processing.
questions.code:
Requirements:
• Baseline: 2 vCPUs, 4GB RAM
• Peak: 8 vCPUs, 16GB RAM (business hours)
• Cost optimization is important
• Consistent performance needed
questions.question: Choose the appropriate EC2 instance type for a specific workload.
options: Use m5.large with Scheduled Scaling
Use c5.2xlarge instances with Auto Scaling
Use t3.medium with burstable performance
Use t3.xlarge with unlimited burst mode
questions.explanation: m5.large provides consistent baseline performance for regular operations, and Scheduled Scaling can automatically add capacity during predictable business hour spikes, optimizing both performance and cost.

questions.title: Optimizing Storage Costs
questions.situation: Your company has 3 types of data: active user files (daily access), backup files (monthly access), and compliance archives (yearly access, 7-year retention).
questions.code:
Data Types:
• User files: 500GB, accessed daily
• Backups: 2TB, accessed monthly
• Archives: 10TB, accessed yearly, must retain 7 years
questions.question: Select the right S3 storage strategy for different data access patterns.
options: Store everything in S3 Standard for simplicity
S3 Standard for user files, S3 Standard-IA for backups, S3 Glacier Deep Archive for compliance
S3 Intelligent-Tiering for all data types
S3 One Zone-IA for all data to minimize costs
questions.explanation: This strategy matches storage classes to access patterns: Standard for frequent access, Standard-IA for infrequent monthly access, and Glacier Deep Archive for long-term retention with rare access.

questions.title: Choosing the Right Database
questions.situation: You're building a social media platform that needs to store user profiles, posts, comments, and real-time chat messages with global distribution requirements.
questions.code:
Requirements:
• User profiles: Structured data, ACID compliance
• Posts/Comments: Fast reads, eventual consistency OK
• Chat messages: Real-time, low latency globally
• Expected: 1M users, global audience
questions.question: Select the appropriate AWS database service for your application needs.
options: Use RDS MySQL for everything
RDS for user profiles, DynamoDB for posts/comments, ElastiCache for chat
RDS for profiles, DynamoDB Global Tables for posts, DynamoDB with DAX for chat
Aurora Global Database for everything
questions.explanation: This approach uses the right tool for each job: RDS for ACID-compliant user data, DynamoDB Global Tables for globally distributed posts with eventual consistency, and DynamoDB with DAX for ultra-low latency chat.

questions.title: Network Security Architecture
questions.situation: You need to deploy a web application with frontend, API backend, and database tiers while ensuring security best practices and internet access where needed.
questions.code:
Architecture:
• Web servers: Need internet access (inbound/outbound)
• API servers: Outbound internet only (for API calls)
• Database: No internet access
• All tiers need to communicate with each other
questions.question: Design a secure VPC architecture for a three-tier web application.
options: Single public subnet with security groups for all tiers
Public subnet for web, private subnets for API/DB, NAT Gateway for API outbound access
All private subnets with VPN access only
Public subnets for web/API, private subnet for DB only
questions.explanation: This follows security best practices: public subnet for web tier (needs inbound internet), private subnets for API/DB (more secure), and NAT Gateway allows API servers secure outbound internet access without exposing them to inbound traffic.

questions.title: Dynamic Scaling Configuration
questions.situation: Your e-commerce site experiences traffic spikes during flash sales (10x normal traffic in minutes) and needs to scale quickly while avoiding unnecessary costs during normal periods.
questions.code:
Traffic Pattern:
• Normal: 100-200 concurrent users
• Flash sale: 2000+ users in < 5 minutes
• Sales announced on social media (unpredictable timing)
• Cost optimization important during low traffic
questions.question: Configure Auto Scaling to handle unpredictable traffic patterns efficiently.
options: Use Scheduled Scaling for known sale times
Target Tracking Scaling on CPU utilization (70% target)
Step Scaling with multiple CloudWatch alarms for aggressive scaling
Predictive Scaling based on historical patterns
questions.explanation: Step Scaling with multiple CloudWatch alarms allows for aggressive scaling during traffic spikes (add many instances quickly when CPU > 80%) while also scaling down during normal periods. This handles unpredictable spikes better than gradual target tracking.

questions.title: Load Balancer Strategy
questions.situation: You have a microservices application with HTTP APIs, WebSocket connections for real-time features, and need SSL termination, path-based routing, and health checks.
questions.code:
Requirements:
• HTTP REST APIs on different paths (/api/users, /api/orders)
• WebSocket connections for real-time notifications
• SSL termination at load balancer
• Advanced health checks
• Cost-effective solution
questions.question: Choose the right load balancing solution for a microservices architecture.
options: Application Load Balancer with target groups
Classic Load Balancer for simplicity
Network Load Balancer for high performance
Multiple Classic Load Balancers for each service
questions.explanation: Application Load Balancer supports Layer 7 routing (path-based), WebSocket connections, SSL termination, and advanced health checks. It's perfect for microservices with different routing requirements.

questions.title: Compute Architecture Decision
questions.situation: You need to implement three services: a file processing service (triggered by S3 uploads), a user authentication API (steady traffic), and a batch data processing job (runs nightly).
questions.code:
Services:
1. File processor: Triggered by uploads, processing takes 30 seconds
2. Auth API: Steady 1000 requests/hour, needs low latency
3. Batch job: Runs for 2 hours nightly, processes 1TB data
questions.question: Decide between serverless and containerized solutions for different use cases.
options: Use Lambda for everything
Use ECS for everything
Lambda for file processing, ECS for auth API, ECS/Batch for batch job
Lambda for file processing and batch job, ECS for auth API
questions.explanation: This matches each service to the optimal compute model: Lambda for event-driven file processing, ECS for the steady-state API (better cost for consistent load), and ECS/Batch for long-running batch processing (Lambda has 15-minute limit).

questions.title: IAM Security Best Practices
questions.situation: You have developers, DevOps engineers, and data analysts who need different levels of access to AWS resources. Security requires principle of least privilege and audit trails.
questions.code:
Teams:
• Developers: EC2, RDS, S3 buckets for their projects only
• DevOps: Full infrastructure access, cannot access sensitive data
• Data Analysts: Read-only S3 data buckets, Athena, no infrastructure
• All actions must be logged and auditable
questions.question: Design secure IAM policies for a team-based development environment.
options: Create individual IAM users with attached policies for each person
Share IAM credentials among team members for simplicity
Use root account with MFA for all operations
Use IAM roles with groups, enable CloudTrail, implement resource tagging for access control
questions.explanation: IAM roles with groups provide scalable permission management, CloudTrail ensures all actions are logged, and resource tagging allows fine-grained access control based on project ownership while maintaining least privilege.

questions.title: Multi-Region Disaster Recovery
questions.situation: Your financial application requires 99.9% uptime, <1 hour RTO (Recovery Time Objective), and <15 minutes RPO (Recovery Point Objective). Primary region is us-east-1.
questions.code:
Requirements:
• RTO: < 1 hour (time to restore service)
• RPO: < 15 minutes (acceptable data loss)
• Cost-conscious but uptime critical
• Database: 500GB, high transaction volume
• Application: Stateless web services
questions.question: Design a disaster recovery strategy for a critical business application.
options: Backup and Restore: Daily snapshots to secondary region
Pilot Light: Core services ready in secondary region, scale up during disaster
Multi-Site Active-Active: Full deployment in both regions
Warm Standby: Scaled-down version running in secondary region
questions.explanation: Warm Standby meets the RTO/RPO requirements cost-effectively. It runs a smaller version of the environment that can quickly scale up, with database replication ensuring the 15-minute RPO, while being more cost-effective than active-active.

questions.title: AWS Cost Optimization
questions.situation: Your startup's AWS bill is $15K/month: 60% EC2, 25% RDS, 15% other services. Traffic varies significantly, and you need to cut costs by 40% while maintaining performance.
questions.code:
Current Setup:
• 20 x m5.large instances (always on)
• RDS MySQL db.r5.xlarge (always on)
• 5TB S3 Standard storage
• Data transfer costs from multiple AZs
questions.question: Optimize AWS costs for a growing startup without impacting performance.
options: Switch everything to smaller instance types
Implement Reserved Instances, Spot Instances for non-critical workloads, S3 lifecycle policies, and RDS optimization
Move everything to a single AZ to reduce data transfer
Migrate to on-premises to avoid cloud costs
questions.explanation: This comprehensive approach addresses the major cost drivers: Reserved Instances for predictable workloads (up to 75% savings), Spot Instances for fault-tolerant tasks, S3 lifecycle policies for storage optimization, and RDS right-sizing or Aurora Serverless for variable workloads.

questions.title: Large-Scale Migration Planning
questions.situation: You need to migrate a monolithic .NET application with SQL Server database, file shares, and batch jobs. 500 users, 2TB database, minimal downtime allowed, tight deadline.
questions.code:
Legacy System:
• Monolithic .NET Framework app on Windows Server
• SQL Server 2016 (2TB database)
• Shared file storage (500GB)
• Nightly batch processing
• <4 hours downtime allowed for cutover
questions.question: Plan the migration strategy for a legacy enterprise application to AWS.
options: Use AWS Application Migration Service for infrastructure, RDS for database, staged migration approach
Rewrite the entire application as cloud-native microservices
Lift-and-shift to EC2 with gradual modernization
Keep on-premises and use AWS for backup only
questions.explanation: AWS Application Migration Service provides automated lift-and-shift with minimal downtime, RDS handles the database migration with point-in-time recovery, and a staged approach allows testing and rollback capabilities while meeting the tight deadline and downtime requirements.

questions.title: The Number to Memorise
questions.situation: To convert 'per day' into 'per second' quickly, you need the seconds in a day.
questions.question: The single most useful constant for capacity math.
options: About 86,400 (and you usually round to ~100,000 for fast math)
About 3,600 (and you usually round to 1,000)
About 10,000
questions.explanation: 24 x 3,600 = 86,400 seconds per day. For fast estimation people round it to ~100,000 (10^5), so 'X per day' divided by 100,000 gives a quick average per-second rate. Memorising ~100K seconds/day is the highest-leverage constant in estimation math.

questions.title: Daily Requests to Average QPS
questions.situation: Your API serves 1 billion requests per day, spread fairly evenly.
questions.question: The most common conversion in a design interview.
options: About 1,000 requests/second
About 10,000 requests/second
About 100,000 requests/second
About 1 million requests/second
questions.explanation: 1,000,000,000 / 86,400 ~= 11,600/s, or using the ~100,000 sec/day shortcut, 1e9 / 1e5 = 10,000/s. So roughly 10K average QPS. The shortcut gets you within ~15% of the exact number, which is all estimation needs.

questions.title: Average vs Peak
questions.situation: Your average traffic is 10,000 QPS. You are sizing capacity for the system.
questions.question: Why you never size for the average.
options: Provision for exactly 10,000 QPS, the average
Provision for 100x the average to be totally safe
Provision for a peak that is typically 2-3x the average (or more for spiky workloads), so plan for ~20,000-30,000+ QPS with headroom
Peak does not matter if the average is known
questions.explanation: Traffic is bursty: daily peaks commonly run 2-3x the daily average, and event-driven spikes (launches, news, flash sales) go far higher. Sizing for the average guarantees you fall over at peak. A reasonable default is to estimate peak at 2-3x average and add headroom, then revisit for known spike patterns.

questions.title: Powers of Two as Data Sizes
questions.situation: You need quick data-size intuition for estimation.
questions.question: The KB/MB/GB shortcuts.
options: They are all roughly equal to a thousand
2^10 ~ 1 million, 2^20 ~ 1 billion, 2^30 ~ 1 trillion
2^10 ~ 1 thousand, 2^20 ~ 1 million, 2^30 ~ 1 billion
questions.explanation: 2^10 = 1,024 ~ 1 thousand (a KB), 2^20 = 1,048,576 ~ 1 million (a MB), 2^30 ~ 1 billion (a GB), 2^40 ~ 1 trillion (a TB). Memorising that each 10 powers of two is about 3 orders of magnitude lets you convert between bytes and human numbers instantly.

questions.title: Sizing a User Table
questions.situation: You have 100 million users. Each user profile row is about 1 KB.
questions.question: Users times row size.
options: About 100 GB total
About 100 MB total
About 1 TB total
About 100 TB total
questions.explanation: 100,000,000 users x 1 KB = 100,000,000 KB = ~100 GB (since 1 million KB ~ 1 GB). This kind of users x row-size product is the bread and butter of storage estimation; once you have raw size you multiply by replication factor and add indexes/overhead.

questions.title: Latency Numbers, Ordered
questions.situation: Order these from fastest to slowest: a main-memory (RAM) reference, an SSD random read, a round trip within the same datacenter, a round trip from California to Europe and back.
questions.question: Know the hierarchy cold.
options: Same-DC round trip < RAM reference < SSD read < CA-to-Europe round trip
RAM reference (~100 ns) < SSD random read (~16-100 us) < same-DC round trip (~0.5 ms) < CA-to-Europe round trip (~150 ms)
SSD read < RAM reference < CA-to-Europe < same-DC
They are all roughly the same once you account for caching
questions.explanation: The canonical hierarchy: RAM reference ~100 ns, SSD random read ~16-100 us (100-1000x slower than RAM), a same-datacenter round trip ~0.5 ms, and a transcontinental round trip ~150 ms (bounded by the speed of light). Each step is roughly an order of magnitude or more. Knowing this ordering lets you reason about where a design will be slow before you build it.

questions.title: DAU to System QPS
questions.situation: A social feed has 100 million daily active users, and each user makes about 10 feed requests per day.
questions.question: From users to load.
options: About 1,000 QPS average
About 100,000 QPS average
About 10,000 QPS average
About 1 million QPS average
questions.explanation: 100M users x 10 requests = 1 billion requests/day. Divided by ~100,000 sec/day, that is ~10,000 QPS average, and you would then size for ~20-30K+ at peak. Reads usually dominate a feed, so you would also split this into read vs write paths.

questions.title: Egress Bandwidth
questions.situation: Your CDN origin serves 10,000 images per second, and each image averages 200 KB.
questions.question: Traffic times object size.
options: About 2 MB/s
About 200 MB/s
About 200 GB/s
About 2 GB/s
questions.explanation: 10,000 images/s x 200 KB = 2,000,000 KB/s = ~2 GB/s (since a million KB ~ a GB). That is ~16 Gbps of egress, which immediately tells you a single origin will not do and you need a CDN and careful egress-cost planning. Bandwidth estimates are rate x object-size.

questions.title: Daily Log Volume
questions.situation: A service handles 1,000 requests/second and writes a ~1 KB log line per request, all day.
questions.question: Rate times size times time.
options: About 86 GB/day
About 86 MB/day
About 1 TB/day
About 8 GB/day
questions.explanation: 1,000 req/s x 1 KB = 1 MB/s of logs. Over 86,400 seconds that is ~86,400 MB ~= 86 GB/day. This is why log retention and sampling matter: a modest 1K QPS service generates tens of GB of logs daily, which is real money at cloud storage and ingestion prices.

questions.title: Cache Hit Ratio and Effective Latency
questions.situation: A cache hit takes 1 ms and serves 90% of reads; a miss takes 100 ms (it goes to the database). What is the approximate average read latency?
questions.question: Weighted-average latency.
options: About 1 ms, because most reads hit
About 11 ms (0.9 x 1 ms + 0.1 x 100 ms)
About 100 ms, dominated by misses
About 50 ms, the midpoint
questions.explanation: Effective latency is a weighted average: 0.9 x 1 ms + 0.1 x 100 ms = 0.9 + 10 = ~11 ms. Notice the 10% of slow misses dominate the average, that is why raising a 90% hit rate to 99% (0.99 x 1 + 0.01 x 100 = ~2 ms) is such a big win. The tail of misses, not the common hit, drives the number.

questions.title: Reading 1 MB Sequentially
questions.situation: Roughly how long to read 1 MB sequentially from main memory versus from a fast SSD?
questions.question: Throughput, not just latency.
options: Both take about 1 second
Memory is slower than SSD for sequential reads
Memory: tens of microseconds; SSD: a few hundred microseconds to ~1 ms; both far faster than a network fetch from another continent
Both take about 100 ms
questions.explanation: Sequential bandwidth is high: reading 1 MB from RAM is on the order of tens of microseconds, and from a fast SSD on the order of a few hundred microseconds to about a millisecond. Both crush a cross-continent network round trip (~150 ms). The lesson: for bulk data, sequential local reads are cheap; the expensive thing is round trips and random access, not raw bytes.

questions.title: Annual Write Storage
questions.situation: Users post 10 million 300-byte messages per day. Roughly how much raw message storage per year (ignore replication and indexes)?
questions.question: Scale a daily rate to a year.
options: About 1 GB/year
About 1 PB/year
About 100 TB/year
About 1 TB/year
questions.explanation: 10M x 300 bytes = 3,000,000,000 bytes = ~3 GB/day. Over 365 days that is ~1,000 GB ~= ~1 TB/year of raw message text. You would then multiply by replication factor (often 3x) and add indexing/metadata overhead, but the raw figure is ~1 TB/year.

questions.title: Round Trips in a Latency Budget
questions.situation: Your p99 latency budget is 200 ms, and each cross-continent round trip costs ~150 ms.
questions.question: Why chatty designs miss SLAs.
options: You can afford at most one such round trip; a chatty design with multiple sequential cross-continent calls blows the budget, so co-locate or parallelise
You can comfortably fit several cross-continent round trips in the budget
Latency budgets do not apply to distributed calls
Adding more round trips reduces total latency
questions.explanation: With a 200 ms budget and ~150 ms per transcontinental round trip, one round trip already eats most of it; two sequential ones (300 ms) miss entirely. This is why estimation matters before design: you either reduce round trips (batch, co-locate data near compute) or parallelise independent calls so they overlap. Counting round trips against the budget is a core back-of-envelope check.

questions.title: What is CI/CD?
questions.situation: You're joining a new team and they mention CI/CD practices. You want to understand what this means.
questions.question: What does CI/CD stand for?
options: Code Integration / Code Delivery
Continuous Integration / Continuous Deployment
Central Integration / Central Distribution
Cloud Integration / Cloud Deployment
questions.explanation: CI/CD stands for Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment (or Continuous Delivery). It's a set of practices that automate the software delivery process, from code commits to production deployment.

questions.title: Purpose of Continuous Integration
questions.situation: Your team has multiple developers committing code daily. You need to understand why CI is important.
questions.question: What is the primary purpose of Continuous Integration?
options: To make code reviews optional
To automatically merge all code without testing
To deploy code directly to production
To detect integration issues early by frequently merging and testing code changes
questions.explanation: Continuous Integration helps catch bugs and integration issues early by automatically building and testing code changes whenever developers commit. This reduces integration problems and makes it easier to maintain code quality.

questions.title: Benefits of CI/CD
questions.situation: Your manager asks why your team should invest time setting up CI/CD pipelines.
questions.question: Which of the following is a key benefit of implementing CI/CD?
options: It eliminates the need for testing
It prevents developers from making mistakes
It removes the need for code reviews
It allows faster, more reliable software releases with reduced manual work
questions.explanation: CI/CD automates repetitive tasks like building, testing, and deploying code, which leads to faster release cycles, fewer manual errors, and more reliable deployments. Teams can ship features and fixes more quickly with confidence.

questions.title: Basic Pipeline Stages
questions.situation: You're designing your first CI/CD pipeline and need to understand the common stages.
questions.question: What are the typical stages in a basic CI/CD pipeline?
options: Write, Review, Approve
Build, Test, Deploy
Code, Commit, Push
Plan, Design, Execute
questions.explanation: A typical CI/CD pipeline consists of Build (compile code and create artifacts), Test (run automated tests), and Deploy (release to environments). These stages ensure code quality before reaching production.

questions.title: Version Control in CI/CD
questions.situation: Your team is setting up CI/CD. Someone suggests skipping version control to save time.
questions.question: Why is version control essential for CI/CD?
options: It's not essential, CI/CD can work without it
It only helps with documentation
It's only needed for large teams
It tracks code changes, enables collaboration, and triggers automated pipelines
questions.explanation: Version control (like Git) is fundamental to CI/CD. It tracks all code changes, enables team collaboration, and most importantly, triggers CI/CD pipelines when code is committed. Without it, automated pipelines wouldn't know when to run.

questions.title: Automated Testing
questions.situation: You're setting up automated tests in your pipeline. Which tests should run first?
questions.question: What type of test runs first in a CI/CD pipeline?
options: Manual testing by QA team
End-to-end tests (testing full user workflows)
Unit tests (testing individual components)
Performance tests
questions.explanation: Unit tests should run first because they're fast, test small pieces of code in isolation, and quickly catch basic issues. If unit tests fail, there's no point running slower integration or end-to-end tests.

questions.title: Build Artifacts
questions.situation: Your CI pipeline successfully completes the build stage. What has it created?
questions.question: What is a build artifact in CI/CD?
options: A backup of the source code
A list of bugs found
Documentation for the code
The compiled/packaged application ready for deployment
questions.explanation: A build artifact is the output of the build process - typically a compiled application, Docker image, or packaged file that can be deployed. It's the tangible result that gets promoted through environments.

questions.title: Deployment Environments
questions.situation: Your pipeline deploys to multiple environments. Where should you do final validation?
questions.question: Which environment is typically used for final testing before production?
options: Development
Production
Staging
Local machine
questions.explanation: Staging is a production-like environment used for final testing before releasing to actual users. It mirrors production configuration and data, allowing you to catch issues before they affect real users.

questions.title: Pipeline Triggers
questions.situation: You want your pipeline to run automatically. What should trigger it?
questions.question: What typically triggers a CI/CD pipeline to run?
options: Only manual button clicks
When the server restarts
Code commits, pull requests, or scheduled times
Only on weekends
questions.explanation: CI/CD pipelines are typically triggered by code events (commits, pull requests), schedules (nightly builds), or manual triggers. Automatic triggers ensure code is continuously tested and integrated.

questions.title: Deployment vs Delivery
questions.situation: Your team is debating whether to implement Continuous Deployment or Continuous Delivery.
questions.question: What's the difference between Continuous Deployment and Continuous Delivery?
options: There is no difference, they're the same thing
Delivery is faster than Deployment
Deployment is only for large companies
Deployment automatically releases to production; Delivery stops at a manual approval step
questions.explanation: Continuous Delivery means code is always ready to deploy but requires manual approval for production. Continuous Deployment automatically deploys every change that passes tests directly to production without human intervention.

questions.title: CI/CD Tools
questions.situation: You need to choose a CI/CD tool for your project.
questions.question: Which of these is a popular CI/CD tool?
options: Microsoft Word
Photoshop
GitHub Actions
MySQL
questions.explanation: GitHub Actions is a popular CI/CD platform that runs workflows based on repository events. Other common tools include Jenkins, GitLab CI, CircleCI, and Azure DevOps.

questions.title: Build Status Indicators
questions.situation: You see a green checkmark next to your latest commit in GitHub.
questions.question: What does a green checkmark on a build typically mean?
options: The code has been deployed to production
Someone approved your code
The build is currently running
All pipeline checks passed successfully
questions.explanation: A green checkmark (or 'passing' status) indicates that all CI/CD pipeline checks - builds, tests, and validations - completed successfully. Red X means failure, yellow/orange means in progress or pending.

questions.title: Handling Pipeline Failures
questions.situation: You pushed code and the CI pipeline shows a red X with 'Tests failed'.
questions.question: Your pipeline fails on a test. What should you do first?
options: Review the logs to understand which test failed and why
Delete the failing test
Immediately push more code to fix it
Ask someone else to fix it
questions.explanation: When a pipeline fails, always check the logs first to understand what went wrong. The logs show which test failed and the error details, helping you identify and fix the root cause.

questions.title: Deployment Rollback
questions.situation: A new deployment causes issues in production. Your team mentions rolling back.
questions.question: What is a rollback in CI/CD?
options: Reverting to the previous working version of the application
Rolling logs to a backup
Restarting all servers
Moving servers to a different location
questions.explanation: A rollback means reverting to a previous stable version of your application when a new deployment causes problems. It's a safety mechanism to quickly restore service while you investigate and fix the issue.

questions.title: Code Reviews in CI/CD
questions.situation: You're using pull requests with your CI/CD setup.
questions.question: How do code reviews fit into a CI/CD workflow?
options: CI/CD runs tests on pull requests before code is merged and reviewed
Code reviews happen only after deployment
Code reviews are not needed with CI/CD
CI/CD replaces the need for human review
questions.explanation: CI/CD complements code reviews by automatically running tests on pull requests. This gives reviewers confidence that code works before they review it, and ensures only tested code gets merged into the main branch.

questions.title: Managing Dependencies
questions.situation: Your build works locally but fails in CI with the same code.
questions.question: Why is it important to specify exact dependency versions in CI/CD?
options: To ensure consistent, reproducible builds across all environments
To make builds slower
It's not important, any version works
To use the oldest possible dependencies
questions.explanation: Specifying exact dependency versions (like in package-lock.json or requirements.txt) ensures everyone - developers, CI systems, and production - uses the same versions. This prevents 'works on my machine' issues.

questions.title: Branching Strategy
questions.situation: Your team needs to set up automated deployments from Git.
questions.question: Which branch is typically used for production deployments?
options: main (or master)
developer-sandbox
feature/new-button
Any branch is fine
questions.explanation: The main (or master) branch typically represents the production-ready code. Feature branches are used for development, then merged to main after review and testing. Production deployments trigger from the main branch.

questions.title: Pipeline Efficiency
questions.situation: Your pipeline takes 2 hours to run. Developers are frustrated.
questions.question: Why should CI/CD pipelines run as fast as possible?
options: Fast feedback helps developers fix issues quickly and maintain productivity
Slower pipelines are more thorough
Speed doesn't matter in CI/CD
It only matters for large teams
questions.explanation: Fast pipelines give developers quick feedback on their changes, allowing them to fix issues while the code is fresh in their minds. Slow pipelines frustrate developers and slow down the entire development process.

questions.title: Setting Up Your First Pipeline
questions.situation: You're setting up a CI/CD pipeline for a web application that needs to be tested and deployed to production.
questions.code:
# Your application:
- Unit tests
- Integration tests
- Docker image build
- Deploy to staging
- Deploy to production
questions.question: What's the correct order of stages in a basic CI/CD pipeline?
options: Build → Test → Deploy
Build → Unit Tests → Integration Tests → Deploy to Staging → Deploy to Production
Test → Build → Deploy
Deploy → Test → Build
questions.explanation: The correct order follows the principle of fail fast: build first, run unit tests (fastest), then integration tests (slower), deploy to staging for verification, and finally to production. This catches issues early and reduces waste.

questions.title: Git Branching for CI/CD
questions.situation: Your team needs to deploy features frequently while maintaining production stability. Multiple developers work on features simultaneously.
questions.question: Which branching strategy works best with automated deployments?
options: Trunk-based development with feature flags and automated deployments from main branch
Create a branch for each environment (dev, staging, prod)
Long-lived feature branches merged monthly
Everyone commits directly to main branch
questions.explanation: Trunk-based development with short-lived branches and feature flags enables continuous integration, reduces merge conflicts, and allows controlled feature releases. Combined with automated deployments, it supports rapid delivery.

questions.title: Test Automation Strategy
questions.situation: You need to balance test coverage with pipeline speed. Your pipeline is taking 45 minutes to run.
questions.code:
# Current situation:
# - 200 unit tests (2 minutes)
# - 50 integration tests (15 minutes)
# - 20 end-to-end tests (28 minutes)
# Total: 45 minutes
questions.question: How should you structure your automated tests in a CI pipeline?
options: Run only end-to-end tests since they test everything
Run all tests in parallel regardless of type
Follow the test pyramid: many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, minimal E2E tests. Run unit tests on every commit, integration tests before merge, E2E tests before deployment
Skip automated tests and rely on manual QA
questions.explanation: The test pyramid prioritizes fast, focused unit tests that run frequently, with fewer but comprehensive integration tests, and minimal slow E2E tests. This balances coverage with speed and gives rapid feedback.

questions.title: Managing Environment Configuration
