After losing 2 nodes and splitting the remaining 3 into 2 and 1, neither side has 3 votes, so no leader is elected and writes halt. This is by design: it is the mechanism that prevents split-brain (two leaders) at the cost of availability when you lose quorum.

questions.title: Split-Brain
questions.situation: After a partition heals, you discover two nodes both believed they were the primary and each accepted conflicting writes.
questions.question: Recognise the worst failure mode.
options: This is split-brain: two leaders accepted divergent writes, and you now have conflicting state to reconcile or data loss
This is normal and the writes will automatically merge correctly
This cannot happen if you use TCP instead of UDP
This only affects reads, not writes
questions.explanation: Split-brain is when a partition leaves two nodes each acting as the authoritative primary, accepting writes that conflict. When the partition heals you have divergent histories, and resolving them means conflict resolution or, often, losing one side's writes. Quorum/fencing mechanisms exist precisely to make this impossible by ensuring only one side can hold leadership.

questions.title: Idempotency and Retries
questions.situation: A client sends a 'charge $10' request, the server processes it, but the response is lost. The client retries.
questions.question: Make retries safe.
options: Retries are always safe, so no special handling is needed
An idempotency key lets the server recognise the retry and not charge twice
The server should reject all retries to be safe
Use UDP so lost responses do not trigger retries
questions.explanation: On an unreliable network a lost response is indistinguishable from a lost request, so clients must retry, and a naive retry double-charges. An idempotency key (a unique token per logical operation) lets the server detect 'I already did this one' and return the original result instead of repeating the side effect. It is the standard pattern for safe retries on non-idempotent operations.

questions.title: Ordering Events Across Servers
questions.situation: Two events happen on two servers. You want to know which happened first, so you compare their system clock timestamps.
questions.question: Why wall-clock timestamps lie.
options: Wall-clock timestamps are reliable because NTP keeps clocks perfectly in sync
The server with the higher IP address is always first
Clock skew between servers means timestamps can disagree with real causal order; use logical clocks (Lamport or vector clocks) to order events
You should use the database's auto-increment ID, which is globally ordered across servers
questions.explanation: Physical clocks drift and NTP only bounds the error, it does not eliminate it, so two servers can disagree by milliseconds or more. An event with a later real cause can carry an earlier timestamp. Logical clocks (Lamport timestamps, or vector clocks for detecting concurrency) capture happens-before relationships without trusting wall time. Per-server auto-increment IDs are not globally ordered.

questions.title: PACELC Extends CAP
questions.situation: Your system has no partition right now. A teammate says 'so CAP does not apply, we get consistency and low latency for free.'
questions.question: The trade-off that exists even without partitions.
options: Correct, with no partition there is no trade-off
Without a partition, all systems become linearizable automatically
PACELC only matters for NoSQL databases
PACELC says: if Partitioned, choose A or C; Else (normal operation) choose between Latency and Consistency, so the trade-off persists even with a healthy network
questions.explanation: PACELC extends CAP with the part CAP ignores: even with no partition (the 'Else' branch), you still trade Latency against Consistency. Synchronously replicating to a quorum before acknowledging gives stronger consistency but higher latency; acknowledging early and replicating async gives lower latency but weaker consistency. The trade-off does not disappear when the network is healthy.

questions.title: The Problem With Two-Phase Commit
questions.situation: In a two-phase commit, all participants vote 'yes' in the prepare phase. Then the coordinator crashes before sending the commit decision.
questions.question: Why 2PC is called a blocking protocol.
options: Participants are stuck holding locks and cannot unilaterally decide commit or abort; they block until the coordinator recovers
Participants can safely abort on their own after a short timeout
Each participant commits independently to avoid waiting
The transaction silently rolls back with no consequences
questions.explanation: After voting yes, a participant has promised it can commit and must hold its locks. If the coordinator dies before announcing the decision, participants cannot safely decide alone: committing risks inconsistency if others aborted, and aborting risks the opposite. They block until the coordinator (or a recovery process) resolves it. This blocking weakness is why consensus protocols like Raft/Paxos and three-phase variants are preferred for fault tolerance.

questions.title: Fallacies of Distributed Computing
questions.situation: A new service assumes the network is reliable, latency is zero, bandwidth is infinite, and topology never changes.
questions.question: Spot the false assumption.
options: These are reasonable assumptions inside a single datacenter
These are the classic fallacies of distributed computing; each is false and ignoring them produces fragile systems
They are only false on the public internet, not internal networks
Modern cloud networking has made all of these true
questions.explanation: These are straight out of the eight fallacies of distributed computing (the network is reliable, latency is zero, bandwidth is infinite, the network is secure, topology does not change, there is one administrator, transport cost is zero, the network is homogeneous). Every one is false, even inside a datacenter, and systems built as if they were true fail in production the first time the network misbehaves.

questions.title: Read Repair and Hinted Handoff
questions.situation: In a Dynamo-style store, a replica was down during a write and missed it. Later a read touches that replica and finds a stale value.
questions.question: How eventually-consistent stores heal.
options: The stale replica is permanently corrupt and must be rebuilt from scratch
The read fails because the replicas disagree
Read repair updates the stale replica with the newest value seen during the read; hinted handoff would have stored the missed write for delivery when the replica returned
Nothing can be done until an admin manually copies the data
questions.explanation: Eventually-consistent stores self-heal. Read repair: when a read sees replicas disagree, it pushes the newest version back to the stale ones. Hinted handoff: when a replica is down during a write, another node stores a 'hint' and replays the write once the replica recovers. Together with anti-entropy (Merkle-tree) repair, these keep replicas converging without manual intervention.

questions.title: The Exactly-Once Myth
questions.situation: A vendor claims their message system guarantees exactly-once delivery over an unreliable network.
questions.question: What 'exactly-once' really means.
options: Believable: exactly-once delivery is a solved problem
It just requires a fast enough network
Exactly-once is only possible with UDP
Exactly-once delivery is impossible in general; what is achievable is at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing, giving exactly-once effects
questions.explanation: True exactly-once delivery is impossible when nodes and networks can fail, because a sender cannot distinguish a lost message from a lost acknowledgement. The practical guarantee is at-least-once delivery combined with idempotent consumers (or deduplication), which yields exactly-once processing semantics, the effect happens once even though the message may arrive more than once. 'Exactly-once' as marketed is almost always this.

questions.title: Vector Clocks vs Lamport Clocks
questions.situation: You need to detect whether two updates were truly concurrent (neither caused the other), so you can flag a conflict.
questions.question: Detecting concurrency, not just order.
options: Vector clocks can tell concurrent events apart from causally ordered ones; a single Lamport timestamp only gives a total order and cannot distinguish concurrency
A single Lamport timestamp tells you whether two events were concurrent
Wall-clock timestamps are sufficient to detect concurrency
Concurrency cannot be detected in distributed systems
questions.explanation: A Lamport clock gives a consistent total order but loses information: if event A has a smaller timestamp than B, you cannot tell whether A happened-before B or they were concurrent. Vector clocks track a counter per node, so comparing two vectors reveals causally-before, causally-after, or concurrent (neither dominates). That concurrency signal is exactly what conflict-detecting stores need.

questions.title: Detecting a Dead Node
questions.situation: A node stops responding to heartbeats for 10 seconds. Your system declares it dead and promotes a replica. The node was actually just slow and comes back.
questions.question: The limits of failure detection.
options: Heartbeats give perfect, instant failure detection
You cannot perfectly distinguish a slow node from a dead one over an async network; tune timeouts and use fencing so a wrongly-declared-dead node cannot cause split-brain when it returns
Longer timeouts eliminate all false positives with no downside
A node that misses one heartbeat is definitely dead
questions.explanation: On an asynchronous network you fundamentally cannot tell 'crashed' from 'slow or partitioned', so any failure detector trades false positives (declaring a live node dead) against detection latency. Short timeouts react fast but mis-fire; long timeouts are safe but slow. Because a wrongly-evicted node may return believing it is still valid, you need fencing (tokens, leases) so its late actions are rejected, preventing split-brain.

questions.title: Dockerfile Best Practices
questions.situation: You need to create a Dockerfile for a Node.js web application that has dependencies in package.json.
questions.code:
// Your app structure:
├── package.json
├── package-lock.json
├── src/
│   └── app.js
└── public/
    └── index.html
questions.question: Choose the most efficient Dockerfile for a Node.js application.
options:
FROM node:16-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["npm", "start"]

FROM node:16
COPY . /app
WORKDIR /app
RUN npm install
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["npm", "start"]

FROM node:16
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN npm install
CMD ["node", "src/app.js"]

FROM ubuntu
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y nodejs npm
COPY . /app
WORKDIR /app
RUN npm install
CMD ["npm", "start"]
questions.explanation: Option B uses Alpine for smaller image size, leverages Docker layer caching by copying package files first, uses npm ci for production builds, and follows proper WORKDIR practices.

questions.title: Docker Networking
questions.situation: You have a web application container that needs to connect to a PostgreSQL database container.
questions.question: How should two containers communicate in a multi-container application?
options: Use --link flag when running containers
Use localhost and map ports to host
Create a custom bridge network and connect both containers to it
Connect containers using IP addresses
questions.explanation: Custom bridge networks provide better isolation, automatic DNS resolution between containers, and are the recommended approach for multi-container applications.

questions.title: Data Persistence
questions.situation: You're running PostgreSQL in a container and need to ensure data persists across container restarts and updates.
questions.question: What's the best way to persist database data in a containerized PostgreSQL?
options: Use bind mounts to map host directory
Copy data files during container build
Use --volumes-from another container
Create a named volume and mount it to /var/lib/postgresql/data
questions.explanation: Named volumes are managed by Docker, provide better performance, work across different host systems, and are the recommended way to persist database data.

questions.title: Optimizing Image Size
questions.situation: Your Go application needs to be compiled, but you don't want build tools in the final production image.
questions.code:
// You have:
- main.go (your application)
- go.mod and go.sum (dependencies)
- Need: minimal production image
questions.question: You need to build a Go application with minimal final image size.
options:
FROM golang:1.19
COPY . /app
WORKDIR /app
RUN go build -o myapp
CMD ["./myapp"]

FROM golang:1.19 AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY go.* ./
RUN go mod download
COPY . .
RUN go build -o myapp

FROM alpine:latest
RUN apk --no-cache add ca-certificates
COPY --from=builder /app/myapp /
CMD ["/myapp"]

FROM alpine:latest
RUN apk add --no-cache go
COPY . /app
WORKDIR /app
RUN go build -o myapp
CMD ["./myapp"]

FROM scratch
COPY main.go /
CMD ["go", "run", "main.go"]
questions.explanation: Multi-stage builds allow you to use a full build environment in the first stage, then copy only the compiled binary to a minimal final image, significantly reducing size.

questions.title: Container Health Monitoring
questions.situation: Your web application runs on port 3000 and has a /health endpoint that returns HTTP 200 when healthy.
questions.question: How do you properly implement health checks for a web application container?
options: HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --retries=3 CMD curl -f http://localhost:3000/health || exit 1
RUN curl -f http://localhost:3000/health
HEALTHCHECK CMD ps aux | grep node
No health check needed - Docker handles this automatically
questions.explanation: The HEALTHCHECK instruction with proper interval, timeout, and retry settings using the application's health endpoint is the correct approach for monitoring container health.

questions.title: Container Security
questions.situation: You're preparing a Docker image for production deployment and need to follow security best practices.
questions.question: What's the most important security practice when building production Docker images?
options: Always run as root user for maximum compatibility
Create and use a non-root user, avoid unnecessary packages, and use specific image tags
Use the latest tag for all base images to get updates
Install all possible dependencies to avoid runtime issues
questions.explanation: Running as non-root, minimizing attack surface by avoiding unnecessary packages, and using specific tags (not 'latest') are fundamental Docker security practices.

questions.title: Images vs Containers
questions.situation: One teammate says 'just run the image' and another says 'restart the container'. You want to use the terms precisely.
questions.question: Use the core Docker vocabulary correctly.
options: They are two names for the same thing
A container is a read-only template and an image is a running instance of it
An image is a read-only template, and a container is a runnable instance created from that image
An image can only ever produce a single container
questions.explanation: An image is an immutable, layered template. You create one or many containers from a single image; each container is an isolated instance with its own writable layer. Think class versus instance.

questions.title: Running Your First Container
questions.situation: You want to run the official nginx image in the background and reach it on host port 8080.
questions.question: Start a container in the background with a published port.
options: docker run -d -p 8080:80 nginx
docker start -d -p 8080:80 nginx
docker run -p 80:8080 nginx
docker exec -d -p 8080:80 nginx
questions.explanation: docker run creates and starts a new container. -d runs it detached (in the background), and -p 8080:80 publishes host port 8080 to container port 80. docker start only restarts an existing container; docker exec runs a command in a running one.

questions.title: Listing Containers
questions.situation: You started a container but `docker ps` shows nothing. It seems to have exited right away.
questions.question: Find a container that exited immediately.
options: docker images, which lists your containers
docker logs, which lists all containers
Nothing, an exited container is gone for good
docker ps -a, which includes stopped and exited containers
questions.explanation: docker ps shows only running containers. Add -a (all) to include stopped and exited ones, then docker logs <id> tells you why it exited. docker images lists images, not containers.

questions.title: Building an Image
questions.situation: You have a Dockerfile in the current directory and want an image named myapp with tag v1.
questions.question: Build and tag an image from a Dockerfile.
options: docker run -t myapp:v1 .
docker build -t myapp:v1 .
docker build myapp:v1
docker create myapp:v1 .
questions.explanation: docker build builds an image from a Dockerfile. -t sets the name:tag and the trailing . is the build context (the current directory). Leaving off the context path is one of the most common first-time errors.

questions.title: Dockerfile Instructions
questions.situation: You are reading a Dockerfile for the first time and want to understand the foundational instruction.
questions.question: Know what the core Dockerfile instructions do.
options: FROM, which sets the base image the build starts from
RUN, which starts the container
CMD, which copies your application files in
EXPOSE, which downloads the base image
questions.explanation: A Dockerfile starts FROM a base image (aside from an optional leading ARG). RUN executes build-time commands, COPY brings files into the image, and CMD sets the default command the container runs at startup.

questions.title: Docker Compose Basics
questions.situation: Your compose.yaml defines a web service and a db service.
questions.code:
services:
  web:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"
  db:
    image: postgres:16
questions.question: Understand what `docker compose up` does for a multi-service app.
options: It builds a single image containing both web and db
It starts only the first service listed
It creates and starts both services on a shared network so they reach each other by service name
It runs both services but keeps them on isolated networks by default
questions.explanation: docker compose up brings every defined service up together and puts them on a shared default network, so web can reach the database at the hostname 'db'. It is the standard way to run a multi-container app locally.

questions.title: Publishing Ports
questions.situation: Your app listens on port 3000 inside the container. You run `docker run -p 3000:8080 myapp` and cannot reach it at localhost:3000.
questions.question: Get the host-to-container port mapping the right way round.
options: Containers cannot publish ports below 8080
The mapping is backwards: -p is host:container, so you sent host 3000 to container 8080 where nothing listens. Use -p 3000:3000
You must add -d or published ports are ignored
localhost is never reachable from a container
questions.explanation: The -p flag uses host:container order. -p 3000:8080 forwards host port 3000 to container port 8080, but the app listens on 3000 inside, so nothing answers. Use -p 3000:3000 (or -p 8080:3000 to reach it on host port 8080).

questions.title: Getting a Shell in a Container
questions.situation: A container is running and you want a shell inside it to look around and debug.
questions.question: Open an interactive shell inside a running container.
options: docker run -it <container> sh, to reuse the running container
docker attach <container> sh
docker shell <container>
docker exec -it <container> sh
questions.explanation: docker exec runs a new command in an already-running container, and -it gives you an interactive terminal. docker run would start a brand new container instead, and docker attach connects to the main process rather than opening a new shell.

questions.quizTitle: eBPF for Network Observability and Security Quiz
questions.title: Why not just write a kernel module?
questions.situation: You're standing up fleet-wide network visibility on a few thousand hosts. A custom .ko kernel module would give you the data, but the platform team has a hard rule: nothing that can take down the kernel at runtime. You reach for eBPF instead and have to justify why it's different.
questions.code:
# Loading a custom kernel module: one bug = kernel panic
$ sudo insmod mynetstats.ko
# a null deref in here can crash the whole host

# Loading an eBPF program: rejected at load time if unsafe
$ sudo bpftool prog load netstats.o /sys/fs/bpf/netstats
libbpf: prog 'count_bytes': BPF program load failed: Permission denied
# the kernel verifier refused it; the host stays up
questions.question: You need per-connection network stats from every production host. Ops refuses to load custom kernel modules because one bad module can panic the box. What makes eBPF a safer fit?
options: eBPF programs run entirely in userspace, so they physically cannot touch kernel data structures
Every eBPF program is checked by an in-kernel verifier and runs in a restricted sandbox, so an unsafe program is rejected at load time instead of crashing the kernel
eBPF programs are compiled into the kernel image at boot, so they are reviewed before the system starts
eBPF disables the part of the kernel that can panic, trading safety for a small performance hit
questions.explanation: eBPF programs run inside the kernel, but before the kernel accepts one, the verifier walks every possible path and proves the program terminates, never reads out-of-bounds memory, and only touches data it's allowed to. If it can't prove safety, the load fails (often with a cryptic -EPERM or -EINVAL) and nothing runs. That's the key difference from a kernel module: a module trusts you completely and a single bug panics the host, while an eBPF program is checked first. It does not run in userspace, it is not baked into the boot image, and it does not switch off kernel safety features.

questions.quizTitle: eBPF for Network Observability and Security Quiz
questions.title: Getting counts out to a dashboard
questions.situation: The drop counter lives inside the kernel-side program. Your Go agent runs in userspace and needs to scrape the current value every few seconds. There's no return value to catch, the program just runs per packet and exits.
questions.question: Your XDP program increments a counter every time it drops a packet. That code runs in the kernel. How does your userspace agent read those counts to ship them to a dashboard?
options: A map: a shared key/value structure that both the kernel program and userspace can read and write, looked up by name or file descriptor
The program returns the counter as its exit code, and userspace reads it from the return value
The kernel writes the value to a log file with bpf_printk, and userspace tails the file
A shared environment variable that the kernel updates and userspace reads with getenv
questions.explanation: Maps are how eBPF programs and userspace exchange data. They're kernel-resident key/value stores (arrays, hashes, per-CPU variants, ring buffers, and more) that the program updates from inside the kernel and that userspace reads through a file descriptor, often pinned under /sys/fs/bpf so multiple processes can share it. The program's actual return value is a verdict for the hook (like XDP_PASS or XDP_DROP), not a place to stash data. bpf_printk exists but it's a debugging aid that writes to the trace pipe, not a metrics channel, and there's no shared environment variable between kernel and userspace.

questions.quizTitle: eBPF for Network Observability and Security Quiz
questions.title: Where XDP sits in the stack
questions.situation: You're filtering unwanted traffic at the edge of each node and want to spend as few CPU cycles as possible per dropped packet. A colleague suggests XDP but isn't sure why it's cheaper than filtering higher up the stack.
questions.question: Your team is choosing a hook point for a high-volume packet filter. Someone proposes XDP because it's 'the fastest.' Where does an XDP program actually run, and why is that fast?
options: Inside each application socket, so it sees fully reassembled application-layer data
In netfilter, replacing iptables rules with a faster equivalent
At the earliest point in the receive path, in the NIC driver before the kernel builds an sk_buff, working on raw packet bytes
In userspace next to your agent, which is why it avoids kernel overhead
questions.explanation: XDP (eXpress Data Path) attaches at the very start of the receive path, in the NIC driver, before the kernel allocates an sk_buff (the heavyweight per-packet metadata structure). Because that allocation is one of the more expensive steps, dropping or redirecting a packet at XDP avoids almost all per-packet cost, which is what makes it ideal for line-rate filtering and DDoS mitigation. It works on raw bytes, so it sees Ethernet and IP headers, not reassembled application data. It's not inside sockets, not part of netfilter, and not in userspace, it runs in the kernel driver context.

questions.quizTitle: eBPF for Network Observability and Security Quiz
questions.title: Filtering happens, but only inbound
questions.situation: Your policy needs to block certain outbound connections from a node, not just inbound ones. You attached your filter as XDP and tested it: connections from outside are blocked correctly, but the node still happily sends traffic out to blocked destinations.
questions.code:
$ sudo bpftool net attach xdp name policy dev eth0
$ # inbound: blocked correctly
$ # outbound from this host: still goes through

$ sudo bpftool net
xdp:
eth0(2) driver id 41
# nothing on the egress path...
questions.question: You wrote an XDP program to enforce a policy on both inbound and outbound traffic. Inbound works. Outbound traffic sails right through. Why?
options: XDP needs XDP_TX to handle egress; add it as a second return code in the same program
XDP only runs on the receive path (ingress); to act on egress traffic you need a tc BPF program attached to the egress hook, which operates on the sk_buff
Outbound traffic skips XDP because it's encrypted; disable TLS offload on the NIC
The program is fine, but bpftool can't display egress XDP; the policy is actually being enforced
questions.explanation: XDP is an ingress-only hook. It lives in the driver's receive path, so by design it never sees packets the host is sending out. For egress (and for ingress when you want sk_buff context), you use tc BPF programs attached via the clsact qdisc, which has both an ingress and an egress hook. tc runs slightly later than XDP because the sk_buff already exists, but that's the trade for being able to act in both directions. XDP_TX bounces a received packet back out the same interface, it does not give you a hook on locally generated egress traffic, and this has nothing to do with TLS.

questions.quizTitle: eBPF for Network Observability and Security Quiz
questions.title: Dropping a SYN flood cheaply
questions.situation: During the flood, perf top shows the kernel burning most of its time allocating and freeing sk_buffs for packets that iptables drops a moment later. You want those packets gone before the kernel does any of that work.
questions.code:
$ perf top
  18.4%  [kernel]  __alloc_skb
  12.1%  [kernel]  kfree_skb
   9.7%  [kernel]  nf_hook_slow
   ...

# iptables rule currently doing the drop:
-A INPUT -p tcp --syn -m limit --limit 1/s -j DROP
questions.question: A SYN flood is hammering a node at millions of packets per second. iptables is dropping them, but the box is pinned at 100% softirq CPU. Where should you drop these packets to spend the least CPU?
options: Move the rule earlier in the iptables INPUT chain so it matches before other rules
Switch to nftables, which drops packets before the sk_buff is allocated
Add more conntrack buckets so the firewall can track and drop the flood faster
Drop the packets at XDP with XDP_DROP, before the sk_buff is ever allocated, so each dropped packet costs almost nothing
questions.explanation: The CPU is being spent on __alloc_skb and kfree_skb, the sk_buff lifecycle. iptables and nftables both run after the sk_buff exists, so they can't avoid that cost, no matter where you put the rule. An XDP program returning XDP_DROP runs in the driver before the sk_buff is allocated, so a dropped packet costs little more than the inspection itself. This is exactly why XDP is the standard tool for volumetric DDoS mitigation (Cloudflare and Facebook both built XDP-based packet filters for this). Adding conntrack capacity makes it worse, since you'd track attack packets you intend to discard.

questions.quizTitle: eBPF for Network Observability and Security Quiz
questions.title: kube-proxy and the iptables wall
questions.situation: Your platform team runs a large cluster. kube-proxy in iptables mode writes a rule chain per Service and endpoint, and `iptables-save` now dumps hundreds of thousands of lines. Adding or removing a Service causes a noticeable stall while the chains are rewritten.
questions.code:
$ iptables-save | wc -l
284119

$ # every Service adds KUBE-SVC-* and KUBE-SEP-* chains
-A KUBE-SERVICES -d 10.96.0.10/32 -p tcp --dport 53 -j KUBE-SVC-TCOU7...
-A KUBE-SVC-TCOU7... -j KUBE-SEP-AAAA...
-A KUBE-SVC-TCOU7... -j KUBE-SEP-BBBB...
# ... matched roughly linearly per packet
questions.question: A cluster with thousands of Services has slow service updates and high latency on the first packet of new connections. kube-proxy in iptables mode is generating enormous rule chains. What does an eBPF-based dataplane change?
options: It rewrites the same iptables rules faster by batching them, cutting the update stall
It moves the iptables rules into a kernel module so they're compiled instead of interpreted
It replaces the linear iptables chains with eBPF programs that do service lookups and load balancing through hash-map lookups, so cost stays roughly constant as Services grow
It caches DNS responses in eBPF so Service resolution no longer hits iptables
questions.explanation: kube-proxy's iptables mode encodes every Service and endpoint as rules, and packet matching plus rule rewrites scale poorly as the cluster grows. An eBPF dataplane like Cilium's kube-proxy replacement does service ClusterIP-to-backend translation and load balancing using eBPF maps: a hash lookup keyed by service and a backend table. Lookups are roughly O(1) instead of walking chains, and updating a Service is a map write rather than regenerating a giant ruleset. It does not just batch iptables faster, it doesn't 'compile' iptables into a module, and it isn't a DNS cache. IPVS mode helps somewhat but still isn't map-based the way eBPF is.

questions.quizTitle: eBPF for Network Observability and Security Quiz
questions.title: Compiled here, won't load there
questions.situation: Your tracing program reads a field out of a kernel struct. It works on your laptop. On older production kernels the same compiled .o either fails verification or reads garbage, because that struct's layout shifted between kernel versions. Recompiling on each target with BCC is the old way and you'd rather not.
questions.question: Your eBPF object loads fine on your 5.15 dev kernel but fails to load on a 5.4 production node, reading a struct field at the wrong offset. You don't want to ship kernel headers and a compiler to every host. What fixes this?
options: Pin the program to a single kernel version and maintain a separate build per kernel you run
Use CO-RE (Compile Once, Run Everywhere): build against BTF type info and emit relocations so the loader patches struct offsets to match the running kernel
Statically link the kernel headers into the eBPF object so offsets travel with it
Disable the verifier's type checks on the older kernel so the mismatched offset is accepted
questions.explanation: The root problem is that kernel struct layouts change between versions, so a hard-coded field offset compiled on one kernel is wrong on another. CO-RE solves this with BTF (BPF Type Format): the compiler records which field you wanted, the object carries relocations, and at load time libbpf reads the running kernel's BTF (from /sys/kernel/btf/vmlinux) and patches each access to the correct offset. One object file then runs across many kernels without shipping headers or a compiler. Maintaining a build per kernel is the pain CO-RE removes, you can't statically embed offsets that match every kernel, and you never want to disable the verifier's safety checks.

questions.quizTitle: eBPF for Network Observability and Security Quiz
questions.title: Finding which connections retransmit
questions.situation: p99 latency spikes a few times an hour with no obvious cause. You think packets are being lost and retransmitted, but a full packet capture on a 10 Gbps host is too heavy to leave running, and it won't cleanly tell you which flows retransmit.
questions.code:
# attach to the kernel's retransmit path and emit one event per retransmit
$ sudo /usr/share/bcc/tools/tcpretrans
TIME     PID    IP LADDR:LPORT          T> RADDR:RPORT          STATE
01:55:05 0      4  10.0.0.7:443         R> 10.0.2.31:51234     ESTABLISHED
01:55:05 0      4  10.0.0.7:443         R> 10.0.2.44:48820     ESTABLISHED
# near-zero overhead: fires only when a retransmit actually happens
questions.question: An app sees intermittent tail latency. You suspect TCP retransmissions but don't want to run tcpdump continuously on a busy host. How do you attribute retransmits to specific connections with low overhead?
options: Attach an eBPF program to the kernel's retransmit function or tracepoint, so an event fires only when a retransmit occurs, carrying the connection's addresses and ports
Lower the host's TCP retransmission timeout so retransmits show up sooner in tcpdump
Poll /proc/net/snmp every second and diff the global TCP retransmit counter
Mirror all traffic to a second NIC and run tcpdump there to avoid load on the primary
questions.explanation: eBPF lets you attach to a specific kernel event, here the retransmit path (a kprobe on tcp_retransmit_skb or the matching tracepoint), so your program runs only when a retransmit actually happens and can read the socket's source/destination addresses and ports right there. That's near-zero overhead because there's no per-packet work and no copying full packets to userspace, which is why bcc's tcpretrans and bpftrace one-liners are the go-to here. Polling /proc/net/snmp gives you a single global counter with no per-connection attribution, lowering the RTO changes behavior rather than observing it, and port-mirroring just moves the capture cost around.

questions.quizTitle: eBPF for Network Observability and Security Quiz
questions.title: Counters that don't add up under load
questions.situation: Your eBPF program bumps a per-key byte counter in a BPF_MAP_TYPE_HASH on every packet. At a few hundred thousand packets per second across 16 cores, the counter update becomes a hotspot and totals come in lower than reality because of contention on the shared entry.
questions.question: A shared hash map counter is updated on every packet across all CPUs. Under heavy load the numbers look low and the update path shows up hot in profiles. What map change fixes the contention?
options: Wrap each update in a bpf_spin_lock so concurrent writes are serialized correctly
Switch to a per-CPU map (BPF_MAP_TYPE_PERCPU_HASH): each CPU updates its own copy with no cross-CPU contention, and userspace sums the per-CPU values when it reads
Increase max_entries so there are more buckets and less hashing collision
Move the counter into a BPF_MAP_TYPE_ARRAY, which is lock-free for writes
questions.explanation: When every CPU hammers the same map entry, you get cache-line bouncing and contention, and atomics on a single shared value become the bottleneck. A per-CPU map gives each CPU its own private copy of the value, so updates on the hot path never coordinate across cores. When userspace reads the map it gets one value per CPU and sums them, trading a slightly more complex read for a contention-free write path. That's the standard pattern for high-frequency counters and stats. A spin lock makes serialization explicit but keeps the contention you're trying to remove, more buckets doesn't help when the collisions are on the same key, and a plain ARRAY is still a single shared value per index.

questions.quizTitle: eBPF for Network Observability and Security Quiz
questions.title: Blocking an action in the kernel, not just logging it
questions.situation: You already log suspicious file opens with a tracing program, but logging is after the fact. The ask now is enforcement: when a process that shouldn't touch /etc/shadow tries to open it, the open must fail, decided in-kernel rather than by a userspace watcher that could be too slow.
questions.question: Security wants to actually prevent certain processes from opening a sensitive file, and to do it in the kernel so it can't be raced. You're choosing between classic seccomp and an eBPF LSM program. Which fits?
options: Use seccomp-bpf: attach a filter to the open syscall that denies it for the whole process tree
Use a tracing kprobe on the open path and have userspace kill the process when it sees a match
Attach an eBPF LSM program to the file_open hook and return a non-zero value to deny the operation in-kernel at the security decision point
Add a Linux capability rule so the process loses permission to read the file
questions.explanation: eBPF LSM programs (BPF_PROG_TYPE_LSM, available since kernel 5.7) attach to the same Linux Security Module hooks that SELinux and AppArmor use. Returning a non-zero value from the hook makes the kernel deny the operation right at the security decision point, with full context like the file and the calling task, so there's no race with a userspace watcher. seccomp-bpf filters syscalls by number and argument values but works on raw syscall arguments (it can't safely dereference a path pointer to match the file), so it's the wrong tool for path-based file policy. A tracing kprobe plus userspace kill is reactive and racy, and a capability rule is too coarse for a single path. Tetragon builds on these eBPF enforcement hooks.

questions.quizTitle: eBPF for Network Observability and Security Quiz
questions.title: Decoding a verifier rejection
questions.situation: You're parsing packet headers in XDP. The code compiles cleanly, but bpftool refuses to load it with a packet-access error pointing at the line where you dereference the Ethernet header. You stare at it and the logic seems fine.
questions.question: Your XDP program reads the Ethernet header and the verifier rejects it with 'invalid access to packet'. The C looks correct. What is the verifier insisting on?
options: The program must be compiled with a newer Clang; older Clang emits packet accesses the verifier can't follow
You have to copy the packet into a stack buffer with bpf_xdp_load_bytes before reading any field
ctx->data and ctx->data_end must be read with bpf_probe_read because they are kernel pointers
You must bounds-check the access against data_end before dereferencing: prove `data + sizeof(*eth) <= data_end`, or the verifier assumes the read could run past the packet
questions.explanation: The verifier cannot assume the packet is long enough to hold the header you're about to read. It tracks data and data_end as a range and requires you to prove, with an explicit comparison, that the bytes you dereference fall inside that range. Adding `if ((void *)(eth + 1) > data_end) return XDP_DROP;` before touching eth->h_proto satisfies it: now every path that dereferences eth has first established the bytes exist. This is the single most common XDP verifier error. It isn't about Clang version, you don't need to copy the packet to the stack for a simple header read, and ctx->data/data_end are special direct-packet-access pointers, not kernel pointers you'd read with bpf_probe_read.

questions.quizTitle: eBPF for Network Observability and Security Quiz
questions.title: Line-rate program, fraction of the throughput
questions.situation: You benchmarked the same XDP program on a NIC with native support and got line-rate drops. On this host it's slow and softirq CPU is high, even though the attach succeeded with no error. The driver on this box is older.
questions.code:
$ sudo bpftool net
xdp:
eth0(2) generic id 57
        ^^^^^^^
# compare to the fast host:
xdp:
eth0(2) driver id 57
        ^^^^^^
questions.question: You attached an XDP drop program expecting near line-rate, but throughput is a fraction of that and CPU is high. bpftool shows the program attached. What likely happened at attach time?
options: It loaded in generic (SKB) mode because the driver lacks native XDP, so the program runs after the sk_buff is built, losing most of XDP's advantage
The program JIT-compilation was disabled, so it's running interpreted; enable the JIT to fix it
Generic mode means the program is offloaded to the NIC and the CPU number is misreported
The map got too large and spilled to swap, slowing every packet
questions.explanation: XDP has three attach modes. Native (driver) mode runs in the driver before the sk_buff exists, which is where the big win comes from. Offload mode runs on a capable SmartNIC. Generic (SKB) mode is the kernel's fallback when the driver has no native XDP support: it runs the program after the stack has already allocated the sk_buff, so you pay almost all the per-packet cost XDP is meant to skip. The attach succeeds, which is why it's easy to miss, but `bpftool net` showing 'generic' instead of 'driver' is the tell. The fix is a NIC/driver with native XDP support (or to force native mode and confirm the driver supports it). It's not a JIT toggle, generic is not offload, and maps don't swap.

questions.quizTitle: eBPF for Network Observability and Security Quiz
questions.title: Streaming events without losing them
questions.situation: You ship per-event records (exec, connect, file open) from the kernel to a userspace agent. You're using a perf event array (one ring per CPU). During spikes some CPUs overflow and drop records, and stitching a global ordering from per-CPU streams is awkward and memory-hungry.
questions.question: Your security program emits an event per process exec to userspace through a perf buffer. Under bursts you see lost events and your userspace consumer struggles to order them across CPUs. What's the better primitive on modern kernels?
options: Keep the perf buffer but raise each CPU's buffer to the largest size allowed, which removes drops entirely
Switch event delivery to a map the userspace agent polls on a timer instead of a streaming buffer
Use the BPF ring buffer (BPF_MAP_TYPE_RINGBUF): one shared MPSC buffer that preserves submission order across CPUs and uses memory more efficiently than per-CPU perf buffers
Write events into a per-CPU hash map and reconstruct ordering from timestamps in userspace
questions.explanation: The perf event array is per-CPU: you size a ring for every CPU, a busy CPU can overflow and drop while others sit idle, and because records leave on separate per-CPU streams there's no global ordering. The BPF ring buffer (kernel 5.8+) is a single buffer shared across CPUs with multi-producer support. It preserves the order in which events were submitted, wastes far less memory than over-provisioning N per-CPU rings, and supports a reserve/commit API that avoids an extra copy. That's why it's the recommended primitive for streaming variable-size events to userspace today. Just growing per-CPU buffers delays drops without fixing the per-CPU imbalance or the ordering problem, polling adds latency, and rebuilding order from timestamps is fragile.

questions.quizTitle: How Does It Work So Fast? - System Design Speed Tricks
questions.title: Instant Credit Card Validation
questions.situation: You are building a checkout page for an online store. Users keep getting frustrated because they submit their card number, wait 3 seconds for the payment API to respond, and then learn they mistyped a digit. Your product manager asks you to catch obvious typos instantly, right in the browser, before the form is submitted. A colleague mentions that credit card numbers have a built-in checksum.
questions.code:
# The Luhn Algorithm (Mod 10 check):
# Card number: 4539 1488 0343 6467
#
# Step 1: Starting from the rightmost digit, double every second digit:
#   4  5  3  9  1  4  8  8  0  3  4  3  6  4  6  7
#   8  5  6  9  2  4  16 8  0  3  8  3  12 4  12 7
#
# Step 2: If doubling produces a number > 9, subtract 9:
#   8  5  6  9  2  4  7  8  0  3  8  3  3  4  3  7
#
# Step 3: Sum all digits:
#   8+5+6+9+2+4+7+8+0+3+8+3+3+4+3+7 = 80
#
# Step 4: If total mod 10 == 0, the number is valid
#   80 % 10 == 0 -> Valid!
questions.question: You need to understand how e-commerce checkout forms can validate a credit card number before sending anything to the payment processor.
options: The Luhn algorithm, which uses a checksum built into the card number to detect single-digit typos without any network call
A local database of valid card number prefixes that the browser checks against to verify the issuing bank
A lightweight HEAD request to the payment processor that validates the number faster than a full charge request
A regex pattern that matches the format rules for Visa, Mastercard, and Amex card numbers
questions.explanation: The Luhn algorithm is a checksum formula that catches the vast majority of accidental typos in credit card numbers. It works entirely client-side with no network call. The last digit of every card number is a check digit calculated so that the Luhn formula produces a total divisible by 10. If you mistype a single digit, the checksum fails instantly. It catches about 95% of random single-digit errors and all single transposition errors. Regex can check format (length, prefix) but cannot verify the checksum. A network call defeats the purpose of instant validation. Bank prefix databases exist (BIN tables) but they verify the issuer, not whether the full number is correctly typed.

questions.quizTitle: How Does It Work So Fast? - System Design Speed Tricks
questions.title: Username Availability at Scale
questions.situation: You work on the signup flow for a social platform with 400 million registered usernames. As users type a desired username, you want to show a green check or red X in real time. Querying the database on every keystroke would generate tens of thousands of queries per second during peak registration hours. The team needs a data structure that can answer 'is this username taken?' in constant time and fits entirely in memory.
questions.code:
# Bloom Filter for username lookup:
# Size: ~500 MB for 400M usernames at 1% false positive rate
#
# Insert 'alice_dev':
#   hash1('alice_dev') -> bit 14209
#   hash2('alice_dev') -> bit 87432
#   hash3('alice_dev') -> bit 203847
#   Set bits 14209, 87432, 203847 to 1
#
# Check 'bob_codes':
#   hash1('bob_codes') -> bit 55123  (is it 1? yes)
#   hash2('bob_codes') -> bit 87432  (is it 1? yes)
#   hash3('bob_codes') -> bit 99201  (is it 1? no)
#   -> At least one bit is 0 -> DEFINITELY NOT in the set
#
# Key property:
#   'Possibly taken' -> confirm with DB query
#   'Definitely available' -> no DB query needed
questions.question: You need to check if a username is already taken across hundreds of millions of accounts without hitting the database for every keystroke.
options: A bloom filter - a probabilistic data structure that can definitively say 'not taken' but may have false positives for 'taken'
A hash table of all usernames loaded into memory, using consistent hashing to distribute across multiple app servers
A Redis sorted set with all usernames, using binary search to check availability in O(log n) time
A pre-computed trie of all username prefixes that returns availability predictions as the user types
questions.explanation: A bloom filter is the go-to data structure for this problem. It uses a bit array and multiple hash functions to test set membership. The critical property: if any hash position is 0, the item is definitely not in the set (username is available, no DB query needed). If all positions are 1, the item might be in the set (possible false positive), so you fall back to a DB query. For 400 million usernames with a 1% false positive rate, the bloom filter needs roughly 500 MB of RAM, which is very manageable. A full hash table of 400M usernames would need tens of gigabytes. Redis sorted sets still require a network round-trip per check. A trie would use even more memory than a hash table for this many entries.

questions.quizTitle: How Does It Work So Fast? - System Design Speed Tricks
questions.title: Autocomplete Search Suggestions
questions.situation: You are building an autocomplete feature for a search bar on a documentation site with 50,000 page titles. When the user types 'kub', the dropdown should instantly show 'Kubernetes', 'Kubernetes Pods', 'Kubelet Configuration', etc. The suggestions must appear within 10ms. A naive approach of scanning all 50,000 titles with a string prefix match takes too long when the prefix is short (like 'k'), returning thousands of candidates.
questions.code:
# Trie structure for autocomplete:
#
#           (root)
#          /     \
#        k        d
#        |         \
#        u          n
#        |           \
#        b            s
#       / \
#      e    l
#      |    |
#   rnetes  et  <- 'kubelet'
#      |
# 'kubernetes'
#
# Lookup 'kub':
#   1. Walk: root -> k -> u -> b  (3 steps)
#   2. Collect all leaf nodes below 'b'
#   3. Return ranked results
#   Time: O(prefix_length + results)
questions.question: You need to understand which data structure powers the instant dropdown suggestions that appear as you type in a search bar.
options: A trie (prefix tree) that organizes strings by shared prefixes, allowing you to find all matches by walking the tree to the prefix node
An inverted index that maps every possible substring to a list of matching documents
A hash map with every possible prefix as a key and pre-computed result lists as values
A B-tree index on the titles column, using a SQL LIKE query with a prefix wildcard
questions.explanation: A trie (also called a prefix tree) is the classic data structure for autocomplete. Each node represents a character, and paths from root to leaf spell out complete strings. To find all completions for 'kub', you walk the tree in 3 steps to reach the 'b' node, then collect all descendants. The time complexity is O(prefix_length + number_of_results), which is independent of the total dataset size. An inverted index of all substrings would use enormous memory (every substring of every title). Pre-computing all prefix results in a hash map works but uses a lot of memory and is hard to update. SQL LIKE queries with short prefixes are slow because they scan too many rows, even with a B-tree index.

questions.quizTitle: How Does It Work So Fast? - System Design Speed Tricks
questions.title: URL Shortener Redirect Speed
questions.situation: Your company runs a link shortener handling 50,000 redirects per second. Each short URL (like sho.rt/a3Bf9x) must resolve to the original long URL as fast as possible. The database has 8 billion URL mappings. Reading from the database takes 5-15ms, but most redirects go to a small set of popular links (the top 1% of links account for 80% of traffic). You need to bring the p99 redirect latency under 5ms.
questions.code:
# Base62 encoding for short URL generation:
# Characters: [0-9a-zA-Z] = 62 chars
# 6 chars = 62^6 = 56.8 billion combinations
#
# ID: 1234567890
# Base62: 1234567890 -> '1LY7VK'
#
# Redirect flow:
#   GET /a3Bf9x
#   1. Check in-memory cache (LRU, ~10M entries)
#      -> HIT: return 301 redirect (~0.5ms)
#      -> MISS: continue
#   2. Check Redis cache
#      -> HIT: return 301, promote to memory cache (~2ms)
#      -> MISS: continue
#   3. Query database
#      -> Return 301, populate both caches (~10ms)
#
# Cache hit rate: ~99.2% (memory + Redis combined)
questions.question: You need to design a URL shortener that redirects users in under 5ms, even with billions of stored URLs.
options: Use a hash table with consistent hashing to distribute all 8 billion URLs across application servers, keeping everything in memory
Use Base62 encoding to generate short codes from sequential IDs, combined with a multi-layer cache (in-memory LRU + Redis) in front of the database
Store all mappings in a distributed key-value store like DynamoDB with global tables for sub-5ms reads from any region
Pre-compute redirects as static files served by a CDN, regenerating the files hourly
questions.explanation: The standard URL shortener design uses Base62 encoding to convert a numeric ID into a compact alphanumeric string (6 characters give you 56.8 billion possible URLs). The speed comes from multi-layer caching. An in-memory LRU cache on each app server handles the hottest links in sub-millisecond time. Redis serves as a shared second-layer cache for warm links. The database is only hit for cold links that nobody has accessed recently. With the 80/20 distribution described, the combined cache hit rate exceeds 99%, meaning fewer than 1% of requests ever touch the database. Keeping all 8 billion URLs in memory would require terabytes of RAM. DynamoDB global tables add complexity and still have higher latency than local memory. Static CDN files cannot work for billions of dynamic URLs that are created continuously.

questions.quizTitle: How Does It Work So Fast? - System Design Speed Tricks
questions.title: Real-Time Typing Indicators
questions.situation: You are building a team chat application. When someone starts typing in a channel, other members should see a 'typing...' indicator within 200ms. The app currently uses REST API polling every 2 seconds to check for new messages, but a 2-second delay on typing indicators feels sluggish. The team needs a protocol that pushes typing events to connected clients instantly without polling.
questions.code:
# WebSocket typing indicator flow:
#
# 1. Client A opens WebSocket connection (persistent TCP):
#    ws://chat.example.com/ws?channel=engineering
#
# 2. Client A starts typing:
#    Client A -> Server: {"type": "typing", "user": "alice"}
#
# 3. Server broadcasts to channel subscribers:
#    Server -> Client B: {"type": "typing", "user": "alice"}
#    Server -> Client C: {"type": "typing", "user": "alice"}
#
# 4. Client A stops typing (3-second timeout):
#    Server -> Client B: {"type": "stop_typing", "user": "alice"}
#
# Latency: ~50ms (no HTTP overhead, no polling delay)
# Connection: persistent, full-duplex
questions.question: You need to understand how messaging apps show 'User is typing...' with near-zero latency.
options: Server-Sent Events (SSE) with a dedicated endpoint that streams typing events to each client as they occur
WebSocket connections that maintain a persistent full-duplex channel, allowing the server to push typing events to subscribers instantly
HTTP long polling where the client holds an open request and the server responds only when a typing event occurs
gRPC bidirectional streaming over HTTP/2, using protocol buffers for efficient typing event serialization
questions.explanation: WebSockets are the standard choice for typing indicators in chat apps. They provide a persistent, full-duplex TCP connection between client and server. Once established, either side can send messages at any time with minimal overhead (just a 2-byte frame header vs. hundreds of bytes for HTTP headers). When Alice types, her client sends a small JSON frame to the server, which broadcasts it to all channel members over their existing WebSocket connections. The total latency is typically under 50ms. SSE is one-directional (server to client only), so the typing event from the client would still need a separate HTTP request. Long polling has higher latency because each event requires a new HTTP response/request cycle. gRPC streaming works but is uncommon in browser-based chat apps due to limited browser support for gRPC.

questions.quizTitle: How Does It Work So Fast? - System Design Speed Tricks
questions.title: CDN Edge Server Selection
questions.situation: Your company serves static assets (images, CSS, JS) through a CDN with 300 edge locations worldwide. A user in Tokyo requests an image. Without any special routing, the DNS for your CDN domain resolves to a single IP address pointing to your origin server in Virginia, adding 200ms of round-trip latency. You need every user to automatically reach the closest edge server. The networking team mentions anycast as the solution.
questions.code:
# Anycast routing for CDN:
#
# Traditional unicast: 1 IP = 1 server
#   cdn.example.com -> 203.0.113.50 (Virginia)
#   User in Tokyo -> 200ms RTT to Virginia
#
# Anycast: 1 IP = 300 servers
#   cdn.example.com -> 198.51.100.1 (same IP, all 300 PoPs)
#   BGP routing sends packets to the nearest PoP
#
#   User in Tokyo -> Tokyo PoP (5ms RTT)
#   User in London -> London PoP (3ms RTT)
#   User in Sao Paulo -> Sao Paulo PoP (8ms RTT)
#
# How it works:
#   1. All 300 edge servers announce the SAME IP prefix via BGP
#   2. Internet routers pick the shortest AS path
#   3. User traffic naturally flows to the closest PoP
#   4. If a PoP goes down, BGP withdraws the route
#      -> traffic shifts to next-closest PoP automatically
questions.question: You need to understand how a CDN routes a user's request to the nearest edge server without a centralized routing service.
options: GeoDNS resolves the CDN domain to different IP addresses based on the client's geographic location derived from their DNS resolver IP
Anycast routing where all edge servers announce the same IP address via BGP, and internet routing protocols deliver packets to the topologically nearest server
A centralized load balancer that inspects the client's source IP, determines their region, and proxies the request to the nearest edge server
HTTP redirect chains where the origin server responds with a 302 redirect to the nearest edge URL based on the client's IP geolocation
questions.explanation: Anycast is the primary routing mechanism used by major CDNs (Cloudflare, AWS CloudFront, Fastly). Every edge server in the network advertises the same IP address prefix via BGP. When a user sends a packet to that IP, the internet's BGP routing tables direct it to the topologically closest server, which is typically also the geographically closest. This happens at the network layer with zero application involvement. If an edge server fails, it stops announcing the BGP route, and traffic automatically shifts to the next closest location within seconds. GeoDNS is a complementary technique but is less precise because it relies on the DNS resolver's location, not the client's. A centralized load balancer would be a single point of failure and add latency. HTTP redirects add an extra round trip before the user gets their content.

questions.quizTitle: How Does It Work So Fast? - System Design Speed Tricks
questions.title: Edge Cache Hit Optimization
questions.situation: Your news website serves 2 million unique images. After enabling a CDN, you expected a big performance boost, but your cache hit rate is only 35%. Investigation reveals that each edge PoP has limited storage and your images have low individual popularity - most images are viewed only a few times before being evicted from the edge cache. The CDN provider suggests a tiered caching architecture to improve hit rates without increasing edge storage.
questions.code:
# Two-tier CDN caching:
#
# Without tiered caching:
#   User -> Edge PoP (MISS) -> Origin (slow)
#   Each of 300 PoPs maintains its own cache
#   Same image fetched from origin 300 times
#
# With tiered caching (shield / mid-tier):
#   User -> Edge PoP (MISS) -> Regional Shield (HIT) -> done
#   User -> Edge PoP (MISS) -> Regional Shield (MISS) -> Origin
#
#   300 edge PoPs -> 8 regional shields -> 1 origin
#   Image fetched from origin at most 8 times (once per region)
#
# Cache-Control header strategy:
#   Images:     Cache-Control: public, max-age=86400
#   HTML:       Cache-Control: public, max-age=60, s-maxage=300
#   API:        Cache-Control: private, no-store
#              (s-maxage = CDN cache time, separate from browser)
questions.question: You need to maximize the cache hit rate at CDN edge servers for a media-heavy website.
options: Increase the TTL on all assets to 30 days so images stay cached longer at each edge PoP
Use origin shield (tiered caching) to add a regional mid-tier cache between edge PoPs and the origin, reducing origin fetches and improving aggregate hit rates
Pre-warm all 2 million images to every edge PoP using a background job that requests each URL from each location
Switch to a pull-through cache architecture where edge servers proxy directly to the origin with no caching, relying on HTTP keep-alive for speed
questions.explanation: Origin shield (also called tiered caching or mid-tier caching) adds a caching layer between the edge PoPs and your origin server. Instead of 300 edge PoPs each independently fetching images from the origin, requests from a region funnel through a single regional shield node. That shield has a much larger effective cache because it aggregates traffic from dozens of edge PoPs. If an image is popular in Asia, the Tokyo shield caches it once and serves all Asian edge PoPs. This collapses cache misses dramatically. Increasing TTL helps but does not solve the problem of low per-PoP popularity - the images are evicted due to limited storage, not expired TTLs. Pre-warming 2 million images to 300 PoPs means 600 million requests, which is impractical and wasteful. Disabling caching entirely defeats the purpose of a CDN.

questions.quizTitle: How Does It Work So Fast? - System Design Speed Tricks
questions.title: DNS Resolution Speed
questions.situation: A junior engineer on your team is confused about DNS performance. She points out that resolving example.com requires contacting the root nameserver, then the .com TLD server, then the authoritative nameserver - at least three network round trips. Yet when she runs dig example.com, the response comes back in 0.3ms. She asks you to explain where the caching happens and why DNS feels instant for most requests.
questions.code:
# DNS caching layers (from fastest to slowest):
#
# Layer 1: Browser cache
#   Chrome caches DNS for up to 60 seconds
#   Lookup time: ~0ms (in-process memory)
#
# Layer 2: OS resolver cache
#   Linux: systemd-resolved, nscd
#   macOS: mDNSResponder
#   Windows: DNS Client service
#   Lookup time: ~0.1ms (local IPC)
#
# Layer 3: Router / home gateway cache
#   Most home routers run a caching DNS forwarder
#   Lookup time: ~1ms (LAN hop)
#
# Layer 4: ISP recursive resolver
#   Or public resolver: 8.8.8.8, 1.1.1.1
#   Caches responses for thousands of users
#   Lookup time: ~5-20ms (network hop)
#
# Layer 5: Full recursive resolution
#   Root -> TLD -> Authoritative
#   Only happens on cold cache across all layers
#   Lookup time: ~50-200ms (3+ network hops)
#
# Typical TTL: 300s (5 min) to 86400s (24 hours)
# Cache hit rate at ISP resolver: ~90%+
questions.question: You need to understand why most DNS lookups resolve in under 1ms despite the hierarchical nature of the DNS system.
options: DNS is fast because modern resolvers use UDP instead of TCP, and UDP packets are processed faster by network hardware
Multiple caching layers - browser, OS, router, and ISP resolver - mean that full recursive lookups rarely happen, and most queries are answered from a nearby cache
DNS uses anycast so the root and TLD nameservers are always located within a few milliseconds of any user
Modern DNS resolvers prefetch records before they expire, so there is never a cache miss during normal browsing
questions.explanation: DNS performance comes from aggressive caching at every layer of the resolution path. The browser caches recent lookups for 60 seconds or more. The OS maintains its own resolver cache. Home routers typically cache DNS responses for all devices on the network. The ISP's recursive resolver caches results shared across thousands of subscribers, giving it a very high hit rate. By the time a query reaches the ISP resolver, the chance of needing a full recursive lookup (root -> TLD -> authoritative) is small. When it does happen, it takes 50-200ms, but the result is cached for the duration of the TTL (often 5 minutes to 24 hours). UDP helps with speed, but the primary reason DNS feels instant is caching, not protocol choice. Anycast is used by root servers but does not eliminate the multi-hop resolution process. Prefetching exists in some resolvers but is not the main reason for fast lookups.

questions.quizTitle: How Does It Work So Fast? - System Design Speed Tricks
questions.title: Load Balancer Health Check Design
questions.situation: Your application runs behind an Nginx load balancer with 10 backend servers. Last night, one backend's database connection pool was exhausted, causing it to return 500 errors. The load balancer kept sending traffic to it for 5 minutes because health checks were only pinging the / endpoint, which returned 200 even though the app could not process real requests. You need to design health checks that detect this kind of failure.
questions.code:
# Shallow health check (what you have now):
GET /healthz -> 200 OK  # just checks if the process is alive

# Deep health check (what you need):
GET /health/ready -> checks:
  - Database connection: SELECT 1
  - Redis connection: PING
  - Disk space: > 500MB free
  - Memory: < 90% used
  Response: 200 if ALL pass, 503 if ANY fail

# Nginx upstream health check config:
upstream backend {
    server 10.0.1.1:8080;
    server 10.0.1.2:8080;
    # ...
}

# Check every 5 seconds, mark unhealthy after 3 failures,
# mark healthy again after 2 successes
# interval=5s fails=3 passes=2
questions.question: You need to configure health checks that remove unhealthy backends quickly without causing false positives.
options: Use TCP-level health checks that verify the port is open, since they have lower overhead than HTTP checks
Implement a deep health check endpoint that verifies database, cache, and resource availability - not just process liveness - and configure the load balancer to check it with a failure threshold
Monitor error rates from real user traffic and remove backends that exceed a 5% error threshold
Run a separate monitoring agent on each backend that kills the process if dependencies are unreachable, relying on process restarts
questions.explanation: A deep health check (also called a readiness check) verifies that the application can actually serve requests, not just that the process is running. It tests critical dependencies like the database connection pool, cache connectivity, and system resources. The load balancer sends this check at a regular interval (e.g., every 5 seconds) and removes a backend after a configurable number of consecutive failures (e.g., 3 failures = 15 seconds to detect). The passes threshold prevents flapping when a backend recovers. TCP checks only confirm the port is open, which would have missed the database pool exhaustion scenario. Real-traffic error monitoring works but reacts slower because you need enough requests to calculate a reliable error rate. Killing the process is heavy-handed and causes connection drops for in-flight requests.

questions.quizTitle: How Does It Work So Fast? - System Design Speed Tricks
questions.title: Bloom Filter Tuning Trade-offs
questions.situation: Your team deployed the bloom filter for username checks, but the false positive rate is 8%, meaning 8% of available usernames are incorrectly flagged as 'possibly taken,' triggering unnecessary database queries. The product team complains that users see brief loading spinners too often when typing available names. You need to reduce the false positive rate to under 1% while keeping the bloom filter in memory on a server with 4 GB of RAM available for this purpose.
questions.code:
# Bloom filter math:
#
# n = number of items (400 million usernames)
# m = number of bits in the filter
# k = number of hash functions
# p = false positive probability
#
# Formula: m = -(n * ln(p)) / (ln(2))^2
#
# Current config (p = 8%, too high):
#   m = -(400M * ln(0.08)) / (ln(2))^2
#   m = ~1.2 billion bits = ~150 MB
#   k = (m/n) * ln(2) = ~3 hash functions
#
# Target config (p = 1%):
#   m = -(400M * ln(0.01)) / (ln(2))^2
#   m = ~3.83 billion bits = ~478 MB
#   k = (m/n) * ln(2) = ~7 hash functions
#
# Target config (p = 0.1%):
#   m = -(400M * ln(0.001)) / (ln(2))^2
#   m = ~5.75 billion bits = ~718 MB
#   k = ~10 hash functions
questions.question: You need to configure a bloom filter's parameters to balance memory usage against false positive rates for a production system.
options: Double the number of hash functions from 3 to 6 while keeping the bit array the same size, since more hashes reduce false positives
Increase the bit array from 1.2 billion to 3.83 billion bits (~478 MB) and use 7 hash functions to achieve a 1% false positive rate
Replace the bloom filter with a cuckoo filter, which eliminates false positives entirely while using the same amount of memory
Partition the bloom filter by first character of the username so each partition has fewer items and a lower false positive rate
questions.explanation: The false positive rate of a bloom filter depends on both the bit array size (m) and the number of hash functions (k), relative to the number of items (n). Simply adding more hash functions without increasing the bit array actually makes things worse - more bits get set to 1, increasing collisions. The correct approach is to increase the bit array size. For 400 million items at a 1% false positive rate, you need approximately 3.83 billion bits (478 MB), well within the 4 GB budget. The optimal number of hash functions is k = (m/n) * ln(2), which works out to about 7. Cuckoo filters do support deletion (which bloom filters do not) and can be more space-efficient, but they do not eliminate false positives. Partitioning by first character does not change the overall false positive rate because the formula depends on the ratio m/n, not the absolute values.

questions.quizTitle: How Does It Work So Fast? - System Design Speed Tricks
questions.title: Scaling WebSocket Presence Across Servers
questions.situation: Your chat app has grown to 500,000 concurrent WebSocket connections. A single server can handle about 50,000 connections, so you now run 12 WebSocket servers behind a load balancer. The problem: when Alice is connected to Server 3 and starts typing, only users on Server 3 see the typing indicator. Users on Servers 1, 2, and 4-12 see nothing because the broadcast is local to Server 3. You need cross-server event delivery.
questions.code:
# Problem: local broadcast only reaches one server
#
# Server 3 (Alice's connection):
#   Alice types -> broadcast to Server 3 clients -> OK
#
# Server 7 (Bob's connection):
#   Bob is in the same channel but sees nothing
#
# Solution: pub/sub backbone
#
# Redis Pub/Sub:
#   Server 3: Alice types
#   Server 3: PUBLISH channel:engineering:typing '{"user":"alice"}'
#   Server 7: SUBSCRIBE channel:engineering:typing
#   Server 7: receives event -> broadcasts to local clients
#
# All 12 servers subscribe to channels they have members in
# Redis handles fan-out between servers
# Each server handles fan-out to its own clients
questions.question: You need to design a system where typing indicators work correctly when channel members are connected to different WebSocket servers.
options: Use sticky sessions to ensure all members of a channel are routed to the same WebSocket server
Store typing state in a shared database and have each server poll every 200ms for changes
Use a pub/sub system like Redis Pub/Sub as a message backbone where all servers subscribe to channel events and broadcast locally
Use WebSocket server-to-server direct connections where each server maintains TCP connections to all other servers
questions.explanation: Redis Pub/Sub (or similar systems like NATS or Kafka) is the standard solution for cross-server WebSocket event delivery. Each WebSocket server subscribes to Redis channels corresponding to the chat channels it has active members in. When Alice types on Server 3, that server publishes the event to Redis, which fans it out to all subscribing servers. Each server then broadcasts locally to its connected clients. This decouples servers cleanly. Sticky sessions by channel do not work because a single user might be in dozens of channels, and channels have members scattered across servers. Database polling at 200ms intervals introduces unacceptable latency and database load. Direct server-to-server mesh connections create O(n^2) connections and become unmanageable as you scale beyond a handful of servers.

questions.quizTitle: How Does It Work So Fast? - System Design Speed Tricks
questions.title: Load Balancer Algorithm for Mixed Workloads
questions.situation: Your API gateway load-balances across 6 backend servers. Most requests (image metadata lookups) complete in 5ms, but about 10% of requests (image processing jobs) take 2-3 seconds. With round-robin balancing, you notice that some servers accumulate slow requests and their response times spike while other servers sit idle. During peak traffic last Tuesday, one server had 15 in-flight image processing requests while another had zero, causing timeout errors for users routed to the overloaded server.
questions.code:
# Round-robin problem with mixed workloads:
#
# Time 0: All servers at 0 active requests
# Server 1: gets 3 slow (image processing) requests
# Server 2: gets 3 fast (metadata) requests
# Server 3: gets 2 slow + 1 fast request
#
# After 100ms:
# Server 1: 3 active (all still processing)
# Server 2: 0 active (all completed)
# Server 3: 2 active (slow ones still running)
#
# Round-robin sends next request to Server 1 (worst choice!)
#
# Least-connections approach:
# Server 1: 3 active -> skip
# Server 2: 0 active -> PICK THIS ONE
# Server 3: 2 active -> skip
#
# Nginx config:
# upstream api_backend {
#     least_conn;
#     server 10.0.1.1:8080;
#     server 10.0.1.2:8080;
#     server 10.0.1.3:8080;
# }
questions.question: You need to select the right load balancing algorithm for a service with highly variable request processing times.
options: Weighted round-robin with higher weights assigned to servers with more CPU cores
Random selection, which statistically distributes load evenly across all servers
Least-connections algorithm, which routes each new request to the server with the fewest active in-flight requests
IP hash, which ensures the same client always reaches the same server for connection affinity
questions.explanation: Least-connections is the right algorithm when request durations vary significantly. It tracks the number of active (in-flight) requests per backend server and routes new requests to the server currently handling the fewest. This naturally avoids piling up slow requests on one server. When Server 1 has 3 active slow requests, new traffic goes to Server 2 (which has 0 active). This self-balances regardless of whether requests take 5ms or 3 seconds. Round-robin (even weighted) ignores current server load and can overload servers that happen to receive a batch of slow requests. Random selection has the same problem. IP hash provides session affinity but does nothing for load distribution across mixed workloads. Some advanced load balancers also support 'least latency' or 'peak EWMA' algorithms that consider response time in addition to connection count.

questions.quizTitle: How Does It Work So Fast? - System Design Speed Tricks
questions.title: DNS TTL Strategy for Zero-Downtime Migration
questions.situation: Your team is migrating the production API from an on-premise data center (IP 10.20.30.40) to AWS (IP 54.200.100.50). The current DNS record for api.example.com has a TTL of 86400 seconds (24 hours). If you update the DNS record right when the migration happens, some clients will still resolve the old IP for up to 24 hours because their resolvers cached the previous answer. The old servers will be decommissioned 2 hours after migration. You need a plan to minimize the window where clients hit a dead IP.
questions.code:
# DNS migration timeline:
#
# Current state:
#   api.example.com  A  10.20.30.40  TTL=86400 (24h)
#
# Phase 1: Lower TTL (48 hours before migration)
#   api.example.com  A  10.20.30.40  TTL=60 (1 min)
#   Wait 24h+ for old cached records to expire
#
# Phase 2: Update the record (migration day)
#   api.example.com  A  54.200.100.50  TTL=60
#   All resolvers pick up new IP within ~60 seconds
#
# Phase 3: Raise TTL back (after confirming success)
#   api.example.com  A  54.200.100.50  TTL=3600 (1h)
#
# $ dig +short api.example.com
# 54.200.100.50
questions.question: You need to plan a DNS change for a server migration without causing downtime due to stale cached records.
options: Update the DNS record and the old server simultaneously, relying on clients to retry failed connections to the new IP automatically
Lower the DNS TTL to 60 seconds at least 24 hours before the migration, then update the A record on migration day so all caches refresh within a minute
Add the new IP as a second A record so clients can reach either server, then remove the old record after migration
Use a CNAME record pointing to a load balancer hostname so you only need to update the load balancer target, not the DNS
questions.explanation: The standard approach for DNS migrations is the TTL step-down pattern. You lower the TTL well in advance (at least as long as the current TTL, so all existing cached entries expire under the old TTL). By the time you change the IP, all resolvers are caching with the short TTL and will pick up the new address within 60 seconds. After confirming the migration is successful, you raise the TTL back to a reasonable value to reduce DNS query volume. Simply updating the record without lowering TTL first means some clients cache the old IP for up to 24 hours. Adding dual A records causes split traffic, which is unpredictable and hard to monitor. A CNAME to a load balancer is a good long-term architecture, but it does not solve the immediate problem because the CNAME itself has a TTL that must be managed the same way.

questions.title: Database Connection Pool Exhausted
questions.situation: It's 2 PM on Black Friday, traffic is 10x normal, and your application is throwing database connection errors. Customers are abandoning carts and revenue is dropping fast.
questions.code:
ERROR logs:
[ERROR] HikariPool-1 - Connection is not available, request timed out after 30000ms
[ERROR] Could not obtain connection from pool within 30 seconds
[ERROR] Database connection pool exhausted

Monitoring shows:
- CPU: 25% (normal)
- Memory: 60% (normal) 
- Active DB connections: 100/100 (maxed out)
- Response time: 15+ seconds
questions.question: Your e-commerce site is down during Black Friday sales. Users can't check out.
options: Restart the database server immediately
Scale up the database instance to a larger size
