Increase connection pool size, add read replicas, and implement connection timeout tuning
Enable database query caching and hope it helps
questions.explanation: Connection pool exhaustion during traffic spikes requires immediate pool tuning and load distribution. Increasing pool size provides immediate relief, read replicas distribute load, and proper timeouts prevent connection leaks.

questions.title: Application Memory Leak
questions.situation: Every 6 hours, your API servers run out of memory and restart. This started after yesterday's deployment. Memory usage grows from 500MB to 8GB over time.
questions.code:
Symptoms:
- Memory usage: 500MB → 2GB → 4GB → 8GB → OOM kill
- Heap dump shows growing object references
- Restart cycle: Every 6 hours
- Started after: v2.3.1 deployment yesterday

Monitoring data:
- Request rate: Normal (1000 req/min)
- CPU: Normal (30%)
- Memory: Growing continuously
- GC frequency: Increasing
questions.question: Your Node.js API server memory usage keeps growing until it crashes.
options: Rollback to previous version, analyze heap dumps, and identify the memory leak in recent code changes
Add more memory to the servers
Restart servers every 4 hours with a cron job
Scale horizontally by adding more server instances
questions.explanation: Memory leaks require root cause analysis. Rollback provides immediate relief for users, heap dump analysis identifies the leak source, and reviewing recent changes helps pinpoint the problematic code.

questions.title: Load Balancer Health Check Failures
questions.situation: Servers are being removed from the load balancer pool one by one. The remaining servers are getting overloaded and also failing health checks, creating a death spiral.
questions.code:
Load Balancer Status:
- Server 1: UNHEALTHY (removed from pool)
- Server 2: UNHEALTHY (removed from pool)  
- Server 3: WARNING (high CPU due to increased load)
- Server 4: WARNING (high CPU due to increased load)

Health Check: GET /health
- Timeout: 5 seconds
- Expected: HTTP 200
- Current response time: 8-12 seconds
questions.question: Your load balancer is marking healthy servers as unhealthy, causing cascading failures.
options: Disable health checks temporarily until servers recover
Manually add servers back to the pool via load balancer admin
Increase health check timeout, investigate why /health endpoint is slow, and scale up remaining servers
Deploy new servers and replace the failing ones
questions.explanation: Health check failures during load spikes often indicate timeout issues rather than actual server problems. Increasing timeout prevents false negatives, investigating the health endpoint addresses root cause, and scaling provides immediate relief.

questions.title: DNS Resolution Failure
questions.situation: You updated DNS records 2 hours ago to point to new servers. About 30% of users report the site is unreachable, while others see it fine. Support tickets are flooding in.
questions.code:
DNS Change Made:
myapp.com A record: 1.2.3.4 → 5.6.7.8 (TTL: 300 seconds)

User Reports:
- "Site not loading" (30% of users)
- "Works fine for me" (70% of users)
- Geographic pattern: Issues mostly in Asia/Europe

Dig results:
$ dig myapp.com @8.8.8.8
;; ANSWER SECTION:
myapp.com. 300 IN A 5.6.7.8

$ dig myapp.com @1.1.1.1  
;; ANSWER SECTION:
myapp.com. 300 IN A 1.2.3.4
questions.question: After a DNS change, some users can't reach your site while others can.
options: Wait for DNS propagation to complete (up to 48 hours)
Revert DNS changes immediately and investigate the new servers
Clear DNS cache on all ISPs globally
Keep both old and new servers running, ensure new servers are healthy, and wait for TTL expiration
questions.explanation: During DNS transitions, keep old infrastructure running until propagation completes. Verify new servers are actually working correctly, and let TTL naturally expire rather than forcing changes that could make things worse.

questions.title: SSL Certificate Expired at Midnight
questions.situation: It's 6 AM and you're getting reports that users see 'Your connection is not secure' warnings. The SSL certificate expired at midnight, but your monitoring didn't alert you.
questions.code:
Browser Error:
"Your connection is not secure"
"NET::ERR_CERT_DATE_INVALID"

Certificate Info:
- Domain: api.myapp.com
- Expired: Today at 00:00:00 UTC
- Issuer: Let's Encrypt
- Valid from: 3 months ago

Current Status:
- Website: Inaccessible (security warnings)
- API: Failing (SSL handshake errors)
- Mobile app: Can't connect to backend
questions.question: Your SSL certificate expired overnight and users are getting security warnings.
options: Disable SSL temporarily and use HTTP until new certificate is ready
Renew SSL certificate immediately, update server configuration, and implement certificate monitoring
Ask users to ignore the security warning and continue
Switch to a different domain name that has a valid certificate
questions.explanation: SSL certificate renewal is critical for security and user trust. Renew immediately using automated tools like certbot, update server configs, and implement monitoring to prevent future expirations.

questions.title: Production Server Running Out of Disk Space
questions.situation: Log files have grown to fill the disk, new deployments are failing, and the database can't write transaction logs. You need to free space immediately without losing important data.
questions.code:
Disk Usage:
$ df -h
Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/sda1        50G   49G  500M  98% /

Largest directories:
$ du -sh /* | sort -hr | head -5
25G    /var/log
15G    /opt/app/uploads
5G     /tmp
2G     /var/cache
1G     /home

Critical Errors:
- "No space left on device" in application logs
- Database: "Cannot write to transaction log"
- Deployment: "Failed to extract package"
questions.question: Your main application server is at 98% disk usage and applications are starting to fail.
options: Delete everything in /tmp and /var/cache immediately
Add more disk space to the server
Restart the server to clear temporary files
Compress and archive old logs, clean temporary files, move uploads to external storage, and set up log rotation
questions.explanation: Systematic cleanup preserves important data while freeing space. Compress/archive logs for potential debugging, clean safe temporary files, move uploads to scalable storage, and implement rotation to prevent recurrence.

questions.title: Kubernetes Pods in CrashLoopBackOff
questions.situation: You deployed a new version 30 minutes ago. Pods start, run for 10 seconds, then crash. Kubernetes keeps restarting them but they never become ready.
questions.code:
kubectl get pods:
NAME                    READY   STATUS             RESTARTS   AGE
api-deployment-abc123   0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   8          30m
api-deployment-def456   0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   8          30m
api-deployment-ghi789   0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   8          30m

kubectl logs api-deployment-abc123:
Starting application...
Connecting to database...
Fatal error: Environment variable DB_PASSWORD not found
Exiting with code 1
questions.question: After a deployment, all your application pods are crashing and restarting continuously.
options: Rollback deployment, verify ConfigMap/Secret configuration, and redeploy with correct environment variables
Increase pod memory and CPU limits
Scale the deployment to more replicas
Restart the Kubernetes cluster
questions.explanation: CrashLoopBackOff usually indicates configuration issues. Rollback provides immediate service restoration, then investigate missing environment variables, ConfigMaps, or Secrets before attempting redeploy.

questions.title: Network Partition Between Services
questions.situation: The frontend can't reach the user service, the user service can't reach the database, but everything appears to be running. Network timeouts are occurring between different subnets.
questions.code:
Service Status:
✅ Frontend pods: Running
✅ User service pods: Running  
✅ Database: Running
✅ Load balancers: Healthy

Errors:
- Frontend → User Service: "Connection timeout after 30s"
- User Service → Database: "Connection refused"
- Ping between subnets: 100% packet loss

Infrastructure:
- Frontend: Subnet A (10.0.1.0/24)
- User Service: Subnet B (10.0.2.0/24)
- Database: Subnet C (10.0.3.0/24)
questions.question: Your microservices can't communicate with each other due to network issues.
options: Restart all the services to reset network connections
Check security groups, NACLs, route tables, and firewall rules between subnets
Increase network timeouts in application configuration
Deploy all services to the same subnet
questions.explanation: Network partitions are usually caused by infrastructure changes to security groups, NACLs, route tables, or firewalls. Systematic checking of network policies between subnets will identify the blocking rule.

questions.title: Cascading Service Failures
questions.situation: The payment service went down, but now your entire platform is experiencing failures. Services that don't even use payments are timing out and becoming unresponsive.
questions.code:
Failure Timeline:
14:30 - Payment service: High error rate
14:32 - Order service: Timeouts calling payments
14:35 - User service: High CPU (retry storms)
14:37 - Frontend: 500 errors
14:40 - Database: Connection pool exhausted
14:42 - Load balancer: All backends unhealthy

Current State:
- Payment service: DOWN
- Order service: Degraded (retry loops)
- User service: Overloaded 
- Database: Unresponsive
- Frontend: Completely down
questions.question: One service failure is triggering a domino effect across your entire system.
options: Implement circuit breakers, isolate the payment service, enable graceful degradation, and restore services in dependency order
Restart all services simultaneously to reset the system state
Fix the payment service first, then wait for other services to recover
Scale up all services to handle the increased load
questions.explanation: Cascading failures require immediate isolation of the root cause and systematic recovery. Circuit breakers prevent retry storms, graceful degradation maintains partial functionality, and dependency-order recovery prevents re-triggering the cascade.

questions.title: Database Corruption During Peak Hours
questions.situation: It's peak shopping hours and the database is throwing corruption errors. Some user orders are being lost, payment data is inconsistent, and you need to maintain data integrity while keeping the service running.
questions.code:
Database Errors:
[ERROR] Table 'orders' is marked as crashed and should be repaired
[ERROR] Incorrect key file for table 'users'; try to repair it
[ERROR] Got error 127 from storage engine

Impact:
- Lost orders: ~50 in the last hour
- Payment mismatches: $15,000 in pending transactions
- User complaints: Cannot access order history
- Business impact: $2,000/minute revenue loss

System Status:
- Primary DB: Partial corruption
- Read replicas: 15 minutes behind
- Application: Degraded performance
questions.question: Your primary database is reporting data corruption errors during the busiest time of day.
options: Take the database offline immediately and run full repair
Continue running and fix corruption during maintenance window
Failover to read replica, promote it to primary, run repair on original primary in background
Restore from last night's backup and lose recent data
questions.explanation: Data corruption during peak hours requires immediate failover to preserve business continuity. Promoting a read replica minimizes data loss, allows continued operations, and provides time to properly repair the corrupted primary database offline.

questions.quizTitle: Building an Internal Developer Platform Quiz
questions.title: IDP Core Purpose
questions.situation: Your engineering organization has grown to 150 developers. Teams spend significant time filing tickets to the platform team for infrastructure provisioning, environment setup, and deployment configuration. Leadership asks you to propose a solution.
questions.code:
# Current workflow:
# 1. Developer opens Jira ticket for new service
# 2. Platform team provisions infrastructure (2-3 days)
# 3. Developer opens ticket for CI/CD pipeline (1-2 days)
# 4. Developer opens ticket for monitoring setup (1 day)
# Total lead time: 4-6 days per new service
questions.question: What is the primary goal of building an internal developer platform (IDP)?
options: Reduce developer cognitive load by providing self-service capabilities with golden paths and sensible defaults
Replace all infrastructure engineers with automation scripts
Force all developers to learn Kubernetes and Terraform so they can manage infrastructure themselves
Centralize all deployment decisions with a dedicated release management team
questions.explanation: An IDP reduces cognitive load by abstracting infrastructure complexity behind self-service interfaces. Developers get golden paths (pre-configured, opinionated workflows) with sensible defaults while retaining the ability to customize when needed. The goal is not to eliminate platform engineers or force developers to learn infrastructure tools, but to create a productive middle ground where developers can self-serve common tasks.

questions.quizTitle: Building an Internal Developer Platform Quiz
questions.title: Platform Abstraction Layer
questions.situation: Your platform currently supports AWS EKS for compute. However, some teams have expressed interest in serverless workloads, and the company may expand to multi-cloud in the future. You need to define how developers interact with the platform.
questions.code:
# Option A: Direct Kubernetes manifests
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: my-service
spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: my-service:v1.2
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: "256Mi"
            cpu: "250m"

# Option B: Platform-level spec
apiVersion: platform.internal/v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: my-service
spec:
  tier: standard
  scaling:
    min: 2
    max: 10
  ports:
    - 8080
questions.question: You are designing the abstraction layer for your IDP. Which approach best balances developer experience with flexibility?
options: Expose raw Kubernetes YAML directly so developers have full control over every field
Build a higher-level abstraction (like Option B) that maps to underlying infrastructure, hiding implementation details while allowing overrides
Use a GUI-only approach with no configuration files so developers never see YAML
Let each team define their own custom resource definitions and deployment formats
questions.explanation: A higher-level abstraction like a platform-specific API (Option B) gives developers a simpler interface focused on what they care about (scaling, ports, tier) while the platform team manages the translation to underlying infrastructure. This approach enables portability across cloud providers, enforces organizational standards, and allows power users to add overrides when needed. Raw Kubernetes YAML creates tight coupling, GUI-only lacks version control, and per-team formats create fragmentation.

questions.quizTitle: Building an Internal Developer Platform Quiz
questions.title: Service Catalog Design
questions.situation: Your organization runs 200+ microservices. New developers struggle to understand service ownership, dependencies, and how to get started. On-call engineers waste time figuring out who owns what during incidents.
questions.code:
# Backstage catalog-info.yaml
apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1
kind: Component
metadata:
  name: payment-service
  description: Handles payment processing
  annotations:
    github.com/project-slug: org/payment-service
    pagerduty.com/service-id: P12345
  tags:
    - payments
    - java
spec:
  type: service
  lifecycle: production
  owner: team-payments
  dependsOn:
    - component:user-service
    - resource:payments-db
  providesApis:
    - payment-api
questions.question: What should a well-designed service catalog in an IDP provide?
options: A comprehensive registry showing ownership, dependencies, APIs, documentation links, health status, and scaffolding templates for new services
A searchable list of service names and their Git repository URLs only
A spreadsheet maintained manually by engineering managers with service information
An auto-generated list from Kubernetes namespace labels with no additional metadata
questions.explanation: A well-designed service catalog (like Backstage) serves as the single source of truth for all software assets. It should include ownership information for incident response, dependency graphs for impact analysis, API documentation for integration, health status for operational awareness, and scaffolding templates for consistent service creation. A simple list of repos or a manual spreadsheet quickly becomes outdated and lacks the rich context teams need.

questions.quizTitle: Building an Internal Developer Platform Quiz
questions.title: Golden Path Templates
questions.situation: Your organization wants to standardize how new services are created. Currently, developers copy an existing service repo and manually modify it, often missing security configurations, monitoring setup, or CI/CD pipeline definitions.
questions.code:
# Backstage software template
apiVersion: scaffolder.backstage.io/v1beta3
kind: Template
metadata:
  name: microservice-template
  title: Standard Microservice
spec:
  owner: platform-team
  type: service
  parameters:
    - title: Service Info
      properties:
        name:
          type: string
        owner:
          type: string
          ui:field: OwnerPicker
        tier:
          type: string
          enum: [standard, critical]
  steps:
    - id: create-repo
      action: publish:github
    - id: register-catalog
      action: catalog:register
    - id: create-infra
      action: custom:provision-infra
questions.question: How should you implement golden path templates for new service creation in your IDP?
options: Provide a wiki page with step-by-step instructions for manually setting up each component
Use scaffolding templates that generate complete, production-ready projects with CI/CD, monitoring, security configs, and catalog registration in a single workflow
Clone a reference repository and let developers figure out what to change
Require developers to submit a form and have the platform team manually create everything
questions.explanation: Scaffolding templates (like Backstage Software Templates) automate the entire service creation workflow. They collect required inputs through a form, then execute steps to create the repository with proper structure, configure CI/CD pipelines, provision infrastructure, set up monitoring, and register the service in the catalog. This ensures consistency, enforces security standards, and eliminates the error-prone manual copying approach. Wiki instructions and manual processes do not scale with team growth.

questions.quizTitle: Building an Internal Developer Platform Quiz
questions.title: Platform as a Product
questions.situation: Your platform team has built several tools, but adoption is low. Developers complain the tools are hard to use, poorly documented, and do not solve their actual pain points. The team has been building features based on what they think developers need.
questions.code:
# Platform adoption metrics dashboard
┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Platform Adoption (Q1 2026)          │
├──────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Self-service deploys:     23%  ↓     │
│ Template usage:           15%  ↓     │
│ Portal daily active users: 8%  ↓     │
│ Support tickets:         +40%  ↑     │
│ Developer satisfaction:   3.2/10     │
└──────────────────────────────────────┘
questions.question: What does it mean to treat your internal developer platform 'as a product'?
options: Mandate platform usage through company policy and block alternative tools
Build as many features as possible to cover every possible use case
Apply product management practices: research user needs, prioritize based on impact, iterate with feedback, measure adoption, and market the platform internally
Hire more platform engineers to build tools faster
questions.explanation: Treating a platform as a product means applying the same practices used for external products: conducting user research (developer interviews, surveys), defining a product roadmap based on actual pain points, iterating quickly with feedback loops, measuring success through adoption metrics and developer satisfaction, and actively marketing features to internal users. Mandating usage creates resentment and workarounds. Building everything at once leads to bloated, unfocused tools. The platform should be so good that developers choose to use it.

questions.quizTitle: Building an Internal Developer Platform Quiz
questions.title: Backstage Plugin Architecture
questions.situation: You need to display deployment status from ArgoCD, on-call schedules from PagerDuty, and cost data from your cloud billing system in the Backstage portal. These integrations do not exist as community plugins.
questions.question: Your team chose Backstage as the foundation for your IDP portal. How should you extend it to integrate with your internal systems?
options: Fork the Backstage repository and modify core source code directly for each integration
Embed each external tool as an iframe within Backstage pages
Skip the portal and have developers bookmark each tool's native UI separately
Build custom plugins using Backstage's plugin architecture, keeping integrations modular and independently deployable
questions.explanation: Backstage's plugin architecture is designed for exactly this use case. Custom plugins are modular, independently testable, and upgradeable without modifying Backstage core. Each plugin registers its own APIs, components, and routes. Forking the core makes upgrades extremely difficult. Iframes provide a poor user experience with no data integration. Separate bookmarks defeat the purpose of a unified developer portal. The plugin model lets you maintain clean separation while presenting a unified experience.

questions.quizTitle: Building an Internal Developer Platform Quiz
questions.title: Self-Service Infrastructure
questions.situation: Developers need PostgreSQL databases, Redis caches, and RabbitMQ instances for their services. Currently, they submit tickets to the infrastructure team, leading to 3-5 day wait times. You want to enable self-service while maintaining security and cost controls.
questions.code:
# Developer-facing resource request
apiVersion: platform.internal/v1
kind: Database
metadata:
  name: orders-db
  owner: team-orders
spec:
  engine: postgresql
  version: "15"
  tier: standard        # Maps to predefined instance size
  backup: daily
  environment: production
---
# Platform translates to Terraform/Crossplane behind the scenes
# Enforces: encryption at rest, VPC placement, backup policy,
# credential rotation, cost limits per tier
questions.question: How should your IDP enable developers to provision infrastructure resources like databases and message queues?
options: Give developers direct access to the AWS console to create resources manually
Pre-provision a fixed pool of resources and assign them on request
Require developers to write their own Terraform modules for each resource
Provide a self-service API with predefined tiers that enforces guardrails (encryption, networking, cost limits) while abstracting infrastructure complexity
questions.explanation: A self-service API with predefined tiers gives developers speed and autonomy while the platform team maintains control through guardrails. The platform translates simple, high-level specs into properly configured infrastructure (using tools like Crossplane or Terraform). Guardrails enforce encryption, network policies, backup schedules, and cost limits automatically. Direct AWS access risks misconfiguration and cost overruns. Pre-provisioned pools waste resources. Requiring Terraform expertise from every developer increases cognitive load.

questions.quizTitle: Building an Internal Developer Platform Quiz
questions.title: Measuring Platform Success
questions.situation: Six months after launching your IDP, leadership asks for evidence of its impact. You need to present metrics that demonstrate real value, not vanity metrics.
questions.code:
# Potential metrics to track
metrics:
  dora:
    deployment_frequency: "3x/week -> 5x/day"
    lead_time_for_changes: "2 weeks -> 2 days"
    change_failure_rate: "15% -> 5%"
    mttr: "4 hours -> 45 minutes"
  platform_specific:
    time_to_first_deploy: "6 days -> 30 minutes"
    self_service_ratio: "23% -> 85%"
    developer_satisfaction: "3.2 -> 8.1"
    support_tickets: "200/month -> 45/month"
questions.question: Which metrics best indicate that your IDP is successfully improving developer productivity?
options: DORA metrics (deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate, MTTR) combined with platform-specific metrics (time to first deploy, self-service ratio, developer satisfaction)
Number of platform features shipped and lines of platform code written
Total cost savings from reducing infrastructure team headcount
Number of developers who logged into the portal at least once
questions.explanation: Effective IDP measurement combines DORA metrics (which measure software delivery performance) with platform-specific metrics. DORA metrics show improvement in deployment frequency, lead time, failure rate, and recovery time. Platform metrics like time-to-first-deploy, self-service ratio, and developer satisfaction directly measure the platform's impact. Features shipped and login counts are vanity metrics. Cost savings from headcount reduction misrepresents the platform's purpose, which is to amplify productivity, not eliminate roles.

questions.quizTitle: Building an Internal Developer Platform Quiz
questions.title: Platform Team Topology
questions.situation: Your organization is adopting the Team Topologies model. The platform team currently operates as a gatekeeper -- every infrastructure change must go through them. Stream-aligned teams feel blocked and frustrated by the bottleneck.
questions.code:
# Current interaction model (anti-pattern)
Stream Team -> Ticket -> Platform Team -> Review -> Approve -> Provision
Avg cycle time: 5 days

# Target interaction model
Stream Team -> Self-Service Platform API -> Automated Provisioning
Platform Team: Maintains APIs, guardrails, golden paths
Avg cycle time: 15 minutes
questions.question: According to Team Topologies, how should a platform team interact with stream-aligned (feature) teams?
options: The platform team should review and approve every change to ensure quality
Platform teams should be embedded within each stream-aligned team
The platform team should provide self-service APIs and golden paths, acting as an enabling team that reduces cognitive load for stream-aligned teams
Stream-aligned teams should build and maintain their own platform tools independently
questions.explanation: In Team Topologies, a platform team provides self-service capabilities that reduce the cognitive load of stream-aligned teams. The platform acts as a 'thinnest viable platform' with golden paths and self-service APIs. The platform team is not a gatekeeper (which creates bottlenecks) or embedded (which does not scale). Stream-aligned teams consuming platform capabilities through well-designed interfaces is the key to scaling engineering organizations. The platform team focuses on making the platform so easy to use that it becomes the path of least resistance.

questions.quizTitle: Building an Internal Developer Platform Quiz
questions.title: Infrastructure Orchestration Choice
questions.situation: Your platform team is designing the self-service infrastructure layer. Developers will request resources through the platform API. You need to decide the underlying orchestration engine. Your organization already runs Kubernetes clusters and wants infrastructure provisioning to integrate with GitOps workflows.
questions.code:
# Crossplane Composite Resource Definition
apiVersion: apiextensions.crossplane.io/v1
kind: CompositeResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: xdatabases.platform.example.com
spec:
  group: platform.example.com
  names:
    kind: XDatabase
  versions:
    - name: v1alpha1
      schema:
        openAPIV3Schema:
          properties:
            spec:
              properties:
                engine:
                  type: string
                  enum: [postgresql, mysql]
                tier:
                  type: string
                  enum: [small, medium, large]
questions.question: When building the infrastructure provisioning layer of your IDP, when would you choose Crossplane over Terraform?
options: Always choose Terraform because it has more provider support and is the industry standard

Choose Crossplane when you want Kubernetes-native infrastructure management with continuous reconciliation, GitOps integration, and the ability to expose custom APIs (XRDs) to developers as platform abstractions
Always choose Crossplane because it is newer and therefore better
Use both simultaneously for every resource to ensure redundancy
questions.explanation: Crossplane excels in IDP scenarios where you want Kubernetes-native infrastructure management. Its key advantages for IDPs include: Composite Resource Definitions (XRDs) that let you create custom platform APIs, continuous reconciliation that detects and corrects drift automatically, native GitOps integration with tools like ArgoCD, and a familiar Kubernetes API model. Terraform is still excellent for one-time provisioning and has broader provider coverage, but Crossplane's reconciliation loop and custom API capabilities make it particularly well-suited for self-service platforms. Neither tool is universally better; the choice depends on your requirements.

questions.quizTitle: Building an Internal Developer Platform Quiz
questions.title: Portal Architecture Decisions
questions.situation: You are architecting the developer portal (UI) for your IDP. It needs to aggregate data from 15+ backend systems (Git, CI/CD, monitoring, cloud providers, on-call, documentation). Some systems have slow APIs, and the portal must remain responsive.
questions.code:
# Architecture options

# Option A: Direct API calls from frontend
Browser -> GitHub API
Browser -> ArgoCD API
Browser -> PagerDuty API
# Problem: CORS, auth sprawl, slow rendering

# Option B: Backend-for-frontend (BFF)
Browser -> Portal BFF -> GitHub API
                      -> ArgoCD API
                      -> PagerDuty API
# Benefits: caching, auth consolidation, data aggregation

# Option C: Portal BFF + async data pipeline
Browser -> Portal BFF -> Cache Layer
Collector Service -> GitHub/ArgoCD/PagerDuty -> Cache Layer
questions.question: What is the recommended architecture for a developer portal that serves as the UI layer of your IDP?
options: Direct browser-to-API calls for each backend system to minimize latency
A monolithic backend that stores copies of all data from every system
A backend-for-frontend pattern with caching and optional async data collection for slow sources, providing a unified API to the portal frontend
Server-side rendering that calls all 15 APIs on each page load
questions.explanation: A backend-for-frontend (BFF) pattern is ideal for developer portals aggregating many data sources. The BFF provides a unified API that handles authentication to backend systems, caches responses from slow APIs, aggregates data from multiple sources into single responses, and shields the frontend from backend API changes. For particularly slow data sources, an async collector can pre-fetch and cache data. Direct browser calls create CORS and auth issues. A monolithic data store becomes a synchronization nightmare. Server-side rendering blocking on 15 APIs creates unacceptable page load times.

questions.quizTitle: Building an Internal Developer Platform Quiz
questions.title: Environment Management
questions.situation: Your organization runs 50 microservices. Developers need isolated environments to test changes that span multiple services. Currently, there is a single shared staging environment that is constantly broken due to conflicting deployments from different teams.
questions.code:
# Namespace-per-PR approach
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: preview-pr-1234
  labels:
    managed-by: platform
    ttl: 24h
    owner: team-checkout
---
# Platform creates:
# - Isolated namespace with service dependencies
# - Routes: pr-1234.preview.internal.dev
# - Seeded test data
# - Auto-cleanup after TTL or PR merge
questions.question: How should your IDP handle developer environment provisioning for testing and staging?
options: Maintain multiple full copies of the entire production environment for each team
Use a single shared staging environment with a deployment calendar to avoid conflicts
Provide on-demand, ephemeral preview environments (namespace-per-PR or similar) with automatic provisioning of dependencies, routing, and TTL-based cleanup
Have developers test everything locally using Docker Compose with mocked dependencies
questions.explanation: Ephemeral preview environments (namespace-per-PR) give each developer or PR an isolated environment with real service dependencies. The platform handles provisioning, DNS routing, test data seeding, and automatic cleanup. This eliminates staging conflicts, enables parallel development, and provides production-like testing. Full environment copies are prohibitively expensive. Shared staging with calendars slows teams down. Local Docker Compose testing with mocks misses integration issues. Ephemeral environments balance cost, isolation, and fidelity.

questions.quizTitle: Building an Internal Developer Platform Quiz
questions.title: IDP Adoption Strategy
questions.situation: Your platform team has built the first version of the IDP with self-service deployments and a service catalog. However, most teams continue using their existing manual processes. You have 6 months to reach 80% adoption.
questions.code:
# Adoption tracking
teams_total: 25
teams_onboarded: 4

# Adoption blockers (from developer survey)
blockers:
  - "Didn't know the platform existed"        # 35%
  - "Existing process works fine for us"       # 25%
  - "Missing features we need"                 # 20%
  - "Too complex to migrate"                   # 15%
  - "Don't trust it for production"            # 5%
questions.question: What is the most effective strategy for driving adoption of a newly built IDP across your organization?
options: Mandate adoption through an executive decree with a hard deadline for all teams
Wait for organic adoption as developers naturally discover the platform
Rebuild the platform from scratch to address all reported missing features before promoting it further
Start with enthusiastic early adopters, collect feedback, iterate on pain points, provide migration support, showcase success stories, and gradually expand while addressing blockers systematically
questions.explanation: Successful IDP adoption follows a product-led growth strategy. Start with early adopters who are eager to try new tools, use their feedback to improve the platform, then leverage their success stories to attract the next wave of teams. Address blockers systematically: improve documentation for awareness, provide migration guides and hands-on support, and prioritize the most impactful missing features. Mandating adoption creates resistance and surfaces problems at scale. Waiting passively wastes momentum. Rebuilding delays value delivery indefinitely.

questions.title: VirtualService vs DestinationRule
questions.situation: You're onboarding two new backend engineers to your service mesh. They keep mixing up which resource handles what, and you need to give them a clear answer before they start writing configs.
questions.code:
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: reviews
spec:
  hosts:
  - reviews
  http:
  - route:
    - destination:
        host: reviews
        subset: v2
---
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: reviews
spec:
  host: reviews
  subsets:
  - name: v2
    labels:
      version: v2
questions.question: Your team just installed Istio and a junior engineer asks what the difference is between a VirtualService and a DestinationRule.
options: VirtualService and DestinationRule are interchangeable; use whichever your team prefers
VirtualService decides how requests are routed to a service, while DestinationRule defines policies that apply after routing has picked a destination (subsets, load balancing, TLS, circuit breaking)
VirtualService handles ingress traffic only, DestinationRule handles east-west traffic only
DestinationRule creates the service, VirtualService exposes it to the cluster
questions.explanation: VirtualService answers 'which destination should this request go to?' based on matches on hosts, headers, URIs, and weights. DestinationRule answers 'once I picked that destination, how do I talk to it?' It defines subsets (named groupings of pods by label), load balancing algorithm, TLS settings, connection pool limits, and outlier detection. You almost always need both: a VirtualService references a subset, and the DestinationRule is what actually defines that subset.

questions.title: Defining subsets for version routing
questions.situation: Your reviews service has deployments labeled version: v1 and version: v2 running in the same namespace. You want to address them separately in routing rules, but there's no clean way to reference them yet.
questions.code:
# Current Deployments
kubectl get pods -l app=reviews --show-labels
NAME            READY   LABELS
reviews-v1-abc  2/2     app=reviews,version=v1
reviews-v2-xyz  2/2     app=reviews,version=v2

# You want to route like this:
http:
- route:
  - destination:
      host: reviews
      subset: v1
    weight: 90
  - destination:
      host: reviews
      subset: v2
    weight: 10
questions.question: You need to split traffic between two versions of the same service. What's the right way to tell Istio which pods belong to each version?
options: Create two separate Kubernetes Services, one per version, and route to each
Add a VirtualService with match rules on pod names
Define subsets in a DestinationRule that map subset names to pod label selectors
Use Kubernetes NetworkPolicies to tag pods by version
questions.explanation: Subsets are defined in a DestinationRule and map a friendly name (like 'v1' or 'canary') to a set of pod labels. Once defined, VirtualServices can reference them by name. You do NOT need separate Kubernetes Services per version, that's the whole point of subsets. NetworkPolicies have nothing to do with routing, and matching on pod names defeats the purpose of labels.

questions.title: Canary deploy at 5% traffic
questions.situation: Payments is your highest-risk service. Your SRE lead wants a slow ramp: 5% first, bake for an hour, then 25%, then 50%, then 100%. You already have a DestinationRule with v1 and v2 subsets defined. Now write the VirtualService for the 5% step.
questions.code:
# DestinationRule already exists:
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: payments
spec:
  host: payments
  subsets:
  - name: v1
    labels:
      version: v1
  - name: v2
    labels:
      version: v2
questions.question: You're rolling out v2 of the payments service. You want 5% of traffic to go to v2 and 95% to stay on v1. Which config is correct?
options: Two VirtualServices, one routing to v1 and one routing to v2, and let Istio balance them
One VirtualService with two destinations under a single route, each with a weight field (95 and 5) that sums to 100
Scale v2 to 5% of the replica count of v1 and route 100% to 'payments'
Set a header match 'canary: true' and hope 5% of clients send it
questions.explanation: Weighted routing is done inside a single HTTPRoute with multiple destination entries, each carrying a weight. The weights must sum to 100. Two separate VirtualServices for the same host create undefined behavior, Istio does not merge them predictably. Relying on replica counts is a common misconception: traffic is routed by the mesh, not distributed by pod count. And header-based canaries target specific clients, not a random percentage.

questions.title: Route internal testers to v2
questions.situation: Your product team wants dogfooding: employees should see the new checkout flow (v2) but external customers should keep the stable version (v1). The request from the internal portal always carries x-user-type: internal set by the auth proxy.
questions.code:
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: checkout
spec:
  hosts:
  - checkout
  http:
  # ??? which rules go here ???
questions.question: You want internal employees (requests carrying x-user-type: internal) to hit v2 while everyone else stays on v1. How do you express this in a VirtualService?
options: A single route with weight 50/50 and let Istio figure it out
Use a DestinationRule with an outlier that ejects non-internal users
Two HTTP rules: the first with a match on headers x-user-type: internal routing to subset v2, then a fallback rule with no match routing to subset v1
Put both rules inside a single match block, since Istio evaluates them in parallel
questions.explanation: Istio evaluates HTTP rules in order and takes the first match. Put the specific rule (header match on x-user-type: internal going to v2) first, then a default rule with no match going to v1. Ordering matters: if the default rule is first, everyone gets v1 because the generic match eats the request. Weights are for percentages, not for conditional routing. Outlier detection is a health check mechanism, not a routing filter.

questions.title: Adding retries for a flaky dependency
questions.situation: Your recommendations service talks to a catalog service. When catalog rolls out a new version, pods briefly 503 while terminating. You see user-facing errors. You want the sidecar to transparently retry so restarts don't leak to users.
questions.code:
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: catalog
spec:
  hosts:
  - catalog
  http:
  - route:
    - destination:
        host: catalog
    retries:
      # ??? which settings ???
questions.question: A downstream service occasionally returns 503s during pod restarts. You want Istio to retry these failures up to 3 times. Which config does this correctly?
options: attempts: 3, perTryTimeout: 2s, retryOn: 5xx,reset,connect-failure,refused-stream
attempts: 3, retryOn: 4xx (because we want to retry bad requests)
maxRetries: 3 at the DestinationRule connection pool level
timeout: 10s on the route (timeouts automatically retry in Istio)
questions.explanation: The retries block on an HTTPRoute supports attempts, perTryTimeout, and retryOn. You almost always want perTryTimeout: otherwise a slow response eats your entire request timeout in a single try. retryOn should include 5xx plus connection-level failures (reset, connect-failure, refused-stream). Retrying 4xx is usually wrong, those are client errors and retrying won't fix them. maxRetries at the DestinationRule is for circuit breaking concurrency limits, not per-request retries. And timeouts do not automatically retry.

questions.title: Ejecting a sick pod from the pool
questions.situation: Your payments service has 10 replicas. One pod has a stuck database connection and returns 500s for every request. Without outlier detection, Istio's default round-robin keeps sending 10% of traffic to the broken pod. Users are seeing errors.
questions.code:
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: payments
spec:
  host: payments
  trafficPolicy:
    outlierDetection:
      consecutive5xxErrors: 5
      interval: 30s
      baseEjectionTime: 30s
      maxEjectionPercent: 50
questions.question: One pod in your service keeps returning 500s while the others are healthy. You want Istio to stop sending traffic to that pod automatically. Where do you configure this?
options: This won't work because outlier detection is configured on the VirtualService, not DestinationRule
This restarts any pod returning 5xx responses via Kubernetes liveness
This blocks users whose requests got 5 consecutive 5xx responses

This ejects the unhealthy pod from the load balancing pool after 5 consecutive 5xx responses within the 30s interval, keeps it out for 30s, and ensures no more than 50% of endpoints are ejected at once
questions.explanation: Outlier detection lives on DestinationRule under trafficPolicy and works at the endpoint (pod) level, not the pod lifecycle level. Istio does not restart pods, that's the kubelet's job via liveness probes. consecutive5xxErrors is the threshold that triggers ejection, interval is the scan window, baseEjectionTime is how long the pod stays ejected, and maxEjectionPercent caps how much of the pool can be removed at once (so you don't eject everything during a shared outage). The ejected pod is re-added automatically after baseEjectionTime and gets probed again.

questions.title: Protecting a slow backend with connection pools
questions.situation: Your legacy inventory service has a hard connection limit at 100. During spikes, clients open 500+ connections and the service crashes. Scaling the legacy service isn't an option in the next 6 months. You need the mesh to shed load before it reaches the service.
questions.code:
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: inventory
spec:
  host: inventory
  trafficPolicy:
    connectionPool:
      tcp:
        maxConnections: 100
      http:
        http1MaxPendingRequests: 50
        http2MaxRequests: 200
        maxRequestsPerConnection: 10
questions.question: A backend service can only handle 100 concurrent connections before it falls over. How do you protect it with Istio?
options: This is useless; Istio cannot limit connection counts, only retry attempts
These are soft suggestions that Envoy logs but does not enforce
These settings cap concurrent TCP connections, pending HTTP/1.1 requests, in-flight HTTP/2 streams, and requests reused per connection. Excess traffic is rejected with 503 so the backend stays up
These settings only apply to ingress traffic coming from the gateway
questions.explanation: Connection pool settings are part of the circuit breaker family in Istio. They're enforced by each client-side Envoy sidecar, meaning every caller respects the limit from their side. When the pool is full, Envoy rejects new requests with 503 instead of piling on to the backend. http1MaxPendingRequests matters for HTTP/1.1 (no multiplexing), http2MaxRequests for HTTP/2 (many streams per connection). maxRequestsPerConnection forces periodic reconnects, useful when you have sticky load balancers in front of you. This applies to any traffic the sidecar proxies, not just ingress.

questions.title: Retries are making the incident worse
questions.situation: The auth service is having a bad day. It's already overloaded at 2x normal traffic because of a memory leak. Every service that depends on it has attempts: 5 configured. Now auth is seeing 10x the request rate and is completely down. You need to stop the bleeding.
questions.code:
# Current config on many services:
retries:
  attempts: 5
  perTryTimeout: 3s
  retryOn: 5xx,reset,connect-failure,refused-stream

# Metrics during incident:
auth_request_rate_normal:   2000 rps
auth_request_rate_current: 10000 rps (5x amplification)
auth_error_rate: 95%
questions.question: During an outage, your dashboards show request rate to the failing service is 5x normal. Retries are amplifying load. What's the fix?
options: Drop attempts to 1-2, add a retryBudget (or use Envoy's retry budget via EnvoyFilter) so retries cannot exceed a small percent of active requests, and combine with circuit breaking on the client side so a failing dependency is dropped quickly
Increase attempts to 10 so retries eventually succeed
Remove all retries globally since they are always dangerous
Set perTryTimeout to 0 so retries stop when the original request times out
questions.explanation: Retry storms are a classic incident amplifier. The fix is layered: lower attempts (1-2 is usually enough for transient failures), add a retry budget so total retry traffic can't grow without bound, and use circuit breaking (outlier detection + connection pool limits) so a sick dependency is cut off quickly instead of retried into the ground. More attempts makes it worse, not better. Removing all retries is overkill and hurts transient-failure recovery. perTryTimeout: 0 is invalid and wouldn't address amplification anyway. Think of retries as a dangerous tool that trades a bit of extra load for resilience, you must bound that trade.

questions.title: Shadowing production traffic to a new version
questions.situation: v2 of the search service has a new ranking algorithm. You want to send it the same requests v1 gets so you can compare results offline, but you cannot risk v2 bugs reaching users. No response from v2 should ever make it back to the client.
questions.code:
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: search
spec:
  hosts:
  - search
  http:
  - route:
    - destination:
        host: search
        subset: v1
      weight: 100
    mirror:
      host: search
      subset: v2
    mirrorPercentage:
      value: 100.0
questions.question: You want to test v2 with real production requests without affecting users. How do you use Istio to shadow traffic?
options: This sends 100% of traffic to both v1 and v2, and returns whichever responds first
This is invalid; you cannot have route and mirror in the same HTTPRoute
This sends 100% to v1 only, and mirror is just a placeholder for future versions
This routes 100% of traffic to v1 and also forwards a fire-and-forget copy to v2; v2's response is discarded and its errors never reach the client
questions.explanation: Mirroring (also called shadowing) sends a copy of the request to the mirror destination fire-and-forget. The client only ever sees the response from the primary route. v2's response is discarded, and its errors, latency, and side effects do not affect the user. Be careful about side effects though: if v2 writes to a shared database, mirroring can cause duplicate writes. Production mirroring is usually paired with an isolated test environment for the mirror target. mirrorPercentage lets you dial mirror traffic down (useful when v2 is resource-constrained).

questions.title: Injecting failures to test resilience
questions.situation: Your resilience team is running a game day. They want to verify clients handle slow upstreams gracefully. Rather than breaking the actual service, they want Istio to inject controlled failures so behavior is deterministic and easy to turn off.
questions.code:
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: ratings
spec:
  hosts:
  - ratings
  http:
  - fault:
      delay:
        percentage:
          value: 10.0
        fixedDelay: 5s
      abort:
        percentage:
          value: 2.0
        httpStatus: 503
    route:
    - destination:
        host: ratings
        subset: v1
questions.question: You want to inject a 5-second delay into 10% of requests to test your client's timeout handling. What does this config do?
options: Adds a 5s delay to every request and returns 503 for all of them
Fails if both delay and abort are set together in the same fault block
Only takes effect on ingress gateway, not for service-to-service calls

Injects a 5-second delay into 10% of requests and returns a 503 to 2% of requests (independently), before forwarding the rest normally to ratings v1. Delay and abort percentages are evaluated separately
questions.explanation: Fault injection has two independent dials: delay (add latency) and abort (return an error). Percentages are applied independently, so you can stack them, 10% of requests get delayed, and 2% of requests get aborted with a 503. A single request could even hit both (unlucky). This runs on the client-side Envoy, so it works for both ingress and service-to-service traffic. Use it to validate that clients have proper timeouts, that retries fire correctly, and that your dashboards detect degraded dependencies. Turn it off when the game day ends, fault injection left in prod is a footgun.

questions.title: My VirtualService changes don't take effect
questions.situation: You're debugging a canary rollout. You applied a new VirtualService that should send 10% of traffic to v2, but all requests are still hitting v1 based on metrics. kubectl get virtualservice shows your resource. Logs from the ingress gateway show it's not matching your rule.
questions.code:
# Your VirtualService:
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: productpage
  namespace: default
spec:
  hosts:
  - productpage.default.svc.cluster.local
  http:
  - route:
    - destination: { host: productpage, subset: v1 }
      weight: 90
    - destination: { host: productpage, subset: v2 }
      weight: 10

# Check:
kubectl get gateway -A
NAME         NAMESPACE        HOSTS
main-gw      istio-system     ["*.example.com"]

# The VirtualService is missing: spec.gateways
questions.question: You apply a VirtualService but traffic still behaves the old way. istioctl analyze reports no issues. What's the most likely cause?
options: You need to restart istiod for VirtualService changes to take effect

The VirtualService is missing the gateways field, so for ingress traffic it only applies to mesh-internal traffic. Add gateways: [istio-system/main-gw] (or include 'mesh' explicitly) so it binds to the ingress gateway
The subsets weren't declared in a DestinationRule (but istioctl analyze would have caught this)
VirtualServices can only live in the istio-system namespace
questions.explanation: When you omit the gateways field, the VirtualService defaults to the reserved value 'mesh', meaning it only applies to sidecar-to-sidecar traffic inside the mesh. Ingress traffic from an Istio gateway will ignore it. To route external traffic you must explicitly list your gateway: gateways: [istio-system/main-gw, mesh] if you want both ingress and internal. Other common gotchas in this family: hosts must match what the gateway accepts, and the VirtualService namespace matters for cross-namespace gateway references. istiod does not need a restart, config is pushed dynamically. And istioctl analyze catches many issues but not semantic binding mismatches like this one.

questions.title: Tuning outlier detection for bursty traffic
questions.situation: Your checkout service occasionally gets burst traffic (flash sales). During bursts, some pods return a few 5xx responses as they warm up. Your current outlier detection ejects them aggressively, reducing pool size, which spreads more load on remaining pods and creates a feedback loop. On-call is paging at every sale.
questions.code:
# Current (too aggressive):
outlierDetection:
  consecutive5xxErrors: 3
  interval: 10s
  baseEjectionTime: 60s
  maxEjectionPercent: 100

# Observed: during a flash sale, 8 out of 10 pods briefly eject,
# pool shrinks to 2 pods, load explodes on survivors, full outage.
questions.question: Your outlier detection is ejecting healthy pods during brief traffic spikes, causing cascading failures. How do you tune it for bursty workloads?
options: Raise consecutive5xxErrors to 10+, lower baseEjectionTime to 10-15s for faster recovery, cap maxEjectionPercent at 30-50 to always keep most pods in rotation, and consider splitUpstreamConfig or adding warmup so pods ramp in slowly
Disable outlier detection entirely; it always causes cascading failures under load
Lower consecutive5xxErrors to 1 so ejection is instant
Set maxEjectionPercent to 100 to ensure sick pods can always be ejected no matter what
questions.explanation: Outlier detection is useful but has to be tuned for the workload's variance. Under bursty traffic, a too-low consecutive5xxErrors threshold turns transient blips into permanent ejections. The fix is higher tolerance (10+ errors before ejection), shorter ejection (10-15s so pods rejoin fast if they recover), and a hard cap on ejection percentage (never take more than ~30-50% of the pool out of rotation, so the survivors aren't crushed). Disabling entirely removes a useful safety net; setting threshold to 1 makes the feedback loop worse; 100% ejection guarantees outages during correlated failures (bad config push, shared dependency going down).

questions.title: Declarative vs Scripted Pipelines
questions.question: What is the primary difference between Declarative and Scripted Jenkins pipelines?
options: Declarative uses more verbose syntax than Scripted
Scripted pipelines are faster than Declarative pipelines
Declarative pipelines cannot use Groovy code
Declarative provides structured syntax with predefined sections, while Scripted offers full Groovy flexibility
questions.explanation: Declarative pipelines use a more structured, opinionated syntax with predefined sections (pipeline, agent, stages, steps), making them easier to read and maintain. Scripted pipelines use pure Groovy, offering maximum flexibility but requiring more scripting knowledge.

questions.title: Pipeline Agent Definition
questions.question: In a Declarative pipeline, which section defines where the pipeline or stage executes?
options: agent
node
executor
slave
questions.explanation: The 'agent' section specifies where the pipeline or stage executes. You can define agents as 'any', 'none', 'label', 'docker', or 'kubernetes' to control execution environments.

questions.title: Parallel Stage Execution
questions.question: How do you execute multiple stages in parallel in a Declarative pipeline?
options: Use the 'parallel' keyword inside a stage with nested stages
Define stages with the same name
Use 'async' and 'await' keywords
Parallel execution is not supported in Declarative pipelines
questions.explanation: Use the 'parallel' directive inside a stage to run multiple nested stages concurrently. Each nested stage runs in its own thread, significantly reducing overall pipeline execution time.

questions.title: Post-Build Actions
questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'post' section in a Jenkins pipeline?
options: To define pre-build actions
To specify actions that run after stages complete, based on build status
To send HTTP POST requests
To schedule future builds
questions.explanation: The 'post' section defines actions to run after stages complete. It supports conditions like 'always', 'success', 'failure', 'unstable', 'changed', 'fixed', and 'regression' to execute cleanup, notifications, or other post-build tasks.

questions.title: Jenkins Shared Libraries
questions.question: In Jenkins, what is a Shared Library used for?
options: Storing build artifacts
Managing Jenkins plugins
Sharing reusable pipeline code and functions across multiple projects
Configuring agent workspaces
questions.explanation: Shared Libraries allow you to create reusable Groovy code that can be imported and used across multiple pipelines. They're stored in version control and loaded using @Library annotation, promoting DRY principles and consistency.

questions.title: Docker Registry Authentication
questions.question: Which Jenkins credential type should you use for Docker registry authentication?
options: Secret text
SSH Username with private key
Certificate
Username with password
questions.explanation: 'Username with password' is the standard credential type for Docker registry authentication. Jenkins securely stores the credentials and provides them to the pipeline via the credentials() binding.

questions.title: Docker Agent Configuration
questions.question: What does the following agent configuration do?
options: Runs the pipeline stages inside a Node.js 18 Docker container
Installs Docker on the Jenkins agent
Deploys the application to a Docker container
Builds a Docker image named node:18
questions.explanation: The docker agent configuration runs the entire pipeline (or stage) inside a Docker container using the specified image. This ensures a consistent, isolated build environment without requiring the tools to be installed on the Jenkins agent.

questions.title: Credential Access in Pipelines
questions.question: How do you access a Jenkins credential in a pipeline?
options: Reading from a file in the workspace
Using environment variables or withCredentials step
Using System.getenv()
Credentials cannot be accessed in pipelines
questions.explanation: Use the credentials() function in an environment block or the withCredentials step to securely access credentials. Jenkins automatically masks these values in console output and cleans them up after use.

questions.title: Dependency Caching Strategies
questions.question: What is the recommended way to cache dependencies (like npm or Maven) in Jenkins pipelines?
options: Store them in the workspace between builds
Commit them to version control
Use Docker volumes or custom workspace locations with stash/unstash
Download them fresh every build
questions.explanation: Use Docker volumes to persist dependency caches, or use custom workspace locations that persist between builds. For multi-stage pipelines, stash/unstash can save and restore files between stages. Some plugins also provide cache management features.

questions.title: Conditional Stage Execution
questions.question: What does the 'when' directive control in a Declarative pipeline?
options: When to schedule the pipeline
When to trigger downstream jobs
When to clean the workspace
Conditional execution of a stage based on specified criteria
questions.explanation: The 'when' directive allows conditional execution of stages. Common conditions include branch, environment, changelog, expression, and tag. Multiple conditions can be combined with allOf or anyOf.

questions.title: Essential Git Plugin
questions.question: Which Jenkins plugin is essential for Git integration in pipelines?
options: GitHub Plugin
Git Plugin
SCM API Plugin
Pipeline SCM Step Plugin
questions.explanation: The Git Plugin is the core plugin for Git integration, providing the 'checkout scm' step and Git-related functionality. While other plugins add specific features, Git Plugin is the foundation.

questions.title: Pipeline Options Configuration
questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'options' directive in a Jenkins pipeline?
options: To configure pipeline-wide settings like timeouts and build retention
To define command-line options for scripts
To set environment variables
To specify available build parameters
questions.explanation: The 'options' directive configures pipeline-wide settings such as timestamps, timeouts, build discarders, retry logic, and skipDefaultCheckout. These apply to the entire pipeline execution.

questions.title: Error Handling and Retries
questions.question: How do you handle errors and implement retry logic in Jenkins pipelines?
options: Errors cannot be handled in pipelines
Using the error() function only
Using try-catch blocks and the retry step
Setting failFast to false
questions.explanation: Use try-catch-finally blocks for error handling and the retry step for automatic retries. You can also use catchError to catch errors without failing the build, and the error() step to explicitly fail with a message.

questions.title: Git Webhook Triggers
questions.question: What is the recommended way to trigger a Jenkins pipeline from a Git webhook?
options: Use SCM polling every minute
Manually trigger builds
Configure a webhook in the Git repository pointing to Jenkins, and enable 'GitHub hook trigger' or 'Generic Webhook Trigger'
Use cron expressions
questions.explanation: Configure a webhook in your Git repository (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket) to send events to Jenkins. Use the 'GitHub hook trigger for GITScm polling' option or the Generic Webhook Trigger plugin for instant build triggering on code changes.

questions.title: Node vs Agent Differences
questions.question: What is the difference between 'node' and 'agent' in Jenkins pipelines?
options: They are identical and interchangeable
'node' allocates executors, 'agent' does not
'agent' is deprecated
'node' is used in Scripted pipelines, 'agent' in Declarative pipelines
questions.explanation: 'node' is used in Scripted pipelines to allocate an executor and workspace. 'agent' is the Declarative pipeline equivalent, providing similar functionality with more structured syntax and additional options like docker and kubernetes.

questions.title: Performance Optimization Strategies
questions.question: How can you optimize Jenkins pipeline performance for large projects?
options: Use parallel stages, Docker layer caching, stash/unstash for artifacts, and skipDefaultCheckout
Disable all plugins
Run everything sequentially
Increase the number of executors only
questions.explanation: Optimize performance by: running independent stages in parallel, using Docker layer caching, leveraging stash/unstash for artifacts between stages, using skipDefaultCheckout when appropriate, implementing incremental builds, and using agent labels to utilize appropriate resources.

questions.title: Pipeline as Code Best Practices
questions.question: What is the best practice for managing Jenkins pipeline definitions?
options: Store them only in Jenkins UI
Email the Jenkinsfile to team members
Store in a shared network drive
Store Jenkinsfile in version control at the repository root (Pipeline as Code)
questions.explanation: Store the Jenkinsfile in version control (typically at repository root) following the 'Pipeline as Code' principle. This enables versioning, code review, branching, and ensures the pipeline definition travels with the code.

questions.title: File Permissions
questions.situation: You're troubleshooting why a user can't execute a script, and you run 'ls -l' to check file permissions.
questions.code:
$ ls -l deploy.sh
-rwxr-xr-- 1 devops team 1234 Dec 1 10:00 deploy.sh
questions.question: What does the permission 'rwxr-xr--' mean in Linux?
options: Owner can read/write, group can read/execute, others can read/write
Everyone can read/write/execute
Owner can read/write/execute, group can read/execute, others can only read
Only owner can read the file
questions.explanation: rwx (owner) = read, write, execute permissions; r-x (group) = read and execute only; r-- (others) = read only. The owner (devops) has full control, the group (team) can read and run it, and others can only view it.

questions.title: Process Management
questions.situation: Your application server is running slow. You need to identify which process is consuming the most CPU and memory.
questions.question: Which command shows real-time system resource usage and running processes?
options: ls -la
top
ps aux
df -h
questions.explanation: The 'top' command provides a real-time, interactive view of running processes, CPU usage, memory consumption, and system load. 'ps aux' shows a snapshot of processes, 'ls -la' lists files, and 'df -h' shows disk space usage.

questions.title: System Logs
questions.situation: An application crashed overnight. You need to check system logs to find error messages.
questions.question: Where are system logs typically stored in Linux?
options: /usr/logs
/home/logs
/etc/logs
/var/log
questions.explanation: /var/log is the standard directory for system and application logs in Linux. Common files include /var/log/syslog (general system), /var/log/auth.log (authentication), and /var/log/nginx/ (web server logs).

questions.title: Text Search
questions.situation: You need to find all occurrences of 'ERROR' in your application logs from the past week.
questions.code: You want to search for 'ERROR' in /var/log/app.log
questions.question: Which command searches for specific text patterns in files?
options: search ERROR /var/log/app.log
cat ERROR /var/log/app.log
find /var/log/app.log ERROR
grep 'ERROR' /var/log/app.log
questions.explanation: 'grep' (Global Regular Expression Print) searches for patterns in files. The command 'grep ERROR /var/log/app.log' will find all lines containing 'ERROR'. You can add flags like -i (case-insensitive), -n (line numbers), or -r (recursive).

questions.title: Git Staging
questions.situation: You've made changes to multiple files in your project and want to prepare them for commit.
questions.code:
$ git status
Modified: app.js
Modified: config.yaml
Modified: README.md
questions.question: Which command stages all modified files for commit?
options: git commit -a
git stage --all
git add .
git push
questions.explanation: 'git add .' stages all changes in the current directory and subdirectories. This prepares files to be included in the next commit. 'git commit -a' commits tracked files but doesn't stage new files. 'git push' sends commits to remote, and 'git stage --all' is not a valid command.

questions.title: Git Branching
questions.situation: Your team follows Git Flow. You're starting work on a new feature and need to explain why you're creating a separate branch.
questions.question: What's the purpose of creating a feature branch in Git?
options: Branches are only for fixing bugs
Branches isolate development work from the main codebase, allowing parallel development and easy rollback
Branches are required by Git and serve no practical purpose
Branches permanently split the codebase into separate projects
questions.explanation: Feature branches isolate new development from the stable main branch. This allows: 1) Multiple developers to work in parallel without conflicts, 2) Code review before merging to main, 3) Easy rollback if needed, 4) Clean commit history. Once complete, branches are merged back and can be deleted.

questions.title: Git Merge vs Rebase
questions.situation: Your feature branch is behind main. A senior developer asks whether you want to merge or rebase to get the latest changes.
questions.question: What's the main difference between 'git merge' and 'git rebase'?
options: They do exactly the same thing
Merge creates a new commit combining branches, rebase rewrites history by moving commits to a new base
Rebase is faster but merge is safer
Merge deletes the branch, rebase keeps it
questions.explanation: 'git merge' creates a new merge commit that combines the changes from both branches, preserving the full history. 'git rebase' rewrites commit history by applying your commits on top of another branch, creating a linear history. Merge is safer (doesn't rewrite history), rebase creates cleaner history but should not be used on shared branches.

questions.title: Git Remote Operations
questions.situation: You start your workday and need to get the latest code that your teammates pushed yesterday.
questions.code: $ git pull origin main
questions.question: What does 'git pull' do?
options: Sends your local commits to the remote repository
Fetches remote changes and merges them into your current branch
Creates a new branch from remote
Deletes remote branches
questions.explanation: 'git pull' is a combination of 'git fetch' (downloads remote changes) and 'git merge' (merges them into your current branch). It's the most common way to sync your local repository with remote updates. Equivalent to running 'git fetch' followed by 'git merge'.

questions.title: Container Concepts
questions.situation: A junior developer asks why we 'run' an image to create a container. You need to explain the relationship.
questions.question: What's the main difference between a Docker image and a container?
options: Containers are templates, images are running processes
There is no difference, the terms are interchangeable
Images are stored templates, containers are running instances of those images
Images can be modified, containers cannot
questions.explanation: Docker images are read-only templates that contain application code, runtime, libraries, and dependencies. Containers are running instances created from images. Think of images as classes and containers as objects in programming. You can run multiple containers from a single image, each isolated from the others.

questions.title: Docker Commands
questions.situation: You have an nginx image and want to start a web server container from it.
questions.code: You want to run nginx and expose port 80
questions.question: Which command starts a container from an image?
options: docker create nginx
docker execute nginx
docker start nginx
docker run nginx
questions.explanation: 'docker run' creates and starts a new container from an image. Example: 'docker run -d -p 80:80 nginx' runs nginx in detached mode and maps port 80. 'docker start' restarts an existing stopped container, 'docker create' only creates (doesn't start), and 'docker execute' isn't a valid command.

questions.title: Dockerfile Basics
questions.situation: You need to containerize a Node.js application. Your team lead mentions creating a Dockerfile.
questions.question: What is the purpose of a Dockerfile?
options: A Dockerfile is a text document containing instructions to build a Docker image
A Dockerfile runs containers
A Dockerfile stores container logs
A Dockerfile manages Docker networks
questions.explanation: A Dockerfile is a text file with instructions (FROM, RUN, COPY, CMD, etc.) that Docker uses to build an image. It defines the base image, dependencies, files to include, and startup commands. Running 'docker build' with a Dockerfile creates an image that can then be used to run containers.

questions.title: Docker Image Layers
questions.situation: You notice when rebuilding an image that some steps say 'Using cache'. You want to understand how this works.
questions.code:
Step 3/8 : RUN npm install
 ---> Using cache
 ---> a1b2c3d4e5f6
questions.question: Why are Docker images built in layers?
options: Layers have no purpose, they're just how Docker works internally
Layers slow down Docker operations
Layers enable caching and sharing, making builds faster and images smaller
Each layer requires separate storage, making images larger
questions.explanation: Docker's layered architecture allows: 1) Caching - unchanged layers are reused, speeding up builds, 2) Sharing - multiple images can share common layers (e.g., same base OS), 3) Efficiency - only changed layers need to be downloaded/uploaded. Each Dockerfile instruction creates a new layer. Order matters: put frequently changing instructions last.

questions.title: CI/CD Pipeline Basics
questions.situation: You're interviewing for a junior DevOps role and need to explain CI/CD fundamentals.
questions.question: What does CI/CD stand for and what's its purpose?
options: Code Integration / Code Deployment - manual process for releasing software
Container Installation / Container Distribution - Docker deployment system
Cloud Integration / Cloud Development - cloud-only development workflow
Continuous Integration / Continuous Delivery - automates building, testing, and deploying code changes
questions.explanation: CI/CD automates software delivery: Continuous Integration (CI) automatically builds and tests code when developers commit changes, catching bugs early. Continuous Delivery/Deployment (CD) automates releasing to staging and production. Benefits: faster releases, fewer bugs, consistent deployments, reduced manual work. Common tools: Jenkins, GitLab CI, GitHub Actions, CircleCI.

questions.title: Pipeline Stages
questions.situation: Your team is setting up a new pipeline. You need to identify the common stages in order.
questions.question: What are typical stages in a CI/CD pipeline?
options: Build -> Test -> Deploy -> Monitor
Deploy -> Build -> Test -> Monitor
Test -> Deploy -> Build -> Monitor
Monitor -> Test -> Build -> Deploy
questions.explanation: Standard pipeline flow: 1) Build - compile code, install dependencies, 2) Test - run unit, integration, security tests, 3) Deploy - release to staging/production, 4) Monitor - track application health. Each stage must pass before proceeding. Failed tests block deployment, preventing bugs from reaching production.

questions.title: Cloud Service Models
questions.situation: During an interview, you're asked to explain cloud service models with examples.
questions.question: What's the difference between IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS?
options: IaaS provides infrastructure (VMs, storage), PaaS provides platforms (runtime environments), SaaS provides complete applications
They're all the same, just different names
IaaS is cheapest, SaaS is most expensive
Only large companies use IaaS, startups use SaaS
questions.explanation: IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service): Rent VMs, storage, networks - you manage OS and above (AWS EC2, Azure VMs). PaaS (Platform as a Service): Provider manages infrastructure and runtime, you deploy code (Heroku, Google App Engine). SaaS (Software as a Service): Ready-to-use applications (Gmail, Salesforce). More control = more management responsibility.

questions.title: Load Balancing
questions.situation: Your web application runs on multiple servers. You need to explain why you need a load balancer.
questions.question: What is the purpose of a load balancer?
options: Load balancers distribute incoming traffic across multiple servers for high availability and performance
Load balancers store data
Load balancers are only for large enterprises
Load balancers replace the need for multiple servers
questions.explanation: Load balancers distribute traffic across multiple backend servers, providing: 1) High availability - if one server fails, traffic routes to healthy servers, 2) Better performance - requests spread across multiple servers, 3) Scalability - easily add/remove servers, 4) Health checks - automatically detect and avoid unhealthy servers. Examples: AWS ALB/NLB, nginx, HAProxy.

questions.title: Bash Scripting
questions.situation: You're writing your first deployment script and see this line at the top of examples.
questions.code:
#!/bin/bash
echo 'Deploying application...'
questions.question: What does the shebang line '#!/bin/bash' do in a script?
options: It specifies which interpreter should execute the script
It's a comment that has no effect
It makes the script executable
It's required for all text files
questions.explanation: The shebang (#!) tells the system which interpreter to use to execute the script. #!/bin/bash uses the Bash shell, #!/usr/bin/python3 uses Python. Without it, the system uses the default shell. To run the script directly (./script.sh), you also need execute permissions (chmod +x script.sh).

questions.title: Basic Monitoring Metrics
questions.situation: Your team is setting up monitoring for a new service. You need to know which metrics matter most.
questions.question: What are the four golden signals of monitoring?
options: CPU, Memory, Disk, Network
Latency, Traffic, Errors, Saturation
Uptime, Users, Revenue, Bugs
Logs, Metrics, Traces, Events
questions.explanation: The Four Golden Signals (from Google SRE): 1) Latency - how long requests take, 2) Traffic - how many requests per second, 3) Errors - rate of failing requests, 4) Saturation - how 'full' your system is (CPU, memory, disk). These metrics quickly indicate service health and help diagnose issues. Track these first before adding more detailed metrics.

questions.title: What is a Kubernetes Operator?
