questions.situation: You're in a technical interview and the interviewer wants to understand your knowledge of Operators at a conceptual level.
questions.question: The interviewer asks you to explain the fundamental concept of Kubernetes Operators.
options: A Kubernetes Operator is a method of packaging, deploying, and managing applications using custom resources and controllers that extend the Kubernetes API
A Kubernetes Operator is a built-in Kubernetes component that manages cluster nodes
A Kubernetes Operator is a command-line tool for deploying Helm charts
A Kubernetes Operator is a type of pod that runs privileged containers
questions.explanation: A Kubernetes Operator is a pattern that uses Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) and custom controllers to automate application management. It encapsulates operational knowledge (like how to deploy, scale, backup, and upgrade an application) in code.

questions.title: Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs)
questions.situation: The interviewer asks you to describe what Custom Resource Definitions are and how they relate to Operators.
questions.code:
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: databases.example.com
spec:
  group: example.com
  versions:
    - name: v1
      served: true
      storage: true
      schema:
        openAPIV3Schema:
          type: object
          properties:
            spec:
              type: object
              properties:
                size:
                  type: integer
                version:
                  type: string
  scope: Namespaced
  names:
    plural: databases
    singular: database
    kind: Database
    shortNames:
      - db
questions.question: Explain the role of CRDs in the Operator pattern.
options: CRDs are configuration files that store application secrets
CRDs are only used for monitoring and logging purposes
CRDs replace the need for Deployments and StatefulSets
CRDs extend the Kubernetes API by defining new resource types that can be managed like built-in resources (pods, services)
questions.explanation: CRDs extend the Kubernetes API by allowing you to define custom resource types. Once a CRD is created, users can create instances of that custom resource using kubectl, just like built-in resources. The Operator's controller then watches these custom resources and acts on them.

questions.title: The Reconciliation Loop
questions.situation: The interviewer wants to understand the core control loop pattern that drives Operators.
questions.question: Describe how the reconciliation loop works in an Operator.
options: The reconciliation loop runs once when a resource is created and never again
The reconciliation loop continuously compares desired state (spec) with actual state and takes actions to converge them
The reconciliation loop is triggered manually by the cluster administrator
The reconciliation loop only handles delete operations
questions.explanation: The reconciliation loop is the heart of an Operator. It continuously watches for changes to custom resources and compares the desired state (defined in the spec) with the actual state of the system. When differences are detected, it takes actions to bring the actual state in line with the desired state.

questions.title: Operators vs Helm Charts
questions.situation: The interviewer asks you to compare Operators with Helm charts and explain when each is appropriate.
questions.question: When would you choose an Operator over a Helm chart?
options: Operators and Helm are identical; use whichever you prefer
Use Helm only for stateless applications and Operators only for databases
Use Operators when you need ongoing operational automation (scaling, backups, failover); use Helm for simple deploy-and-forget applications
Always use Helm because Operators are deprecated
questions.explanation: Helm is great for templating and one-time deployment of applications. Operators excel when you need ongoing Day-2 operations: automatic scaling, backups, upgrades, failover, and self-healing. For stateful applications like databases that require complex operational knowledge, Operators are typically the better choice.

questions.title: Building an Operator with Operator SDK
questions.situation: Your team needs to build a custom Operator for managing a proprietary database. The interviewer asks about your approach.
questions.code:
# Initialize a new Operator project
operator-sdk init --domain example.com --repo github.com/example/db-operator

# Create an API (CRD and controller)
operator-sdk create api --group cache --version v1 --kind Database --resource --controller

# Generated project structure:
# .
# ├── api/v1/database_types.go    # CRD type definitions
# ├── controllers/
# │   └── database_controller.go  # Reconciliation logic
# ├── config/
# │   ├── crd/                    # CRD manifests
# │   ├── rbac/                   # RBAC permissions
# │   └── manager/                # Operator deployment
# └── main.go
questions.question: How would you start building a new Operator?
options: Use Operator SDK to scaffold the project, generate CRD types, and create controller boilerplate, then implement the reconciliation logic
Write all Kubernetes API interactions from scratch without any framework
Copy an existing Operator and modify the code
Use kubectl plugins to auto-generate Operators
questions.explanation: Operator SDK provides scaffolding commands that generate project structure, CRD type definitions, controller boilerplate, RBAC configurations, and build/deployment manifests. This significantly accelerates development and ensures best practices are followed.

questions.title: Status Subresource
questions.situation: The interviewer asks about separating spec and status in your custom resources.
questions.code:
apiVersion: example.com/v1
kind: Database
metadata:
  name: my-database
spec:
  size: 3
  version: "14.5"
status:
  phase: Running
  replicas: 3
  readyReplicas: 3
  conditions:
    - type: Ready
      status: "True"
      lastTransitionTime: "2024-01-15T10:30:00Z"
questions.question: What is the purpose of the status subresource in a custom resource?
options: Status stores the resource's YAML manifest backup
Status is where the controller reports the actual observed state, separate from the desired state in spec
Status contains user-provided configuration
Status is only used for logging purposes
questions.explanation: The status subresource separates the desired state (spec) from the observed state (status). Users update spec to declare what they want, while the controller updates status to report what actually exists. This separation enables optimistic concurrency and clearer ownership.

questions.title: Finalizers for Cleanup
questions.situation: Your Operator provisions AWS RDS instances. The interviewer asks how you ensure RDS instances are deleted when the custom resource is deleted.
questions.question: How do finalizers help with resource cleanup in Operators?
options: Finalizers automatically restart pods when they crash
Finalizers are used to encrypt sensitive data
Finalizers speed up the deletion process
Finalizers prevent resource deletion until cleanup logic runs, allowing the controller to delete external resources before the Kubernetes object is removed
questions.explanation: Finalizers prevent a resource from being deleted until cleanup is complete. When a resource with finalizers is deleted, Kubernetes sets deletionTimestamp but keeps the resource. The controller detects this, performs cleanup (like deleting external cloud resources), then removes the finalizer to allow final deletion.

questions.title: Owner References and Garbage Collection
questions.situation: Your Database Operator creates Pods, Services, and ConfigMaps. The interviewer asks how to handle cleanup.
questions.question: How do you ensure child resources are automatically deleted when the parent custom resource is deleted?
options: Set owner references on child resources so Kubernetes garbage collection automatically deletes them when the parent is deleted
Manually delete all child resources in the reconciliation loop
Use a CronJob to periodically clean up orphaned resources
Child resources must be deleted before creating the parent resource
questions.explanation: Owner references create a parent-child relationship. When the parent (custom resource) is deleted, Kubernetes garbage collection automatically deletes all resources that have an owner reference pointing to it. This is the recommended pattern for managing dependent resources.

questions.title: Level-Triggered vs Edge-Triggered Reconciliation
questions.situation: The interviewer asks about the design philosophy behind how controllers respond to changes.
questions.question: Explain why Kubernetes controllers use level-triggered reconciliation.
options: Controllers use edge-triggered logic, responding only to change events
Controllers use a hybrid approach that changes based on cluster load
Controllers use level-triggered logic, comparing current state against desired state regardless of what changed
Controllers don't respond to changes; they run on a fixed schedule
questions.explanation: Kubernetes controllers are level-triggered: they reconcile based on the current state vs desired state, not on what specific event occurred. This makes controllers resilient - if events are missed or duplicated, the controller still converges to the correct state by examining the current situation.

questions.title: Operator Capability Levels
questions.situation: The interviewer asks how mature your Operator is and what capabilities it provides.
questions.code:
Operator Capability Levels:

Level 1 - Basic Install
  - Automated application provisioning
  - Basic configuration management

Level 2 - Seamless Upgrades
  - Application version upgrades
  - Patch management

Level 3 - Full Lifecycle
  - Backup and restore
  - Failure recovery

Level 4 - Deep Insights
  - Metrics and alerts
  - Log processing
  - Workload analysis

Level 5 - Auto Pilot
  - Horizontal/vertical scaling
  - Auto-tuning
  - Anomaly detection
questions.question: Describe the Operator maturity model and capability levels.
options: Operator maturity is determined by lines of code
Capability levels range from Basic Install (Level 1) to Auto Pilot (Level 5), each adding more sophisticated automation like upgrades, backups, monitoring, and auto-scaling
All Operators must implement all 5 levels to be production-ready
Capability levels only apply to database Operators
questions.explanation: The Operator Capability Model defines 5 maturity levels: Basic Install, Seamless Upgrades, Full Lifecycle (backup/restore), Deep Insights (monitoring), and Auto Pilot (auto-scaling/tuning). This helps teams understand what capabilities an Operator provides and plan their implementation roadmap.

questions.title: Controller vs Operator: What's the Difference?
questions.situation: You're discussing Kubernetes architecture and the interviewer wants to know if you understand the nuanced difference between Controllers and Operators.
questions.question: Explain the difference between a Kubernetes Controller and an Operator.
options: Controllers and Operators are completely interchangeable terms
Controllers only manage pods, while Operators manage all other resources
An Operator is a controller that manages Custom Resources (CRDs) and encodes domain-specific operational knowledge, while controllers manage built-in Kubernetes resources
Operators are deprecated in favor of controllers
questions.explanation: A Controller is a control loop that watches the state of your cluster and makes changes to move toward the desired state. An Operator is a specific type of controller that uses Custom Resources to manage applications and their components. The key difference is that Operators encode domain-specific knowledge (like how to backup a database) rather than generic Kubernetes operations.

questions.title: Preventing Infinite Reconciliation Loops
questions.situation: The interviewer noticed your Operator keeps triggering reconciliation even when nothing has changed. They ask how to fix this.
questions.question: How do you prevent your Operator from entering an infinite reconciliation loop?
options: Always use Update() instead of Patch() for all changes
Check if the actual state already matches desired state before making any modifications, and use Status subresource for state tracking
Add a random sleep between reconciliation calls
Disable the reconciliation loop after 10 iterations
questions.explanation: Infinite loops occur when every reconciliation triggers another one. To prevent this: (1) Always check if changes are actually needed before updating, (2) Use Status subresource to track state without triggering Spec watches, (3) Use Patch instead of Update to only modify changed fields, (4) Avoid updating metadata like annotations unnecessarily.

questions.title: Admission Webhooks: Mutating and Validating
questions.situation: The interviewer asks how to add validation and default values to your Custom Resources before they're persisted.
questions.question: Explain the role of admission webhooks in Operators.
options: Webhooks are only used for authentication
Validating webhooks modify requests, mutating webhooks reject them
All validation must be done in the reconciliation loop
Mutating webhooks modify requests (add defaults), validating webhooks reject invalid requests - both run before the resource is persisted to etcd
questions.explanation: Admission webhooks intercept API requests before persistence. Mutating webhooks can modify requests (e.g., setting default values). Validating webhooks can accept or reject requests (e.g., enforce business rules). Using webhooks for validation is more efficient than doing it in the reconciliation loop because invalid resources are rejected immediately.

questions.title: Operator Performance Optimization
questions.situation: Your Operator is managing 5000+ custom resources and the interviewer asks how you would optimize its performance.
questions.question: What techniques can you use to optimize Operator performance in large clusters?
options: Remove all caching and query the API server directly for freshest data
Use informer caches, event filtering with predicates, rate limiting, concurrent reconciliation, and indexed lookups
Process all resources sequentially to avoid race conditions
Increase API server timeout to handle slow operations
questions.explanation: Key optimization techniques: (1) Informer caches reduce API server load, (2) Predicates filter unnecessary events (e.g., only trigger on spec changes), (3) Rate limiting prevents overwhelming the cluster during error storms, (4) Concurrent reconciliation (MaxConcurrentReconciles) parallelizes work, (5) Field indexers enable efficient lookups instead of listing all resources.

questions.title: Operator Security and RBAC
questions.situation: The security team is reviewing your Operator before production deployment. The interviewer asks about security measures.
questions.code:
# Minimal RBAC - only grant what's needed
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: database-operator-role
rules:
- apiGroups: ["example.com"]
  resources: ["databases"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "update", "patch"]
- apiGroups: ["example.com"]
  resources: ["databases/status"]
  verbs: ["update", "patch"]
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods", "services"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "create", "delete"]
# Note: No cluster-wide permissions unless absolutely necessary
questions.question: What security best practices should an Operator follow?
options: Grant cluster-admin to simplify RBAC configuration
Run the operator pod as root for maximum compatibility
Follow least-privilege RBAC, run as non-root, use network policies, enable TLS for webhooks, and avoid storing secrets in CRD specs
Security is handled by Kubernetes automatically, no special configuration needed
questions.explanation: Operator security best practices: (1) Least-privilege RBAC - only grant permissions actually needed, (2) Run as non-root with read-only filesystem where possible, (3) Use NetworkPolicies to restrict pod communication, (4) TLS for all webhook endpoints, (5) Don't store sensitive data in CRD specs - use Secret references instead, (6) Implement proper input validation in webhooks.

questions.title: Multi-Tenant Operator Design
questions.situation: Your company offers a managed database service. The interviewer asks how your Operator would handle multiple customers on the same cluster.
questions.question: How do you design an Operator that safely serves multiple tenants?
options: Use a single namespace for all tenants to simplify management
Give each tenant cluster-admin access to manage their own resources
Operators cannot support multi-tenancy; use separate clusters instead
Use namespace isolation, namespace-scoped CRDs, RBAC per tenant, resource quotas, and network policies to ensure tenant isolation
questions.explanation: Multi-tenant Operator design requires: (1) Namespace isolation - each tenant gets dedicated namespace(s), (2) Namespace-scoped CRDs instead of cluster-scoped, (3) RBAC limiting each tenant to their namespaces, (4) ResourceQuotas preventing any tenant from consuming excessive resources, (5) NetworkPolicies preventing cross-tenant communication, (6) Consider tenant labels/annotations for additional filtering.

questions.title: Creating Your First Pod
questions.situation: You need to deploy an nginx web server in a Kubernetes cluster.
questions.code:
# Goal: Create a pod named 'web-server' running nginx:1.20
# The pod should be accessible on port 80
questions.question: What's the correct way to create a pod running nginx?
options:
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: web-server
spec:
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx:1.20
    ports:
    - containerPort: 80
EOF
kubectl run web-server --image=nginx:1.20
kubectl create pod web-server --image=nginx:1.20 --port=80
kubectl run web-server --image=nginx:1.20 --port=80
questions.explanation: While 'kubectl run' creates pods quickly, using YAML manifests with 'kubectl apply' is the best practice as it's declarative, version-controllable, and allows for more complex configurations.

questions.title: Exposing Your Application
questions.situation: Your nginx pod is running, but you need to make it accessible from outside the cluster.
questions.question: How do you expose a pod to external traffic?
options: kubectl expose pod web-server --type=ClusterIP --port=80
kubectl expose pod web-server --type=NodePort --port=80
kubectl create service web-server --port=80
kubectl expose pod web-server --type=LoadBalancer --port=80
questions.explanation: LoadBalancer service type exposes the service externally using a cloud provider's load balancer, making it accessible from outside the cluster. NodePort only works if you can access cluster nodes directly.

questions.title: Scaling Applications
questions.situation: You have a deployment called 'web-app' with 1 replica, but you need 5 replicas to handle traffic.
questions.code:
# Current state:
# deployment.apps/web-app   1/1     1            1           2m
# Need: 5 replicas running
questions.question: Your application is experiencing high traffic. How do you scale it?
options: kubectl scale pod web-app --replicas=5
kubectl scale deployment web-app --replicas=5

kubectl edit deployment web-app
# Change replicas: 5
kubectl patch deployment web-app -p '{"spec":{"replicas":5}}'
questions.explanation: kubectl scale deployment is the most direct and common way to scale a deployment. While edit and patch work, scale is specifically designed for this purpose and is more intuitive.

questions.title: Debugging Failed Pods
questions.situation: A pod named 'app-pod' keeps restarting and shows CrashLoopBackOff status.
questions.code:
$ kubectl get pods
NAME      READY   STATUS             RESTARTS   AGE
app-pod   0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   4          2m
questions.question: Your pod is in CrashLoopBackOff state. How do you diagnose the issue?
options: kubectl delete pod app-pod
kubectl describe pod app-pod && kubectl logs app-pod
kubectl restart pod app-pod
kubectl get events
questions.explanation: kubectl describe shows pod events and status details, while kubectl logs shows the application's output. Together, they provide comprehensive debugging information for pod issues.

questions.title: Managing Configuration
questions.situation: Your application needs database connection settings that might change between environments.
questions.code:
# You have these config values:
# DB_HOST=postgres.example.com
# DB_PORT=5432
# DB_NAME=myapp
questions.question: How do you inject configuration into a pod without rebuilding the image?
options: kubectl create configmap db-config --from-literal=DB_HOST=postgres.example.com --from-literal=DB_PORT=5432 --from-literal=DB_NAME=myapp
kubectl create secret db-config --from-literal=DB_HOST=postgres.example.com
kubectl set env deployment/app DB_HOST=postgres.example.com
Rebuild the Docker image with the config values
questions.explanation: ConfigMaps are specifically designed for non-sensitive configuration data. They can be mounted as volumes or exposed as environment variables, keeping configuration separate from application code.

questions.title: Data Persistence
questions.situation: You're running a PostgreSQL database pod that needs to retain data even if the pod is recreated.
questions.question: How do you ensure database data survives pod restarts?
options: Use hostPath volume to mount host directory
Create a PersistentVolumeClaim and mount it to the database pod
Use emptyDir volume for data storage
Store data in the container's filesystem
questions.explanation: PersistentVolumeClaims provide durable storage that survives pod restarts and rescheduling. They abstract the underlying storage implementation and can be dynamically provisioned.

questions.title: Resource Management
questions.situation: You need to ensure your application pod doesn't use more than 500Mi of memory and 0.5 CPU cores.
questions.code:
# Pod should be limited to:
# Memory: 500Mi
# CPU: 0.5 cores (500m)
questions.question: How do you prevent a single pod from consuming all cluster resources?
options: Set NODE_OPTIONS='--max-old-space-size=500' environment variable
Use cgroups on the host system

Set resources.limits in the pod specification:
  limits:
    memory: "500Mi"
    cpu: "500m"
Configure the container runtime limits
questions.explanation: Kubernetes resource limits in the pod specification enforce hard limits on CPU and memory usage, preventing pods from consuming excessive cluster resources and affecting other workloads.

questions.title: Zero-Downtime Deployments
questions.situation: You need to update your web application from version 1.0 to 2.0 without any downtime.
questions.code:
# Current: myapp:1.0 (3 replicas)
# Target: myapp:2.0 (zero downtime)
questions.question: How do you update your application without service interruption?
options: kubectl delete deployment myapp && kubectl create deployment myapp --image=myapp:2.0
kubectl set image deployment/myapp container-name=myapp:2.0
kubectl scale deployment myapp --replicas=0 && kubectl scale deployment myapp --replicas=3
kubectl replace -f new-deployment.yaml
questions.explanation: kubectl set image triggers a rolling update, gradually replacing old pods with new ones. Kubernetes ensures availability by maintaining running instances during the update process.

questions.title: Securing Pod Communication
questions.situation: Your frontend pods should only communicate with backend pods, and backend pods should only accept traffic from frontend pods.
questions.question: How do you restrict network traffic between pods for security?
options: Use iptables rules on each node
Configure firewall rules in the cloud provider
Create NetworkPolicy resources to define allowed traffic
Use service mesh like Istio for all traffic control
questions.explanation: NetworkPolicies are Kubernetes-native resources that define rules for pod-to-pod communication. They work at the cluster level and are enforced by the CNI plugin.

questions.title: Permission Denied Emergency
questions.situation: Your web server can't read files in /var/www/html after a deployment. The application owner is 'webapp' and group is 'www-data'. Files should be readable by the web server but not writable by others.
questions.code:
Current permissions:
-rw------- 1 root root index.html
-rw------- 1 root root style.css
drwx------ 2 root root images/
questions.question: Fix file permissions for a web application that suddenly stopped working.
options: chown -R webapp:www-data /var/www/html && find /var/www/html -type f -exec chmod 644 {} \; && find /var/www/html -type d -exec chmod 755 {} \;
chmod 777 /var/www/html/*
chown webapp:www-data /var/www/html/* && chmod 644 /var/www/html/*.* && chmod 755 /var/www/html/*/
chmod -R 755 /var/www/html
questions.explanation: This command properly sets ownership recursively, then sets appropriate permissions: 644 for files (read/write for owner, read for group/others) and 755 for directories (executable needed to enter directories).

questions.title: High CPU Usage Investigation
questions.situation: Your server's CPU usage is at 95% and users are complaining about slow response times. You need to quickly identify the culprit process and take action.
questions.code:
$ top
%Cpu(s): 95.2 us,  2.1 sy,  0.0 ni,  2.7 id
Something is consuming CPU but top output is scrolling too fast to see clearly.
questions.question: Identify and manage a process consuming excessive CPU resources.
options: ps aux | head -10
top -n 1 -o %CPU | head -20
ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head -10
htop --sort-key PERCENT_CPU
questions.explanation: ps aux --sort=-%cpu sorts processes by CPU usage in descending order and shows the top 10 CPU consumers. This gives a clear, static view of which processes are using the most CPU.

questions.title: Disk Space Crisis
questions.situation: Your server's root partition is 98% full and applications are failing. You need to quickly identify what's consuming space and free it up safely.
questions.code:
$ df -h
Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/sda1        20G   19G  200M  98% /

Applications are logging 'No space left on device' errors.
questions.question: Free up disk space when the root filesystem is 98% full.
options: rm -rf /tmp/* /var/log/*
du -sh /* | sort -hr
du -sh /* 2>/dev/null | sort -hr && du -sh /var/log/* | sort -hr
find / -size +100M -exec ls -lh {} \;
questions.explanation: This command finds the largest directories in root, suppresses permission errors, and then specifically checks log files which are often safe to clean. It's systematic and avoids dangerous deletions.

questions.title: Application Error Investigation
questions.situation: Users reported errors between 14:00-15:00 today. You need to find error messages in the application log file '/var/log/app.log' and count how many occurred.
questions.code:
Log format:
2024-06-21 14:23:15 INFO User login successful
2024-06-21 14:24:32 ERROR Database connection failed
2024-06-21 14:25:01 WARN Cache miss for user:12345

Need: Find all ERROR messages from 14:00-15:00 hour
questions.question: Find error patterns in application logs during a production incident.
options: grep ERROR /var/log/app.log
grep '2024-06-21 14:.*ERROR' /var/log/app.log | wc -l
awk '/2024-06-21 14:/ && /ERROR/' /var/log/app.log | wc -l
sed -n '/2024-06-21 14:/,/2024-06-21 15:/p' /var/log/app.log | grep ERROR | wc -l
questions.explanation: This grep pattern matches the date, hour (14:), and ERROR in the same line, then counts the occurrences with wc -l. It's precise and efficient for the specific time range needed.

questions.title: Network Connection Troubleshooting
questions.situation: Your web application can't connect to database server 'db.company.com' on port 5432. You need to systematically check network connectivity and identify where the connection is failing.
questions.code:
Error: Connection to db.company.com:5432 failed
Timeout after 30 seconds

Need to check: DNS resolution, network path, port accessibility
questions.question: Diagnose why your application can't connect to a database server.
options: nslookup db.company.com && ping db.company.com && nc -zv db.company.com 5432
ping db.company.com
telnet db.company.com 5432
traceroute db.company.com && netstat -an | grep 5432
questions.explanation: This systematic approach first checks DNS resolution (nslookup), then basic connectivity (ping), and finally tests the specific port (nc -zv). It diagnoses each layer of the connection.

questions.title: Log Data Analysis Pipeline
questions.situation: You need to find the top 10 IP addresses making the most requests in your Apache access log and show their request counts.
questions.code:
Apache log format:
192.168.1.100 - - [21/Jun/2024:14:23:15 +0000] "GET /index.html HTTP/1.1" 200 1024
10.0.0.50 - - [21/Jun/2024:14:23:16 +0000] "POST /api/login HTTP/1.1" 200 256

Goal: Top 10 IPs by request count
questions.question: Extract and analyze specific data from web server access logs.
options: cut -d' ' -f1 /var/log/apache2/access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -10
awk '{print $1}' /var/log/apache2/access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -10
grep -o '^[0-9.]*' /var/log/apache2/access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -10
sed 's/ .*//' /var/log/apache2/access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -10
questions.explanation: awk '{print $1}' extracts the first field (IP address), sort groups identical IPs, uniq -c counts occurrences, sort -nr sorts by count in reverse order, and head -10 shows the top 10.

questions.title: Stubborn Process Termination
questions.situation: A Java application (PID 1234) is completely unresponsive and consuming 100% CPU. It's not responding to normal termination requests, and you need to stop it without affecting other processes.
questions.code:
$ ps aux | grep java
user  1234  99.9  25.0 2048000 1024000 ?  R  14:23  45:32 java -jar myapp.jar

Process is unresponsive to user input and consuming excessive resources.
questions.question: Safely terminate a hung application process that's not responding to normal signals.
options: kill -9 1234
kill 1234 && sleep 5 && kill -9 1234
kill 1234; if ps -p 1234 > /dev/null; then sleep 10; kill -TERM 1234; sleep 5; kill -KILL 1234; fi
pkill -f 'java -jar myapp.jar'
questions.explanation: This approach tries graceful termination first (SIGTERM), waits, then escalates to SIGKILL only if needed. It checks if the process still exists and follows the proper signal escalation sequence.

questions.title: Bulk Configuration Update
questions.situation: You need to change the database host from 'localhost' to 'db.internal' in all .conf files within /etc/myapp/ and its subdirectories, but only if the line contains 'db_host='.
questions.code:
Files contain lines like:
db_host=localhost
api_host=localhost  # Should NOT change this
cache_host=redis.local

Only change db_host lines from localhost to db.internal
questions.question: Update configuration values across multiple files in a directory structure.
options: sed -i 's/localhost/db.internal/g' /etc/myapp/*.conf
find /etc/myapp -name '*.conf' -exec sed -i 's/localhost/db.internal/g' {} \;
find /etc/myapp -name '*.conf' -exec sed -i '/db_host=/s/localhost/db.internal/g' {} \;
grep -r 'db_host=localhost' /etc/myapp --include='*.conf' | sed 's/localhost/db.internal/'
questions.explanation: This command finds all .conf files recursively, then uses sed with a pattern address '/db_host=/' to only modify lines containing 'db_host=', preventing unintended changes to other localhost references.

questions.title: Performance Bottleneck Investigation
questions.situation: Your server is experiencing slow response times. You need to check CPU, memory, disk I/O, and network to identify the bottleneck. Users report intermittent timeouts.
questions.code:
Symptoms:
• Application response time: 30+ seconds (normally <2s)
• Users getting timeouts
• No obvious error messages in logs

Need to check all system resources systematically
questions.question: Identify system bottlenecks during performance issues using command-line tools.
options: top && free -h && df -h
vmstat 1 5 && iostat -x 1 5 && sar -n DEV 1 5
htop && iotop && nethogs
uptime && cat /proc/loadavg && cat /proc/meminfo
questions.explanation: This combination provides comprehensive system monitoring: vmstat shows CPU/memory over time, iostat shows disk I/O statistics, and sar shows network statistics. The '1 5' samples every second for 5 iterations, revealing patterns.

questions.title: Security Audit - Suspicious Files
questions.situation: Security team suspects a breach. You need to find files modified in the last 24 hours, world-writable files, and files with unusual ownership in system directories.
questions.code:
Investigation needed:
• Files modified in last 24 hours in /usr, /bin, /sbin
• World-writable files that shouldn't be
• Files owned by unusual users in system directories

Security incident response protocol active
questions.question: Find potentially compromised files and unusual permissions for security investigation.
options: find /usr /bin /sbin \( -mtime -1 -o -perm -002 -o ! -user root \) -ls | tee /tmp/security_audit.log
find /usr /bin /sbin -mtime -1 -ls
find /usr /bin /sbin -mtime -1 -o -perm -002 -o ! -user root | tee /tmp/security_audit.log
ls -la /usr /bin /sbin | grep $(date +%Y-%m-%d)
questions.explanation: This command uses proper grouping with parentheses to find files that match ANY of the suspicious criteria: recently modified (-mtime -1), world-writable (-perm -002), or not owned by root (! -user root). The -ls provides detailed output and tee logs results.

questions.title: Emergency Backup and Recovery
questions.situation: You need to create an emergency backup of /home/users before a risky system update. The backup must be compressed, exclude cache directories, and include integrity verification.
questions.code:
Requirements:
• Backup /home/users to /backup/emergency_backup.tar.gz
• Exclude .cache and .tmp directories
• Compress for space efficiency
• Verify backup integrity
• System must remain operational
questions.question: Create a compressed backup while the system is running and verify its integrity.
options: tar -czf /backup/emergency_backup.tar.gz /home/users
tar --exclude='*.cache' --exclude='*.tmp' -czf /backup/emergency_backup.tar.gz /home/users && tar -tzf /backup/emergency_backup.tar.gz > /dev/null
tar --exclude='*/.cache' --exclude='*/.tmp' -czf /backup/emergency_backup.tar.gz /home/users && echo $? && tar -tzf /backup/emergency_backup.tar.gz | wc -l
tar --exclude='*/.cache' --exclude='*/.tmp' -czf /backup/emergency_backup.tar.gz -C / home/users && tar -tzf /backup/emergency_backup.tar.gz > /dev/null && echo 'Backup verified successfully'
questions.explanation: This command properly excludes cache/tmp directories with correct patterns, uses -C to avoid absolute paths in the archive, compresses the backup, verifies integrity by listing contents, and provides confirmation of successful verification.

questions.title: System Maintenance Automation
questions.situation: You need to automate weekly maintenance: clean old logs (>30 days), remove temp files, update package cache, and restart a service only if configuration changed. Script must handle errors gracefully.
questions.code:
Weekly maintenance tasks:
1. Remove logs older than 30 days from /var/log/myapp/
2. Clean /tmp files older than 7 days
3. Update package manager cache
4. Restart myapp service only if config changed in last week
5. Log all actions with timestamps
questions.question: Create a maintenance script that handles multiple system cleanup tasks safely.
options:
find /var/log/myapp -mtime +30 -delete
find /tmp -mtime +7 -delete
apt update
service myapp restart

#!/bin/bash
set -e
find /var/log/myapp -name '*.log' -mtime +30 -delete 2>/dev/null || true
find /tmp -mtime +7 -type f -delete 2>/dev/null || true
apt update -qq
if [ $(find /etc/myapp/ -name '*.conf' -mtime -7 | wc -l) -gt 0 ]; then
  systemctl restart myapp
fi

crontab -e
0 2 * * 0 find /var/log/myapp -mtime +30 -delete && find /tmp -mtime +7 -delete

#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
log() { echo "$(date): $1" | tee -a /var/log/maintenance.log; }
log "Starting maintenance"
find /var/log/myapp -name '*.log' -mtime +30 -delete && log "Old logs cleaned" || log "Error cleaning logs"
find /tmp -mtime +7 -type f -delete && log "Temp files cleaned" || log "Error cleaning temp"
apt update -qq && log "Package cache updated" || log "Error updating cache"
if [ $(find /etc/myapp/ -name '*.conf' -mtime -7 | wc -l) -gt 0 ]; then
  systemctl restart myapp && log "Service restarted" || log "Error restarting service"
else
  log "No config changes, service restart skipped"
fi
log "Maintenance completed"
questions.explanation: This script includes proper error handling (set -euo pipefail), logging function with timestamps, conditional service restart based on config changes, and comprehensive error reporting. It follows bash scripting best practices for production use.

questions.quizTitle: Running Your First Chaos Experiment with Litmus Quiz
questions.title: Why deliberately break things?
questions.situation: You pitched a Litmus rollout to your team. Leadership is nervous about the word 'chaos' and wants a one-sentence reason this is not just reckless.
questions.code:
# A typical first experiment:
#   Hypothesis: 'If one checkout pod dies, the service still serves traffic'
#   Method:     pod-delete on 1 replica out of 3
#   Probe:      HTTP 200 on /healthz throughout the run
#   Result:     pass = hypothesis holds, fail = we learned something
questions.question: Your manager pushes back on a chaos engineering proposal: 'Why would we intentionally cause failures in a system we're trying to keep stable?' What's the right framing?
options: It replaces integration tests so QA can be shut down
It generates synthetic load for SLO dashboards
You inject controlled, scoped faults to test specific hypotheses about how the system behaves, finding weaknesses before real outages do
It is a compliance requirement for SOC 2 and has no other purpose
questions.explanation: Chaos engineering is hypothesis-driven. You state 'I believe the system will behave like X under failure Y', then inject Y in a small, controlled blast radius and check whether X actually holds. If the hypothesis fails, you've found a bug or a gap in your resilience design before a real outage does. It is not a replacement for integration testing, and it is not load generation. Compliance frameworks may reward it, but that is a side effect, not the point.

questions.quizTitle: Running Your First Chaos Experiment with Litmus Quiz
questions.title: What ChaosCenter actually is
questions.situation: Fresh install of Litmus 3.x on a kind cluster. You see Deployments for litmusportal-frontend, litmusportal-server, mongo, and chaos-operator. The teammate wonders if ChaosCenter is the thing that breaks the pods.
questions.code:
helm repo add litmuschaos https://litmuschaos.github.io/litmus-helm/
helm install chaos litmuschaos/litmus \
  --namespace=litmus \
  --create-namespace

kubectl -n litmus get pods
# NAME                                  READY   STATUS
# chaos-litmus-frontend-...             1/1     Running
# chaos-litmus-server-...               1/1     Running
# chaos-mongo-0                         1/1     Running
questions.question: You ran the Helm chart from the Litmus docs and now you have a litmus namespace with several Deployments. A teammate asks what ChaosCenter is and where the experiments actually run.
options: ChaosCenter is the web UI and control plane (workflows, projects, RBAC, dashboards). Actual chaos is executed in target clusters by the chaos-operator and per-experiment runner/helper pods
ChaosCenter is the pod that runs every experiment directly; the frontend is just for browsing logs
ChaosCenter is a CRD; it has no Deployments or services
ChaosCenter is the kernel module that injects faults at the node level
questions.explanation: ChaosCenter is the management plane: a React frontend, a GraphQL server, and a MongoDB store for users, projects, and workflow history. It does not run faults itself. The chaos-operator (and on workload clusters, the subscriber agent) reconciles ChaosEngine resources and spawns short-lived runner and helper pods that perform the actual fault injection. Separating control plane from execution plane is what lets one ChaosCenter target many clusters.

questions.quizTitle: Running Your First Chaos Experiment with Litmus Quiz
questions.title: ChaosEngine vs ChaosExperiment
questions.situation: A new engineer copies snippets from the Litmus Hub. They wrote a ChaosExperiment and a ChaosEngine that both look like they describe pod-delete and they're not sure which one actually runs the fault.
questions.code:
# ChaosExperiment: defines the fault and its tunables (a template)
apiVersion: litmuschaos.io/v1alpha1
kind: ChaosExperiment
metadata:
  name: pod-delete
spec:
  definition:
    image: litmuschaos/go-runner:latest
    args: ["-c", "./experiments -name pod-delete"]
    env:
      - name: TOTAL_CHAOS_DURATION
        value: "30"
---
# ChaosEngine: binds the experiment to a target app and triggers a run
apiVersion: litmuschaos.io/v1alpha1
kind: ChaosEngine
metadata:
  name: cart-pod-delete
spec:
  appinfo:
    appns: shop
    applabel: "app=cart"
    appkind: deployment
  chaosServiceAccount: litmus-admin
  experiments:
    - name: pod-delete
questions.question: Reviewing a PR, you see two new YAMLs: one ChaosExperiment named pod-delete and one ChaosEngine named cart-pod-delete. What is the relationship between them?
options: They are duplicates; you only need one of them

ChaosExperiment is the reusable fault definition (image, args, default env); ChaosEngine references it and applies it to a specific target. You install experiments once and create a ChaosEngine per run
ChaosEngine runs in the control plane; ChaosExperiment runs in the data plane and they communicate over gRPC
ChaosExperiment is created automatically from ChaosEngine; you never write one yourself
questions.explanation: Think of ChaosExperiment as a template: it points at a runner image, declares supported env vars, and lives in a namespace alongside its ServiceAccount and Role. A ChaosEngine is the actual run: it picks a target via appinfo, overrides env, attaches probes, and tells the operator 'go execute this experiment now'. You typically install the experiment set once per namespace (often via the chaos-charts) and then create many ChaosEngines over time.

questions.quizTitle: Running Your First Chaos Experiment with Litmus Quiz
questions.title: Stuck in Initialized: missing RBAC
questions.situation: You're testing pod-delete in the 'shop' namespace. You set chaosServiceAccount: default in the ChaosEngine because you wanted to get going quickly. The runner pod never spawns and events show 'pods is forbidden: User system:serviceaccount:shop:default cannot list pods'.
questions.code:
kubectl -n shop describe chaosengine cart-pod-delete
# Events:
#   Warning  ChaosResourcesOperationFailed  chaos-operator
#   Unable to filter target pods:
#   pods is forbidden: User "system:serviceaccount:shop:default"
#   cannot list resource "pods" in API group "" in the namespace "shop"
questions.question: You applied a ChaosEngine for pod-delete. The status stays at 'Initialized' for 10 minutes and no chaos runs. kubectl describe shows events about forbidden access to pods. What's the fix?
options: Restart the chaos-operator pod; the default SA gets pod permissions on restart
Set hostNetwork: true on the ChaosEngine so it bypasses RBAC
Run kubectl auth can-i and ignore the failure; pod-delete works without RBAC because it uses the API server's bootstrap account
Each experiment ships with a ServiceAccount, Role, and RoleBinding. Apply those manifests and point chaosServiceAccount at the experiment's SA (often litmus-admin) instead of default
questions.explanation: Litmus runs experiments with the privileges of the ServiceAccount you name in chaosServiceAccount. The default SA in a namespace has almost no permissions, so the chaos-runner cannot list, delete, or exec into pods. Each experiment in the Litmus Hub ships with the matching RBAC manifest (look for rbac.yaml beside experiment.yaml). Apply that and reference its SA. Granting cluster-admin is overkill; use the per-experiment scoped Role, which gives only the verbs that experiment actually needs.

questions.quizTitle: Running Your First Chaos Experiment with Litmus Quiz
questions.title: annotationCheck and silent no-ops
questions.situation: You enabled annotationCheck because you want only Deployments that explicitly mark themselves as chaos-ready to be targeted. The Deployment in question does not have the litmuschaos.io/chaos annotation. The run completes in seconds with the target untouched.
questions.code:
spec:
  annotationCheck: "true"
  appinfo:
    appns: shop
    applabel: "app=cart"
    appkind: deployment
  experiments:
    - name: pod-delete

# But the target Deployment looks like this:
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: cart
  labels:
    app: cart
  # no litmuschaos.io/chaos annotation
questions.question: You set annotationCheck: 'true' in your ChaosEngine to limit blast radius to opted-in workloads. The experiment finishes immediately with status 'Skipped' and no pods were touched. Why?
options: annotationCheck only works in the litmus namespace; move the target there

When annotationCheck is true, Litmus only targets workloads with the annotation litmuschaos.io/chaos: 'true'. Without it, the run is skipped on purpose. Either add the annotation to the Deployment or set annotationCheck: 'false'
annotationCheck is deprecated and should be removed
The experiment ran but Litmus suppresses logs when the target uses a label rather than an annotation
questions.explanation: annotationCheck is an opt-in safety control. With it set to 'true', Litmus refuses to inject faults into any workload that has not annotated itself with litmuschaos.io/chaos: 'true'. This is exactly the behavior you want for shared clusters: it makes it impossible for someone in a neighbouring namespace to accidentally include your service in their experiment. The fix is to add the annotation to the target's pod template (or its parent workload), not to disable the check.

questions.quizTitle: Running Your First Chaos Experiment with Litmus Quiz
questions.title: Probes: how Litmus knows you survived
questions.situation: Pod-delete killed one of three replicas. Kubernetes recreated it, but the Service routed traffic to the dying pod for several seconds because readiness was misconfigured. The customer-facing impact is real, but the chaos run is green.
questions.code:
# Add a probe to the experiment so Litmus checks steady state itself:
experiments:
  - name: pod-delete
    spec:
      probe:
        - name: cart-healthz
          type: httpProbe
          mode: Continuous
          runProperties:
            probeTimeout: 2
            interval: 1
            retry: 1
            probePollingInterval: 2
          httpProbe/inputs:
            url: http://cart.shop.svc:8080/healthz
            insecureSkipVerify: false
            method:
              get:
                criteria: ==
                responseCode: "200"
questions.question: Your pod-delete experiment ran and ended with verdict 'Pass'. But Grafana shows the cart service returned 5xx for 40 seconds during the run. Why did Litmus call it a pass and how do you make it fail next time?
options: Litmus passes if the chaos action completed, regardless of app behavior. Add probes (httpProbe, cmdProbe, k8sProbe, promProbe) that assert your steady-state hypothesis. A failing probe flips the verdict to Fail
Probes are only for metrics export; they cannot change the verdict
The experiment verdict tracks pod recreation time only; service availability is out of scope
Set strictCheck: true on ChaosEngine; that is the only way to involve health checks
questions.explanation: Without probes, the verdict only confirms the fault was injected (a pod was deleted). Probes are how you tell Litmus what 'healthy' means. Continuous mode runs the probe throughout the chaos window; if any sample fails the criteria, the experiment fails. Use httpProbe for HTTP endpoints, cmdProbe to run a shell command inside a pod, k8sProbe to assert on Kubernetes resources, and promProbe to query a PromQL expression. The probe is the hypothesis; the chaos is the experiment.

questions.quizTitle: Running Your First Chaos Experiment with Litmus Quiz
questions.title: Tuning pod-delete intensity
questions.situation: Your team is graduating from 'one pod, one shot' experiments to sustained pressure runs. You want to keep killing pods at a steady rate while the load test runs in parallel.
questions.code:
experiments:
  - name: pod-delete
    spec:
      components:
        env:
          - name: TOTAL_CHAOS_DURATION
            value: "___"
          - name: CHAOS_INTERVAL
            value: "___"
          - name: PODS_AFFECTED_PERC
            value: "___"
          - name: FORCE
            value: "false"
          - name: GRACE_PERIOD
            value: "___"
questions.question: You want pod-delete to kill half of the cart pods every 30 seconds for 5 minutes, with a 10-second grace period. Which env vars do you set on the experiment spec?
options: TOTAL_CHAOS_DURATION=5, CHAOS_INTERVAL=30, PODS_AFFECTED_PERC=2, GRACE_PERIOD=10
TOTAL_CHAOS_DURATION=300, CHAOS_INTERVAL=30, PODS_AFFECTED_PERC=50, GRACE_PERIOD=10
TOTAL_CHAOS_DURATION=300m, CHAOS_INTERVAL=30s, PODS_AFFECTED_PERC=0.5, GRACE_PERIOD=10s
DURATION=5m, FREQUENCY=30s, RATIO=half
questions.explanation: TOTAL_CHAOS_DURATION and CHAOS_INTERVAL are unitless seconds (so 5 minutes is 300, and 30s is 30). PODS_AFFECTED_PERC is a whole-number percentage from 1 to 100, not a fraction or count. GRACE_PERIOD is also seconds and controls how long Kubernetes waits before SIGKILL after SIGTERM, which directly affects whether your app gets to drain connections. FORCE=true uses SIGKILL immediately, which is useful for testing the absence of graceful shutdown but should not be your default.

questions.quizTitle: Running Your First Chaos Experiment with Litmus Quiz
questions.title: appinfo and target discovery
questions.situation: The team uses app=cart across cart-api, cart-worker, and cart-cron. You only want pod-delete to touch cart-api. Right now the chaos-runner discovers every pod with that label across the namespace.
questions.code:
spec:
  appinfo:
    appns: shop
    applabel: "app=cart"
    appkind: deployment

# All three Deployments share the label:
kubectl -n shop get deploy -l app=cart
# NAME          READY
# cart-api      3/3
# cart-worker   2/2
# cart-cron     1/1
questions.question: Your ChaosEngine has appinfo.applabel='app=cart' and appns='shop'. Multiple Deployments in the shop namespace share that label. The experiment kills pods from all of them. How do you scope to just one Deployment?
options: Use a more specific label combination (for example app=cart,component=api) so applabel matches exactly one parent workload. Litmus discovers the parent workload via the label and only touches its pods
appinfo accepts a name field; set name: cart-api
Move cart-api into its own namespace; appinfo cannot distinguish workloads in the same namespace
Set appkind: pod and list pod names individually under appinfo.pods
questions.explanation: appinfo is intentionally simple: a namespace, a label selector, and a kind. Litmus uses that selector to find the parent workload (Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet), then targets its pods. There is no name field. The right move is to make your labels precise enough that the selector picks the workload you mean. Best practice: standardize on app.kubernetes.io/name and app.kubernetes.io/component, then chaos selectors become unambiguous across the cluster.

questions.quizTitle: Running Your First Chaos Experiment with Litmus Quiz
questions.title: Triggering chaos from CI
questions.situation: You have ChaosCenter running and a chaos workflow defined in the UI. The CI job needs to start a run, wait for the verdict, and exit non-zero if any probe failed.
questions.code:
- name: Run pod-delete in staging
  run: |
    litmusctl config set-account \
      --endpoint=https://chaos.example.com \
      --token=$LITMUS_TOKEN
    litmusctl create workflow \
      --file=./chaos/pod-delete-cart.yaml \
      --project-id=$PROJECT_ID \
      --chaos-infra-id=$INFRA_ID
    litmusctl get workflow-runs \
      --project-id=$PROJECT_ID --workflow-id=...
questions.question: Your team wants every pre-production deploy to run a 60-second pod-delete with probes against the new build, then promote or roll back based on the result. How do you drive that from a GitHub Actions job?
options: ChaosCenter has no CLI; you must use the GraphQL endpoint directly
Use kubectl apply on the workflow YAML in the litmus namespace; ChaosCenter polls etcd for new ChaosEngines and reports back over webhooks
litmusctl is the official CLI for ChaosCenter. It authenticates with a token, creates/runs workflows, and exposes run state so CI can poll and fail the build on a failed verdict
Trigger workflows by sending a SIGUSR1 to the chaos-operator pod; it picks the next file in /etc/litmus/queue
questions.explanation: litmusctl is the supported CLI for ChaosCenter. It wraps the GraphQL API so you can script account setup, infra registration, workflow creation, run triggers, and run inspection. In CI, you typically generate a service-account token in ChaosCenter, store it as a secret, and have the job create the workflow run and poll until it reaches Completed or Failed. Doing this with raw kubectl skips ChaosCenter entirely, which means no dashboards, no probe results, and no centralized RBAC.

questions.quizTitle: Running Your First Chaos Experiment with Litmus Quiz
questions.title: Probe modes: when does the check run?
questions.situation: A teammate read mode names quickly and assumed EOT meant 'every operational tick'. They want a probe that fires every second while chaos is happening, plus one that verifies recovery after.
questions.code:
probe:
  - name: live-traffic
    type: httpProbe
    mode: ___          # fires throughout the chaos window
  - name: recovered
    type: httpProbe
    mode: ___          # fires once, at end of test
  - name: warm-baseline
    type: httpProbe
    mode: ___          # fires once, before chaos starts
questions.question: You add an httpProbe in 'EOT' mode expecting it to run continuously during chaos. Instead it runs once after chaos finishes. What does each probe mode actually do?
options: live-traffic: Continuous, recovered: EOT, warm-baseline: SOT
live-traffic: OnChaos, recovered: SOT, warm-baseline: EOT
live-traffic: Edge, recovered: Once, warm-baseline: Bootstrap
All probes share one mode globally; set spec.probeMode: Continuous
questions.explanation: Litmus probe modes are SOT (Start of Test, fires once before chaos), EOT (End of Test, fires once after chaos), Edge (fires both before and after, useful for differential checks), Continuous (polls throughout the chaos window at probePollingInterval), and OnChaos (continuous but only during the chaos action, not the surrounding setup/teardown). Pick the mode based on the question you're answering: 'were we healthy before?' is SOT, 'did we recover?' is EOT, 'were we healthy the whole time?' is Continuous or OnChaos.

questions.quizTitle: Running Your First Chaos Experiment with Litmus Quiz
questions.title: First chaos run in production
questions.situation: You've been running chaos in staging for two months without surprises. Now you have a 30-minute window in production. The CTO is in the Slack channel and one regression here will set the program back a year.
questions.code:
# A production-safe ChaosEngine:
spec:
  annotationCheck: "true"
  jobCleanUpPolicy: retain
  experiments:
    - name: pod-delete
      spec:
        components:
          env:
            - name: TOTAL_CHAOS_DURATION
              value: "60"
            - name: PODS_AFFECTED_PERC
              value: "10"
        probe:
          - name: slo-error-budget
            type: promProbe
            mode: Continuous
            runProperties: {probeTimeout: 5, interval: 5, retry: 1}
            promProbe/inputs:
              endpoint: http://prom:9090
              query: |
                sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="cart",code=~"5.."}[1m]))
                / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="cart"}[1m]))
              comparator: {type: float, criteria: "<", value: "0.01"}
questions.question: Leadership has cautiously approved one chaos experiment in production. Which set of guardrails should be in place before you click 'Run'?
options: Maximum blast radius (100% of pods), no probes, run during peak traffic so the signal is loud
Skip annotationCheck so you do not have to touch Deployment manifests; trust the namespace boundary instead

Small blast radius (single workload, low percentage), annotationCheck on, probes tied to a real SLO, abort criteria documented, kubectl delete chaosengine rollback rehearsed, off-peak window, on-call paged in advance
Run the experiment, then write down what happened in a postmortem the next week
questions.explanation: The point of production chaos is to learn safely, not to prove bravery. The well-known practices: shrink blast radius (small percentage, single workload, single zone if possible), use annotationCheck so only opted-in workloads can be hit, attach a probe that watches an actual SLI (error rate, latency, queue depth) so the system itself fails the run when users are affected, write the abort procedure on a sticky note (kubectl delete chaosengine NAME is usually enough), run off-peak with on-call aware, and have a clear rollback path. Increase blast radius across runs as confidence grows.

questions.quizTitle: Running Your First Chaos Experiment with Litmus Quiz
questions.title: Composing multi-fault scenarios
questions.situation: Single-fault experiments are not enough anymore. Your team wants to chain faults in a specific order, with probes between steps and parallel branches, and to keep the whole scenario as one reviewable artifact in git.
questions.code:
# A workflow chains experiments with steps and probes:
kind: Workflow
metadata:
  name: az-failure-scenario
spec:
  templates:
    - name: scenario
      steps:
        - - name: latency-on-node
            template: pod-network-latency
        - - name: drain-node
            template: node-drain
        - - name: kill-survivors
            template: pod-delete
            arguments:
              parameters:
                - name: appns
                  value: shop
questions.question: You want to simulate a partial AZ outage: induce network latency on one node, then drain it, then run pod-delete on remaining replicas elsewhere. How do you orchestrate this in Litmus?
options: Chain multiple ChaosEngines in a single namespace; the chaos-operator notices order and serializes them automatically
Use ChaosWorkflow (built on Argo Workflows) to declare steps, parameters, and parallel branches as one YAML artifact. ChaosCenter renders it visually and litmusctl runs it
Workflows are only for ChaosCenter and not available to GitOps users; use a Bash script that applies and waits between kubectl applies
You must write a custom Operator; Litmus does not support multi-experiment scenarios
questions.explanation: ChaosWorkflow is a thin layer over Argo Workflows. Each step references an experiment template (pod-delete, node-drain, pod-network-latency), passes parameters, and can run sequentially or in parallel using the standard Argo steps/dag syntax. Probes still attach to each individual experiment. The workflow YAML is reviewable in git, runs identically from CI via litmusctl, and gives you a single status object for the whole scenario instead of correlating four separate ChaosEngine runs.

questions.quizTitle: Running Your First Chaos Experiment with Litmus Quiz
questions.title: Debugging a run that just hangs
questions.situation: You inherited a chaos workflow from a previous teammate. It worked in staging; in prod it just sits. The on-call wants to know if they should kill it or wait.
questions.code:
kubectl -n shop get chaosengine cart-pod-delete -o jsonpath='{.status}'
kubectl -n shop get pods -l name=cart-pod-delete
# NAME                              READY   STATUS              RESTARTS
# pod-delete-helper-...             0/1     ImagePullBackOff    0
# cart-pod-delete-runner            1/1     Running             0
kubectl -n shop logs cart-pod-delete-runner
kubectl -n shop logs pod-delete-helper-... --previous
kubectl -n litmus logs deploy/chaos-operator-ce
questions.question: A ChaosEngine has been in 'Running' for 40 minutes. Probes are not firing, no pods are being deleted, and the dashboard shows no progress. Where do you look, in order?
options: Delete the ChaosEngine and rerun; if it hangs again, file a Litmus bug
Restart the kubelet on the node; stuck experiments are almost always a kubelet issue
Disable RBAC temporarily; chaos-operator can finish the run with elevated permissions

Check ChaosEngine status, then runner pod logs, then helper pod logs (often the actual fault injector), then chaos-operator logs in the litmus namespace, then ServiceAccount RBAC and probe configuration. ImagePullBackOff on a helper is a common cause
questions.explanation: Litmus has a layered execution model: chaos-operator reconciles the ChaosEngine, spawns a runner pod, and the runner spawns helper pods that do the actual fault injection on target nodes. A hang almost always shows up at one of those layers. ChaosEngine status tells you the current phase; runner logs show high-level orchestration; helper logs show whether the fault actually injected (or got stuck on image pull, network policy, or capabilities). RBAC and probe misconfiguration are common silent failures. Restarting kubelet or disabling RBAC are not real fixes.

questions.quizTitle: Message Queues and Delivery Guarantees Quiz
questions.title: The Three Delivery Semantics
questions.situation: You are choosing the delivery guarantee for an order-processing pipeline.
questions.question: The vocabulary every queue conversation starts with.
options: At-most-once may lose messages but never duplicates; at-least-once never loses but may duplicate; exactly-once means each message takes effect once
They all mean the same thing in practice
At-least-once means messages are never delivered more than the queue size
Exactly-once is the easiest to implement and the default everywhere
questions.explanation: At-most-once: deliver and forget, so a failure can drop a message but you never see duplicates. At-least-once: keep retrying until acknowledged, so you never lose a message but can deliver it more than once. Exactly-once: each message affects the system exactly one time, which is the hardest to achieve and almost always built as at-least-once delivery plus idempotency. Knowing which you have determines everything downstream.

questions.quizTitle: Message Queues and Delivery Guarantees Quiz
questions.title: Surviving At-Least-Once
questions.situation: Your queue guarantees at-least-once delivery, so a payment message can be delivered twice.
questions.question: The consumer-side defence against duplicates.
options: Trust the queue and charge the card on every message
Make the consumer idempotent: deduplicate on a message/business id so processing the same message twice has the same effect as once
Switch to at-most-once so you never see duplicates
Add a sleep before processing to avoid duplicates
questions.explanation: At-least-once means duplicates are a when, not an if. The consumer must be idempotent: track a unique id (payment id, message id) and skip or no-op if already processed, often via a unique constraint or an idempotency key. Then a redelivery is harmless. Idempotency at the consumer is how real systems get 'effectively-once' behaviour on top of at-least-once delivery.

questions.quizTitle: Message Queues and Delivery Guarantees Quiz
questions.title: Acks and Visibility Timeouts
questions.situation: A consumer pulls a message from an SQS-style queue, starts working, but crashes before acknowledging. The visibility timeout is 30 seconds.
questions.question: Why an unacked message comes back.
options: The message is lost forever
The message is deleted immediately on receipt
After the visibility timeout expires without an ack, the message becomes visible again and is redelivered to another consumer
The queue blocks all other messages until that consumer recovers
questions.explanation: Pulling a message hides it for the visibility timeout rather than deleting it. The consumer must acknowledge (delete) it after successful processing. If it crashes and the timeout passes with no ack, the broker assumes failure and redelivers, which is exactly what produces at-least-once semantics. Set the timeout longer than worst-case processing time, or you get duplicate work while the first consumer is still busy.

questions.quizTitle: Message Queues and Delivery Guarantees Quiz
questions.title: Dead-Letter Queues
questions.situation: One malformed message keeps failing, getting redelivered, failing again, blocking the queue.
questions.question: Where bad messages go to be examined.
options: Delete the entire queue and start over
Acknowledge every message immediately so nothing fails
Increase the visibility timeout to infinity
Route messages that exceed a max-retries threshold to a dead-letter queue, so the main queue keeps flowing and failures can be inspected later
questions.explanation: A dead-letter queue (DLQ) captures messages that fail more than a configured number of times. This stops a single poison message from being retried forever and blocking healthy traffic, and it preserves the failures for debugging, alerting, or manual replay. A DLQ with a max-receive-count is the standard pattern for isolating bad messages without losing them.

questions.quizTitle: Message Queues and Delivery Guarantees Quiz
questions.title: Ordering Is Not Global
questions.situation: You assume a partitioned log like Kafka delivers all messages in the exact global order they were produced.
questions.question: A common, costly misconception.
options: No: ordering is guaranteed only within a partition (or key), not across partitions; to keep related events ordered you must route them to the same partition via a partition key
Correct, Kafka guarantees total global ordering across all partitions
Ordering is never guaranteed anywhere in Kafka
Ordering depends only on the number of consumers
questions.explanation: Partitioned logs scale by spreading messages across partitions, and ordering is preserved only within a single partition. Across partitions there is no global order. To keep a customer's events in order, you pick a partition key (e.g. customer id) so all their events land on one partition. Expecting global ordering, or using a random key for events that must stay ordered, is a classic source of subtle bugs.

questions.quizTitle: Message Queues and Delivery Guarantees Quiz
questions.title: The Exactly-Once Myth
questions.situation: A vendor claims their queue offers true end-to-end exactly-once delivery with no effort on your part.
questions.question: What 'exactly-once' really means.
options: Believe it: exactly-once delivery over an unreliable network is trivially solved

Be skeptical: exactly-once delivery is impossible in general over unreliable networks; what systems actually provide is at-least-once delivery plus idempotency/transactions to get exactly-once processing (effectively-once)
Exactly-once is the same as at-most-once
Exactly-once requires turning off all retries
questions.explanation: You cannot guarantee a message is delivered exactly once across an unreliable network, because the sender can never be sure an ack was lost vs the message was lost. Real 'exactly-once' is engineered: at-least-once delivery combined with idempotent consumers or transactional/atomic commits (e.g. Kafka transactions tying offset commit to output). The honest framing is exactly-once processing, not magic exactly-once delivery.

questions.quizTitle: Message Queues and Delivery Guarantees Quiz
questions.title: Consumer Lag and Backpressure
questions.situation: Producers write 50,000 messages/second; consumers process 30,000/second. This runs for hours.
questions.question: When producers outrun consumers.
options: Nothing happens, queues have infinite capacity
The queue automatically slows producers with no consequences
Lag grows without bound: the backlog (and storage/memory) keeps increasing, latency climbs, and you must scale consumers, shed load, or apply backpressure to producers
Consumers will magically speed up to match
questions.explanation: A sustained producer rate above consumer throughput means lag grows forever: the backlog, end-to-end latency, and broker storage all climb until something breaks. You monitor consumer lag and respond by scaling out consumers, increasing parallelism (partitions), shedding or sampling load, or applying backpressure so producers slow down. A queue absorbs bursts, it does not fix a permanent throughput deficit.

questions.quizTitle: Message Queues and Delivery Guarantees Quiz
questions.title: Work Queue vs Pub/Sub
questions.situation: You need a job processed by exactly one worker. Separately, you need an event seen by every interested service.
questions.question: Two fundamentally different delivery shapes.
options: Both need the same delivery model
Competing consumers means every consumer gets every message
Pub/sub guarantees only one subscriber ever receives a message

A work queue (competing consumers) delivers each message to one worker among many; pub/sub (fan-out) delivers each message to every subscriber. The first load-balances work, the second broadcasts events
questions.explanation: A work queue with competing consumers spreads messages so each job runs once on one of several workers, that is how you parallelise processing. Pub/sub (or Kafka consumer groups, each group a separate subscriber) fans a message out to every interested party. Mixing these up, e.g. expecting all workers to see every job, or expecting one subscriber to absorb a broadcast, breaks the design. Pick the topology that matches the intent.

questions.quizTitle: Message Queues and Delivery Guarantees Quiz
questions.title: The Poison Message
questions.situation: A consumer repeatedly crashes on the same message, recovers, gets redelivered the same message, and crashes again.
questions.question: One message that keeps killing the consumer.
options: It is a poison message: it must be capped with a retry/redelivery limit and routed to a DLQ, otherwise it blocks the partition/queue and starves all other messages
This is normal and self-resolves
Adding more consumers fixes a poison message
Poison messages only occur with at-most-once delivery
questions.explanation: A poison message is one that can never be processed successfully (bad schema, unhandled edge case). Without a redelivery cap it loops forever, and in an ordered partition it blocks everything behind it. The fix is a max-delivery count that diverts it to a dead-letter queue so the rest of the stream proceeds, plus alerting so a human investigates. Unbounded retries on a poison message turn one bad record into an outage.

questions.quizTitle: Message Queues and Delivery Guarantees Quiz
questions.title: When You Commit the Offset
questions.situation: In a Kafka consumer, you choose whether to commit the offset before or after processing the message.
questions.question: The decision that sets your delivery semantics.
options: It makes no difference to delivery guarantees

Commit before processing risks losing a message on a crash (at-most-once); commit after processing risks reprocessing on a crash (at-least-once). The order of commit vs work decides which guarantee you get
Committing after processing guarantees exactly-once with no other work
You should never commit offsets at all
questions.explanation: If you commit the offset first and then crash mid-processing, that message is skipped on restart: at-most-once (possible loss). If you process first and crash before committing, the message is redelivered: at-least-once (possible duplicate). There is no commit order that gives exactly-once by itself, you add idempotency or Kafka transactions for that. This single choice is where consumers accidentally lose or duplicate data.

questions.quizTitle: Message Queues and Delivery Guarantees Quiz
questions.title: Producer Acks and Durability
questions.situation: A producer can wait for acks=1 (leader only) or acks=all (leader plus in-sync replicas) before considering a write successful.
questions.question: How hard the broker promises to keep your message.
options: Both give identical durability
acks=1 is more durable than acks=all

acks=all is more durable: the write is acknowledged only after replicas have it, so a leader failure won't lose the message, at the cost of higher latency; acks=1 is faster but can lose a just-written message if the leader dies before replication
Acks only affect consumers, not durability
questions.explanation: With acks=1 the leader acknowledges as soon as it has the message locally; if it crashes before replicas copy it, that message is gone. With acks=all the broker waits until the in-sync replicas have it, so a single broker loss won't lose data, trading latency for durability. Durability is a producer-side choice too, not just a consumer concern, and 'fast but lossy' vs 'slower but safe' is a deliberate tradeoff.

questions.quizTitle: Message Queues and Delivery Guarantees Quiz
questions.title: Queue vs Log (Replay)
questions.situation: After a bug, you want to reprocess the last 24 hours of events through a fixed consumer.
questions.question: A key difference between RabbitMQ-style and Kafka-style systems.
options: Always possible: every message system retains everything forever
Only at-most-once systems support replay
Replay requires deleting the topic first

A retained log (like Kafka) lets you reset the consumer offset and replay within the retention window; a classic queue typically removes a message once acknowledged, so it is gone and cannot be replayed
questions.explanation: A log-structured broker keeps messages for a retention period independent of consumption, so consumers track an offset and can rewind to reprocess history, great for bug fixes and new consumers backfilling. A traditional message queue deletes a message once it is acknowledged, so there is nothing to replay. Whether you can 'reprocess last 24h' depends on choosing a retained log vs a consume-and-delete queue up front.

questions.quizTitle: Message Queues and Delivery Guarantees Quiz
questions.title: The Dual-Write Problem and the Outbox
questions.situation: Your service must update its database and publish an event. It writes the DB, then crashes before publishing to the queue.
questions.question: Keeping the database and the queue consistent.
options: This is the dual-write problem: the DB and queue can diverge. The transactional outbox pattern writes the event into an outbox table in the same DB transaction, then a relay reliably publishes it, so the state change and the event are atomic
No problem, the two are always atomic
Just publish to the queue first, that removes all risk
Use two separate transactions and hope they both succeed
questions.explanation: Writing to a database and a message broker are two separate systems with no shared transaction, so a crash between them leaves state and events inconsistent (the dual-write problem). The transactional outbox writes the event row in the same local DB transaction as the state change, then a separate relay (polling or change-data-capture) publishes outbox rows to the broker at-least-once. The DB commit is the single source of truth, so the event is never lost or phantom-published.

questions.title: Purpose of Monitoring
questions.situation: Your team is launching a new web application. Your manager asks why you need to implement monitoring.
questions.question: What is the primary purpose of monitoring in a production system?
options: To track user behavior and sell data to advertisers
To make colorful dashboards for presentations
To detect problems early, ensure system health, and make informed decisions
To replace the need for testing and quality assurance
questions.explanation: Monitoring helps detect issues before they impact users, ensures systems are healthy and performing well, and provides data for capacity planning and optimization. It's a proactive approach to system reliability.

questions.title: CPU Metrics
questions.situation: You check your monitoring dashboard and notice the CPU metric showing 95% utilization for the past hour.
questions.question: Your web server's CPU usage is consistently at 95%. What does this indicate?
options: The system is working perfectly and efficiently
The server is likely overloaded and may need scaling or optimization
This is normal for all web servers
You should immediately restart the server
questions.explanation: Sustained high CPU usage (above 80-90%) typically indicates the server is struggling to handle the load. This can lead to slow response times, timeouts, and poor user experience. You should investigate the cause and consider scaling or optimization.

questions.title: Memory Usage
questions.situation: You're setting up monitoring for a new application server and need to track memory consumption.
questions.question: Which metric indicates how much RAM is actively being used by applications?
options: Disk space
CPU load average
Network bandwidth
Memory usage / RAM utilization
questions.explanation: Memory usage or RAM utilization tracks how much of your system's memory is being used by running processes. High memory usage can lead to swapping, performance degradation, or out-of-memory errors.

questions.title: Disk Space Alerts
questions.situation: You're configuring disk space monitoring for your database server. You want to be notified before running out of space.
questions.question: At what disk usage percentage should you typically set an alert?
options: 50% - alert when half full
70-80% - provide time to investigate and take action
99% - wait until the last moment
25% - alert when mostly empty
questions.explanation: Setting alerts at 70-80% disk usage gives you adequate warning time to investigate log growth, clean up unnecessary files, or add more storage before critical issues occur. Waiting until 99% is too late.

questions.title: Network Monitoring
questions.situation: Your application seems slow, and you suspect network issues. Which metric should you check?
questions.question: Which metric measures the amount of data transferred over the network?
options: Disk IOPS
Memory usage
CPU percentage
Network bandwidth / throughput
questions.explanation: Network bandwidth or throughput measures how much data is being transferred over the network. High usage can indicate legitimate traffic spikes, DDoS attacks, or misconfigured applications sending excessive data.

questions.title: Logging vs Monitoring
questions.situation: Your team is discussing whether to implement logging or monitoring for the new application.
