questions.question: What is the key difference between logging and monitoring?
options: Monitoring is free; logging costs money
They are exactly the same thing with different names
Logging is for developers; monitoring is only for operations
Logging records discrete events; monitoring tracks metrics over time
questions.explanation: Logging captures specific events and messages (like errors, user actions, or transactions), while monitoring tracks numerical metrics over time (like CPU usage, request rates, or response times). Both are essential and complementary.

questions.title: Alert Configuration
questions.situation: You're setting up your first alerts for a production system. What should you prioritize?
questions.question: What makes a good alerting rule?
options: Only alert the CEO directly for maximum visibility
Alert on every single metric change to catch everything
Alert only on actionable issues that require immediate attention
Never set up alerts - check dashboards manually every hour
questions.explanation: Good alerts are actionable (require human intervention), important (affect users or business), and have clear ownership. Too many alerts cause alert fatigue, while too few mean missing critical issues.

questions.title: Health Check Endpoints
questions.situation: You're deploying an API service and need to set up monitoring. The documentation mentions implementing a health check endpoint.
questions.question: What is a health check endpoint in a web application?
options: A security feature to scan for viruses
An endpoint that returns the application's operational status
A page that shows employee health insurance information
A backup system for data recovery
questions.explanation: A health check endpoint (typically /health or /healthz) is a simple URL that returns whether the application is running properly. Monitoring systems regularly check this endpoint to verify the service is alive and responding.

questions.title: Uptime Monitoring
questions.situation: Your SLA promises 99.9% uptime. Your manager asks how much downtime is acceptable per month.
questions.question: What does 99.9% uptime mean?
options: About 7 hours per month
About 43 minutes per month
About 3.65 days per year
No downtime ever allowed
questions.explanation: 99.9% uptime (three nines) means the service can be down for approximately 0.1% of the time. Per month (30 days), this equals about 43.2 minutes of acceptable downtime. 99.99% (four nines) would be about 4.3 minutes per month.

questions.title: Monitoring Tools
questions.situation: Your team needs to choose a monitoring solution for tracking CPU, memory, and application metrics over time.
questions.question: Which tool is commonly used for time-series metrics and monitoring?
options: Git
Prometheus
Slack
Microsoft Word
questions.explanation: Prometheus is a popular open-source monitoring system designed for collecting and storing time-series data. It's widely used with Grafana for visualization. Other popular options include Datadog, New Relic, and CloudWatch.

questions.title: Dashboard Design
questions.situation: You're creating your first monitoring dashboard for your team. What information is most important?
questions.question: What should a good monitoring dashboard display?
options: Key metrics that indicate system health and performance
Only colorful graphs to impress management
Every possible metric available in the system
Personal information about team members
questions.explanation: Effective dashboards focus on the most important metrics (KPIs) that indicate system health, like error rates, response times, throughput, and resource usage. They should be clear, actionable, and not overwhelming with unnecessary information.

questions.title: SLA Understanding
questions.situation: You're joining a new team and hear them discussing SLAs. What are they talking about?
questions.question: What is an SLA (Service Level Agreement)?
options: A type of software license
A team lunch schedule agreement
A commitment to a specific level of service quality and availability
A security audit checklist
questions.explanation: An SLA is a formal commitment between a service provider and customer defining expected service levels, typically including uptime guarantees, response times, and support availability. Violating SLAs can result in penalties or refunds.

questions.title: Response Time Monitoring
questions.situation: Your API is working without errors, but users are complaining. You check the response time metric and see it's 5 seconds per request.
questions.question: Why is monitoring API response time important?
options: Response time doesn't matter as long as requests eventually complete
5 seconds is fast enough for any application
Slow response times lead to poor user experience and potential timeouts
Response time only matters for mobile applications
questions.explanation: Response time directly impacts user experience. Slow responses frustrate users, can cause timeouts, and may indicate performance issues like database bottlenecks, inefficient code, or resource constraints. Most APIs should respond in milliseconds to a few seconds.

questions.title: Error Rate Metrics
questions.situation: Your monitoring dashboard shows the error rate climbing from 0.1% to 5% over the last hour.
questions.question: What does an increasing error rate indicate?
options: Indicates a problem that needs immediate investigation
This is normal fluctuation - ignore it
Users are making mistakes - provide better documentation
The monitoring system is broken
questions.explanation: A sudden increase in error rate typically signals a problem: recent code deployment issues, infrastructure problems, dependency failures, or increased load causing failures. This requires immediate investigation to prevent widespread user impact.

questions.title: Log Severity Levels
questions.situation: Your application encounters a database connection failure. What log level should this be recorded at?
questions.question: Which log level should you use for recording errors that need attention?
options: ERROR
INFO
DEBUG
TRACE
questions.explanation: ERROR level is for problems that need attention but don't crash the application. DEBUG is for detailed diagnostic info, INFO is for general informational messages, and TRACE is for very detailed debugging. FATAL/CRITICAL is for application-stopping errors.

questions.title: Observability Basics
questions.situation: Your team is implementing observability practices. What should you focus on?
questions.question: What are the three pillars of observability?
options: Development, staging, and production
CPU, memory, and disk
Frontend, backend, and database
Logs, metrics, and traces
questions.explanation: The three pillars of observability are: Logs (discrete events), Metrics (numerical data over time), and Traces (request flows through distributed systems). Together they provide comprehensive insight into system behavior.

questions.title: Alert Fatigue
questions.situation: Your team receives 50 alerts per day, but most aren't critical. Engineers start ignoring alerts.
questions.question: What is alert fatigue and why is it problematic?
options: When alerts are too quiet and people fall asleep
When the monitoring system gets tired and stops working
When too many non-critical alerts cause teams to ignore all alerts
A medical condition from working too many on-call shifts
questions.explanation: Alert fatigue occurs when teams receive too many alerts, especially false positives or low-priority notifications. This leads to desensitization where critical alerts are missed or ignored. Solution: create clear, actionable alerts and reduce noise.

questions.title: Data Retention
questions.situation: Your Prometheus setup keeps high-resolution data for 15 days but aggregates older data into hourly summaries.
questions.question: Why do monitoring systems typically aggregate older metrics data?
options: To confuse engineers looking at historical data
To save storage space while maintaining historical trends
Because old data is less important and should be deleted
Aggregation happens automatically and can't be controlled
questions.explanation: Storing every data point forever would require enormous storage. Aggregation (downsampling) reduces granularity for older data while preserving trends. For example, keeping 1-minute resolution for 30 days, then hourly for a year, provides useful history without excessive storage costs.

questions.title: Collecting Application Metrics
questions.situation: You're running a Node.js web application and need visibility into performance metrics.
questions.code:
# Metrics needed:
# - Request rate (requests/second)
# - Response time (p50, p95, p99)
# - Error rate (%)
# - Active connections
questions.question: Your application needs to track response times, error rates, and throughput. What's the best approach?
options: Use console.log() to print metrics and grep the logs
Manually track metrics in a spreadsheet
Only monitor when problems occur
Instrument code with Prometheus client library, expose /metrics endpoint, and scrape with Prometheus server
questions.explanation: Prometheus is the industry standard for metrics collection. Instrument your code with client libraries to expose metrics at /metrics, then Prometheus scrapes and stores time-series data. This enables powerful querying with PromQL, alerting, and visualization with Grafana. It's designed for high-cardinality metrics and dynamic environments.

questions.title: Centralizing Logs
questions.situation: Developers need to search logs across all services to debug issues. Currently, they SSH into each server.
questions.question: Your microservices architecture has 50 containers across 10 servers. How do you search logs?
options: SSH into each container and use grep
Email logs to developers daily
Use centralized logging with ELK Stack (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana) or Loki for aggregation, indexing, and search
Store logs only on local disk
questions.explanation: Centralized logging solutions like ELK Stack or Loki aggregate logs from all services into a searchable system. Logs are shipped (via Filebeat, Fluentd, or Promtail), indexed, and made searchable through a web UI. This enables correlation across services, retention policies, and eliminates the need to SSH into individual servers.

questions.title: Setting Up Effective Alerts
questions.situation: Your team gets too many alerts (50+ per day), causing alert fatigue. Critical issues are being missed.
questions.code:
# Current alerts:
# - Disk usage > 50% (fires constantly)
# - Any HTTP 404 error
# - CPU > 30%
# - Memory usage increases
# Result: Alert fatigue, missed critical issues
questions.question: What's the best strategy for alerting on application issues?
options: Alert on symptoms (user-facing issues like high error rates, slow response times) not causes, use severity levels, and set meaningful thresholds
Send all alerts to everyone on the team
Disable all alerts to reduce noise
Only alert during business hours
questions.explanation: Effective alerting focuses on symptoms users experience (errors, latency) rather than low-level metrics (CPU, memory). Use severity levels (critical, warning, info), set thresholds based on SLOs, and alert on rate of change rather than absolute values. Implement on-call rotations with escalation policies. This reduces noise while catching real issues.

questions.title: Debugging Microservices
questions.situation: Request latency is 5 seconds, but you don't know which of the 8 services in the call chain is slow.
questions.code:
# Request flow:
# API Gateway → Auth → UserService → 
# ProductService → InventoryService → 
# PricingService → CartService → PaymentService
# Total: 5 seconds (expected: 500ms)
questions.question: A user request touches 8 microservices. One service is slow. How do you identify the bottleneck?
options: Add timing logs to every service and correlate them manually
Restart all services and hope the issue resolves
Implement distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry, Jaeger, or Zipkin to track requests across services with trace IDs
Check each service individually until you find the slow one
questions.explanation: Distributed tracing instruments each service to propagate trace IDs through the request chain. Tools like Jaeger or Zipkin visualize the entire request flow, showing time spent in each service, dependencies, and bottlenecks. This is essential for debugging microservices architectures where requests span multiple services.

questions.title: Understanding Service Levels
questions.situation: You need to define reliability targets for your API service.
questions.code:
# Your API:
# - Current uptime: 99.5%
# - Customer contract requires 99.9%
# - You want to track availability
questions.question: What's the difference between SLI, SLO, and SLA?
options: SLI is what you measure (availability %), SLO is your internal target (99.95%), SLA is contractual commitment to customers (99.9%)
They're all the same thing with different names
SLA is more important, ignore SLI and SLO
Only enterprise companies need these, startups don't
questions.explanation: SLI (Service Level Indicator) is the actual measurement (e.g., % of successful requests). SLO (Service Level Objective) is your internal target (99.95% success rate). SLA (Service Level Agreement) is the contractual commitment to customers (99.9%) with penalties if missed. SLOs should be stricter than SLAs to provide a buffer. These form the foundation of site reliability engineering.

questions.title: The Four Golden Signals
questions.situation: You can only monitor 4 metric categories for your web application. Which should you choose?
questions.question: Which metrics are most important for monitoring a web service?
options: CPU, Memory, Disk, Network
Number of users, Revenue, Conversions, Bounce rate
Server count, Container count, Pod count, Node count
Latency, Traffic, Errors, Saturation (The Four Golden Signals)
questions.explanation: The Four Golden Signals from Google's SRE book are: Latency (response time), Traffic (requests/second), Errors (error rate), and Saturation (resource utilization). These metrics indicate user experience and system health better than infrastructure metrics alone. They apply to almost any service and help identify issues quickly.

questions.title: Preventing Alert Fatigue
questions.situation: Team morale is low due to constant alerts. Many alerts auto-resolve before anyone can investigate.
questions.code:
# Alert problems:
# - 60% auto-resolve within 5 minutes
# - 30% require no action
# - 10% are actionable issues
# On-call engineers burning out
questions.question: Your on-call engineer receives 100 alerts per week. Most aren't actionable. How do you fix this?
options: Increase alert thresholds so they fire less often
Ignore alerts that auto-resolve
Implement alert aggregation, set minimum duration before alerting, use warning vs critical severity, and create runbooks for each alert
Hire more engineers to handle the alerts
questions.explanation: Combat alert fatigue by: aggregating related alerts, requiring issues persist for minimum duration (e.g., 5 minutes) before alerting, using severity levels appropriately, creating clear runbooks for each alert, and regularly reviewing/removing noisy alerts. Every alert should be actionable and require human intervention. Auto-resolving alerts indicate improper thresholds.

questions.title: The Three Pillars of Observability
questions.situation: You're implementing a complete observability stack. How should you use each pillar?
questions.question: How do metrics, logs, and traces work together in observability?
options: Only use metrics, logs and traces are redundant
Use metrics to identify WHEN issues occur, logs to understand WHAT happened, traces to see WHERE in distributed systems. Correlate all three for complete observability
Use logs for everything, they contain all information
Metrics, logs, and traces are competing solutions, choose one
questions.explanation: The three pillars complement each other: Metrics show trends and trigger alerts (WHEN), Logs provide detailed context and error messages (WHAT), Traces show request flows through distributed systems (WHERE). Modern observability correlates all three using common identifiers (trace IDs, user IDs) to enable drilling down from high-level metrics to specific log entries and traces.

questions.title: Managing High-Cardinality Metrics
questions.situation: Your monitoring system is slow and expensive. You're tracking metrics with high-cardinality labels like user_id, session_id, and request_id.
questions.code:
# Metric:
# http_request_duration{user_id="...", endpoint="...", method="..."}
# - 10M users
# - 100 endpoints  
# - 4 HTTP methods
# = 4 billion time series!
questions.question: You want to track request latency by user ID (10 million users). What's the problem?
options: This is fine, track everything with maximum detail
Use sampling and exemplars for high-cardinality data, keep metrics aggregated, use logs or traces for individual request details
Delete old metrics to save space
Switch to a more expensive monitoring solution
questions.explanation: High-cardinality labels create massive numbers of time series, crushing performance and costs. Instead: keep metrics aggregated by low-cardinality labels (endpoint, status code), use sampling for high-cardinality data, use exemplars (links from metrics to traces), and store detailed per-request data in logs or traces. This provides necessary detail without overwhelming the metrics system.

questions.quizTitle: Multi-Region Active-Active Architecture on AWS Quiz
questions.title: Active-Active or Just Warm Standby?
questions.situation: Leadership asked for an active-active deployment across us-east-1 and eu-west-1. The current setup keeps both regions fully deployed and healthy, but Route 53 sends all live traffic to us-east-1. eu-west-1 only starts receiving requests when a health check fails and traffic shifts over. A new engineer asks whether this is really active-active.
questions.code:
Route 53 record set:
  app.example.com  FAILOVER  PRIMARY    -> us-east-1 ALB
  app.example.com  FAILOVER  SECONDARY  -> eu-west-1 ALB

Normal state: 100% of traffic -> us-east-1
eu-west-1: deployed, healthy, 0 live requests
questions.question: Your team calls the setup active-active, but one region only takes traffic during a failover. What actually defines active-active?
options: Nothing, this is active-passive: only one region serves live traffic, and the second takes over only on failover
It is active-active because both regions are deployed and healthy at the same time
It is active-active because the standby keeps instances running instead of scaling up from zero
It is active-active because both regions can reach the same primary database
questions.explanation: Active-active means every region serves live production traffic at the same time and shares the real load. What is described here is active-passive (warm standby): both regions are deployed and ready, but only us-east-1 takes traffic until a failover shifts it to eu-west-1. Having a healthy, warm, or even fully scaled second region does not make it active-active if that region sits idle during normal operation. The give-away is the FAILOVER routing policy with a single primary. To make it active-active you serve traffic to both regions at once, for example with latency-based or weighted records, and run the data layer so each region can handle its own share of writes.

questions.quizTitle: Multi-Region Active-Active Architecture on AWS Quiz
questions.title: Sending Users to Their Nearest Region
questions.situation: You run identical stacks in us-east-1 and eu-west-1, both live. Users in Europe report sluggish page loads. You check and they are resolving to the US endpoint. You want every user to land on whichever region answers fastest for them, and you want it to adjust as network conditions change.
questions.code:
$ dig +short app.example.com   # from a host in Frankfurt
52.0.0.10      # us-east-1 ALB  (~95 ms RTT)

# desired:
#   Frankfurt user -> eu-west-1   (~12 ms RTT)
#   Virginia user  -> us-east-1   (~8 ms RTT)
questions.question: European users keep hitting the US region and seeing slow responses. Which Route 53 policy fixes the latency?
options: Weighted routing with a fixed 50/50 split between the two regions
Latency-based routing, which sends each user to the region with the lowest measured network latency
Geolocation routing keyed only to the user's country code
Simple routing that returns both region IPs and lets the client choose
questions.explanation: Latency-based routing is the right tool. Route 53 keeps latency measurements between AWS regions and user networks and answers each query with the region that is fastest for that user, adjusting as conditions change. Weighted 50/50 ignores where the user is and would still send half of Europe to the US. Geolocation routing maps users by country or continent, which sounds similar but routes by political geography rather than measured latency, so it can miss the actually-fastest region and needs careful default rules. Simple routing returns records in no useful order and gives the client no latency signal at all.

questions.quizTitle: Multi-Region Active-Active Architecture on AWS Quiz
questions.title: Traffic Still Flowing to a Dead Region
questions.situation: us-east-1 is having a bad day: its ALB is returning 503s for most requests. You use latency-based records for us-east-1 and eu-west-1. Despite the failures, Route 53 keeps handing out the us-east-1 address to a chunk of users, and they get errors instead of being sent to the healthy region.
questions.code:
app.example.com  LATENCY  us-east-1  -> 52.0.0.10   (ALB returning 503)
app.example.com  LATENCY  eu-west-1  -> 34.0.0.20   (healthy)

Observed: us-east-1 still served to ~40% of users despite the 503s
questions.question: Your unhealthy region keeps getting traffic even though it is returning errors. What is missing from the Route 53 setup?
options: Drop the DNS TTL to zero so every client re-resolves on each request
Switch to weighted routing and set the failed region's weight to 0 by hand
Attach a Route 53 health check to each regional record so unhealthy endpoints are dropped from answers automatically
Enable DynamoDB global tables so the data layer fails over
questions.explanation: Route 53 only knows an endpoint is unhealthy if you attach a health check to the record. With health checks in place, Route 53 stops returning the failing region and serves only healthy answers, automatically and within the check interval. A zero TTL is impossible to honor in practice and just hammers your resolvers while still handing out the bad address. Manually setting a weight to 0 works only if a human is awake and watching, which defeats the point of fast failover. DynamoDB global tables handle the data layer, not DNS routing, so they would not stop traffic going to a broken front end.

questions.quizTitle: Multi-Region Active-Active Architecture on AWS Quiz
questions.title: A Database That Takes Writes in Both Regions
questions.situation: Your active-active app serves users from us-east-1 and ap-southeast-2. You want each region to write to a local database with single-digit millisecond latency, and you want those writes replicated to the other region automatically. You do not want app code reaching across the ocean for every write.
questions.code:
Requirements:
  - region-local writes (low latency) in BOTH regions
  - automatic async replication between regions
  - no single 'writer region' funneling normal writes
questions.question: You need both regions to accept writes locally with low latency. Which AWS database does that without forwarding writes to one region?
options: Aurora Global Database with one primary writer cluster
RDS Multi-AZ, with the standby promoted in the second region
DynamoDB global tables, which give each region a read/write replica with async cross-region replication
ElastiCache for Redis global datastore
questions.explanation: DynamoDB global tables are built for multi-active writes. Each region holds a full read/write replica, writes are accepted locally, and DynamoDB replicates them to the other regions asynchronously, usually within a second. Aurora Global Database has a single writer region; the others are read-only, and even write forwarding sends the write back to that one primary, so it is not truly multi-active for writes. RDS Multi-AZ is a single-region high-availability feature, not cross-region active-active. ElastiCache global datastore has one primary region for writes and read-only secondaries, so it does not give you local writes everywhere either.

questions.quizTitle: Multi-Region Active-Active Architecture on AWS Quiz
questions.title: Writes Failing in the Second Region
questions.situation: You set up Aurora Global Database with a primary cluster in us-east-1 and a secondary in eu-west-1, then pointed the EU app at the EU cluster endpoint. Reads work fine in Europe, but every INSERT and UPDATE from the EU app fails. The team expected active-active writes out of the box.
questions.code:
ERROR:  cannot execute INSERT in a read-only transaction

-- EU app connected to: aurora-euw1.cluster-xyz.eu-west-1.rds.amazonaws.com
-- primary writer cluster lives in: us-east-1
questions.question: You chose Aurora Global Database expecting writes in both regions, but the secondary rejects every write. Why?
options: The secondary replica is lagging too far behind to accept writes right now
Aurora Global Database has a single writer region; secondary regions are read-only unless you enable write forwarding or promote the secondary
The secondary cluster is missing a read replica node, so writes have nowhere to land
Global Database replicates only schema, so the EU writes need a separate replication path
questions.explanation: Aurora Global Database uses one writer region. Secondary regions expose read-only endpoints, so writing directly to them fails with a read-only transaction error. You have two options: enable write forwarding (the secondary forwards writes to the primary, which adds cross-region latency and still funnels through one writer), or promote the secondary during a failover so it becomes the new primary. Replication lag does not flip a replica into accepting writes. The secondary is not missing nodes, and Global Database replicates real data, not just schema. The point to remember: Aurora Global Database is great for low-latency cross-region reads and fast disaster recovery, but it is not multi-active for writes the way DynamoDB global tables are.

questions.quizTitle: Multi-Region Active-Active Architecture on AWS Quiz
questions.title: Two Regions Update the Same Item
questions.situation: You run DynamoDB global tables across us-east-1 and eu-west-1. A user's profile gets updated in both regions within a few hundred milliseconds, before replication catches up. Both writes succeed locally. You need to know which value survives once the regions sync.
questions.question: The same DynamoDB item is written in both regions at nearly the same instant. How is the conflict resolved?
options: DynamoDB rejects both writes and returns a conflict error to the application
DynamoDB merges the two items field by field and keeps both attributes
DynamoDB keeps both versions and returns them as a list on the next read
Last writer wins: the write with the later timestamp ('light') is kept and the other is overwritten
questions.explanation: DynamoDB global tables resolve concurrent cross-region writes with last-writer-wins, using an internal timestamp. The later write (theme: light at 10:00:00.250) is kept and the earlier one is dropped once replication reconciles. There is no application-visible conflict error and no automatic field-level merge, so a write you thought succeeded can be silently overwritten by one from another region. This shapes your design: if losing a write is unacceptable, do not let two regions own the same item. Common patterns are routing each item or user to a 'home' region, using conditional writes, or modeling updates as append-only events you reconcile yourself instead of overwriting a row.

questions.quizTitle: Multi-Region Active-Active Architecture on AWS Quiz
questions.title: Missing the Last Few Seconds of Writes
questions.situation: us-east-1 fails hard. You promote the eu-west-1 Aurora secondary to primary and bring the app back up there. Most things work, but a handful of orders placed in the last couple of seconds before the failure never made it to Europe and are now lost. Leadership asks how to describe and bound that loss.
questions.code:
12:00:03.9  order #8841 committed in us-east-1
12:00:04.0  us-east-1 becomes unreachable
12:00:04.0  replication to eu-west-1 had reached: 12:00:03.6

Lost writes: everything committed between 12:00:03.6 and 12:00:04.0
questions.question: After failing over to the secondary region, the most recent writes are gone. Which metric does that data loss map to?
options: RPO (recovery point objective): the data-loss window, set by cross-region replication lag at the moment of failure
RTO (recovery time objective): how long recovery takes, set mainly by DNS propagation
MTTR (mean time to repair): set by how fast the on-call engineer responds
SLA: the regional uptime percentage AWS commits to
questions.explanation: RPO is the amount of data you can afford to lose, measured as a time window, and it is set by how far behind your replication was when the source region died. Async cross-region replication always carries some lag, so writes committed inside that lag window are lost on an unplanned failover. RTO is different: it is how long it takes to be running again, not how much data you lose. MTTR is about repair time, and an SLA is a vendor uptime commitment, neither of which describes the lost-writes window. To shrink RPO you reduce replication lag or move to synchronous replication, but synchronous cross-region writes add latency to every transaction, which is the trade-off you are buying.

questions.quizTitle: Multi-Region Active-Active Architecture on AWS Quiz
questions.title: Duplicate Charges During Failover
questions.situation: When us-east-1 got slow, clients timed out and retried, and Route 53 sent the retries to eu-west-1. Some of those original requests had actually succeeded in us-east-1 before the timeout. Now you have duplicate orders and a few double charges, because the same logical request ran in both regions.
questions.code:
client -> POST /orders (timeout, no response)   # us-east-1 already committed it
client -> POST /orders (retry -> eu-west-1)      # commits a SECOND order

Result: 2 orders, 2 charges for 1 user action
questions.question: Clients retry against the new region during failover and you get duplicate orders. What stops the double side effects?
options: Raise the Route 53 TTL so clients stop retrying so quickly
Use idempotency keys so a repeated request with the same key is processed once, even across regions
Switch all reads to DynamoDB strongly consistent reads
Hold a global lock in the primary region for every write
questions.explanation: Idempotency keys are the standard fix. The client generates a unique key per logical action and sends it with the request; the server records the key with its result, so a retry carrying the same key returns the original outcome instead of doing the work twice. That is what protects you when retries land in a different region. Raising the TTL does not stop a client from retrying after a timeout. Strongly consistent reads only affect read freshness within DynamoDB, not duplicate writes across regions. A global lock in one region would force every write through a single point, destroying the low-latency region-local writes that make active-active worth doing, and it would not even be reachable when that region is the one failing.

questions.quizTitle: Multi-Region Active-Active Architecture on AWS Quiz
questions.title: User Uploads Missing in the Other Region
questions.situation: Your app lets users upload images. Uploads in us-east-1 land in an S3 bucket there, and the EU app reads from a separate EU bucket. EU users see broken images for anything uploaded on the US side, and the US side has the same problem in reverse. You want each region to keep its own local copy of every object so reads stay fast and available even if one region is down.
questions.code:
us-east-1: s3://app-assets-use1   (US uploads land here)
eu-west-1: s3://app-assets-euw1   (EU app reads here)

EU user requests an image uploaded in us-east-1 -> 404
questions.question: Objects uploaded in one region are missing when served from the other. What gives each region a local copy?
options: Turn on S3 Transfer Acceleration on both buckets
Put a single CloudFront distribution in front of the us-east-1 bucket
Set up S3 Cross-Region Replication in both directions so each bucket replicates its objects to the other
Enable S3 versioning on both buckets
questions.explanation: S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) copies objects from one bucket to a bucket in another region automatically. For active-active you configure it in both directions so an upload in either region replicates to the other, giving each region a local, independently-available copy. Transfer Acceleration only speeds uploads to a single bucket over the AWS edge network; it does not create a second copy. A single CloudFront distribution in front of the US bucket still has a hard dependency on that one bucket and region, so if us-east-1 is down, EU reads fail. Versioning is a prerequisite you must enable for CRR, but on its own it just keeps object history inside the same bucket and does nothing cross-region. Note that CRR is async, so expect a small replication delay and design for the case where an object has not arrived yet.

questions.quizTitle: Multi-Region Active-Active Architecture on AWS Quiz
questions.title: DNS Caching Slows Down Your Failover
questions.situation: You measured your failover and it is too slow. Even with low TTLs, some clients and intermediate resolvers cache the old DNS answer and keep connecting to the failed region for minutes. You want failover that does not depend on clients re-resolving DNS, ideally with fixed IP addresses your customers can allowlist.
questions.code:
TTL set to 60s, but observed:
  - mobile clients pinning DNS for 5+ minutes
  - a corporate resolver ignoring the TTL entirely
=> traffic still hitting the failed region long after failover
questions.question: Clients keep hitting the dead region because they cached the DNS answer. What fails over faster than DNS?
options: AWS Global Accelerator: static anycast IPs that route over the AWS backbone and shift away from an unhealthy region without any DNS change
Drop the Route 53 TTL to 1 second and rely on clients honoring it
Put CloudFront in front and let edge caching handle the failover
Switch the records to Route 53 latency-based routing
questions.explanation: AWS Global Accelerator gives you two static anycast IP addresses that stay constant while it steers traffic over the AWS backbone to the nearest healthy endpoint. When a region goes unhealthy, Global Accelerator reroutes within seconds at the network layer, so clients keep using the same IPs and never need to re-resolve DNS. That sidesteps the whole DNS-caching problem and hands you fixed IPs to allowlist. Lowering the TTL to 1 second does not help when clients and resolvers ignore TTLs, which many do. CloudFront is built for caching content at the edge, not for failing over a dynamic active-active backend. Latency-based routing is still DNS, so it inherits the same caching delays you are trying to escape.

questions.quizTitle: Multi-Region Active-Active Architecture on AWS Quiz
questions.title: A Failover Switch That Works During an Outage
questions.situation: During a regional event, your health-check-driven failover flapped: traffic bounced between regions as checks went green and red, amplifying the damage. You want an operator-controlled on/off switch to shift traffic away from a region and keep it there, and it has to keep working even when the affected region's control plane is impaired.
questions.code:
Incident timeline:
 12:01 health check fails  -> traffic shifts to eu-west-1
 12:02 check flaps green   -> traffic shifts BACK to us-east-1 (still broken)
 12:03 check fails again   -> shifts again ...
Result: route flapping made the outage worse
questions.question: Automated health-check failover flapped and made the incident worse. You want a reliable manual traffic switch. What does AWS offer?
options: Lower the health check failure threshold so it reacts faster
A Lambda triggered by a CloudWatch alarm that rewrites the Route 53 records
Set Global Accelerator endpoint weights to 0 for the bad region
Route 53 Application Recovery Controller routing controls: a highly available, operator-driven on/off switch for traffic, built to work during a regional impairment
questions.explanation: Route 53 Application Recovery Controller (ARC) routing controls give you exactly this: a deliberate, human-operated switch to shift traffic between cells or regions, backed by a cluster of five Regional endpoints so you can still flip it even when one region is in trouble. It also supports safety rules so you do not accidentally turn everything off at once. Lowering the health check threshold makes flapping worse, not better. A Lambda-plus-alarm setup depends on the very region and control plane that may be failing, and it is one more thing to break mid-incident. Global Accelerator weights help shape traffic but are not the durable, dependency-light manual control that ARC routing controls are built to be. The broader lesson: for the worst incidents you want a dependable manual override, not just reactive automation.

questions.quizTitle: Multi-Region Active-Active Architecture on AWS Quiz
questions.title: Both Regions Keep Writing During a Partition
questions.situation: A network partition cuts replication between us-east-1 and eu-west-1 for several minutes. Your DynamoDB global tables keep accepting writes in both regions the whole time. When the link heals, the regions reconcile and some conflicting writes get resolved by last-writer-wins. An architect asks you to name the trade-off being made and whether it fits a high-availability app.
questions.code:
Partition window (regions cannot replicate):
  us-east-1: accepts writes locally   (stays available)
  eu-west-1: accepts writes locally   (stays available)
Heal: reconcile via last-writer-wins, some writes overwritten

Question: availability or strong consistency?
questions.question: The link between regions breaks but both keep accepting writes. What consistency stance is that, and is it the right one?
options: It blocks writes in both regions until the link heals, choosing consistency over availability (a CP system)

It chooses availability over strong consistency (an AP system): both regions stay writable and conflicts reconcile later by last-writer-wins, which fits a high-availability app that tolerates eventual consistency
It elects a single region through a consensus protocol so writes stay strongly consistent during the partition
It guarantees no conflicts can happen because every write is globally serialized first
questions.explanation: This is the CAP trade-off in practice. During a partition you cannot have both perfect consistency and full availability, so you pick one. DynamoDB global tables choose availability and partition tolerance (AP): every region keeps serving writes, and the system accepts that data temporarily diverges and reconciles afterward with last-writer-wins. For most high-availability active-active apps that is the right call, because staying up matters more than being perfectly consistent for a few minutes, as long as your data model can tolerate eventual consistency and the occasional overwritten write. A CP system would block writes during the partition to stay consistent, trading away the availability you built active-active to get. There is no magic global serialization that removes the trade-off; if you need strong consistency you accept reduced availability instead, and you make that choice per workload.

questions.quizTitle: Multi-Region Active-Active Architecture on AWS Quiz
questions.title: Failover Stalls Because the API Is Throttled
questions.situation: Your failover runbook scales eu-west-1 from half capacity up to full only after us-east-1 fails, and it does that by calling the EC2 and Auto Scaling APIs during the incident. In a real regional event those control-plane calls get throttled and slow, so eu-west-1 never reaches full capacity in time and the failover effectively stalls while users get errors.
questions.code:
Failover step (runs DURING the incident):
  call autoscaling:SetDesiredCapacity  eu-west-1: 10 -> 20
  call ec2:RunInstances                (throttled, slow, partial)
=> healthy region cannot absorb the shifted load fast enough
questions.question: Your failover tries to scale up the healthy region by calling AWS APIs mid-incident, and it stalls. Which principle did you break?
options: Least privilege: the automation holds too many IAM permissions
Eventual consistency: the Auto Scaling group has not converged yet
Immutable infrastructure: you should be baking AMIs instead of scaling
Static stability: the healthy region should already hold enough pre-provisioned capacity so failover needs no control-plane actions during the event
questions.explanation: This is a static stability problem. A statically stable design keeps the standby or peer region already provisioned with enough capacity to take the full load, so failing over needs no new control-plane actions (no scaling up, no new instances, no extra API calls) at the worst possible moment. Control planes are exactly what gets stressed and throttled during a large regional event, so depending on them to grow capacity mid-incident is fragile. Pre-scale eu-west-1 to handle 100% before you ever need it, even though that idle headroom costs more in steady state, because that headroom is what buys you a reliable failover. Least privilege, eventual consistency, and immutable infrastructure are all real concerns, but none of them is why this failover stalled: the failure is the runtime dependency on the control plane to add capacity during the event.

questions.title: TCP/IP Stack Understanding
questions.situation: You're debugging a connectivity issue where packets are reaching the server but the application isn't responding. Understanding the network stack will help you identify where to look.
questions.code:
tcpdump output:
SYN packets arriving at port 443
No SYN-ACK response
Application logs show no incoming requests
questions.question: Which layer of the OSI model handles end-to-end communication and ensures data delivery?
options: Transport Layer (Layer 4) - Manages TCP/UDP connections and port numbers
Network Layer (Layer 3) - Routes packets between networks
Application Layer (Layer 7) - Handles HTTP, DNS, and application protocols
Data Link Layer (Layer 2) - Manages MAC addresses and switches
questions.explanation: The Transport Layer (Layer 4) is responsible for end-to-end communication, handling TCP/UDP connections, port numbers, and ensuring reliable data delivery. In this scenario, the issue is likely at Layer 4 (firewall blocking the port) or Layer 7 (application not listening).

questions.title: CIDR and Subnetting
questions.situation: You're setting up a VPC subnet for a microservices cluster and need to ensure you have enough IP addresses for 12 containers plus future growth.
questions.code:
Subnet: 10.0.1.0/28
Required IPs: 12 containers + 2 load balancers
AWS reserves 5 IPs per subnet (network, gateway, DNS, broadcast, reserved)
questions.question: How many usable IP addresses are available in a 10.0.1.0/28 subnet?
options: 14 usable IPs (16 total - 2 for network and broadcast)
11 usable IPs (16 total - 5 reserved by AWS)
16 usable IPs (all addresses in the range)
32 usable IPs (/28 means 32 addresses)
questions.explanation: /28 provides 2^(32-28) = 16 total IP addresses. AWS reserves 5 IPs in every subnet: network address (.0), VPC router (.1), DNS (.2), future use (.3), and broadcast (.255). This leaves 11 usable IPs, which wouldn't be enough for your 14 services. You'd need at least a /27 (27 usable IPs).

questions.title: CIA Triad Fundamentals
questions.situation: Your security team is implementing a disaster recovery strategy and needs to justify the cost of multi-region encrypted backups.
questions.code:
Backup Strategy:
- AES-256 encryption at rest
- Replicated to us-east-1, eu-west-1, ap-south-1
- Daily snapshots with 30-day retention
- Cross-account backup copies
questions.question: A database backup is encrypted at rest and replicated to three regions. Which CIA principle does this primarily address?
options: Confidentiality - encryption prevents unauthorized access to backup data
Integrity - checksums ensure data hasn't been tampered with
Availability - multi-region replication ensures data can be recovered if one region fails
All three equally - encryption (C), replication (A), and versioning (I)
questions.explanation: This strategy addresses all three CIA principles: Confidentiality through encryption, Integrity through cross-account copies and versioning (implied by retention), and Availability through multi-region replication. The multi-region aspect primarily addresses Availability, but the complete strategy covers all three.

questions.title: Zero Trust Architecture
questions.situation: Your company is moving from a traditional perimeter-based security model to Zero Trust. Leadership wants to understand the fundamental principle.
questions.code:
Old Model (Perimeter Security):
- VPN access = full internal network access
- Trust all traffic inside the firewall
- Single authentication at entry point

New Model (Zero Trust):
- Verify every request
- Least privilege access
- Assume breach
questions.question: Which statement best describes the Zero Trust security model?
options: Trust but verify - allow internal traffic but log everything for audit
Defense in depth - use multiple layers of firewalls and security tools
Never trust, always verify - authenticate and authorize every request regardless of network location
Principle of least privilege - give users minimum permissions needed
questions.explanation: Zero Trust's core principle is 'never trust, always verify' - every request must be authenticated and authorized, regardless of whether it comes from inside or outside the network. This eliminates the concept of a trusted internal network. While least privilege is a component, the fundamental shift is treating every request as potentially hostile.

questions.title: Security Groups vs NACLs
questions.situation: You need to block traffic from a specific IP range that's been identified as malicious. Should you use Security Groups or NACLs?
questions.code:
Requirement: Block 192.0.2.0/24 from accessing EC2 instances

Option 1 (Security Group):
- Inbound rules: Allow specific ports
- Cannot add explicit deny rules

Option 2 (NACL):
- Inbound rules: Can add deny rules
- Rules evaluated in number order
questions.question: What is the key difference between AWS Security Groups and Network ACLs?
options: Security Groups are stateful and only support allow rules; NACLs are stateless and support both allow and deny rules
Security Groups apply to subnets; NACLs apply to individual instances
Security Groups operate at Layer 7; NACLs operate at Layer 4
Security Groups are evaluated first; NACLs are the last line of defense
questions.explanation: Security Groups are stateful (return traffic is automatically allowed) and only support allow rules - you cannot explicitly deny traffic. NACLs are stateless (you must allow both inbound and outbound) and support both allow and deny rules evaluated in order. For blocking specific IPs, use NACLs since Security Groups cannot create deny rules.

questions.title: SSL/TLS Handshake Process
questions.situation: You're debugging an SSL certificate error and need to understand at which point in the handshake the certificate is validated.
questions.code:
TLS Handshake Steps:
1. Client Hello (supported ciphers, TLS version)
2. Server Hello (selected cipher, TLS version)
3. Server Certificate
4. Server Key Exchange
5. Client Key Exchange
6. Finished messages
questions.question: During the TLS handshake, when does the server send its certificate to the client?
options: After Server Hello - immediately after agreeing on cipher and TLS version
Before cipher negotiation - the certificate determines which ciphers can be used
After Client Key Exchange - once the client proves it can decrypt the certificate
During the Finished step - as part of the final handshake verification
questions.explanation: The server sends its certificate immediately after the Server Hello message, after the cipher suite and TLS version have been agreed upon. The client then validates the certificate (checking chain of trust, expiration, hostname match) before proceeding with key exchange. This is why certificate errors appear early in the connection process.

questions.title: IAM Policy Evaluation
questions.situation: You're implementing organization-wide restrictions using SCPs while individual teams manage their own IAM policies. Understanding evaluation order is critical.
questions.question: A user has an explicit Allow in an IAM policy and an explicit Deny in an SCP (Service Control Policy). What happens?
options: Allow wins - IAM policies are evaluated before SCPs
Most specific wins - the more restrictive Resource condition is used
Neither - conflicting policies cancel each other out, resulting in implicit deny
Deny wins - explicit deny always overrides allow in AWS
questions.explanation: In AWS, an explicit deny always wins, regardless of whether it's in an IAM policy, SCP, permission boundary, or resource policy. AWS policy evaluation follows: 1) Explicit deny = deny, 2) Explicit allow = allow, 3) Default = deny. SCPs set the maximum permissions boundary - even if an IAM policy allows an action, an SCP deny will block it.

questions.title: Kubernetes Network Policies
questions.situation: You're securing a microservices cluster and need to understand the baseline security posture before implementing network policies.
questions.code:
Cluster Setup:
- 50 microservices across 10 namespaces
- No NetworkPolicy resources defined
- Services communicate via ClusterIP
- External traffic via Ingress

Question: Can frontend pods communicate with database pods?
questions.question: What is the default behavior if no NetworkPolicy is applied to a pod in Kubernetes?
options: All traffic is denied - Kubernetes follows a deny-by-default model
All traffic is allowed - pods can communicate with any other pod on any port
Same-namespace traffic allowed - cross-namespace traffic is denied
Only labeled pods can communicate - unlabeled pods are isolated
questions.explanation: By default, Kubernetes allows all pod-to-pod communication. Pods can reach any other pod in any namespace on any port. Once you create a NetworkPolicy selecting a pod, that pod becomes isolated and only allows traffic explicitly defined in NetworkPolicy rules. This is the opposite of firewalls which typically deny by default.

questions.title: Secrets Management Best Practices
questions.situation: Your application needs to connect to a PostgreSQL database. Multiple teams are debating the best approach for credential management.
questions.code:
Requirements:
- Credentials should rotate automatically
- No secrets in git repository
- Audit logging of secret access
- Works with existing PostgreSQL RDS
questions.question: Which approach provides the best security for managing database credentials in Kubernetes?
options: Store credentials in Kubernetes Secrets, mount as environment variables
Use AWS Secrets Manager with IAM roles for service accounts (IRSA) and automatic rotation
Encrypt credentials with KMS and store in ConfigMap
Use HashiCorp Vault with dynamic database credentials
questions.explanation: HashiCorp Vault with dynamic database credentials is the gold standard. Vault generates short-lived credentials on-demand, rotates them automatically, provides audit logging, and revokes access when the lease expires. While AWS Secrets Manager (option 2) is also good, Vault's dynamic secrets are superior because credentials are unique per application and short-lived. Kubernetes Secrets (option 1) are just base64-encoded and don't rotate automatically.

questions.title: Web Application Firewall (WAF)
questions.situation: Your e-commerce site is experiencing attacks. The security team is proposing different solutions based on the attack patterns observed.
questions.code:
Attack Patterns Observed:
1. DDoS from botnet (1M requests/minute)
2. SQL injection in search parameters
3. Port scanning of backend servers
4. Brute force on SSH (port 22)

Proposed Solutions:
- AWS Shield for DDoS
- WAF for application attacks
- Security Groups for port filtering
questions.question: Which attack type is a WAF best suited to prevent?
options: SQL injection - WAF inspects HTTP requests and blocks malicious patterns
DDoS attacks - WAF can rate limit requests from malicious IPs
Port scanning - WAF monitors network traffic on all ports
SSH brute force - WAF can block authentication attempts
questions.explanation: WAF (Web Application Firewall) operates at Layer 7 and is designed to inspect HTTP/HTTPS traffic for application-layer attacks like SQL injection, XSS, and CSRF. While WAF can help with rate limiting for DDoS, dedicated DDoS protection (AWS Shield) is better. Port scanning and SSH attacks happen below Layer 7, so network-level controls (Security Groups, NACLs) are more appropriate.

questions.title: Certificate Lifecycle Management
questions.situation: You're automating certificate renewal for 200 domains and need to set up monitoring alerts. Understanding certificate lifetimes is essential.
questions.code:
Current Setup:
- Let's Encrypt certificates for all domains
- cert-manager in Kubernetes for automation
- Need to set alert threshold

Question: When should we alert if renewal fails?
questions.question: Your company uses Let's Encrypt certificates. What is the maximum validity period before renewal is required?
options: 30 days - Let's Encrypt certificates are valid for 30 days
90 days - Let's Encrypt certificates are valid for 90 days
1 year - standard SSL certificate validity
2 years - maximum validity before CA/Browser Forum changes
questions.explanation: Let's Encrypt certificates are valid for 90 days to encourage automation and limit the impact of key compromise. They recommend renewing at 60 days (30 days before expiry). Set alerts if renewal fails at 60 days, and critical alerts if certificates are within 7 days of expiry. The CA/Browser Forum reduced maximum certificate validity to 1 year in 2020, but Let's Encrypt has always used 90 days.

questions.title: Bastion Host Security
questions.situation: Your infrastructure team is designing secure access to private EC2 instances in a VPC. Database servers have no public IPs.
questions.code:
Architecture:
- Public subnet: Bastion host (public IP)
- Private subnet: Database servers (no public IP)
- Security Groups: Bastion allows SSH from office IP
- Database SG: Allows SSH only from Bastion SG

Access flow: Engineer → Bastion → Database
questions.question: What is the primary purpose of a bastion host (jump box)?
options: Load balancing - distribute SSH connections across multiple private instances
VPN replacement - provide encrypted tunnels to internal resources
SSH key management - centralized storage of SSH private keys
Single point of entry - control and audit all access to private resources
questions.explanation: A bastion host (jump box) provides a single, hardened point of entry to private resources. This allows you to: 1) Apply strict security controls in one place, 2) Enable detailed audit logging of all access, 3) Implement 2FA/MFA at the entry point, 4) Reduce attack surface by keeping other resources private. Modern alternatives include AWS Session Manager (no bastion needed) or Zero Trust access.

questions.title: Defense in Depth Strategy
questions.situation: Your security architect is presenting a comprehensive security strategy to leadership and needs to demonstrate layered security.
questions.code:
Scenario A: Single strong firewall with advanced rules

Scenario B: Multiple layers:
- Perimeter firewall
- WAF on application
- Security groups per service
- IAM roles with least privilege
- Encryption at rest and in transit
- Regular security scanning
questions.question: Which scenario best demonstrates the defense in depth principle?
options: Scenario A - investing in the best single security control is most effective
Both equally - it's about implementation quality, not quantity of controls
Scenario B - multiple overlapping security controls create redundancy
Neither - defense in depth only applies to physical security
questions.explanation: Defense in depth is the practice of layering multiple security controls so that if one fails, others still provide protection. Scenario B demonstrates this: if the perimeter firewall is bypassed, WAF provides application-level protection; if WAF is circumvented, Security Groups limit lateral movement; if an attacker gains access, IAM limits what they can do; and encryption protects data even if accessed. No single control is perfect, so layers are essential.

questions.title: VPN Protocols Comparison
questions.situation: Your company is replacing an old PPTP VPN solution. The team is evaluating OpenVPN, IPSec, and WireGuard for the new remote access solution.
questions.code:
Requirements:
- Support for 500+ remote users
- Mobile device support (iOS, Android)
- Modern encryption (no legacy vulnerabilities)
- Good performance on high-latency connections
- Easy to configure and maintain
questions.question: Which VPN protocol is generally considered most secure and modern?
options: PPTP - widely supported and fast
OpenVPN - mature, audited, and highly configurable
WireGuard - modern, minimal codebase, faster than OpenVPN
IPSec - industry standard with hardware acceleration
questions.explanation: WireGuard is the most modern VPN protocol with significant advantages: only 4,000 lines of code (vs 100,000+ for OpenVPN), uses modern cryptography (Curve25519, ChaCha20), faster handshakes, better roaming on mobile, and easier to audit due to simplicity. Linux kernel included it in 5.6. While OpenVPN (option 2) is also good and more mature, WireGuard is considered the future. PPTP is insecure and deprecated.

questions.title: SIEM and Log Aggregation
questions.situation: Security team wants to implement centralized logging. They're debating between basic log aggregation (ELK stack) vs full SIEM (Splunk, Datadog).
questions.code:
Log Sources:
- Application logs (1 TB/day)
- WAF logs
- VPC Flow Logs
- CloudTrail (API audit logs)
- OS security logs

Objective: Detect security incidents quickly
questions.question: What is the primary benefit of using a SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) system?
options: Cost reduction - SIEM consolidates logs to reduce storage costs
Compliance - SIEM provides log retention for regulatory requirements
Correlation and alerting - SIEM connects events across systems to detect threats
Performance - SIEM makes log queries faster than databases
questions.explanation: SIEM's core value is correlating events across multiple systems to detect security incidents. For example: failed login (App) + failed MFA (Identity) + API calls from unusual location (CloudTrail) + data exfiltration (VPC Flow Logs) = potential breach. Basic log aggregation shows individual events, but SIEM connects dots across systems and time to identify patterns indicating attacks. Modern SIEMs also use ML for anomaly detection.

questions.title: Container Security Best Practices
questions.situation: Your team is hardening container images for production. Multiple security improvements have been proposed.
questions.code:
Current Dockerfile:
FROM ubuntu:latest
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y python3
COPY app.py /app/
USER root
CMD ["python3", "/app/app.py"]

Proposed improvements:
A) Use specific version tags
B) Use minimal base images (alpine, distroless)
C) Run as non-root user
D) Scan for vulnerabilities
questions.question: Which approach most effectively reduces container security risks?
options: A only - version pinning prevents supply chain attacks
C only - running as non-root is the most critical security control
All of the above (A, B, C, D) - defense in depth for containers
B and C - minimal image + non-root user
questions.explanation: Container security requires defense in depth: A) Specific tags prevent unexpected changes and enable reproducible builds; B) Minimal images reduce attack surface (alpine/distroless have far fewer packages); C) Non-root prevents privilege escalation; D) Vulnerability scanning catches known CVEs. Each control addresses different risk vectors. A complete approach includes: minimal images, non-root, specific versions, scanning, read-only filesystems, and runtime security.

questions.title: Security Incident Response
questions.situation: At 2am, your monitoring alerts that unusual data is being exfiltrated from a production database. Multiple team members are on the incident call.
questions.code:
Alert Details:
- 50 GB data transfer to unknown IP (Russia)
- API key compromised (leaked in public GitHub repo)
- Data includes customer PII
- Transfer ongoing

Current state: Investigating root cause
questions.question: During a security incident, what should be the first priority?
options: Containment - immediately stop the data exfiltration and revoke compromised credentials
Root cause analysis - understand exactly how the breach occurred
Evidence preservation - take snapshots before making any changes
Notification - inform customers and regulators of the breach
questions.explanation: The incident response priority order is: 1) Containment (stop ongoing damage), 2) Eradication (remove attacker access), 3) Recovery (restore services), 4) Lessons learned. While evidence preservation is important, stopping ongoing data theft is critical - revoke the API key, block the IP, isolate the database. Take snapshots during containment if possible. Root cause analysis comes after containment. Notification timing depends on regulations (GDPR requires 72 hours).

questions.title: Multi-Factor Authentication
questions.situation: After several employees fell victim to phishing attacks, you're upgrading the company's MFA implementation.
questions.code:
Current: SMS-based OTP codes

Options to evaluate:
1. SMS OTP (current)
2. Authenticator app (TOTP like Google Authenticator)
3. Hardware security keys (FIDO2/WebAuthn like YubiKey)
4. Push notifications (like Duo Mobile)

Threat: Sophisticated phishing with real-time relay attacks
questions.question: Which MFA method provides the strongest security against phishing attacks?
options: SMS OTP - codes are convenient and work on any phone
Hardware security keys (FIDO2) - cryptographic proof that prevents phishing
Authenticator app (TOTP) - more secure than SMS and doesn't require cellular
Push notifications - easiest for users with smart approval workflows
questions.explanation: Hardware security keys using FIDO2/WebAuthn are phishing-resistant because they use public-key cryptography and verify the domain. The key only works on the legitimate site's domain - if a user is on a phishing site, the key won't respond. SMS is vulnerable to SIM swapping and interception. TOTP codes can be phished in real-time relay attacks. Push notifications can be approved accidentally (MFA fatigue attacks). For high-security environments, hardware keys are the gold standard.

questions.quizTitle: On-Call Rotation and Escalation Policy Quiz
questions.title: Picking a Rotation Pattern
questions.situation: You have six engineers across three time zones (US East, UK, India). Today, every alert goes to a shared Slack channel and whoever is awake responds. Pages are missed overnight. Leadership asks you to design the first formal rotation.
questions.code:
Team layout:
- 2 engineers in New York (UTC-5)
- 2 engineers in London (UTC+0)
- 2 engineers in Bengaluru (UTC+5:30)

Current state:
- Single Slack channel for alerts
- 4 missed pages last month between 02:00-06:00 local for whoever was on-duty
- Average ack time at night: 38 minutes
- Average ack time during business hours: 4 minutes
questions.question: A small distributed team is setting up its first on-call rotation.
options: One weekly rotation covering all 24 hours, primary picks one engineer regardless of location
A follow-the-sun rotation with three regional shifts so each engineer is only paged during their working hours
Keep the shared channel but require everyone to install the PagerDuty app on their phones
Rotate daily so nobody gets stuck with a bad week
questions.explanation: Follow-the-sun shifts let each region cover its waking hours. That fixes the root cause: people were being paged while asleep. Single 24-hour rotations create burnout fast for a six-person team. Pushing alerts to a shared channel without ownership is what got them into this mess. Daily rotation adds churn and breaks context between handoffs.

questions.quizTitle: On-Call Rotation and Escalation Policy Quiz
questions.title: When the Primary Doesn't Ack
questions.situation: Your team just configured its first escalation policy in PagerDuty. The primary engineer's phone was on Do Not Disturb. The alert page below shows what happened. You're deciding what step 2 of the escalation should look like.
questions.code:
Incident timeline:
03:17:02  PagerDuty triggers incident #4821 (severity: high)
03:17:03  Primary engineer (Alice) paged - SMS + push + phone call
03:17:04  No response
03:22:00  ??? what happens here ???

Current policy:
level_1:
  notify: alice@team.com
  timeout: 5m
level_2:
  notify: ???
  timeout: 5m
questions.question: An alert fires at 03:17 and nobody acknowledges it. What should the escalation policy do next?
options: Re-page Alice every 5 minutes until she acknowledges, since she is the on-call
Send the alert to the team Slack channel and hope someone sees it
Page the secondary on-call engineer, then escalate to the engineering manager if still unacked after another 5 minutes
Auto-resolve the incident after 15 minutes since nobody is responding
questions.explanation: Escalation exists exactly for the case where the primary cannot respond, phone died, sleeping through it, sick, whatever. Hammering the same person rarely works. Slack channels are not a paging mechanism, nobody has Slack notifications on at 3am. Auto-resolving an unacked incident hides real outages. A proper policy moves to a secondary on a short timeout, then to a manager or wider team if the secondary also doesn't ack.

questions.quizTitle: On-Call Rotation and Escalation Policy Quiz
questions.title: Reading the Signs of Alert Fatigue
questions.situation: You took over as the team's tech lead two months ago. You've noticed some patterns in how people interact with pages. The on-call retro this week included these comments.
questions.code:
Retro notes:
- "I just ack and silence everything now, I'll check in the morning"
- "Half the alerts auto-resolve before I even open my laptop"
- 312 pages last month across 4 engineers (78 per person)
- 71% of pages auto-resolved without action
- 4 engineers asked to drop off the rotation this quarter
- One engineer admitted to muting PagerDuty during a shift
questions.question: Your on-call engineers are starting to behave in concerning ways. Which signal points most clearly to alert fatigue?
options: The team needs more training on how to use PagerDuty effectively
The number of pages and self-resolution rate prove the alerts are not actionable, and people are coping by ignoring them
Engineers are not committed enough to operational excellence
The on-call shifts are probably too short, longer shifts would build muscle memory
questions.explanation: When 71% of pages auto-resolve, the alert is not telling you anything useful, it is just noise. People who ignore or mute pages are not lazy, they are responding rationally to a broken signal. Training cannot fix bad alerts. Longer shifts make burnout worse, not better. The fix is to ruthlessly delete alerts that do not require human action and tune the rest.

questions.quizTitle: On-Call Rotation and Escalation Policy Quiz
questions.title: Spot the Bug in This Escalation Policy
questions.situation: A teammate wrote this policy for a new service and asked for your review before they apply it. The service is customer-facing with a 99.9% availability SLO.
questions.code:
name: payments-api-escalation
rules:
  - level: 1
    notify:
      - alice@team.com
    timeout_minutes: 30
  - level: 2
    notify:
      - bob@team.com
    timeout_minutes: 30
  - level: 3
    notify:
      - cto@company.com
    timeout_minutes: 60
repeat: false
questions.question: Review this PagerDuty-style escalation policy. What's the most serious problem with it?
options: The CTO should not be on an escalation policy, only engineers should
The 30 minute timeout is far too long for a customer-facing service; the SLO allows about 43 minutes of total downtime per month
The policy should use phone calls instead of email notifications
Three escalation levels is too many, two is the standard
questions.explanation: A 99.9% SLO leaves roughly 43 minutes of error budget per month. Waiting 30 minutes before even paging a secondary burns most of your monthly budget on a single incident. For a customer-facing service, level 1 timeouts of 5 to 10 minutes are typical. Notification channel (the policy already includes the engineer's contact, channels are configured per-user), having a leader as a final fallback, and the number of levels are all reasonable choices.

questions.quizTitle: On-Call Rotation and Escalation Policy Quiz
questions.title: Symptom-Based vs Cause-Based Alerts
questions.situation: The on-call team is auditing alerts on the checkout-service. They want to keep one of these two rules and delete the other. The service has an SLO of 99.5% successful requests.
questions.code:
# Rule A
- alert: CheckoutHighCPU
  expr: rate(node_cpu_seconds_total{job="checkout",mode!="idle"}[5m]) > 0.85
  for: 10m
  labels:
    severity: page
  annotations:
    summary: "Checkout service CPU above 85%"

# Rule B
- alert: CheckoutErrorRateHigh
  expr: |
    sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout",status=~"5.."}[5m]))
    / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout"}[5m])) > 0.005
  for: 5m
  labels:
    severity: page
  annotations:
    summary: "Checkout 5xx rate exceeds SLO budget"
questions.question: You have two Prometheus alert rules covering the same service. Which one should you keep?
options: Rule A, because high CPU is a leading indicator and you want to catch problems before users see them
Rule B, because it pages on actual user-facing symptoms tied directly to the SLO
Keep both, since CPU and error rate are independent signals
Delete both and use synthetic monitoring instead
questions.explanation: Page on what users feel, not on causes. High CPU is often fine, a service can run hot and still serve requests perfectly. Paging on CPU produces noise and trains the team to ignore alerts. Rule B fires when actual users are getting errors, which is what your SLO measures. Keep cause-based metrics for dashboards and post-incident analysis, not for waking people up.

questions.quizTitle: On-Call Rotation and Escalation Policy Quiz
questions.title: Choosing the Right Severity
questions.situation: Your team uses a four-level severity matrix. A new alert just fired and you need to triage. The internal admin dashboard is returning 500 errors. Only 5 engineering staff use this dashboard, never customers. It's used to view sales reports.
questions.code:
Severity matrix:
SEV-1: Customer-facing outage or data loss. Page primary + manager. All hands.
SEV-2: Major feature degraded for customers, or full outage of an internal critical tool. Page primary.
SEV-3: Minor customer impact, or internal tool degraded. Ticket only, fix during business hours.
SEV-4: No impact, informational. No page, log only.

Incident details:
- Service: internal-admin-dashboard
- Symptom: HTTP 500 on /reports endpoint
- Users affected: 5 internal staff
- Workaround: query the warehouse directly
- Time: 02:14 local
questions.question: Pick the correct severity for the scenario below using the team's severity matrix.
options: SEV-1, any 500 error indicates a serious problem that needs all-hands attention
SEV-2, the dashboard is broken and internal tools need to stay up
SEV-3, internal tool with a workaround and no customer impact, fix it in the morning
SEV-4, since no customer is affected this is just informational
questions.explanation: Severity should reflect impact, not the size of the error message. No customer is affected, a workaround exists, and only five internal users use the tool. Waking someone up for this trains them to ignore SEV-1s. SEV-1 is reserved for customer-facing pain or data loss. SEV-2 is for major internal tools that block work, a reports page does not qualify. SEV-4 understates it, the dashboard genuinely is broken and needs a ticket and a fix.

questions.quizTitle: On-Call Rotation and Escalation Policy Quiz
questions.title: What to Include in a Handoff
questions.situation: You spent the week on-call. A few incidents are still unresolved, you noticed a noisy alert, and there's a planned database migration tomorrow morning. You have 15 minutes to write the handoff before logging off.
questions.code:
This week's state:
- Open incident #5102: intermittent 502s on cart-service, root cause not found, mitigation: retries enabled
- Alert "DiskUsage85" fired 14 times, every time it cleared itself within 10 minutes
- Planned: db schema migration scheduled for Tuesday 09:00 by data team
- New runbook added for Redis evictions
- Two engineers in EU region taking PTO Mon-Wed
questions.question: You're ending your week-long shift. What belongs in the handoff to the next on-call?
options: A summary of what you fixed this week, since the next on-call needs to know your accomplishments
Open incidents, ongoing investigations, known noisy alerts, planned changes, and any unusual coverage gaps
Just the open incidents, everything else can be found in PagerDuty history
A full retrospective with timelines for every incident you handled
questions.explanation: A good handoff transfers the operational context the next person needs to act fast. Open incidents tell them what is still broken. Noisy alerts let them filter signal from noise. Planned changes prevent them from being surprised by a database migration at 9am. Coverage gaps matter when they need to escalate. What you fixed this week and full retrospectives belong in different documents, the handoff is about what the next person needs in the next 7 days.

questions.quizTitle: On-Call Rotation and Escalation Policy Quiz
questions.title: Multi-Window Burn Rate Alert
questions.situation: Your team is moving away from threshold-based alerts and toward SLO burn rate alerts. A senior SRE proposes this rule for the payments service with a 99.9% availability SLO over 30 days.
questions.code:
- alert: PaymentsErrorBudgetBurn
  expr: |
    (
      sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="payments",status=~"5.."}[1h]))
      / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="payments"}[1h])) > (14.4 * 0.001)
    )
    and
    (
      sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="payments",status=~"5.."}[5m]))
      / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="payments"}[5m])) > (14.4 * 0.001)
    )
  for: 2m
  labels:
    severity: page
questions.question: Why does this SLO alert use two windows instead of one?
options: Two windows just doubles the alert evaluations, it's a mistake
The long window detects sustained burn and the short window makes the alert fire quickly without waiting an hour
The 5 minute window is for tests, it should be removed in production
Two windows let you alert on both the average and the median error rate
questions.explanation: Multi-window multi-burn-rate alerts solve the trade-off between alert latency and false positives. A short window alone fires on every small blip. A long window alone takes too long to detect a real outage. Requiring both to exceed the burn rate threshold gives you fast detection (5m window) while filtering out brief spikes (1h window must also be burning). This is the pattern described in the Google SRE Workbook for SLO-based alerting.

questions.quizTitle: On-Call Rotation and Escalation Policy Quiz
questions.title: Fixing a Noisy Disk Alert
questions.situation: Every time a nightly batch job runs, this alert fires for about 20 minutes while temporary files are written. Then the job cleans up and the alert resolves. The on-call has paged seven times in the last week from this single rule.
questions.code:
- alert: HostDiskUsageHigh
  expr: (1 - node_filesystem_avail_bytes / node_filesystem_size_bytes) > 0.80
  for: 1m
  labels:
    severity: page
  annotations:
    summary: "Disk usage above 80% on {{ $labels.instance }}"

Context:
- Disk reaches 82-86% during nightly batch job 02:00-02:25
- Recovers to 60% after job finishes
- Job runs every night, has run reliably for 18 months
- True disk-full incident in past 18 months: 0
questions.question: This alert paged seven times last week. How do you fix it?
options: Raise the threshold to 90% so the batch job no longer triggers it
Change the alert to predictive: page only if disk is filling at a rate that would hit 100% within 4 hours, and ticket (not page) at static high thresholds
Disable the alert during the 02:00-02:25 window using a silence
Add more disk space to the host so it never crosses 80%
questions.explanation: Static thresholds on disk usage are almost always wrong. Raising the threshold to 90% just delays the problem and hides actual leaks. Silences need to be maintained and break when the batch job moves. Adding disk treats the symptom not the design flaw. A predictive alert based on fill rate catches actual problems (slow leaks, runaway logs) without firing on planned, self-correcting spikes. Pair it with a ticket-level static alert for the unusual case of a sudden jump.

questions.quizTitle: On-Call Rotation and Escalation Policy Quiz
questions.title: Making On-Call Sustainable
questions.situation: Three engineers have left the rotation in the past six months. The remaining engineers are picking up more shifts. One of them, your strongest IC, just sent this Slack message.
questions.code:
Slack message from senior engineer:

"Hey, I need to talk about on-call. Last month I got paged 23 times,
11 of those were between midnight and 5am. I haven't had a full
weekend off in 7 weeks because the rotation is short-staffed.
I know we need coverage but I can't keep doing this. I'm thinking
about looking for another job if this doesn't change."

Current state:
- 4 engineers in rotation, was 7 six months ago
- Average pages per week per engineer: 6
- Page volume trend: increasing
- Compensation: none, on-call is unpaid
questions.question: Your best engineer just asked to leave the rotation. What's the most effective long-term fix?
options: Add on-call pay so people are compensated for the pain
Hire more engineers to spread the rotation across more people
