  - "Got 200 OK but charge never went through"

Traffic: ~2,000 req/s to POST /v1/charges
questions.question: Which SLI best captures what users actually care about for this payment API?
options: Percentage of /healthz pings that return 200 within 1 second
Number of support tickets filed per week about payment issues
Average response time of all API endpoints over a 24-hour window
Percentage of POST /v1/charges requests that return a successful response (non-5xx) within 2 seconds
questions.explanation: Good SLIs measure what users experience on the critical path. A healthz ping (option A) misses slow queries and partial failures entirely. Support tickets (option B) are lagging indicators with too much noise. Average response time (option C) hides outliers since a few 30-second requests vanish in the average. Option D directly measures the user-facing endpoint, combines availability (non-5xx) with latency (under 2s), and matches the complaints you are getting.

questions.quizTitle: SLOs, SLIs, and Error Budgets Quiz
questions.title: Error Budget Calculation
questions.situation: Your team's SLO is 99.9% successful requests over a 30-day rolling window. It is day 20 of the month. You had a bad deploy on day 5 that caused errors for 4 hours, and a network blip on day 15 that caused 30 minutes of partial failures.
questions.code:
SLO: 99.9% success rate (30-day window)
Total requests (30 days): ~50,000,000
Error budget: 0.1% = 50,000 failed requests allowed

Day 5 incident:  38,000 failed requests
Day 15 incident:  6,000 failed requests
Budget used:      44,000 / 50,000 = 88%

Pending deploy: new checkout flow (estimated risk: moderate)
questions.question: How much error budget does this team have left, and what should they do?
options: 88% budget used is fine. Ship the new checkout flow since you still have 12% remaining.
You have 12% budget left with 10 days remaining. Proceed with the deploy but add extra monitoring and a quick rollback plan.
Cancel the deploy entirely. With 88% budget consumed, no deploys should happen until the window resets.
Renegotiate the SLO to 99.5% so the incidents no longer count against you.
questions.explanation: With 12% budget remaining and 10 days left, you are not in crisis but you are tight. Blindly shipping (option A) ignores the risk. A full freeze (option C) is too aggressive since you still have budget to spend. Changing the SLO to hide past incidents (option D) defeats the purpose. The right call is to proceed carefully: deploy with extra monitoring, have a rollback plan ready, and be prepared to freeze if this deploy eats more budget. Error budgets exist to make exactly this kind of risk-aware decision.

questions.quizTitle: SLOs, SLIs, and Error Budgets Quiz
questions.title: SLO Window Types
questions.situation: It is March 3rd. On February 27th, your service had a major outage lasting 6 hours. The SRE dashboard shows two panels for the same 99.9% availability SLO, but they disagree.
questions.code:
Dashboard Panel A (Calendar Month - March):
  SLO: 99.9% availability
  Current: 99.98% ✅
  Status: Healthy

Dashboard Panel B (30-day Rolling):
  SLO: 99.9% availability
  Current: 99.72% ❌
  Status: Budget Exhausted

Outage: Feb 27, 14:00 - 20:00 UTC (6 hours)
questions.question: Why is the team seeing different SLO compliance numbers for the same service?
options: Panel A uses a calendar month reset, so the February outage does not count in March. Panel B uses a rolling 30-day window, so February 27th is still within range.
Panel B is broken. A 6-hour outage 4 days ago should not show as budget exhausted.
Both panels are wrong because they should use the same window type for consistency.
Panel A is correct. Calendar windows are the industry standard and rolling windows inflate incident impact.
questions.explanation: Calendar windows reset at the start of each month, so Panel A sees a fresh slate on March 1st. Rolling windows look back exactly 30 days from right now, so Panel B still includes the Feb 27 outage until March 29. Rolling windows are generally better for SLOs because they do not create a 'free pass' at the start of each month or a panic zone at the end. Calendar windows can incentivize bad behavior like pushing risky deploys on the 1st of the month when the budget is full.

questions.quizTitle: SLOs, SLIs, and Error Budgets Quiz
questions.title: Multi-Window Burn Rate Alerts
questions.situation: Your on-call team is drowning in SLO alerts. The current setup fires whenever the error rate exceeds 0.1% in any 5-minute window. You get paged 15 times a week, but only 2 of those pages lead to actual error budget impact. You need to redesign the alerting.
questions.code:
Current alert (too noisy):
  IF error_rate > 0.1% FOR 5m
  THEN page oncall
  Result: 15 pages/week, 87% false positive rate

Option A:
  IF error_rate > 14.4x budget burn FOR 1h
  AND error_rate > 14.4x budget burn FOR 5m
  THEN page oncall

Option B:
  IF error_rate > 1x budget burn FOR 30d
  THEN page oncall

Option C:
  IF total_errors_today > daily_budget
  THEN send email
questions.question: Which alerting setup will catch real problems without flooding the team with false alarms?
options: Option A: Multi-window burn rate alert, fast burn detection with short confirmation window
Option B: Single long window catches all budget-impacting events
Option C: Daily email is less disruptive than pages
Keep the current setup but increase the threshold to 0.5%
questions.explanation: Option A implements the Google SRE multi-window, multi-burn-rate approach. The 1-hour window detects if you are burning budget 14.4x faster than normal (you would exhaust the entire month's budget in about 2 days at that rate). The 5-minute window confirms the problem is still happening right now, filtering out brief spikes. Option B with a 30-day window reacts too slowly since by the time it fires, the budget is already gone. Option C is not actionable for urgent issues. Simply raising the threshold (option D) does not fix the structural problem of using a single short window.

questions.quizTitle: SLOs, SLIs, and Error Budgets Quiz
questions.title: Error Budget Policy Enforcement
questions.situation: Your team's 99.95% availability SLO has burned through 100% of its error budget on day 18 of the month. The product manager is pushing for a large feature release scheduled for tomorrow. The VP of Engineering asks what the error budget policy says.
questions.code:
Error Budget Status:
  SLO: 99.95% availability (30-day rolling)
  Budget: 21.6 minutes of downtime allowed
  Used: 25 minutes (115% consumed)
  Remaining: -3.4 minutes

Pending work:
  - Feature release (large, touches payment flow)
  - 3 reliability improvements (P1)
  - Database index optimization (reduces p99 latency)

Error Budget Policy (approved by VP Eng):
  Budget > 50%: normal development
  Budget 20-50%: deploy with extra caution
  Budget < 20%: reliability work only
  Budget exhausted: freeze features, reliability only
questions.question: What should happen when the error budget is fully consumed mid-month?
options: Ship the feature anyway since error budget policies are guidelines, not rules
Reset the error budget early and ship everything since the incidents were not the team's fault
Negotiate with the PM to split the feature into smaller releases to reduce risk
Follow the policy: freeze feature releases and focus only on the three reliability improvements and the database optimization
questions.explanation: The error budget policy exists precisely for this situation. When budget is exhausted, the team shifts to reliability-only work. This is not punishment; it is the mechanism that balances feature velocity against reliability. Option A undermines the entire SLO framework. Option C sounds reasonable but still ships features when the policy says not to. Option B removes accountability. The policy was pre-approved by the VP, so the decision is already made. The reliability improvements and database optimization directly help recover the budget for next month.

questions.quizTitle: SLOs, SLIs, and Error Budgets Quiz
questions.title: Setting the Right SLO Target
questions.situation: Your team is launching an internal inventory service that other teams depend on. You are deciding between 99.9% and 99.99% availability. The service runs on a single Kubernetes cluster, uses a managed PostgreSQL database, and has no multi-region failover.
questions.code:
Infrastructure:
  - Single k8s cluster (us-east-1)
  - Managed PostgreSQL (single-region, automated backups)
  - No multi-region failover
  - 3 replicas behind a service mesh

Dependencies:
  - Cloud provider SLA: 99.99% for compute
  - Managed DB SLA: 99.95%
  - Network SLA: 99.99%

Team size: 4 engineers, no dedicated SRE
On-call: shared rotation with another team
questions.question: What SLO target should this team set for their new internal microservice?
options: 99.99% (52 minutes downtime/year) since that matches the cloud provider SLA
99.9% (8.7 hours downtime/year) since the infrastructure and team size cannot realistically support anything higher
99.999% (5 minutes downtime/year) to set an ambitious target that pushes the team to improve
99.95% as a compromise between the database SLA and the compute SLA
questions.explanation: Your SLO cannot be higher than what your weakest dependency can deliver. The managed DB only promises 99.95%, so 99.99% (option A) is already impossible to guarantee. 99.999% (option C) is fantasy for a single-region setup with 4 engineers. More importantly, a 4-person team with shared on-call cannot realistically respond fast enough to maintain 99.99%. Setting an unreachable SLO just means the budget is always exhausted and the policy is always triggered, making the entire system meaningless. 99.9% gives a realistic target with enough budget to ship features while still holding a meaningful reliability bar.

questions.quizTitle: SLOs, SLIs, and Error Budgets Quiz
questions.title: Where to Measure Your SLI
questions.situation: Your web application sits behind a CDN, then a load balancer, then an API gateway, then the application servers. Users report intermittent 502 errors, but your application logs show zero errors. You need to figure out where to measure.
questions.code:
Request path:
  User → CDN → Load Balancer → API Gateway → App Server

Measurement options:
  A: App server access logs
     Shows: 0 errors (all requests it receives succeed)

  B: Load balancer access logs
     Shows: 0.3% 502 errors (gateway timeouts)

  C: CDN edge logs
     Shows: 0.5% errors (includes CDN-level issues)

  D: Synthetic monitoring (external)
     Shows: 0.8% failures (includes DNS, network issues)
questions.question: Where should this team measure their availability SLI to get the most accurate picture of user experience?
options: App server logs (A) since that is where your code runs and you control the quality
Load balancer logs (B) since they capture gateway issues the app server misses
CDN edge logs (C) since they are closest to the full user experience without external noise
Synthetic monitoring (D) since it captures everything the user experiences including network issues
questions.explanation: The best SLI measurement point is as close to the user as possible while still being within your control. App server logs (A) miss the 502s entirely since the requests never reach the app. Load balancer logs (B) catch more but miss CDN-level failures. CDN edge logs (C) capture nearly the full user experience and represent infrastructure you control and can act on. Synthetic monitoring (D) includes external network issues you cannot fix, which would burn error budget on problems outside your control. The gap between C (0.5%) and A (0%) explains exactly why users see errors your app logs miss.

questions.quizTitle: SLOs, SLIs, and Error Budgets Quiz
questions.title: Understanding Burn Rate
questions.situation: A deploy went out at 10:00 AM and the error rate jumped. It is now 10:30 AM. You need to decide whether to roll back immediately or wait to see if it stabilizes.
questions.code:
SLO: 99.9% success rate (30-day window)
Total monthly requests: ~100,000,000
Error budget: 100,000 failed requests

Since deploy (10:00 - 10:30):
  Total requests: 500,000
  Failed requests: 5,000
  Error rate: 1.0%
  Normal error rate: 0.05%

Burn rate = actual_error_rate / budget_error_rate
         = 1.0% / 0.1%
         = 10x
questions.question: At this burn rate, when will the error budget be fully consumed?
options: At 10x burn rate, the entire monthly budget will be gone in about 72 hours. Roll back now since every minute costs 10x the normal budget.
At 10x burn rate, the entire monthly budget will be gone in about 3 days. Wait an hour to see if it stabilizes.
The burn rate math does not matter. 1% error rate is within acceptable range for a new deploy.
At 10x burn rate, the budget is already gone. Declare an incident immediately.
questions.explanation: A 10x burn rate means you are consuming 10 days worth of error budget every day. A 30-day budget at 10x burn rate lasts 30/10 = 3 days (72 hours). While 72 hours sounds like you have time, every minute at this rate costs 10 minutes of budget. Waiting an hour to see (option B) burns 10 hours of budget for no reason. The budget is not gone yet (option D) since 30 minutes at 10x only consumed about 0.7% of monthly budget. But the trend is clear: roll back now, investigate, and redeploy when the root cause is fixed.

questions.quizTitle: SLOs, SLIs, and Error Budgets Quiz
questions.title: Defining What Counts as an Error
questions.situation: You are configuring the error classification for your REST API's availability SLI. The API handles CRUD operations on user profiles. You need to decide which responses count as 'bad' events in your SLI ratio.
questions.code:
Recent response codes from access logs:
  200 OK              - 89.2%  (successful requests)
  201 Created          -  4.1%  (new resources created)
  400 Bad Request      -  3.2%  (invalid user input)
  401 Unauthorized     -  1.5%  (expired tokens)
  404 Not Found        -  1.1%  (missing resources)
  429 Too Many Requests -  0.5%  (rate limited)
  500 Internal Error   -  0.3%  (bugs/crashes)
  503 Service Unavail  -  0.1%  (overloaded)

Question: which codes are 'errors' for the SLI?
questions.question: Which of these HTTP responses should count against the availability SLI for this API?
options: All non-2xx responses (400, 401, 404, 429, 500, 503) since any non-success response is a failure
Only 5xx responses (500, 503) since those indicate the server failed to do its job
5xx responses plus 429 (500, 503, 429) since rate limiting and server errors both mean the user could not complete their request
All 4xx and 5xx responses except 401 since authentication failures are the user's problem
questions.explanation: The key question is: did the service fail to serve a valid request? 400s are the client sending bad data, not a service failure. 401 means the token expired, which is expected behavior. 404 for a missing resource is correct behavior. But 429 means the service refused a valid request because it is overloaded, which is a service-side problem the user should not have to deal with. 500 and 503 are clear server failures. Counting all non-2xx (option A) would mean every typo in a request hurts your SLO, which makes the metric useless for measuring service health.

questions.quizTitle: SLOs, SLIs, and Error Budgets Quiz
questions.title: Composite SLOs for User Journeys
questions.situation: Your checkout flow involves 4 microservices: cart, pricing, payment, and notification. Each has its own SLO. But users only care whether checkout works end-to-end. The product team wants a single SLO for 'checkout success rate'.
questions.code:
Individual service SLOs:
  cart-service:     99.95% availability
  pricing-service:  99.9%  availability
  payment-service:  99.95% availability
  notification-svc: 99.5%  availability

Checkout flow (sequential):
  1. GET  /cart/summary     (cart-service)
  2. POST /pricing/calculate (pricing-service)
  3. POST /payment/charge   (payment-service)
  4. POST /notify/receipt   (notification-service)

Theoretical combined availability:
  0.9995 × 0.999 × 0.9995 × 0.995 = 0.9930 (99.30%)
questions.question: How should you define an SLO for a multi-step user journey that spans several services?
options: Set the checkout SLO at 99.30% since that is the mathematical product of all service availabilities
Do not create a composite SLO. Monitor each service independently and let teams own their own SLOs.
Set the checkout SLO at 99.95% since that is what most of the individual services promise
Set the checkout SLO at 99.9% to match the lowest-availability critical service, and make step 4 (notification) async so it does not block checkout success
questions.explanation: The mathematical worst case (option A) is too pessimistic and does not account for design choices. The notification service is the weakest link at 99.5%, but a failed receipt email should not mean 'checkout failed' since the payment went through. Making notification async removes it from the critical path. With the remaining three services (99.95% × 99.9% × 99.95% = 99.80%), a 99.9% composite SLO is achievable with some headroom by investing in retry logic and graceful degradation. Option B misses the point: users do not care which microservice failed, they care that checkout worked.

questions.quizTitle: SLOs, SLIs, and Error Budgets Quiz
questions.title: Diagnosing Silent Budget Drain
questions.situation: Your API has a 99.9% success rate SLO. No incidents were declared this month, but the error budget dashboard shows 70% consumed on day 10. The on-call log has zero pages. Something is silently eating your budget.
questions.code:
Error budget consumption:
  Day 1-5:   15% consumed (normal)
  Day 6:     25% consumed (jumped 10%)
  Day 7-10:  70% consumed (steady drain)

Recent changes:
  Day 5: Deploy v2.4.1 (new search feature)
  Day 6: No deploys
  Day 7: Deploy v2.4.2 (config update)

Alert config:
  Page if: error_rate > 1% for 5 minutes
  Current error rate: 0.15% (below page threshold)
  Normal error rate:  0.05%

Error breakdown:
  500 errors on /api/search: +200% since day 5
  All other endpoints: normal
questions.question: The error budget is draining faster than expected but there are no incidents. What is the most likely cause?
options: The alerting threshold is too low and needs to be raised to catch these errors
The v2.4.1 deploy introduced a bug in the search endpoint that errors at a rate too low to trigger alerts but high enough to steadily drain the budget
The error budget dashboard is miscalculating. A 0.15% error rate cannot consume 70% of budget in 10 days.
The config update in v2.4.2 is the likely cause since config changes are riskier than code changes
questions.explanation: This is a classic slow-burn scenario. The error rate tripled from 0.05% to 0.15% after the v2.4.1 deploy. That is below the 1% paging threshold, so no one gets alerted. But 0.15% against a 0.1% error budget means you are consuming budget 1.5x faster than allowed, every hour, every day. Over 5 days, that adds up fast. The fix is twofold: roll back or fix the search bug, and implement burn-rate alerting (like multi-window alerts) that catches slow burns before they drain the budget. This is exactly why simple threshold-based alerts are insufficient for SLO monitoring.

questions.quizTitle: SLOs, SLIs, and Error Budgets Quiz
questions.title: SLOs for Async Processing
questions.situation: Your data pipeline consumes events from Kafka, transforms them, and writes to a data warehouse. There are no HTTP endpoints. The analytics team needs data to appear in the warehouse within 15 minutes of the event occurring. You need to define an SLO.
questions.code:
Pipeline:
  Source: Kafka topic (user-events, ~10M events/day)
  Processing: Flink job (transform + enrich)
  Sink: BigQuery table (analytics.user_events)

Current metrics:
  Kafka consumer lag: usually < 1 minute
  Processing time: avg 30s, p99 5 minutes
  End-to-end latency (event time to warehouse): p50=2min, p99=12min

Data quality:
  ~0.01% events fail schema validation → dead letter queue
  ~0.001% events duplicated in warehouse
questions.question: How should you define an SLO for a system that processes messages from a queue instead of serving HTTP requests?
options: SLO: 99.9% of events processed successfully within 15 minutes of event timestamp, measured by comparing event_time to warehouse ingestion_time
SLO: Kafka consumer lag must stay below 1 minute, 99.9% of the time
SLO: Average end-to-end latency under 5 minutes measured daily
SLO: Zero events in the dead letter queue per day
questions.explanation: Option A directly measures what the analytics team cares about: events appearing in the warehouse within 15 minutes. It uses event_time (when it happened) not processing_time (when your system saw it), which is the right anchor. Consumer lag (option B) only measures one piece of the pipeline and misses processing delays. Average latency (option C) hides outliers, and a daily measurement cannot catch problems in time. Zero DLQ events (option D) is unrealistic and does not capture the latency requirement at all. The 99.9% target with 10M events/day allows up to 10,000 events to be slow, which is a reasonable error budget for a data pipeline.

questions.title: The Two From Addresses
questions.situation: A customer forwards you a screenshot: the email claims to be from billing@yourcompany.com. Your logs show the bounce went back to a completely different address at a domain you do not own. Nobody has been hacked. Both addresses were set by the sender, in two different places.
questions.code:
MAIL FROM:<bounces@sender-infra.net>      <- envelope
RCPT TO:<customer@example.com>
DATA
From: Billing <billing@yourcompany.com>   <- header
Subject: Your invoice
questions.question: A message shows one sender in the inbox and a different one in the bounce. Which field does the recipient actually see?
options: The header `From:`, set inside DATA. The envelope `MAIL FROM` governs routing and bounces, and normally survives only as a `Return-Path` header most people never open
Both, concatenated, which is why the screenshot looks odd
The envelope `MAIL FROM`, because that is what the receiving server validated
Whichever one SPF passed on, since receivers display the authenticated address
questions.explanation: SMTP carries the sender twice and does not require the two to match. The envelope `MAIL FROM` is transport: it decides where a bounce goes. The header `From:` is content: it is what the mail client renders. Nothing in the protocol forces agreement, which is precisely why spoofing is trivial and why SPF, DKIM and DMARC exist at all. SPF validates the envelope domain, DKIM signs the message so its signing domain can be verified, and DMARC is the layer that insists one of those authenticated domains matches the header `From:`. If you have never watched this happen at the wire level, it is worth doing once: [Send an Email by Hand](/posts/send-an-email-by-hand-raw-smtp).

questions.title: What SPF Actually Authenticates
questions.situation: You publish a strict SPF record. A phishing message arrives at a customer showing `From: ceo@yourcompany.com`. You check the headers: SPF passed. The record was never wrong.
questions.code:
v=spf1 include:_spf.smtpfa.st -all

# The phishing message:
MAIL FROM:<anything@attacker-domain.com>   SPF checked against THIS
From: ceo@yourcompany.com                  displayed to the human
questions.question: Your SPF record is correct and published. A spoofed email still reaches the inbox showing your domain. How?
options: The SPF record needed `-all` rather than `~all` to be enforced
SPF only authenticates the envelope `MAIL FROM` domain, so an attacker passes SPF on their own domain and puts anything in the header `From:`
The attacker must have compromised one of the hosts in your `include:`
SPF had not propagated yet, so receivers fell back to allowing the message
questions.explanation: SPF authenticates the envelope `MAIL FROM`, and the `HELO` name alongside it. Neither is the address your recipient sees. An attacker sends from their own domain, passes SPF legitimately because it really is their mail server, and writes whatever they like in the header `From:`. SPF passed, and the message is still a forgery. DMARC is what closes the gap, by requiring that at least one mechanism both **passes** and **aligns**: the SPF-authenticated domain or the DKIM signing domain has to match the header `From:`. SPF alone, no matter how strict the `-all`, cannot stop this.

questions.title: Why DMARC Fails When SPF Passes
questions.situation: You send through a provider. Your monitoring shows messages authenticating successfully on both SPF and DKIM, and yet the DMARC aggregate reports keep recording failures. Nothing is misconfigured in the sense of being broken.
questions.code:
From:          news@yourcompany.com
MAIL FROM:     bounces@provider-infra.net   SPF: pass (for provider-infra.net)
DKIM d=        provider-infra.net           DKIM: pass (for provider-infra.net)
DMARC:         fail
questions.question: SPF passes, DKIM passes, DMARC fails. What is the most likely cause?
options: The DMARC record is missing a `pct` tag so receivers cannot decide what to enforce
DKIM and SPF cannot both be evaluated on the same message; receivers pick one
Neither authenticated domain aligns with the header `From:` domain, and DMARC requires alignment, not merely a pass
The DMARC policy is set to `p=none`, which always reports a failure
questions.explanation: DMARC does not ask "did SPF pass?". It asks "did SPF pass **for a domain that matches the header From**, or did DKIM pass for one?". Here both passed for the provider's own domain, which authenticates the provider, not you. The fix is alignment: a custom return-path subdomain on your domain so envelope SPF aligns, or the provider signing with `d=` set to your domain, which needs the key published and the provider configured to use it. DMARC needs only one mechanism to pass and align, not both. DKIM alignment is usually the more durable of the two, because a signature can survive a forwarder that changes the connecting IP, though a list that rewrites signed headers will break it just as thoroughly.

questions.title: The Mailing List Problem
questions.situation: Your DMARC reports show a steady trickle of SPF failures, all from the same handful of receiving domains. The messages are legitimate. They are being forwarded through mailing lists and alumni-style forwarding addresses.
questions.question: A subscriber forwards your newsletter through a mailing list. SPF breaks. Why does DKIM often survive?
options: Forwarders are required by RFC to re-sign with the original private key
SPF is advisory and receivers skip it for forwarded mail
DKIM keys are cached by receivers for 24 hours, so a second delivery reuses the first result
SPF checks the connecting IP, and a forwarder relays from its own IP; DKIM signs the message body and headers, which the forwarder usually leaves intact
questions.explanation: SPF authenticates a connection: this IP is allowed to send for this envelope domain. Put a forwarder in the middle and the connecting IP changes, so SPF either fails or passes for the forwarder's own domain, which does not align with your `From:` either way. DKIM authenticates the message itself with a signature over selected headers and the body, so it keeps verifying wherever the message travels, as long as nothing rewrites what was signed. A list that rewrites a signed header or the body breaks the signature too, which is why ARC exists: it records what an earlier hop concluded, rather than repairing the original signature. This is the practical reason to make sure DKIM aligns rather than relying on SPF alignment alone.

questions.title: The Tag That Disappeared
questions.situation: You rolled out DMARC carefully, using `pct` to apply your policy to a small slice of mail while you watched the reports. That record has been sitting in DNS untouched for a year.
questions.code:
v=DMARC1; p=reject; pct=10; rua=mailto:dmarc@example.com

# What did you think this meant?
# What does a DMARCbis receiver do with it?
questions.question: DMARCbis removed `pct`. What happens to a record that still has `pct=10` on it?
options: The whole record is invalid, so DMARC is not applied at all and the domain is unprotected
Receivers ignore the retired tag and apply `p=reject` to **every message that fails DMARC**, rather than the tenth you had been sampling
Receivers fall back to `p=none` because the record uses a tag they do not recognise
Nothing changes; `pct` is deprecated but receivers are required to keep honouring it
questions.explanation: The record is not rejected as invalid. Receivers parse it, discard the unknown `pct`, and apply the policy to everything that fails DMARC rather than to a sample of it. If `pct=10` was the only thing keeping a misaligned sender delivering, that sender stops, and the change arrives without any deployment of yours. DMARCbis removed `pct` along with `rf` and `ri`. The replacement, `t=y`, is a testing flag rather than a percentage dial: it asks receivers to apply a policy one step softer, so `reject` behaves as `quarantine`. Receivers apply their own judgement on top of all of this in any case. The full list of changes is in [DMARCbis Is Here](/posts/dmarcbis-what-changed-new-dmarc).

questions.title: Policy for Subdomains That Do Not Exist
questions.situation: Your domain has a strict DMARC policy and no subdomain policy set. An attacker sends from billing.yourcompany.com, which has no DNS records at all because it has never existed. You want to say something about subdomains that were never created, without committing to a policy for the real subdomains your other teams use.
questions.code:
v=DMARC1; p=reject; rua=mailto:dmarc@example.com
# note: no sp tag

# Attacker uses:  From: ar@billing.yourcompany.com
# That subdomain has no records of any kind.
questions.question: Which DMARCbis tag lets you set a policy for subdomains that were never created, separately from the real ones?
options: `adkim=s`, since strict alignment refuses any subdomain that cannot sign
`pct=100`, which extends the policy to cover every name under the domain
`np`, which applies only to non-existent subdomains and leaves real ones following `sp`, or `p` when `sp` is absent
`psd`, which declares the domain a public suffix and blocks unknown children
questions.explanation: Without `np`, a non-existent subdomain inherits `sp`, or `p` when `sp` is absent, so it is not unprotected. What `np` buys you is the ability to treat the two cases differently: reject anything from a subdomain that was never created, while keeping a softer policy for the real subdomains other teams are still fixing. The tag is not new to DMARCbis, it came from RFC 9091 and DMARCbis carries it forward. `psd` is for registry operators declaring a public suffix, `adkim` controls alignment strictness rather than which names are covered, and `pct` no longer exists. See [DMARCbis Is Here](/posts/dmarcbis-what-changed-new-dmarc).

questions.title: Reading a Bounce Correctly
questions.situation: Your application sends a receipt and gets a rejection back immediately. The response code starts with 5. Another address in the same batch returned `452 4.2.2 Mailbox full`.
questions.code:
550 5.1.1 <nobody@example.com>: User unknown in virtual mailbox table
452 4.2.2 <full@example.com>: Mailbox full, try again later
questions.question: A send returns `550 5.1.1 User unknown`. What should your system do with that address?
options: Suppress both, because any bounce raises your complaint rate with the receiver
Retry the 550 once to confirm, then suppress if it repeats; discard the 452
Retry both with exponential backoff, since any bounce can be transient under load
Suppress the 550 permanently; the 452 is temporary and should be retried later
questions.explanation: The first digit carries the decision. A 5xx is a permanent failure for this attempt: retrying the same message unchanged will not help, and doing it repeatedly is how sender reputation is spent. A 4xx is temporary, a full mailbox or a greylist or a rate limit, and is meant to be retried until a deadline. Be careful about what a 5xx tells you. `5.1.1 User unknown` is about the address and justifies suppressing it. Other 5xx replies are about the message or your reputation, such as a rejected attachment or a blocked IP, and suppressing the recipient for those punishes the wrong thing. Read the enhanced status code, not just the first digit, before deciding an address is dead. Permanently suppressing a 4xx is its own bug: you quietly stop mailing a customer whose mailbox was briefly full.

questions.title: Where to Start With DMARC
questions.situation: Marketing uses one platform, the product sends transactional mail through another, finance sends invoices from an ERP, and there are three more you only found last week. Nobody knows whether they all authenticate correctly.
questions.code:
# Candidate first records:
v=DMARC1; p=reject;   rua=mailto:dmarc@example.com
v=DMARC1; p=none;     rua=mailto:dmarc@example.com
v=DMARC1; p=quarantine; rua=mailto:dmarc@example.com
questions.question: You are introducing DMARC to a domain that sends through six different services. What is the correct first record?
options: `p=none` with `rua`, which enforces nothing and starts the aggregate reports that tell you who is sending
No DMARC record until all six services are verified, since a wrong record is worse than none
`p=reject`, because anything weaker leaves the domain spoofable while you deliberate
`p=quarantine`, as a middle path that neither blocks legitimate mail nor allows forgeries
questions.explanation: `p=none` is not a weak policy, it is an instrument. It changes nothing about delivery and it turns on the aggregate reports, which are the only way to discover the six services, plus the two nobody remembered. Going straight to `p=reject` on a domain you have not surveyed is how an invoice run silently stops arriving. The sequence that works is: `none` and read the reports, fix alignment for each legitimate sender, then `quarantine`, then `reject`. Under DMARCbis you move through that with the `t=y` testing flag rather than the removed `pct`. One caveat worth knowing before you commit to `reject`: it interacts badly with users who post to mailing lists, because the list rewrites the message and breaks the signature.

questions.title: Making SPF Align
questions.situation: Your DKIM is aligned and DMARC passes on that basis. You want SPF to align as well, for redundancy when a forwarder breaks one of them. The From address must stay hello@yourcompany.com, because it is what customers see, and the existing DKIM alignment must not be disturbed.
questions.code:
# Now
From:      hello@yourcompany.com
MAIL FROM: bounces@provider-infra.net    SPF aligns with the provider, not you

# Wanted
MAIL FROM: bounces@mail.yourcompany.com
questions.question: You need SPF alignment for DMARC while keeping your own address in the From line. What has to change?
options: Add the provider to your SPF record with `include:`, which makes their sending IPs authorised for your domain
Ask the provider to sign with your DKIM key under their own `d=` domain
Set up a custom return path on a subdomain of yours, so the envelope domain becomes `mail.yourcompany.com` and aligns with the header `From:` under relaxed alignment
Set `aspf=r` so relaxed alignment accepts the provider's unrelated domain as close enough
questions.explanation: Alignment compares domains, not IP addresses. Adding `include:` authorises the provider's servers to send for your domain, which matters, but SPF is still evaluated against whatever is in `MAIL FROM`, and that is still the provider's own bounce domain. The fix is a custom return path: the provider gives you DNS records to publish on a subdomain of yours, and the envelope sender moves to it. Relaxed alignment, which is the default, counts a subdomain of your organisational domain as aligned; strict alignment would not. The exact records vary by provider, so follow theirs rather than assuming a CNAME. `aspf=r` is already the default and does not stretch to an unrelated domain. A worked setup, records and all, is in [From DNS to Delivery](/posts/from-dns-to-delivery-smtpfast).

questions.title: The Setting That Makes You an Open Relay
questions.situation: You stand up a mail server for an internal application. Within a day it is sending tens of thousands of messages you did not write, and your IP is on three blocklists.
questions.code:
# Which of these is the mistake?
smtpd_recipient_restrictions =
    permit_mynetworks,
    permit_sasl_authenticated,
    ???
questions.question: Which configuration turns a mail server into an open relay?
options: Listening on port 25 rather than 587, which exposes the server to the public internet
Allowing plaintext AUTH before STARTTLS has been negotiated
Having no SPF record, which lets anyone claim to be your domain
Accepting mail from arbitrary untrusted clients and relaying it onward to arbitrary external destinations you are not responsible for
questions.explanation: An open relay carries mail for strangers to strangers. The defining property is accepting a `RCPT TO` for a destination you are not responsible for, from a client you have no reason to trust. Spammers find these within hours. Note that relaying itself is not the problem: an authenticated user, or a trusted internal network, or a gateway relaying for a domain it is configured to accept, are all legitimate. The word that matters is unauthorised, not unauthenticated. The other options are real issues but none of them makes you carry someone else's mail: plaintext AUTH leaks credentials, and a missing SPF record hurts deliverability. Listening on port 25 is simply what a receiving MTA does. In Postfix the control is `smtpd_relay_restrictions` with `reject_unauth_destination`. The [SMTP Flow Simulator](/games/smtp-flow-simulator) lets you try the conversation an open relay would accept.

questions.title: Which Port for What
questions.situation: Code that works on your laptop times out in production. The connection to port 25 never establishes. Nothing in the logs suggests authentication or TLS.
questions.code:
# laptop:  connect smtp.provider.com:25    ok
# cloud VM: connect smtp.provider.com:25   timeout
questions.question: Your application cannot send mail from a cloud VM on port 25. What is the right response?
options: Use port 587 with authentication and STARTTLS. Many cloud providers block outbound 25 to limit abuse, and 25 is primarily for server-to-server transfer rather than submission
Use port 465, which is the modern replacement for both 25 and 587
Request that the provider unblock port 25, since it is the only port defined for SMTP
Route through a local relay on the VM listening on 25, which avoids the block
questions.explanation: Port 25 is primarily for mail transfer between servers. Port 587 is the submission port: a client authenticates and hands a message to a provider to send on its behalf. Many cloud providers block outbound 25 by default, because an unrestricted VM fleet is a spam cannon, and will unblock it only with a reason. Port 465 is implicit-TLS submission and is equally valid, having been un-deprecated; the distractor is wrong because it claims to replace both, not because 465 is bad. A timeout on its own does not prove a block, so confirm with your provider rather than assuming, but this is a submission problem rather than a firewall argument to win. If you have never watched a submission conversation happen line by line, the [SMTP Flow Simulator](/games/smtp-flow-simulator) walks through it.

questions.title: Why the Suppression List Is Not Optional
questions.situation: A retry job re-queues everything that failed yesterday, including the addresses that came back `550 User unknown`. The volume is small, a few hundred messages.
questions.question: Why must a sending system refuse to send to an address that previously hard bounced?
options: Each retry is billed as a new message, so the cost compounds
Receivers treat repeated delivery to addresses they have said do not exist as a sign of a list you do not maintain, and that feeds the reputation affecting where your good mail lands
The bounce webhook fires again, which double counts your metrics
SMTP forbids resending to an address that returned a 5xx, and the server will refuse the connection
questions.explanation: Sender reputation is largely a judgement about whether you know who your recipients are. Repeatedly mailing addresses a receiver has already said do not exist is clear evidence that you do not, and it feeds into the placement decisions applied to everything else you send. That is why suppression belongs in the send path rather than a cleanup job: it should be impossible to send to a suppressed address, not merely unusual. Suppression is not irreversible, and should not be: an address suppressed by mistake, or corrected later, needs a way back. Billing and duplicated metrics are real consequences too, but they are not the reason the list exists.

questions.title: Rotating a DKIM Key Without Breaking Mail
questions.situation: Your DKIM key has been in place for three years and you want to replace it. Messages you send today may sit in a queue, or be forwarded and re-verified by another hop, for some time after they leave you.
questions.code:
# Selectors let more than one key be live at once
selector1._domainkey.example.com   TXT  v=DKIM1; k=rsa; p=<old>
selector2._domainkey.example.com   TXT  v=DKIM1; k=rsa; p=<new>
questions.question: How do you rotate a DKIM key so that no in-flight mail fails verification?
options: Replace the key in the existing selector record, since DNS propagation is fast enough that the gap is negligible
Publish both keys in the same selector record, and receivers will try each in turn
Rotate during a send freeze, so that no message is ever in flight with the old key
Publish the new key under a second selector, switch signing to it, and remove the old selector only after mail signed with it has aged out
questions.explanation: A DKIM signature names the selector it was signed with, so verification looks up that specific record. Publishing the new key under a second selector means both stay verifiable, and the changeover becomes a change in which key you sign with rather than a change to what receivers can check. Publish the new record first and confirm it resolves, allowing for DNS caching, then switch signing, then leave the old selector in place while mail signed with it is still in flight or being re-verified by forwarders. Verification normally happens when a message is received rather than when someone opens it, so the window is shorter than it sounds, but it is not zero. A single selector record cannot hold two keys, and a send freeze does not help because the problem is mail already sent.

questions.title: What STARTTLS Does Not Give You
questions.situation: A colleague argues that because all your mail is sent over TLS, the anti-spoofing records are redundant. The connection really is encrypted.
questions.code:
220 mail.example.com ESMTP
EHLO client
250-STARTTLS
STARTTLS
220 Ready to start TLS
# ...encrypted from here...
questions.question: Your SMTP connection uses STARTTLS. Which of these is still true?
options: Anyone can still claim to be any sender, because TLS protects the connection and says nothing about who wrote the message
Receivers will treat the message as authenticated and skip SPF
The message is signed, so DKIM becomes unnecessary
The header `From:` is now cryptographically bound to the connecting server
questions.explanation: TLS protects the pipe. It can authenticate the server you connected to, and with client certificates the other direction too, and it stops someone on the path reading or altering the message in transit. What it does not do is say anything about who wrote the message: the party at the other end of a perfectly good encrypted connection can still put any address in the header `From:`. Opportunistic STARTTLS is also downgradeable unless something enforces it, whether MTA-STS, DANE, or a locally configured requirement. And the protection covers one hop, not the whole journey or the message at rest. Encryption and authentication answer different questions, which is why the SPF, DKIM and DMARC apparatus sits on top of connections that were already encrypted.

questions.title: Sending Ten Thousand on Day One
questions.situation: The migration is done, the records are correct, SPF and DKIM both align, DMARC passes. You have a list of 40,000 subscribers and you send to all of them on the first morning.
questions.question: You move to a new sending domain and IP and send your full volume immediately. What is the likely outcome?
options: The provider rate-limits you, but receiver reputation is unaffected because the records are correct
Large receivers throttle or reject the mail, because an unknown sender with sudden high volume matches the shape of a compromised or throwaway sender
Nothing, provided authentication passes; volume is not a reputation input
Delivery succeeds but every message lands in spam permanently, and the domain cannot recover
questions.explanation: Correct authentication shows that the sending domain authorised the message. It says nothing about whether the message is wanted. Reputation is built from history, and a new domain and IP have little or none, so a sudden large volume can resemble the pattern receivers most want to stop. The answer is a warm-up: start with small volumes to your most engaged recipients, where opens and replies are likeliest, and increase as the receivers' own signals allow rather than on a fixed schedule. It is recoverable rather than permanent, though recovery can take longer than the warm-up would have. Worth knowing too that a newly assigned IP is not necessarily a clean one: it may carry whatever the previous tenant left on it. What this looks like for a real list is in [What Sending a Developer Newsletter Actually Takes](/posts/what-sending-a-developer-newsletter-actually-takes).

questions.title: Customer Order Analysis
questions.situation: Your e-commerce company needs to identify customers with pending orders for a customer service follow-up campaign.
questions.code:
Tables:
customers: id, name, email, city
orders: id, customer_id, order_date, status, total_amount

Status values: 'pending', 'shipped', 'delivered', 'cancelled'
Goal: Find customers with pending orders and their order details
questions.question: Find customers who placed orders but haven't received them yet.
options:
SELECT c.name, c.email, o.order_date, o.total_amount 
FROM customers c 
INNER JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id 
WHERE o.status = 'pending'
SELECT c.name, c.email FROM customers c, orders o WHERE c.id = o.customer_id AND o.status = 'pending'
SELECT c.name, c.email FROM customers c WHERE c.id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE status = 'pending')
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id = (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE status = 'pending')
questions.explanation: The INNER JOIN with explicit ON clause is clear and efficient, and includes relevant order details (date and amount) that would be useful for customer service follow-up. It's more readable than subqueries for this scenario.

questions.title: Sales Performance Analysis
questions.situation: Management needs a monthly sales report showing total revenue, number of orders, and average order value by month for the last year.
questions.code:
orders table: id, customer_id, order_date, total_amount, status

Need: Monthly breakdown with:
- Total revenue
- Order count
- Average order value
- Only completed orders (status = 'delivered')
questions.question: Calculate monthly sales metrics for business reporting.
options: SELECT MONTH(order_date), SUM(total_amount), COUNT(*), AVG(total_amount) FROM orders WHERE status = 'delivered' GROUP BY MONTH(order_date)
SELECT SUM(total_amount), COUNT(id), AVG(total_amount) FROM orders WHERE order_date > '2023-01-01'
SELECT order_date, total_amount FROM orders WHERE status = 'delivered' ORDER BY order_date

SELECT 
  DATE_FORMAT(order_date, '%Y-%m') as month,
  SUM(total_amount) as total_revenue,
  COUNT(*) as order_count,
  ROUND(AVG(total_amount), 2) as avg_order_value
FROM orders 
WHERE status = 'delivered' 
  AND order_date >= DATE_SUB(NOW(), INTERVAL 1 YEAR)
GROBY DATE_FORMAT(order_date, '%Y-%m')
ORDER BY month
questions.explanation: This query properly groups by year-month, includes the last year filter, uses descriptive column aliases, rounds the average for readability, and orders results chronologically for reporting purposes.

questions.title: Inventory Management Challenge
questions.situation: Your inventory team needs to identify products where current stock is less than 3 times the average monthly sales, indicating potential stockouts.
questions.code:
Tables:
products: id, name, current_stock, category
order_items: order_id, product_id, quantity, price
orders: id, order_date, status

Goal: Products where current_stock < (3 * avg_monthly_sales)
questions.question: Find products that are running low on stock compared to their sales velocity.
options: SELECT p.name, p.current_stock FROM products p WHERE p.current_stock < (SELECT AVG(oi.quantity) FROM order_items oi WHERE oi.product_id = p.id)

SELECT p.name, p.current_stock,
  (SELECT AVG(oi.quantity) * 3 FROM order_items oi 
   JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.id 
   WHERE oi.product_id = p.id 
     AND o.order_date >= DATE_SUB(NOW(), INTERVAL 1 MONTH)
     AND o.status = 'delivered') as monthly_avg_needed
FROM products p
WHERE p.current_stock < (
  SELECT COALESCE(AVG(oi.quantity) * 3, 0) 
  FROM order_items oi 
  JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.id 
  WHERE oi.product_id = p.id 
    AND o.order_date >= DATE_SUB(NOW(), INTERVAL 1 MONTH)
    AND o.status = 'delivered'
)
SELECT * FROM products WHERE current_stock < 100
SELECT p.name FROM products p, order_items oi WHERE p.id = oi.product_id AND p.current_stock < oi.quantity * 3
questions.explanation: This query properly calculates monthly average sales using delivered orders from the last month, multiplies by 3 for the threshold, uses COALESCE to handle products with no recent sales, and provides useful output for inventory decisions.

questions.title: Top Performers by Category
questions.situation: HR needs to identify the top 3 sales performers in each department for bonus allocation based on total sales in the last quarter.
questions.code:
Tables:
employees: id, name, department, hire_date
sales: id, employee_id, sale_amount, sale_date, status

Goal: Top 3 employees per department by Q4 sales total
questions.question: Rank employees by sales performance within their department.
options: SELECT e.name, e.department, SUM(s.sale_amount) FROM employees e JOIN sales s ON e.id = s.employee_id GROUP BY e.department ORDER BY SUM(s.sale_amount) DESC LIMIT 3
SELECT e.name, e.department, MAX(s.sale_amount) FROM employees e, sales s WHERE e.id = s.employee_id GROUP BY e.department
SELECT DISTINCT e.department, e.name FROM employees e JOIN sales s ON e.id = s.employee_id ORDER BY s.sale_amount DESC

SELECT 
  name, 
  department, 
  total_sales,
  dept_rank
FROM (
  SELECT 
    e.name,
    e.department,
    SUM(s.sale_amount) as total_sales,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY e.department ORDER BY SUM(s.sale_amount) DESC) as dept_rank
  FROM employees e
  JOIN sales s ON e.id = s.employee_id
  WHERE s.sale_date >= DATE_SUB(NOW(), INTERVAL 3 MONTH)
    AND s.status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY e.id, e.name, e.department
) ranked
WHERE dept_rank <= 3
questions.explanation: This query uses window functions to rank employees within each department (PARTITION BY), considers only the last quarter's completed sales, and limits to top 3 per department. It provides exactly what HR needs for bonus decisions.

questions.title: Customer Lifecycle Analysis
questions.situation: Marketing wants to understand customer lifecycle: first purchase date, total orders, total spent, last purchase date, and average days between orders for customers who made multiple purchases.
questions.code:
Tables:
customers: id, name, email, registration_date
orders: id, customer_id, order_date, total_amount, status

Goal: Comprehensive customer behavior metrics for multi-purchase customers
questions.question: Analyze customer behavior across their entire purchase journey.
options: SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id), SUM(o.total_amount) FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id GROUP BY c.id
SELECT c.*, o.* FROM customers c, orders o WHERE c.id = o.customer_id AND o.status = 'delivered'
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers WHERE id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1)

SELECT 
  c.name,
  c.email,
  MIN(o.order_date) as first_purchase,
  MAX(o.order_date) as last_purchase,
  COUNT(o.id) as total_orders,
  SUM(o.total_amount) as total_spent,
  ROUND(AVG(o.total_amount), 2) as avg_order_value,
  CASE 
    WHEN COUNT(o.id) > 1 THEN 
      ROUND(DATEDIFF(MAX(o.order_date), MIN(o.order_date)) / (COUNT(o.id) - 1), 1)
    ELSE NULL 
  END as avg_days_between_orders
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
GROUP BY c.id, c.name, c.email
HAVING COUNT(o.id) > 1
ORDER BY total_spent DESC
questions.explanation: This comprehensive query calculates all requested metrics including the complex average days between orders calculation, filters for multi-purchase customers using HAVING, and provides actionable insights for marketing analysis.

questions.title: E-commerce Database Design
questions.situation: You're designing a database for an online clothing store. Products have multiple variants (size, color) with different prices and stock levels. You need to track inventory and support complex pricing rules.
questions.code:
Requirements:
• Products (name, description, category, brand)
• Variants (size, color, SKU, price, stock)
• Categories can have subcategories
• Price history for analytics
• Efficient inventory queries
questions.question: Design tables for a product catalog with variants and pricing.
options:
CREATE TABLE products (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  name VARCHAR(255),
  description TEXT,
  category VARCHAR(100),
  size VARCHAR(10),
  color VARCHAR(50),
  price DECIMAL(10,2),
  stock INT
);

CREATE TABLE products (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  name VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
  description TEXT,
  brand_id INT,
  category_id INT,
  created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
  FOREIGN KEY (brand_id) REFERENCES brands(id),
  FOREIGN KEY (category_id) REFERENCES categories(id)
);

CREATE TABLE product_variants (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  product_id INT NOT NULL,
  sku VARCHAR(50) UNIQUE NOT NULL,
  size VARCHAR(10),
  color VARCHAR(50),
  stock_quantity INT DEFAULT 0,
  created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
  FOREIGN KEY (product_id) REFERENCES products(id)
);

CREATE TABLE variant_prices (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  variant_id INT NOT NULL,
  price DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL,
  effective_date DATE NOT NULL,
  end_date DATE,
  FOREIGN KEY (variant_id) REFERENCES product_variants(id)
);

CREATE TABLE inventory (
  product_name VARCHAR(255),
  size VARCHAR(10),
  color VARCHAR(50),
  price DECIMAL(10,2),
  quantity INT
);
questions.explanation: This normalized design properly separates products from variants, supports price history, uses foreign keys for data integrity, includes necessary indexes, and allows for complex inventory and pricing queries while maintaining data consistency.

questions.title: Query Performance Optimization
questions.situation: A customer search query is taking 15+ seconds and timing out. The query searches products by name, category, and price range. The products table has 2 million rows.
questions.code:
Current slow query:
SELECT * FROM products 
WHERE (name LIKE '%shirt%' OR description LIKE '%shirt%') 
  AND category IN ('clothing', 'fashion') 
  AND price BETWEEN 20 AND 100
ORDER BY created_date DESC
LIMIT 20;

Table: products (2M rows, no indexes except primary key)
questions.question: Optimize a slow-performing query that's causing production issues.
options: Add ORDER BY created_date to speed up sorting

CREATE INDEX idx_search ON products(category, price, created_date);

SELECT id, name, price, category, created_date 
FROM products 
WHERE category IN ('clothing', 'fashion')
  AND price BETWEEN 20 AND 100
  AND (name LIKE '%shirt%' OR description LIKE '%shirt%')
ORDER BY created_date DESC
LIMIT 20;
SELECT * FROM products WHERE name = 'shirt' AND category = 'clothing' ORDER BY price
questions.explanation: This solution uses FULLTEXT search for efficient text searching, creates a composite index for category and price filtering, adds a separate index for sorting, and selects only needed columns to reduce data transfer.

questions.title: Financial Transaction Integrity
questions.situation: You're implementing a money transfer feature between user accounts. The operation must be atomic - either both accounts are updated or neither, even if the system crashes mid-operation.
questions.code:
Tables:
accounts: id, user_id, balance, currency
transactions: id, from_account, to_account, amount, status, created_at

Transfer $100 from Account A (ID: 123) to Account B (ID: 456)
Current balances: A=$500, B=$200
questions.question: Ensure data consistency in a money transfer operation.
questions.explanation: This solution uses proper transaction control with balance validation, row locking to prevent concurrent modifications, error handling for insufficient funds, and proper rollback mechanisms. It ensures both atomicity and business rule enforcement.

questions.title: Database Technology Selection
questions.situation: Your company is building three new features: user activity tracking (millions of events/day), product catalog (complex relationships), and real-time chat (low latency). Choose the best database approach for each.
questions.code:
Requirements:
1. Activity Tracking: 5M events/day, append-only, analytics queries
2. Product Catalog: Complex relationships, ACID compliance, reporting
3. Real-time Chat: Sub-100ms latency, horizontal scaling, simple queries

Budget allows for multiple database technologies
questions.question: Choose the right database technology for different application requirements.
options: Use MySQL for everything to keep it simple
Use PostgreSQL for all three with different schemas

Activity Tracking: Time-series DB (InfluxDB/TimescaleDB)
Product Catalog: PostgreSQL with proper indexing
Real-time Chat: Redis with persistence + MongoDB for history

Activity Tracking: MongoDB
Product Catalog: Neo4j graph database
Real-time Chat: Cassandra
questions.explanation: This approach matches each use case to optimal technology: time-series DB for high-volume analytics data, PostgreSQL for complex relational data requiring ACID compliance, and Redis for ultra-low latency with MongoDB for chat history persistence.

questions.title: Analytics Data Warehouse Design
questions.situation: Your company needs a data warehouse to analyze sales performance across multiple dimensions: time, geography, products, customers, and sales channels. The data comes from multiple operational systems.
questions.code:
Source systems:
• E-commerce platform (orders, customers)
• POS systems (in-store sales)
• Inventory management (products, categories)
• CRM (customer segments, campaigns)

Analytics needs: Sales trends, customer behavior, product performance, regional analysis
questions.question: Design a data warehouse schema for business intelligence and reporting.
options: Copy all operational tables directly into the warehouse

CREATE TABLE sales_fact (
  sale_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  date_key INT,
  customer_key INT,
  product_key INT,
  store_key INT,
  channel_key INT,
  quantity INT,
  unit_price DECIMAL(10,2),
  total_amount DECIMAL(12,2),
  cost_amount DECIMAL(12,2),
  profit_amount DECIMAL(12,2)
);

-- Dimension tables
CREATE TABLE dim_date (
  date_key INT PRIMARY KEY,
  full_date DATE,
  year INT,
  quarter INT,
  month INT,
  week INT,
  day_of_week INT,
  is_weekend BOOLEAN,
  is_holiday BOOLEAN
);

CREATE TABLE dim_customer (
  customer_key INT PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id VARCHAR(50),
  segment VARCHAR(50),
  acquisition_channel VARCHAR(50),
  lifetime_value_bucket VARCHAR(20)
);

CREATE TABLE dim_product (
  product_key INT PRIMARY KEY,
  product_id VARCHAR(50),
  category VARCHAR(100),
  subcategory VARCHAR(100),
  brand VARCHAR(100),
  price_tier VARCHAR(20)
);
Use a single flat table with all columns for easy querying
CREATE VIEW analytics_view AS SELECT * FROM orders JOIN customers JOIN products
questions.explanation: This star schema design optimizes for analytical queries with a central fact table containing metrics and foreign keys to dimension tables. It supports efficient aggregation, filtering, and drilling down across multiple business dimensions.

questions.title: Database Scaling Strategy
questions.situation: Your social media app has grown from 100K to 10M users. The main database is struggling with read queries (70% of traffic), writes are manageable, but response times are degrading during peak hours.
questions.code:
Current issues:
• Read queries taking 2-5 seconds during peak
• 70% read traffic, 30% write traffic
• Peak: 50K concurrent users
• Main bottlenecks: user feeds, search, analytics
• Budget allows infrastructure investment
questions.question: Design a scaling solution for a rapidly growing application.
options: Upgrade to a larger database server with more CPU and RAM
Implement vertical partitioning by splitting tables across databases

Read Replicas + Caching Strategy:
- Master-slave replication with 3 read replicas
- Redis cache for user sessions and hot data
- CDN for static content
- Application-level read/write splitting
- Eventual consistency acceptable for feeds

Long-term: Horizontal sharding by user_id ranges
Move everything to NoSQL to handle the scale
questions.explanation: This comprehensive scaling strategy addresses the read-heavy workload with read replicas, implements caching for frequently accessed data, and plans for future horizontal scaling. It's cost-effective and addresses the specific 70/30 read/write pattern.

questions.title: Service Level Objectives
questions.situation: Your team needs to define SLOs for a new e-commerce checkout service. The business wants 'five nines' (99.999%) availability, but you need to propose realistic, measurable objectives.
questions.code:
Current metrics:
- Average response time: 250ms
- Peak traffic: 5,000 req/sec
- User-reported issues: ~50/month
- Revenue impact: $10k per minute of downtime
questions.question: What makes a good SLO for a user-facing web service?
options: SLO: 99.9% of requests complete successfully in <500ms, measured at load balancer over 30-day windows
SLO: 99.999% availability measured by uptime checks from monitoring tool
SLO: Zero errors and 100ms response time for all requests
SLO: Match last month's performance metrics exactly
questions.explanation: Good SLOs are: 1) User-centric (what users experience), 2) Measurable (quantifiable from real traffic), 3) Achievable (allows for maintenance and incidents), 4) Business-aligned (balances reliability with development velocity). 99.9% success rate in <500ms is realistic and allows a 0.1% error budget for innovation.

questions.title: Error Budget Management
questions.situation: Your service has a 99.9% availability SLO over 30 days. You've had 2 hours of downtime this month. The product team wants to deploy a risky new feature.
questions.code:
Math:
- 30 days = 43,200 minutes
- 99.9% SLO = 43.2 minutes downtime allowed
- Current downtime = 120 minutes
- Error budget remaining = ?
questions.question: How do you calculate and use error budgets?
options: Deploy the feature - we always ship on schedule
Error budget is exhausted (used 277%). Freeze all deployments until next month, focus on reliability improvements
Error budget is fine - 2 hours is less than 0.1%
Negotiate a new SLO with stakeholders to cover the downtime
questions.explanation: Error budget = (1 - SLO) × time period. For 99.9% over 30 days: 0.1% × 43,200 min = 43.2 min allowed. You've used 120 min (277% of budget). When error budget is exhausted, SRE practice is to halt feature work and prioritize reliability until budget is restored. This balances innovation with stability.

questions.title: Identifying Toil
questions.situation: You're analyzing your team's time allocation. Management asks you to identify and reduce toil to free up time for engineering projects.
questions.question: Which of these activities is considered toil in SRE?
options: Writing automation to eliminate manual certificate renewals
Manually restarting crashed services every week because root cause is unknown
Responding to a novel production incident that requires debugging
Architecting a new deployment pipeline for better reliability
questions.explanation: Toil is work that is: manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical (not strategic), scales linearly with service growth, and provides no enduring value. Manually restarting services is textbook toil. Options 1 and 4 are engineering work (reducing future toil). Option 3 is valuable operational work (novel problems that build expertise).

questions.title: The Four Golden Signals
questions.situation: You're setting up monitoring for a new microservices platform. Following Google SRE practices, you need to implement the four golden signals first.
questions.question: What are the four golden signals for monitoring distributed systems?
options: CPU, Memory, Disk, Network
Errors, Warnings, Info, Debug
Availability, Performance, Security, Cost
Latency, Traffic, Errors, Saturation
questions.explanation: The four golden signals from Google SRE: 1) Latency (request duration), 2) Traffic (demand on system), 3) Errors (failed requests rate), 4) Saturation (resource utilization approaching limits). These provide comprehensive visibility into service health from a user perspective. CPU/memory are resource metrics; the golden signals focus on user experience.

questions.title: Incident Response Structure
questions.situation: Your payment service is down during Black Friday. Multiple teams are in the incident channel. Chaos ensues with everyone trying to debug simultaneously. You need to structure the response.
questions.code:
Current state:
- 15 engineers in Slack channel
- 5 different theories being investigated
- No one communicating to stakeholders
- Conflicting commands to prod systems
questions.question: During a major incident, what roles should be assigned?
options: Everyone should work on the most critical issue they see
Senior engineer takes over and fixes everything while others watch
Assign Incident Commander (coordinates), Ops Lead (executes), Communications Lead (stakeholder updates), and Subject Matter Experts
Split into equal teams and have each team try different solutions
questions.explanation: Effective incident response requires clear roles: Incident Commander (overall coordination, decision-making), Operations Lead (executes commands, follows IC direction), Communications Lead (updates stakeholders/customers), and SMEs (provide expertise). This prevents duplicate work, ensures communication, and creates clear authority. Defined roles reduce chaos and time-to-resolution.

questions.title: Blameless Post-Mortem Culture
questions.situation: After a 4-hour outage caused by a junior engineer's configuration change, you're writing the post-mortem. Some team members want to emphasize 'who made the mistake'.
questions.question: What's the primary goal of a blameless post-mortem?
options: Identify who caused the incident so they can be retrained
Understand systemic failures that allowed the incident and implement preventive measures, focusing on 'what' not 'who'
Document the incident for legal and compliance purposes only
Prove to management that your team followed all procedures correctly
questions.explanation: Blameless post-mortems focus on systems and processes, not people. Goals: 1) Understand root causes and contributing factors, 2) Identify systemic improvements (automation, testing, guardrails), 3) Share learnings across the org, 4) Build psychological safety so people report issues freely. Blaming individuals prevents learning and encourages hiding mistakes.

questions.title: On-Call Rotation Design
questions.situation: Your SRE team is burning out. On-call engineers are paged 15+ times per night, exhausted, and threatening to quit. You need to fix the on-call experience.
questions.code:
Current problems:
- 15 pages per night (mostly false positives)
- On-call engineer handles everything alone
- No clear escalation path
- Same people on-call due to 'hero culture'
questions.question: What makes a healthy on-call rotation?
options: Hire more SREs to reduce on-call frequency
Reduce alert fatigue (tune alerts), define escalation paths, implement follow-the-sun rotation, cap pages per shift, ensure adequate staffing (4+ for 24/7)
Pay engineers more to compensate for difficult on-call
Remove on-call requirement and have team check Slack casually
questions.explanation: Healthy on-call requires: 1) Quality alerts (reduce noise/false positives), 2) Clear escalation paths (on-call isn't alone), 3) Sustainable rotation (follow-the-sun, max 2 weeks), 4) Adequate staffing (4+ people for 24/7), 5) Protected time after incidents, 6) Runbooks for common issues. Throwing money or people at broken alerting doesn't solve root problems.

questions.title: Capacity Planning Strategy
questions.situation: Your service grew 3x last quarter. Infrastructure is at 75% CPU utilization. Black Friday is in 6 weeks with expected 10x traffic spike.
questions.code:
Current state:
- Normal: 1,000 req/s at 75% CPU
- Black Friday: expecting 10,000 req/s
- Provisioning lead time: 2 weeks
- Budget: $50k for new infrastructure
questions.question: How should you approach capacity planning for a growing service?
options: Wait until we hit 90% CPU, then provision more capacity
Provision 10x capacity now to handle the spike
Optimize code performance instead of adding capacity
Use organic growth rate + load testing to forecast demand, provision with headroom, implement auto-scaling, have emergency capacity plan
questions.explanation: Effective capacity planning: 1) Forecast demand using historical growth + known events, 2) Load test to validate capacity needs, 3) Provision with headroom (N+2 for redundancy), 4) Implement auto-scaling for variable load, 5) Have emergency capacity plans. Don't wait until crisis (option 1) or massively over-provision (option 2). Code optimization helps but won't solve 10x growth in 6 weeks.

questions.title: Canary Deployment Process
questions.situation: You're deploying a major API change to 200 production servers. You want to minimize risk of breaking production for all users.
questions.question: What's the correct approach to canary deployments?
options: Deploy to all servers simultaneously for consistency
Deploy to 1% of servers, monitor error rates/latency for 1 hour, gradually increase to 5%, 25%, 50%, 100% with rollback plan at each stage
Deploy to 50% of servers and compare with the other 50%
Deploy to test environment first, then all production servers
questions.explanation: Canary deployment best practices: 1) Start small (1-5% traffic), 2) Monitor key metrics (error rates, latency, business KPIs), 3) Gradually increase (1% → 5% → 25% → 50% → 100%), 4) Set automated rollback triggers, 5) Soak time at each stage (30 min - 2 hours), 6) Have instant rollback capability. This limits blast radius if issues arise.

questions.title: Feature Flag Strategy
questions.situation: Your team is building a new payment provider integration. It's complex, will take 3 months, but you want to deploy code continuously without exposing incomplete features to users.
questions.question: When should you use feature flags?
options: Wait 3 months to merge and deploy everything at once
Use feature flags to hide incomplete work, deploy to prod continuously, gradually enable for internal users then external, with instant kill-switch capability
Deploy to production but use a separate URL that users don't know about
Create a long-lived feature branch and deploy only when complete
questions.explanation: Feature flags enable: 1) Continuous deployment of incomplete features (hidden behind flags), 2) Gradual rollout (internal → beta → full), 3) Instant rollback without redeployment (toggle off), 4) A/B testing, 5) Separation of deploy from release. This reduces risk, enables faster iteration, and provides safety nets. Long-lived branches create merge hell and prevent continuous integration.

questions.title: Circuit Breaker Pattern
questions.situation: Your service calls a payment API that occasionally becomes slow (10s+ timeouts). When this happens, your entire app slows down, request queues fill up, and you start timing out healthy requests too.
questions.code:
Problem cascade:
1. Payment API slows to 10s/request
2. Your app threads wait, get exhausted
3. Request queue fills (1000+ queued)
4. Even non-payment requests timeout
5. Total service outage
questions.question: Why implement circuit breakers in distributed systems?
options: Increase timeout values to wait longer for responses
Add more application servers to handle the load
Implement circuit breaker: detect failures, open circuit (fail fast), periodically test if dependency recovered, close circuit when healthy
Remove the failing dependency and handle payments manually
questions.explanation: Circuit breakers prevent cascading failures: 1) Monitor dependency health (error rate, latency), 2) Open circuit when threshold exceeded (fail fast instead of waiting), 3) Half-open state: periodically test if dependency recovered, 4) Close circuit when healthy. This protects your service from slow/failing dependencies, preserves resources, and enables graceful degradation.

questions.title: Retry Logic & Backoff
questions.situation: Your service occasionally gets 503 errors from a downstream API (1% of requests). You want to retry failed requests but not make the problem worse.
questions.question: What's the correct retry strategy for failed requests?
options: Retry immediately, up to 10 times until success
Never retry - fail fast and return error to user
Implement exponential backoff with jitter: retry with delays of 100ms, 200ms, 400ms, 800ms, max 3 retries, with random jitter to prevent thundering herd
Retry every 1 second for 1 minute
questions.explanation: Effective retry strategy: 1) Exponential backoff (increasing delays: 100ms, 200ms, 400ms...), 2) Jitter (randomization to prevent thundering herd), 3) Limited retries (3-5 max), 4) Only retry transient errors (503, timeout, not 4xx), 5) Respect retry-after headers. Immediate retries can overwhelm struggling service. Random jitter prevents all clients retrying simultaneously.

questions.title: Graceful Degradation
questions.situation: Your e-commerce site depends on: product DB (critical), recommendation engine (nice-to-have), reviews API (nice-to-have). The recommendation engine goes down.
questions.question: How should services handle dependency failures?
options: Return 503 error - site is unavailable until all dependencies are healthy
Keep retrying the recommendation engine until it works
Hide all product listings since we can't show recommendations
Show cached/default recommendations, continue serving core functionality (browse, checkout), log degraded state for monitoring
questions.explanation: Graceful degradation: 1) Identify critical vs non-critical features, 2) Serve core functionality even when optional features fail, 3) Use cached data, defaults, or remove feature temporarily, 4) Clearly communicate degraded state to ops/monitoring, 5) Automatic recovery when dependencies heal. Users can still buy (critical) even without personalized recommendations (nice-to-have).

questions.title: Effective Alert Design
questions.situation: Your team gets 50 alerts per day. Most are false positives or transient issues that self-heal. On-call engineers are ignoring pages. You need to redesign alerts.
questions.code:
Current bad alert:
'CPU > 80%'
- Fires 30 times/day
- Often self-corrects
- No context provided
- Not clearly actionable
questions.question: What makes a good alerting rule?
options: Increase CPU threshold to 95% so it alerts less
Send all alerts to email instead of paging
Alert on symptoms not causes: 'Error rate >1% for 5+ minutes' with runbook link, actionable response, and automatic rollback option
Remove all alerts and rely on user reports
questions.explanation: Good alerts: 1) Symptom-based (error rate, latency) not cause-based (CPU), 2) Actionable (require human response), 3) Include context (runbook, dashboard links), 4) Tuned thresholds (reduce false positives), 5) Appropriate severity and response time. High CPU might be fine if users aren't affected. Alert on user-impacting symptoms with sufficient time window to avoid flapping.

questions.title: Core SRE Principles
questions.situation: Your company is transitioning from traditional ops to SRE. Leadership asks you to explain what makes SRE different from traditional operations.
questions.question: What's a fundamental principle of SRE?
options: SRE applies software engineering practices to operations: automation, measurement (SLOs), and engineering 50% of time on reliability projects
SREs only handle incidents, developers do all other work
SREs maintain 100% uptime through manual processes and careful change control
SRE is just a new name for DevOps
questions.explanation: Core SRE principles: 1) Apply software engineering to operations (automation, tooling), 2) SLOs and error budgets balance reliability with velocity, 3) Limit toil to <50% of time (rest is engineering work), 4) Blameless post-mortems, 5) Shared ownership (devs + SRE), 6) Measure everything. SRE is an implementation of DevOps culture with specific practices from Google.

questions.title: Distributing Traffic
questions.situation: You have 5 application servers and need to ensure even traffic distribution while handling server failures gracefully.
questions.code:
# Current setup:
# - 5 web servers
# - 10,000 req/s
# - Need: High availability and even distribution
questions.question: Your web application receives 10,000 requests per second. How do you distribute traffic across multiple servers?
options: Use a load balancer (like NGINX or AWS ALB) with health checks and round-robin or least-connections algorithm
Use DNS round-robin to distribute traffic
Hard-code different server IPs in the client application
Have users manually choose which server to connect to
questions.explanation: Load balancers provide health checking, session persistence, SSL termination, and intelligent routing algorithms. They can automatically remove failed servers from rotation and distribute traffic based on current load, unlike DNS round-robin which caches IPs and can't react to failures quickly.

questions.title: Reducing Database Load
questions.situation: Product catalog data changes infrequently but is read thousands of times per minute. Database CPU is at 95%.
questions.code:
# Problem:
# - 5,000 reads/min to product_catalog table
# - Data changes once per hour
# - DB CPU at 95%
