questions.question: Your database is overwhelmed with read queries. 80% of queries request the same data repeatedly.
options: Add more database replicas
Upgrade to a larger database server
Denormalize all database tables
Implement Redis or Memcached cache layer with TTL-based expiration for frequently accessed data
questions.explanation: Caching frequently accessed, infrequently changing data dramatically reduces database load. Redis/Memcached can serve thousands of requests per second from memory, reducing database queries by 80-90%. This is more cost-effective than adding replicas or upgrading hardware for read-heavy workloads.

questions.title: Scaling Your Database
questions.situation: Single PostgreSQL instance handling both reads and writes. Write latency increasing as data grows.
questions.question: Your application database has grown to handle millions of users. Write performance is degrading.
options: Keep everything in one database and upgrade hardware
Delete old data to keep database small
Use read replicas for read traffic and implement database sharding for write scalability across multiple database nodes
Switch to NoSQL and hope it scales better
questions.explanation: Read replicas handle read traffic, reducing load on the primary database. Sharding distributes write load across multiple databases by partitioning data (e.g., by user ID ranges or geographic region). This horizontal scaling approach handles growth better than vertical scaling (hardware upgrades) alone.

questions.title: Understanding CAP Theorem
questions.situation: Your system spans multiple data centers. Network issues between data centers occur occasionally.
questions.code:
# CAP Theorem states you can only have 2 of 3:
# - Consistency (all nodes see same data)
# - Availability (system always responds)
# - Partition Tolerance (works despite network failures)
questions.question: You're designing a global e-commerce platform. During a network partition, what can you guarantee?
options: During a partition, choose between Consistency (reject requests to maintain data consistency) or Availability (serve potentially stale data)
You can have all three: Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance
CAP theorem doesn't apply to modern systems
Use blockchain to solve the CAP theorem
questions.explanation: CAP theorem proves you can only achieve 2 of 3 guarantees. During a network partition (which you must tolerate in distributed systems), you must choose: either maintain consistency and reject some requests (CP), or remain available but risk serving stale data (AP). E-commerce often chooses AP for shopping cart, CP for payments.

questions.title: Asynchronous Processing
questions.situation: Video processing is CPU-intensive and slow. Users should get immediate feedback, and the system must handle traffic spikes.
questions.question: Users upload videos that need processing. Processing takes 10 minutes but users expect immediate response.
options: Make users wait 10 minutes for processing to complete
Process videos on the web server synchronously
Reject uploads during high traffic periods
Use a message queue (RabbitMQ, SQS, Kafka) to accept uploads immediately, process asynchronously, and notify users when complete
questions.explanation: Message queues decouple request acceptance from processing. Users get immediate confirmation, uploads are queued, and worker processes handle them asynchronously. This provides better UX, handles traffic spikes gracefully (queue absorbs bursts), and allows independent scaling of web and worker tiers.

questions.title: Architecture Decision
questions.situation: Early-stage startup, small team, requirements are still evolving rapidly.
questions.code:
# Context:
# - Team: 5 developers
# - Stage: MVP development
# - Requirements: Changing frequently
# - Timeline: 3 months to launch
questions.question: You're starting a new project with a team of 5 developers. Should you use microservices?
options: Use microservices from day one to ensure scalability
Start with a well-structured monolith, split into microservices later when team size and complexity justify it
Use serverless functions for everything
Build a distributed monolith (worst of both worlds)
questions.explanation: Monoliths are simpler to develop, test, and deploy initially. With a small team and evolving requirements, microservices add complexity without benefits: more deployment overhead, distributed debugging, network latency, and unclear service boundaries. Start monolithic with clean module boundaries, then split when organizational or technical needs justify the complexity.

questions.title: Global Content Delivery
questions.situation: Web servers are in US-East. Asian users see 2-3 second page load times. Static assets (images, JS, CSS) are 5MB total.
questions.question: Your application serves users worldwide. Users in Asia experience slow page loads.
options: Deploy servers in every country
Tell users to upgrade their internet connection
Use a CDN (CloudFront, Cloudflare) to cache static assets globally and serve from edge locations near users
Compress all files and hope it's enough
questions.explanation: CDNs cache static content at edge locations worldwide, serving users from nearby servers. This dramatically reduces latency by minimizing distance data travels. CDNs also offload traffic from origin servers, provide DDoS protection, and handle traffic spikes. This is far more cost-effective than deploying infrastructure globally.

questions.title: API Protection
questions.situation: Public API is being hammered by a few users making excessive requests, degrading service for others.
questions.code:
# Problem:
# - Some users: 1000s of requests/minute
# - Normal users: 10-20 requests/minute
# - API performance degrading
questions.question: How do you protect your API from abuse while allowing legitimate users full access?
options: Block all users making more than 10 requests per minute
Implement rate limiting with token bucket or sliding window algorithm, return 429 status codes, and provide clear limits in documentation
Remove API documentation so fewer people can use it
Add CAPTCHA to every API request
questions.explanation: Rate limiting with token bucket or sliding window algorithms allows burst traffic while preventing sustained abuse. Return HTTP 429 with Retry-After headers to inform clients. Implement tiered limits (per user, per IP, per API key) and document limits clearly. This protects infrastructure while allowing legitimate high-volume users to request limit increases.

questions.title: Handling Distributed Transactions
questions.situation: Order creation must: deduct inventory, charge payment, create shipping label. Any failure should roll back all changes.
questions.code:
# Distributed transaction across:
# - Inventory Service (deduct stock)
# - Payment Service (charge card)
# - Shipping Service (create label)
# Need: All succeed or all fail
questions.question: In your e-commerce system, an order involves multiple services: inventory, payment, shipping. How do you ensure consistency?
options: Use two-phase commit (2PC) across all services
Hope all services succeed and manually fix inconsistencies
Use Saga pattern with compensating transactions or event-driven eventual consistency with idempotent operations
Put all services in one database to use local transactions
questions.explanation: In microservices, distributed transactions are challenging. The Saga pattern orchestrates a sequence of local transactions, each with compensating transactions for rollback (e.g., refund payment if shipping fails). Event-driven approaches use message queues for reliability and idempotency for retries. 2PC has poor performance and availability. Avoid distributed transactions when possible through careful service boundary design.

questions.title: Creating Your First Resource
questions.situation: You need to create a basic EC2 instance named 'web-server' using the t2.micro instance type.
questions.code:
# Goal: Create t2.micro EC2 instance
# Instance should be tagged with Name: web-server
questions.question: What's the correct way to create an AWS EC2 instance with Terraform?
questions.explanation: The correct Terraform syntax uses 'resource' followed by the resource type and name. AWS provider uses 'aws_instance' as the resource type, and tags are specified as a map.

questions.title: Using Variables
questions.situation: You want to use different instance types for development (t2.micro) and production (t2.large) environments.
questions.code:
# Need: Configurable instance type
# Dev: t2.micro
# Prod: t2.large
questions.question: How do you make your Terraform configuration reusable across environments?
options: Use environment variables like $INSTANCE_TYPE
Create separate .tf files for each environment
Use conditional statements: instance_type = env == "prod" ? "t2.large" : "t2.micro"
questions.explanation: Terraform variables are the proper way to make configurations reusable. They support types, descriptions, defaults, and validation, making your infrastructure code more maintainable.

questions.title: State File Management
questions.situation: Multiple team members need to work on the same Terraform configuration without conflicts.
questions.question: What's the best practice for storing Terraform state in a team environment?
options: Use remote backend like S3 with state locking via DynamoDB
Each team member keeps their own local state file
Store state file in version control (Git)
Share state file via email or file sharing service
questions.explanation: Remote backends like S3 with DynamoDB locking prevent conflicts, provide state history, and enable team collaboration. Local state files cause conflicts and version control storage exposes sensitive data.

questions.title: Code Organization with Modules
questions.situation: You need to create VPCs with subnets and security groups across multiple projects with slight variations.
questions.code:
# Common pattern:
# - VPC with public/private subnets
# - Security groups for web/app/db tiers
# - Used across 5+ projects
questions.question: How should you structure reusable Terraform code?
options: Copy and paste the configuration for each project

Create a Terraform module with configurable parameters:
module "vpc" {
  source = "./modules/vpc"
  
  vpc_cidr = var.vpc_cidr
  environment = var.environment
  project_name = var.project_name
}
Use a single large configuration file for all projects
Create shell scripts to generate Terraform files
questions.explanation: Terraform modules promote reusability, maintainability, and consistency. They encapsulate related resources and can be parameterized for different use cases while maintaining DRY principles.

questions.title: Using Existing Resources
questions.situation: You need to launch EC2 instances in an existing VPC that was created outside of Terraform.
questions.code:
# Existing VPC: vpc-12345678
# Need: Reference existing VPC to create subnets
questions.question: How do you reference existing AWS resources in your Terraform configuration?
options: Hard-code the VPC ID: vpc_id = "vpc-12345678"
Import the VPC into Terraform state first
Create a new VPC instead of using the existing one
questions.explanation: Data sources allow you to query and reference existing resources without managing them in Terraform. This enables integration with existing infrastructure while maintaining clean separation of concerns.

questions.title: Resource Lifecycle Control
questions.situation: You have a production database that should never be accidentally destroyed during terraform apply.
questions.question: How do you prevent accidental deletion of critical resources?
options: Add a comment: # DO NOT DELETE
Use separate Terraform workspace for production
create_before_destroy = false
questions.explanation: The lifecycle.prevent_destroy meta-argument prevents Terraform from destroying the resource, even if the configuration is removed. This is essential for protecting critical resources like databases.

questions.title: Complex Provisioning Scenario
questions.situation: Your application servers need to start only after the database is fully initialized and ready to accept connections.
questions.code:
# Database takes 5+ minutes to initialize
# App servers should wait for DB to be ready
# Terraform doesn't know about the initialization delay
questions.question: How do you handle dependencies between resources that Terraform can't automatically detect?
options: Use time_sleep resource or null_resource with local-exec provisioner
depends_on = [aws_db_instance.database]
Run terraform apply twice
Use separate terraform configurations
questions.explanation: While depends_on handles resource creation order, it doesn't wait for service readiness. time_sleep or null_resource with local-exec can implement custom waiting logic or health checks before proceeding.

questions.title: Secrets in Plain Sight
questions.situation: Your services read the production database password from a Kubernetes Secret. During a review, someone with read access to the namespace runs the command below and the password prints to their terminal in seconds. The team assumed the value was encrypted because it looked like random characters.
questions.code:
$ kubectl get secret db-creds -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d
Sup3rS3cret-Prod-2026

$ kubectl get secret db-creds -o yaml
data:
  password: U3VwM3JTM2NyZXQtUHJvZC0yMDI2   # base64, not encryption
questions.question: A teammate says the Kubernetes Secret already protects the database password. What is the real problem here?
options: Kubernetes Secrets use AES-256 by default, so the only fix is rotating the password more often
Secrets stored this way are only base64-encoded, with no access control, audit trail, or rotation, which is what Vault adds
The password is fine because base64 makes it unreadable to anyone without the decode command
The issue is the YAML output format, so switching to JSON output keeps the value hidden
questions.explanation: base64 is encoding, not encryption. Anyone who can read the Secret can decode it instantly. Kubernetes only encrypts Secrets at rest if you explicitly turn on an EncryptionConfiguration with a KMS provider, and even then anyone with API read access still sees the plaintext. Vault solves the bigger picture: secrets live in one place behind identity-based access policies, every read is written to an audit log, and you can issue short-lived or dynamic credentials instead of one shared static password. The output format (YAML vs JSON) changes nothing about who can read the value.

questions.title: Every Request Returns 503
questions.situation: Your Vault server restarted overnight. This morning every application that reads from Vault is throwing errors, and your own CLI calls fail too. You check the server status and see it came back up but is refusing to serve any secrets.
questions.code:
$ vault status
Key                Value
---                -----
Seal Type          shamir
Initialized        true
Sealed             true
Total Shares       5
Threshold          3

$ curl -s https://vault.internal:8200/v1/secret/data/app | jq .errors
["Vault is sealed"]
questions.question: After a node reboot, every Vault call fails. What do you need to do before secrets work again?
options: Run vault operator init again to generate a fresh master key and bring it online
Restart the Vault process one more time, since sealing clears itself after the service stabilizes
Provide the unseal key shares up to the threshold (3 of 5) so Vault can reconstruct the master key and unseal
Log in with the root token, which automatically unseals the server on first use
questions.explanation: Vault starts sealed every time the process restarts. While sealed, it knows where the encrypted data is but cannot decrypt it because the master key is not in memory. To unseal, you supply unseal key shares until you reach the threshold (here 3 of 5), and Vault reconstructs the master key in memory. The root token is for authentication after unsealing, not for unsealing. Restarting again does nothing. And running vault operator init on an already-initialized server will not re-init it, but treating init as the fix is exactly the kind of mistake that risks data loss, so never reach for it here. The real long-term fix is auto-unseal so a restart does not page anyone.

questions.title: Everything Uses the Root Token
questions.situation: You inherit a Vault setup where every service and every CI job is configured with the same token. You check it and realize it is the original root token created during vault operator init. It has no expiry and can do anything, including delete every secrets engine and create new admin tokens.
questions.code:
$ vault token lookup
Key                 Value
---                 -----
id                  hvs.xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx
policies            ["root"]
ttl                 0s          # never expires
renewable           false

# Same token found in: app configs, CI variables, a Slack message
questions.question: Each microservice authenticates to Vault with the initial root token. Why is this a problem and what should you do?
options: Define least-privilege policies, issue scoped tokens through an auth method per workload, then revoke the root token
Keep the root token but rotate its value every 90 days so a leak has a limited window
Wrap the root token in a Kubernetes Secret so only pods can reach it, which makes it safe to reuse
Set a TTL on the root token so it expires and forces services to re-fetch it automatically
questions.explanation: The root token is meant for initial setup and emergency break-glass, not day-to-day app access. The fix is to give each workload its own identity through an auth method (AppRole, Kubernetes, and so on), attach a policy that grants only the paths it needs, and let it receive a short-lived, scoped token. Once real auth is in place, revoke the root token entirely; you can always regenerate a new one later with the unseal key shares if you genuinely need it. Rotating or wrapping the root token still leaves every service over-privileged, and the root token ignores normal TTL handling, so none of those options reduce the blast radius.

questions.title: Stop Sharing One DB Password
questions.situation: Your platform has a single Postgres password baked into every service. It leaked once in a log, and rotating it required redeploying eight services at the same time to avoid downtime. You want each service to get its own credentials that expire on their own, so a leak is short-lived and rotation is automatic.
questions.code:
$ vault read database/creds/readonly
Key                Value
---                -----
lease_id           database/creds/readonly/3xKp...
lease_duration     1h
username           v-token-readonly-9fA2bQ
password           A1b2-C3d4-E5f6-G7h8

# Vault created this Postgres user on the fly and will drop it at expiry
questions.question: One static Postgres password is shared by every service and rotating it means a coordinated redeploy. Which Vault feature fixes this?
options: Move the static password into the KV v2 engine so it is versioned and can be rolled back
Use the database secrets engine to generate dynamic, short-lived credentials unique to each request
Encrypt the shared password with the Transit engine so services decrypt it at startup
Store the password with response wrapping so each service unwraps its own copy once
questions.explanation: The database secrets engine connects Vault to your database with an admin role and generates fresh credentials on demand. Each service gets a unique username and password tied to a lease, and Vault drops the database user automatically when the lease ends or is revoked. That kills the shared-password problem: a leak only exposes one short-lived account, and rotation happens continuously instead of as a risky redeploy. KV v2 still stores a static secret, just with version history. Transit encrypts data but does not create database users. Response wrapping is a delivery mechanism for an existing secret, not a way to generate new ones.

questions.title: Connections Drop After an Hour
questions.situation: A service reads dynamic Postgres credentials from Vault when it boots, opens a connection pool, and runs fine. Around 60 minutes in, every query starts failing with an authentication error, even though nothing was deployed and the network is healthy. Restarting the pod fixes it for another hour.
questions.code:
# at startup
$ vault read database/creds/app
lease_id        database/creds/app/8aQ...
lease_duration  1h
renewable       true

# ~60 min later, in the app logs
FATAL: password authentication failed for user "v-token-app-7Yk"
questions.question: An app fetches dynamic DB credentials at startup and works fine, then loses database access about an hour later. What is happening?
options: The connection pool is too small, so increase max connections and the auth errors stop
It is a transient network partition to the database that happens to recur every hour
The credential lease expired and Vault revoked the database user, so the app must renew the lease (or re-fetch) before it ends
The KV TTL elapsed, so set the KV secret to never expire and the credentials stay valid
questions.explanation: Dynamic secrets come with a lease and a TTL. When the lease_duration elapses, Vault revokes the credentials at the backend, which here means dropping the Postgres user, so existing sessions and any reconnect start failing. The app needs to renew the lease before it expires (renewable is true) or fetch a new credential and refresh its pool. The cleanest way is to run Vault Agent, which renews leases and rewrites credentials for you. The restart hides the symptom because the app fetches a fresh lease on boot. Pool size and network theories do not explain a clean one-hour cycle, and this is not a KV secret, so KV TTL settings are irrelevant.

questions.title: One Token Reads Everything
questions.situation: During an audit you find the billing service token can list and read all of secret/. It only needs the secrets under its own path. You are on KV version 2, which is mounted at secret/ and stores values under a data/ prefix in the API path. You need to rewrite the policy for least privilege.
questions.code:
# current policy (too broad)
path "secret/*" {
  capabilities = ["read", "list"]
}

# KV v2 read path looks like:
#   secret/data/billing/stripe
#   secret/data/billing/paypal
questions.question: An app token can read every secret under secret/, including other teams' data. Which policy gives it only what it needs?
options: path "secret/*" { capabilities = ["read", "list", "deny"] }  to block other teams' paths
path "secret/billing/*" { capabilities = ["read", "sudo"] }  to read only billing with elevated rights
path "secret/metadata/billing/*" { capabilities = ["read"] }  using the metadata path to fetch billing values
path "secret/data/billing/*" { capabilities = ["read"] }  to read only the billing secrets
questions.explanation: With KV v2, the actual secret values live under the data/ prefix, so a read policy must target secret/data/billing/*, not secret/billing/*. Scoping to that path with only the read capability gives least privilege. Mixing deny into a list of capabilities does not work the way people expect; deny is its own rule that overrides others and you do not combine it with read like that. Adding sudo grants root-level access to special endpoints and is the opposite of least privilege. The metadata/ path only exposes version info and metadata, not the secret values themselves, so that policy would not let the app read its secrets at all.

questions.title: How Does the App Log In?
questions.situation: You are removing the static token your CI pipeline uses to talk to Vault. The pipeline runs outside Kubernetes, so you cannot use the Kubernetes auth method. You want the job to log in, get a short-lived token scoped by policy, and you want to avoid leaving a usable secret sitting in the repo or CI config.
questions.code:
$ vault write auth/approle/login \
    role_id=$ROLE_ID \
    secret_id=$SECRET_ID
Key             Value
---             -----
token           hvs.CAES...    # short-lived, scoped by policy
token_policies  ["ci-deploy"]
token_ttl       20m
questions.question: A CI job and a service need to authenticate to Vault without a hardcoded long-lived token. What is the right approach?
options: Use AppRole: a non-secret role_id plus a short-lived secret_id (delivered wrapped) returns a scoped token
Generate one long-lived token, store it as a masked CI variable, and reuse it for every run
Authenticate with the root token in CI, since pipelines are trusted infrastructure anyway
Put the role_id and secret_id together in the repo so any runner can log in without setup
questions.explanation: AppRole is built for machine and automation logins that cannot use a platform-native method. The role_id is like a username and is not secret on its own. The secret_id is the sensitive half; you generate it short-lived and ideally deliver it response-wrapped so it is single-use and tamper-evident. The job exchanges both for a token scoped by the role's policies with a short TTL. Reusing one long-lived token just recreates the static-secret problem. Using the root token in CI is a huge blast radius. And committing the secret_id to the repo defeats the whole point, since anyone who reads the repo can authenticate.

questions.title: Pods Need Secrets Without Static Tokens
questions.situation: You are wiring up Vault for apps running in Kubernetes. You do not want to bake a Vault token into images or push secret_ids into ConfigMaps. Each deployment already runs under its own ServiceAccount, and you want Vault to trust that identity and hand back a scoped token.
questions.code:
$ vault write auth/kubernetes/role/billing \
    bound_service_account_names=billing \
    bound_service_account_namespaces=payments \
    policies=billing-read \
    ttl=1h

# pod presents its projected ServiceAccount JWT to log in
questions.question: Workloads in Kubernetes need to read from Vault, but you do not want to distribute tokens to pods. How do they authenticate?
options: Mount the root token into each pod as a Secret and let the app use it directly
Use the Kubernetes auth method: the pod presents its ServiceAccount JWT, Vault verifies it via the TokenReview API and returns a scoped token
Store an AppRole secret_id in a ConfigMap so every pod in the namespace can log in
Give every pod the same shared token and rely on network policies to limit who reaches Vault
questions.explanation: The Kubernetes auth method lets a pod authenticate with the ServiceAccount token Kubernetes already projects into it. Vault calls the cluster's TokenReview API to confirm the token is valid and identifies the ServiceAccount, then issues a Vault token scoped by the matching role's policies. No long-lived Vault credential ships in the image. Mounting the root token is a severe over-grant. Putting a secret_id in a ConfigMap exposes it to anyone who can read ConfigMaps, since they are not secret. A single shared token plus network policy still means one leaked token unlocks everything; identity per workload is the point.

questions.title: Encrypt PII Without Holding the Key
questions.situation: A new feature stores sensitive user fields that must be encrypted at the application layer. The security team does not want the AES key living in your codebase, your config, or your database. They want a central place to hold the key, rotate it, and do encrypt and decrypt operations, while your app only ever handles ciphertext.
questions.code:
$ vault write transit/encrypt/pii \
    plaintext=$(echo -n '123-45-6789' | base64)
Key            Value
---            -----
ciphertext     vault:v1:8SDd3W...

# app stores 'vault:v1:...' and calls transit/decrypt to read it back
questions.question: Your app must encrypt user data before storing it, but the team does not want to manage or store the encryption key. Which engine fits?
options: Store a generated AES key in KV v2 and have each service fetch it to encrypt locally
Use the PKI engine to issue a certificate and encrypt the data with its public key
Use the Transit engine: Vault holds the key and performs encrypt and decrypt, so the app never sees the key
Hash the data with the Transit engine so it cannot be reversed and store the hash
questions.explanation: Transit is encryption as a service. The key never leaves Vault; your app sends plaintext, gets back ciphertext tagged with a key version (vault:v1:...), and calls decrypt to reverse it. Because the key stays in Vault you get central key rotation and the ability to rewrap old ciphertext to a new key version without re-encrypting in your app. Storing an AES key in KV defeats the goal, since the key now lives where your services and anyone reading KV can grab it. PKI is for issuing and signing certificates, not bulk data encryption. Transit can also do HMAC, but hashing is one-way and you need to decrypt this data later.

questions.title: Someone Overwrote the Secret
questions.situation: A pipeline bug wrote a blank value over the live payment API key stored in KV. Services are failing. You are on the KV version 2 engine. You need the previous value back fast, and you want to stop this from silently happening again.
questions.code:
$ vault kv metadata get secret/payments/api-key
====== Versions ======
Version    Created Time           Deletion Time
1          2026-05-01T10:00:00Z   n/a
2          2026-06-16T09:14:00Z   n/a   <- current, blank value

$ vault kv get -version=1 secret/payments/api-key   # ?
questions.question: A bad deploy overwrote the production API key in KV with an empty value. Can you get the old one back?
options: The old value is gone; KV only keeps the latest write, so restore the whole cluster from a Raft snapshot
Run vault kv undelete, which rolls every secret in the mount back to its previous state at once
Only a root token can read old versions, so escalate and read the prior value with root
KV v2 keeps version history, so read version 1 to recover the value and consider check-and-set to prevent blind overwrites
questions.explanation: KV version 2 keeps a history of writes, so the previous value is still there. You read it with vault kv get -version=1 and write it back, or use the metadata to roll forward to a known-good value. To stop blind overwrites, turn on check-and-set (cas_required) so a write must reference the version it expects, which makes a racing or buggy write fail instead of clobbering. A full cluster snapshot restore is a heavy, disruptive answer when the data is one command away. undelete works on a deleted version, not as a mount-wide rollback. And version history is governed by policy capabilities on the metadata and data paths, not by needing the root token.

questions.title: Who Read This Secret?
questions.situation: There is a suspicion that a database credential was read by something it should not have been. Security wants the access trail from Vault. You check and realize no audit device was ever enabled, so Vault kept no record of past requests. You need an answer now and a fix so this never happens again.
questions.code:
$ vault audit list
No audit devices are enabled.

$ vault audit enable file file_path=/vault/logs/audit.log
Success! Enabled the file audit device at: file/

# sample entry: request path and identity logged, secret values HMAC'd
questions.question: After a suspected leak, security asks for a log of who accessed a specific secret. You find there is no record. What went wrong and what fixes it?
options: Enable an audit device now; it records every request and response going forward, with sensitive strings HMAC'd, but it cannot recover past activity
Read the access history from the root token's lookup output, which tracks every secret it ever touched
Check the standard server stdout logs, which always contain the full plaintext of every secret read
Re-enable the secrets engine, which rebuilds and exposes the historical access log for that path
questions.explanation: Audit devices are the access trail, and they only record from the moment you enable them. With none enabled, there is no retroactive history to pull, which is exactly why turning one on should be part of the initial bring-up. Once enabled, every request and response is logged, with sensitive values HMAC'd so the log itself is not a secrets leak; you can still match a known value by HMAC'ing it with the same key. Token lookup shows a token's policies and TTL, not a history of secrets it read. Server stdout is operational logging and does not contain secret values. Re-enabling a secrets engine does not reconstruct any access history and would disrupt the mount.

questions.title: Manual Unseal Doesn't Scale
questions.situation: Vault runs in an autoscaling group and nodes get recycled during patching and scaling. Every new node comes up sealed, and someone has to gather three of the five key holders to unseal it, sometimes at 3am. You want nodes to unseal themselves on boot while keeping a strong recovery process for emergencies.
questions.question: Your Vault nodes restart often and each one needs three people to paste unseal keys. How do you make restarts hands-off without weakening security?
options: Write the unseal key shares to a file on each node so a startup script can paste them in automatically
Configure auto-unseal with a cloud KMS (or Transit) seal so nodes unseal on boot; Shamir shares become recovery keys
Lower the unseal threshold to 1 so a single on-call person can unseal each node quickly
Disable the seal entirely in non-public networks so nodes start unsealed and skip the step
questions.explanation: Auto-unseal hands the unsealing step to a trusted external key, usually a cloud KMS or another Vault's Transit engine. On boot a node asks the KMS to decrypt its root key and unseals itself, so autoscaling and patching no longer page anyone. Your Shamir shares are converted into recovery keys, which you keep for break-glass and for operations like generating a new root token. Storing the unseal shares on disk recreates a master key sitting next to the data, which is the risk sealing exists to prevent. Dropping the threshold to 1 destroys the split-knowledge guarantee. There is no option to skip the seal; Vault always boots sealed by design, and trusting the network is not a substitute for protecting the root key.

questions.title: A Node Got Popped
questions.situation: Security confirms one application host was compromised. While it was up, its Vault token requested a stream of dynamic Postgres and AWS credentials, all still within their leases. You need to invalidate everything that token caused to be issued, immediately, and at the backend so the database users and cloud keys actually stop working.
questions.code:
$ vault list sys/leases/lookup/database/creds/app
Keys
----
3xKp...
9fA2...
# plus AWS creds under aws/creds/app

$ vault lease revoke -prefix aws/creds/app
$ vault token revoke <compromised-token>
questions.question: One app server was compromised. Its Vault token had issued many dynamic database and cloud credentials. How do you contain the blast fast?
options: Seal Vault, since a sealed server cannot serve secrets and that stops the leaked credentials from working
Rotate the root token and the unseal keys, which cascades and invalidates all child tokens and leases
Revoke the compromised token and use vault lease revoke -prefix to cascade-revoke the dynamic secrets it issued
Delete the affected KV entries so the application can no longer read the values it cached
questions.explanation: Dynamic secrets are tracked as leases, and revocation reaches back to the backend: revoking a database lease drops the Postgres user, revoking an AWS lease deletes the IAM credentials. Revoke the compromised token (which revokes its leases and any child tokens) and run vault lease revoke -prefix on the paths it used to cascade-revoke everything issued under them. Sealing Vault stops new requests but does nothing to the credentials already handed out; the leaked database and cloud creds keep working until their leases end. Rotating the root token and unseal keys does not revoke unrelated leases. The compromised creds here are dynamic, not KV values, so deleting KV entries misses the actual exposure.

questions.title: Designing Vault for HA
questions.situation: Your current Vault is one node backed by a file storage path. If it dies, every service loses secrets. The previous team ran Vault on a separate Consul cluster for HA, which was a lot to operate. You want HA with automatic leader election and as little extra infrastructure as possible.
questions.question: A single Vault node is a single point of failure. You want high availability with fewer moving parts than the old Consul setup. What storage backend do you pick?
options: Run several Vault nodes that all point at the same file storage path on a shared NFS volume
Put a load balancer in front of two independent Vault nodes that each use their own local file storage
Keep one node but take frequent snapshots, since fast restore is equivalent to high availability
Use Integrated Storage (Raft): a cluster replicates data across nodes with automatic leader election, no separate Consul
questions.explanation: Integrated Storage (Raft) is the standard HA backend now. You run an odd number of nodes (3 or 5), they replicate the data through the Raft consensus protocol, one is the active node and the rest are standbys, and leader election is automatic when the active node fails. It needs no separate Consul cluster, which is exactly the operational simplification you want. The file backend does not support HA at all, and pointing multiple nodes at one file path or one NFS volume leads to corruption, since it has no locking or replication. Two nodes behind a load balancer with separate local storage are two different Vaults with different data, not an HA cluster. Snapshots are for disaster recovery, not availability; a restore still means downtime.

questions.title: Delivering the SecretID Safely
questions.situation: Your provisioning system generates an AppRole secret_id and passes it to a new instance so the app can log in to Vault. You are worried the secret_id could be captured in CI logs, a process list, or by something on the path before the app uses it. You want delivery to be single-use and to detect if anyone touched it first.
questions.code:
$ vault write -wrap-ttl=120s -f auth/approle/role/app/secret-id
Key                Value
---                -----
wrapping_token     hvs.CAESxxxx...   # this is handed to the instance
ttl                120s

# app: vault unwrap <wrapping_token>  -> real secret_id, once only
questions.question: You need to get an AppRole secret_id to a freshly booted instance without it showing up in logs or being silently stolen in transit. What does response wrapping give you?
options: Response wrapping encrypts the secret_id with the Transit engine so only the app holding the key can read it
Response wrapping stores the secret_id in a single-use, short-TTL token; if it is intercepted the unwrap fails, revealing the leak
Response wrapping makes the secret_id permanent and reusable so the instance can re-read it on every restart
Response wrapping replaces the secret_id with the role_id, which is safe to pass around in the clear
questions.explanation: Response wrapping returns a single-use wrapping token instead of the secret itself. The real secret_id is held in the wrapping token's private cubbyhole with a short TTL, and only the holder can unwrap it, exactly once. That gives you tamper evidence: if an attacker intercepts the wrapping token and unwraps it, your app's later unwrap fails, so you immediately know the value leaked and can rotate it. This addresses the secret-zero problem of getting the first credential to a workload safely. It is not Transit encryption; the secret lives in a cubbyhole, not encrypted ciphertext you hand around. It does not make the secret permanent (the opposite, it is single-use and short-lived), and it does not swap in the role_id.

questions.title: What Expand-and-Contract Actually Means
questions.situation: You manage a payments service on PostgreSQL 15. The orders table has a column called user_id that you want to rename to customer_id. The service runs 12 replicas behind a load balancer, deploys roll out one pod at a time, and you cannot pause writes.
questions.code:
Old code path:
  INSERT INTO orders (user_id, amount) VALUES ($1, $2)

Desired final state:
  INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, amount) VALUES ($1, $2)

Problem:
During rollout, some pods write to user_id and some to customer_id at the same time.
questions.question: Your team is renaming a column in a high-traffic table. The lead engineer mentions doing it with the expand-and-contract pattern.
options: Run ALTER TABLE orders RENAME COLUMN user_id TO customer_id in a single migration deployed with the new code
Add the new column, dual-write to both, backfill, switch reads, then drop the old column across separate deploys
Drop user_id and recreate it as customer_id inside a transaction so it is atomic
Take a 5 minute maintenance window during off-hours and rename the column with a brief outage
questions.explanation: Expand-and-contract means you never have a moment where old code and new schema disagree. You first expand the schema (add customer_id), make the app write to both, backfill historical rows, then switch readers, and finally contract (drop user_id). A single RENAME deploys instantly schema-wise but breaks every pod still running the old code. Dropping and recreating inside a transaction does not help, the old pods still reference the missing column. Maintenance windows defeat the purpose of zero-downtime work.

questions.title: Reading the Lock Mode Table
questions.situation: You are reviewing the PostgreSQL lock modes documentation before signing off on a migration plan. Your traffic is mostly SELECTs with a steady stream of INSERTs and UPDATEs. You need to identify which lock mode a migration must avoid acquiring on a busy table if it wants to stay invisible to writers.
questions.code:
Common PostgreSQL table-level lock modes (from weak to strong):

  ACCESS SHARE              (SELECT)
  ROW SHARE                 (SELECT FOR UPDATE)
  ROW EXCLUSIVE             (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE)
  SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE    (VACUUM, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, ANALYZE)
  SHARE                     (CREATE INDEX without CONCURRENTLY)
  SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE       (CREATE TRIGGER, some ALTER TABLE)
  EXCLUSIVE                 (REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY)
  ACCESS EXCLUSIVE          (ALTER TABLE, DROP TABLE, TRUNCATE, REINDEX)
questions.question: Before running a migration on a production table, your teammate asks you which PostgreSQL lock modes are safe alongside normal traffic.
options: ROW EXCLUSIVE, because it conflicts with every other write
SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE, because the name has the word EXCLUSIVE in it
ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, because it conflicts with every other lock mode including plain SELECTs
ACCESS SHARE, because anything with SHARE blocks writes
questions.explanation: ACCESS EXCLUSIVE is the only lock mode that conflicts with every other mode, including ACCESS SHARE which a normal SELECT acquires. When a migration takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, every subsequent query against that table queues behind it. ROW EXCLUSIVE is what normal writes take and they coexist fine. SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE sounds scary but is friendly to readers and writers, it is the lock used by CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY and ANALYZE. ACCESS SHARE is the weakest lock and blocks nothing except ACCESS EXCLUSIVE. The takeaway: any DDL that grabs ACCESS EXCLUSIVE has to be quick or done online via a different strategy.

questions.title: Why Your Index Build Killed Writes
questions.situation: You added an index on a 90 million row table to speed up a slow query. You ran CREATE INDEX during a slow traffic period. Within seconds, every INSERT and UPDATE on that table started timing out. Connections piled up in pg_stat_activity with a wait event of relation. You had to cancel the migration.
questions.code:
-- What you ran:
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_id ON orders (customer_id);

-- What you saw in pg_stat_activity:
SELECT pid, wait_event_type, wait_event, query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state = 'active';

 pid | wait_event_type | wait_event | query
-----+-----------------+------------+----------------------------------
 142 | Lock            | relation   | INSERT INTO orders (...) VALUES
 143 | Lock            | relation   | UPDATE orders SET status=...
 144 | Lock            | relation   | INSERT INTO orders (...) VALUES
questions.question: A regular CREATE INDEX brought your API to its knees during business hours.
options: CREATE INDEX takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, you should have run VACUUM first to release locks
The table was missing statistics, run ANALYZE before creating the index
Plain CREATE INDEX takes a SHARE lock that blocks writes, use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY instead
PostgreSQL cannot build indexes on tables larger than 50 million rows in one shot, partition the table first
questions.explanation: A plain CREATE INDEX takes a SHARE lock on the table. SHARE blocks all writes (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) until the index is built, which on a 90M row table can mean many minutes of write outage. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY does two passes over the table and only takes a SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE lock, which allows writes to continue. The trade-off is it cannot run inside a transaction and is slower overall. VACUUM and ANALYZE do not change locking behavior here. PostgreSQL has no row count cutoff for index creation.

questions.title: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY Left an Invalid Index
questions.situation: You ran CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY overnight. It failed near the end because another session held a transaction open. You check pg_indexes in the morning and find the index exists but queries are not using it. Looking at pg_index, you see indisvalid = false.
questions.code:
SELECT indexname, indexdef
FROM pg_indexes
WHERE tablename = 'orders';

 indexname              | indexdef
------------------------+----------------------------
 idx_orders_customer_id | CREATE INDEX idx_orders_...

SELECT i.indisvalid, i.indisready
FROM pg_index i
JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid = i.indexrelid
WHERE c.relname = 'idx_orders_customer_id';

 indisvalid | indisready
------------+-----------
 f          | t
questions.question: Your concurrent index build failed and now the index is marked INVALID.
options: Run REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_customer_id to rebuild it without locks
Run VACUUM FULL on the orders table to repair the invalid index
Mark it valid by hand with UPDATE pg_index SET indisvalid = true
Leave it alone, PostgreSQL will auto-repair invalid indexes during the next autovacuum cycle
questions.explanation: When CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY fails, it leaves a leftover index marked INVALID. The planner ignores invalid indexes but they still consume disk and slow down writes. REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY rebuilds it in place without blocking writes, the modern fix added in PostgreSQL 12. Alternatively you DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY and recreate. VACUUM FULL does not repair invalid indexes and takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock that would defeat the whole point. Editing pg_index by hand is unsafe, the index data may genuinely be incomplete. Autovacuum does not touch invalid indexes.

questions.title: Adding a NOT NULL Column With a Default
questions.situation: You are running PostgreSQL 14. You need to add a tenant_id INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1 column to a 200 million row events table. You read somewhere this used to be slow but is now fast. Your colleague is convinced you still need to do it in three steps.
questions.question: You need to add a new NOT NULL column to a huge table without locking writers.
options: Option B is mandatory, ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN with a DEFAULT always rewrites the whole table
Option A is fine on PostgreSQL 11+, a constant default no longer rewrites the table
Option A only works if you set the column as nullable first, NOT NULL still forces a rewrite
Both options take the same time, PostgreSQL writes the default into every row regardless
questions.explanation: Since PostgreSQL 11, ADD COLUMN with a constant default no longer rewrites the table. PostgreSQL stores the default in pg_attribute (attmissingval) and synthesizes it for old rows on read. New rows get it written normally. This makes Option A safe on PostgreSQL 11 and up, even with NOT NULL. The catch is the default must be a constant. A volatile default like now() or nextval() will still rewrite the table. Pre-11 advice required the multi-step dance, which is why your colleague learned it that way.

questions.title: Migration Hangs Forever Waiting for a Lock
questions.situation: You started a migration during the deploy pipeline. It runs ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT, which needs an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock. There is a long-running analytics query holding a row lock on orders. Your migration is queued behind it. Worse, every new query against orders is now also queued behind your migration, because it requested an exclusive lock.
questions.code:
SELECT pid, mode, granted, query
FROM pg_locks l
JOIN pg_stat_activity a USING (pid)
WHERE relation = 'orders'::regclass
ORDER BY granted DESC;

 pid  | mode                | granted | query
------+---------------------+---------+----------------------------
 9201 | AccessShareLock     | t       | SELECT ... FROM orders ... (long analytics)
 9304 | AccessExclusiveLock | f       | ALTER TABLE orders ADD ...
 9410 | AccessShareLock     | f       | SELECT id FROM orders WHERE id = $1
 9411 | AccessShareLock     | f       | SELECT id FROM orders WHERE id = $1
questions.question: Your ALTER TABLE has been waiting on a lock for 45 minutes and your deploy is stuck.
options: Run VACUUM ANALYZE orders in another session, it preempts the lock queue
Always wrap migrations with SET lock_timeout = '2s' so they fail fast instead of blocking the world
Increase max_connections so queued queries do not back up
Restart PostgreSQL, the lock queue clears on startup
questions.explanation: When a migration asks for ACCESS EXCLUSIVE and cannot get it, every later query that needs even a SHARE lock queues behind the migration. This is a classic production outage pattern, the migration looks idle but is taking down reads. Setting lock_timeout (and statement_timeout) at the migration session level makes the ALTER fail fast if it cannot get the lock quickly. You then retry. VACUUM ANALYZE does not jump the queue and may itself be blocked. More connections just gives more queue space. Restarting Postgres mid-migration loses connections and is a terrible recovery path.

questions.title: Adding a Foreign Key to a 50M Row Table
questions.situation: Your orders table has a customer_id column. There is no foreign key to customers. Compliance asks you to add one. A single ALTER TABLE ADD CONSTRAINT FOREIGN KEY would scan all 50 million rows under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, taking the table offline for many minutes.
questions.code:
-- Naive approach (locks the table):
ALTER TABLE orders
  ADD CONSTRAINT orders_customer_fk
  FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(id);

-- Goal: same constraint, no lock-out window.
questions.question: You need to enforce a foreign key on a table that already has 50 million rows, ideally without locking the world.
options: Add the constraint with NOT VALID, then run VALIDATE CONSTRAINT in a second step
Add a CHECK constraint instead, foreign keys cannot be added online in Postgres
Create a trigger on orders that fails the insert if customer_id is missing
Drop and recreate the orders table with the foreign key already in place
questions.explanation: ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT ... NOT VALID adds the constraint for new and updated rows only and takes only a brief lock. Existing rows are not checked. Then ALTER TABLE ... VALIDATE CONSTRAINT scans the existing rows but uses only a SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE lock, which does not block reads or writes. Two short locks beat one long one. Triggers are a real solution in some setups but are slower per row and harder to maintain than a real FK. Recreating a 50M row table is downtime, not zero-downtime.

questions.title: Backfilling a Column on a Huge Table
questions.situation: You added a status_normalized column to a 80M row events table. New writes populate it. You need to backfill old rows. A junior engineer suggests UPDATE events SET status_normalized = lower(status). You veto this. Why?
questions.code:
-- What the junior wants to run:
UPDATE events
SET status_normalized = lower(status)
WHERE status_normalized IS NULL;

-- Table size: 80M rows, ~120GB
questions.question: You added a nullable column and now need to fill it for 80 million existing rows.
options: A single UPDATE on 80M rows creates one massive transaction that bloats WAL, blocks vacuum, and risks replication lag
UPDATE is fundamentally unsafe on PostgreSQL, you must use COPY for backfills
It will work but waste an index, you need to drop the index on status first
lower() is not deterministic, the values may differ between calls
questions.explanation: A single UPDATE rewriting 80M rows is one giant transaction. It generates enormous WAL, blocks autovacuum from cleaning up the old row versions until it commits, and ships the entire change to replicas in one burst, causing replication lag spikes. If it fails mid-way, it rolls back the whole thing and you start over. Safe backfills batch the work in chunks of a few thousand rows, sleep briefly between batches, and let autovacuum keep up. Tools like pg_repack or custom scripts that loop over primary key ranges are the standard approach.

questions.title: Changing a Column Type Without Downtime
questions.situation: Your events table uses INTEGER for its id column. You are projecting to hit 2^31 in four months. A direct ALTER TABLE events ALTER COLUMN id TYPE BIGINT would rewrite the entire table under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for hours.
questions.code:
-- Naive (blocks for hours):
ALTER TABLE events ALTER COLUMN id TYPE BIGINT;

-- Current state:
      column_name | data_type
      ------------+----------
       id         | integer
      
-- Target: id is BIGINT, no downtime.
questions.question: You need to change an INTEGER column to BIGINT on a hot table because you are running out of ID space.
options: Add a new BIGINT column id_new, dual-write via trigger, backfill in batches, swap the columns in one short transaction
Run ALTER TABLE inside BEGIN; SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '100ms'; ALTER TABLE ...; COMMIT;
Use ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN id TYPE BIGINT USING id::bigint, the USING clause makes it online
Use logical replication to copy the table to a new one with the correct type, then swap names
questions.explanation: Type changes that require a rewrite cannot be done in place online. The standard pattern is expand-and-contract at the column level: add id_new BIGINT, add a trigger or app-level dual-write to keep both in sync, backfill old rows in batches, then in one short transaction rename the columns and drop the old one. Option D (logical replication to a new table) is also viable but heavier. Option B fails fast but does not change the fact that the rewrite needs hours of ACCESS EXCLUSIVE. The USING clause in Option C still rewrites the table under the same lock. There is no online ALTER COLUMN TYPE for types of different storage size.

questions.title: The Transactional DDL Trap
questions.situation: Your migration tool wraps each migration file in BEGIN ... COMMIT for atomicity. The file below ran for 40 minutes in production, with the table locked the entire time. Every API call on this table timed out for those 40 minutes. The same file ran in 90 seconds in staging.
questions.question: You wrapped a multi-step migration in a transaction. It bites you in production.
options: ALTER TABLE acquired ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, then the UPDATE held it for 40 minutes inside the transaction, blocking every query on the table
PostgreSQL cannot run ALTER TABLE and UPDATE in the same transaction, the lock escalates
CREATE INDEX inside a transaction takes a stronger lock than outside, that was the cause
Autovacuum ran during the migration and competed for locks
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL has transactional DDL, which sounds great until you understand what it costs. Once ALTER TABLE acquires ACCESS EXCLUSIVE inside a transaction, it holds that lock until COMMIT. The 40 minute UPDATE in the same transaction kept the entire table locked the whole time. In staging the table had 10K rows so the UPDATE was fast. In production it had 50M rows and the lock stayed. The fix is to split this into multiple migration files: one ALTER, then a chunked backfill (outside a transaction or in many small transactions), then NOT NULL, then a CONCURRENT index. Never put a long UPDATE in the same transaction as a DDL that took an exclusive lock.

questions.title: Renaming a Table Across a Rolling Deploy
questions.situation: You need to rename the user_events table to events. The deploy will take about 8 minutes to roll all 30 pods. During that window, some pods will reference the old name and some the new name.
questions.question: You want to rename a table. You have 30 application pods that deploy one at a time.
options: Run the RENAME exactly at the midpoint of the rollout to minimize errors on each side
Create a view named user_events that points to the new events table, run RENAME, deploy code, then drop the view
Hold the deploy, run RENAME, then resume the deploy, the gap is brief enough to ignore
PostgreSQL supports both names automatically after a rename for 24 hours, no extra work needed
questions.explanation: The cleanest pattern is to create a compatibility view first. You create events as a view over user_events (or rename and then create user_events as a view over events), so both names resolve correctly during the rollout. Once all pods are on the new code, you drop the view. The midpoint trick still leaves half the pods broken. Pausing the deploy still has a moment where the old name vanishes and any in-flight query fails. PostgreSQL does not keep old names around. Views with the same column shape act as transparent aliases and survive a rolling deploy.

questions.title: Dropping a Column Without Breaking Old Code
questions.situation: The legacy_score column on user_profiles has not been read by any service for months. You want to drop it. You also know that ORM-style INSERT statements sometimes name all columns, so some old code paths still INSERT into legacy_score.
questions.code:
-- Some pods still run:
INSERT INTO user_profiles (id, name, email, legacy_score)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4);

-- Other pods run:
INSERT INTO user_profiles (id, name, email)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3);

-- Goal: drop legacy_score safely.
questions.question: You are removing a deprecated column. What is the safe order of operations?
options: Drop the column immediately, all SELECTs ignore it so writes will be fine
Deploy code that stops writing to legacy_score, wait for the rollout to finish, then ALTER TABLE DROP COLUMN
Mark the column as deprecated in a comment and leave it forever, dropping columns is not safe in Postgres
Rename the column to legacy_score_deprecated first to catch any stragglers
questions.explanation: Drop is also an expand-and-contract problem in reverse. If you DROP COLUMN while old pods are still INSERTing into it, those inserts fail with column does not exist. The safe order is: ship code that no longer writes to the column, wait for the full rollout, then drop. ALTER TABLE DROP COLUMN itself is quick in PostgreSQL because it only marks the column as dropped in the catalog. The actual storage is reclaimed lazily on rewrite. Renaming first just postpones the same problem.

questions.title: When to Reach for pg_repack or pg_squeeze
questions.situation: You deleted 60% of a 400GB table to comply with a retention policy. Disk usage did not drop because PostgreSQL only marks rows as dead. autovacuum reclaims space within the table but does not shrink it. VACUUM FULL would rewrite the table under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for hours.
questions.code:
-- Before:
 table_size  | dead_tuples | live_tuples
 400 GB      | 600M        | 400M

-- After VACUUM:
 table_size  | dead_tuples | live_tuples
 400 GB      | 0           | 400M     <- size unchanged

-- Want: 400 GB --> ~160 GB, no downtime.
questions.question: You want to reclaim disk after a massive DELETE. VACUUM FULL would lock the table for hours.
options: Run VACUUM FULL with a low priority nice value to avoid impacting traffic
Use pg_repack, it rebuilds the table online via triggers and a temporary copy, then swaps with a brief lock
Set autovacuum_naptime to 1 and the space will be reclaimed within a few minutes
Drop the table and restore it from a backup with only the surviving rows
questions.explanation: Standard VACUUM reclaims space inside the file but does not return it to the filesystem. VACUUM FULL does, but holds ACCESS EXCLUSIVE the whole time. pg_repack builds a copy of the table in the background, uses triggers to capture writes during the copy, then swaps the tables atomically with only a brief exclusive lock. pg_squeeze does similar work using logical decoding. nice on the OS does nothing for PostgreSQL lock behavior. Setting autovacuum_naptime to 1 just makes autovacuum poll more often, it does not change what it can do. Restoring from a backup is downtime by definition.

incidents.title: 502s on every rollout
incidents.topic: Pod termination races load balancer deregistration
incidents.scenario:
Your API runs on Kubernetes behind an AWS Application Load Balancer (target type: ip).

Every rolling deployment produces about 10 seconds of 502 errors. Never during normal traffic. Only during rollouts.

Readiness probes pass. New pods are healthy before old ones are removed. The app exits as soon as it receives SIGTERM.

What fixes it?

options.text: Raise replicas from 4 to 8 so fewer requests land on a pod that is shutting down
Add a preStop sleep and make the app drain in-flight requests on SIGTERM
Lower the readiness probe period to 1 second so old pods leave the endpoints faster
Switch the Deployment strategy to Recreate so old and new pods never overlap

incidents.fix:
When Kubernetes deletes a pod, shutdown and endpoint updates happen independently: the kubelet runs the preStop hook and then sends SIGTERM, while the control plane marks the pod's endpoint as terminating and not ready. That update is not instant for the load balancer. The AWS Load Balancer Controller has to see the change and deregister the target, and the ALB keeps sending new requests until that takes effect.

Your app exits on SIGTERM right away. For a few seconds the ALB still routes requests to an IP where nothing is listening, and those requests come back as 502.

The fix is to stay alive longer than the slowest part of that chain:
- a preStop hook that sleeps (10 to 20 seconds is common)
- terminationGracePeriodSeconds longer than the sleep plus your drain time
- an app that stops accepting new connections and finishes in-flight requests on SIGTERM

A) More replicas spread the errors thinner. Every rollout still drops requests.
C) Readiness does not help here. Termination marks the endpoint not ready whatever the probe says. The delay is in the controller and the load balancer, not the probe.
D) Recreate stops all old pods before new ones start. You trade 10 seconds of 502s for real downtime.

The mental model: Kubernetes updates the endpoints and stops the pod at the same time. Your shutdown has to outlast the propagation, not race it.
incidents.lesson: Endpoint updates and container shutdown happen in parallel. Make shutdown outlast the load balancer's view of the pod.
incidents.linkTitle: Kubernetes Beyond the Basics: 7 Concepts That Take You From Junior to Mid-Level

incidents.title: OOMKilled with 18 GiB free
incidents.topic: Container memory limits are enforced per cgroup, not per node
incidents.scenario:
A Java service on Kubernetes restarts a few times a day.

kubectl describe pod shows:
Last State: Terminated
Reason: OOMKilled
Exit Code: 137

The node has 32 GiB of RAM and 18 GiB free. The container's memory limit is 1Gi. Your JVM heap dashboard never goes above 600 MiB. The node's kernel log says: Memory cgroup out of memory: Killed process (java).

What is going on?

options.text: The node is under memory pressure, so the kubelet is evicting the pod
The memory request is too low, so the pod landed on a crowded node
The heap metric is wrong, and the JVM is leaking heap that the dashboard cannot see
The process hit the 1Gi container limit; the heap is only part of its memory

incidents.fix:
The kernel enforces the container's memory limit through cgroups. When usage reaches the limit and reclaim cannot free enough, the kernel runs the cgroup OOM killer. Killing the Java process gives OOMKilled with exit code 137 (128 + SIGKILL). Spare memory on the node does not override the limit, and the kernel log line says it was the cgroup, not the node.

The heap is not the whole JVM. Metaspace, thread stacks (default sizes vary by JVM and platform), the JIT code cache, GC data structures, and direct or native buffers (Netty, compression libraries) all live outside it. A 600 MiB heap leaves only 424 MiB of a 1Gi limit for all of that.

What to do:
- compare the container's working set (container_memory_working_set_bytes) with the limit, not the heap
- size the heap as a share of the limit, for example -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=60 to 75, and leave headroom for native memory
- turn on Native Memory Tracking to see the JVM's own native allocations (it does not count every third-party native library)

A) Eviction looks different: the pod status says Evicted and the node reports memory pressure. Here the kernel log names the memory cgroup.
B) Requests affect scheduling and which pods go first under node memory pressure, but they do not raise the container's hard limit.
C) The heap may be fine. The memory outside the heap is what the dashboard does not show.

The mental model: the node's free memory is not your budget. The container limit is.
incidents.lesson: A container can be OOM-killed at its own limit even when the node has free memory. Measure the container's working set, not just the heap.
incidents.linkTitle: Kubernetes Beyond the Basics: 7 Concepts That Take You From Junior to Mid-Level

incidents.title: The NAT Gateway bill
incidents.topic: S3 traffic from private subnets through a NAT Gateway
incidents.scenario:
Your AWS bill arrives (us-east-1). One line jumped:

NAT Gateway, data processed: $4,460 (last month: $410)

The only change: a new nightly job on EC2 instances in private subnets. It reads about 3,000 GB per night from an S3 bucket in the same region. Same-region transfer from S3 to EC2 is free, so nobody expected a cost.

Which fix removes the NAT charge for this job and keeps the instances private?

options.text: Add an S3 gateway VPC endpoint and route the private subnets' S3 traffic through it
Move the job's instances to a public subnet with public IPs so they skip the NAT Gateway
Compress the objects in S3 so the job reads fewer bytes each night
Replace the NAT Gateway with a self-managed NAT instance on a large EC2 type

incidents.fix:
Same-region transfer from S3 to EC2 is free, but this traffic did not go straight to S3. Instances in a private subnet reach S3's public endpoints through the NAT Gateway, and the NAT Gateway charges for every GB it processes: $0.045 per GB in us-east-1. 3,000 GB a night for 30 nights is 90,000 GB, about $4,050 a month for traffic that was supposed to cost nothing.

An S3 gateway endpoint adds a route for S3's prefix list to the subnet route tables. The traffic skips the NAT Gateway, and gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB have no hourly or per-GB charge. You can also attach an endpoint policy that limits which buckets are reachable.

B) Public instances can skip the NAT Gateway, but then they are no longer private, and you widened the attack surface to solve a routing problem.
C) Fewer bytes means a smaller bill, but you still pay the NAT for every byte that is left.
D) A NAT instance has no per-GB processing fee, but now you run, patch, and size a single point of failure for all outbound traffic. It is a workaround, not a fix.

The mental model: free data transfer is only free on the path you think it takes. Check the route table, not just the price list.
incidents.lesson: Data transfer prices depend on the path. Private subnets reach S3 through the NAT Gateway unless a gateway endpoint gives them another route.

incidents.title: Too many clients at 22% CPU
incidents.topic: PostgreSQL connection exhaustion after scaling the app
incidents.scenario:
Launch day. You scale your API from 10 to 30 pods to handle the traffic.

Ten minutes later, new requests fail with:
FATAL: sorry, too many clients already

PostgreSQL CPU is 22%. Memory is fine. max_connections is 200. Each API pod opens a connection pool of 10. pg_stat_activity shows most sessions idle between queries.

What is the best fix?

options.text: Raise max_connections from 200 to 2,000 so every pod gets its full pool
Move PostgreSQL to an instance with twice the CPU and memory so it can take the extra load
Put PgBouncer in transaction mode in front of PostgreSQL and size the pools to the database
Scale back to 10 pods and put a queue in front of the API to absorb the spike

incidents.fix:
30 pods with 10 connections each want 300 connections. PostgreSQL allows 200 and keeps a few of those for superusers. The immediate failure is connection-slot exhaustion, and pg_stat_activity shows most of those connections sitting idle between queries.

A pooler in transaction mode lets many client connections share a small number of server connections, because a server connection is only held for the length of a transaction. You size the server side to what PostgreSQL handles well (often a small multiple of its CPU cores), and the app can add pods without touching max_connections. Managed options such as RDS Proxy do the same job.

The caveat: transaction mode cannot keep session state across transactions. Session-level SET, session advisory locks, and LISTEN need care or session pooling. Protocol-level prepared statements need PgBouncer 1.21 or later with max_prepared_statements set. Check your app before you switch.

A) Each PostgreSQL connection is a separate backend process with its own memory. 2,000 mostly idle connections cost memory and make contention worse under load.
B) CPU is at 22%. With max_connections still at 200, a bigger instance does not remove the cap.
D) It stops the errors by giving up the capacity you scaled for.

The mental model: connections are a scarce resource on the database side, even when CPU is not. Multiply pods by pool size every time you change either one.
incidents.lesson: Pods times pool size is a number the database has to serve. Pool connections in front of PostgreSQL instead of raising max_connections.

incidents.title: Nine-minute builds for a one-line change
incidents.topic: Docker layer cache invalidation and cold CI runners
incidents.scenario:
Every CI build of your Node.js service takes 9 minutes, even when the change is one line in the README.

The Dockerfile:
FROM node:22
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN npm ci
RUN npm run build

Most of the time is spent in npm ci. CI runners are fresh VMs for every job.

What gives you the biggest win?

options.text: Copy package files first, run npm ci, copy the source, and export the build cache
Move the pipeline to CI runners with twice the CPU and a faster disk
Switch the base image to node:22-alpine so there is far less to download and build
Run npm ci on the CI host first and COPY the finished node_modules into the image

incidents.fix:
Docker caches each instruction as a layer and reuses it until something it depends on changes. COPY . . copies the whole repository, so any change, even to the README, invalidates that layer and every layer after it, including npm ci.

Copy only the dependency manifests first, run npm ci, then copy the source. With a reusable cache, npm ci now reruns only when the package files or earlier layers change, not on every source edit.

There is a second half. A fresh CI VM starts with an empty local cache, so a good layer order alone helps less than you expect. Export the cache and import it on the next run, for example docker buildx build --cache-to type=registry,ref=<image>:buildcache,mode=max --cache-from type=registry,ref=<image>:buildcache . (this needs a builder that supports registry cache, such as the docker-container driver). A .dockerignore that excludes node_modules and build output keeps the build context small too.

B) More CPU makes the same wasted work a little faster.
C) A smaller base image speeds up pulls, but npm ci still reruns on every change. Alpine also uses musl, so native modules can behave differently.
D) It can work, but node_modules built on the CI host may not match the image's OS or CPU architecture, and the image is no longer reproducible from the Dockerfile alone.

The mental model: order Dockerfile instructions from least to most often changed, and remember that on ephemeral runners a cache you do not export does not exist.
incidents.lesson: Order layers from least to most often changed, and export the build cache when your CI runners start empty.
incidents.linkTitle: Docker Best Practices (Introduction to Docker guide)

incidents.title: DNS moved, 4% did not
incidents.topic: Traffic that keeps reaching the old endpoint after a DNS change
incidents.scenario:
You moved your app to a new load balancer.

The day before, you lowered the A record's TTL from 3600 to 60. On Monday at 10:00 you pointed the record at the new load balancer.

It is now Wednesday. 4% of requests still arrive at the old load balancer. dig from three different networks returns the new address.

What do you do next?

options.text: Wait. DNS propagation can take up to 72 hours to reach every resolver on the internet
Purge the old record using the public resolvers' cache flush pages
Lower the TTL again, from 60 to 5 seconds, so clients refresh faster
Check the old load balancer's logs for who still connects, and keep it forwarding

incidents.fix:
Lowering the TTL a day ahead gave ordinary caches time to drop the old 3600-second value, and the new 60-second TTL means normal resolver caching cannot explain traffic two days later. Whatever still reaches the old load balancer is holding on to the old address some other way.

Common causes:
- long-lived connections (HTTP keep-alive pools, WebSockets, gRPC) that never reconnect
- clients that cache DNS results in the process for a long time
- the old IP address hardcoded in a client or proxy configuration
- a few resolvers that do not honour TTLs

The old load balancer's access logs help you find them: source IPs, user agents, and paths. Keep the old endpoint forwarding to the new backend, contact the owners of the remaining clients, and switch it off only when the logs show no more traffic.

A) There is no universal 72-hour propagation period. Ordinary caches expire after the TTL they received, which here was at most an hour.
B) Not the first step. You do not yet know which resolvers the stuck clients use, and flushing unrelated ones does nothing for clients that never look up the name.
C) A lower TTL does not shorten lifetimes already cached, and it does not move existing connections or pinned addresses.

The mental model: DNS only moves new lookups. Plan for the clients that never look again, and never switch off the old endpoint until its logs say nobody uses it.
incidents.lesson: DNS changes only reach clients that look up the name again. Watch the old endpoint's logs before you turn it off.

incidents.title: Four nodes free, pod still Pending
incidents.topic: Zonal EBS volumes pin stateful pods to one availability zone
incidents.scenario:
An EKS cluster spans three availability zones with one node group across all three.

The only node in us-east-1a fails. Your StatefulSet pod, with a 200 GiB EBS volume, is rescheduled and stays Pending. The cluster autoscaler adds a node, in us-east-1b. The pod is still Pending:

0/4 nodes are available: 4 node(s) had volume node affinity conflict.

The four nodes have plenty of free CPU and memory.

What is the right fix?

options.text: Delete the PVC so Kubernetes provisions a new volume in a zone that has free nodes
Change the StorageClass to volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
Get a node into us-east-1a, and split the node group so each zone has its own
Give the pod a higher PriorityClass so it can preempt pods on other nodes

incidents.fix:
An EBS volume lives in one availability zone and can only attach to an instance in that zone. The PersistentVolume carries a node affinity for us-east-1a, so the scheduler can only place this pod on a node in us-east-1a. There is none, so the pod waits.

The new node in us-east-1b does not help. With one node group spanning three zones, the autoscaler cannot reliably add capacity in a specific zone. The cluster autoscaler documentation recommends one node group per zone for workloads with zonal volumes, together with --balance-similar-node-groups. Then 'add a node in us-east-1a' is something it can actually do.

A) Deleting the PVC does not move the existing volume. With a Delete reclaim policy it can delete the disk itself; with Retain the old data stays behind, detached. Either way the new volume starts empty unless you restore a snapshot.
B) WaitForFirstConsumer is the right default: it creates new volumes in the zone where the pod is scheduled. It does nothing for a volume that already exists.
D) Preemption frees space on nodes the pod could use. No usable node exists in us-east-1a, so there is nothing to preempt.

The mental model: a stateful pod is pinned to the zone its disk lives in. Plan capacity per zone, not per cluster.
incidents.lesson: Zonal disks pin pods to zones. Give the autoscaler one node group per zone so it can add capacity where the volume is.
incidents.linkTitle: The anatomy of Kubernetes persistent storage

incidents.title: A refactor that destroys production
incidents.topic: Moving a Terraform resource into a module changes its address
incidents.scenario:
You clean up your Terraform code and move the production database into a module. No settings change.

terraform plan says:
# aws_db_instance.main will be destroyed
# module.database.aws_db_instance.main will be created
Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy.

What is the cleanest fix?

options.text: Add lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true } to the database and apply
Add a moved block from aws_db_instance.main to module.database.aws_db_instance.main and run plan again
Apply with -target=module.database so the new database exists before the old one goes away
Remove the old address with terraform state rm, then terraform import the database at the new address

incidents.fix:
Terraform tracks resources by address. Moving the resource into a module changes its address, and Terraform does not know that aws_db_instance.main and module.database.aws_db_instance.main are the same database. To Terraform, one resource disappeared from the code and a new one appeared, so it plans a destroy and a create.

A moved block (Terraform 1.1 and later, and OpenTofu) records the rename in code:

moved {
